concepts/anni-di-piombo.title: Anni di piombo (Years of Lead)
concepts/anni-di-piombo.content:
Anni di piombo (Years of Lead)
The anni di piombo — the years of lead — is the name given to the decade and more of political violence that gripped Italy from the late 1960s through the early 1980s, the period in which the Republic passed through the greatest crisis of its history. From the bombing of the Banca Nazionale dell’Agricoltura in Milan in December 1969 to the kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro in 1978 and beyond, Italy was the theatre of a terrorism of the far right and of the far left, of bombings in public places and of the assassination of judges, policemen, politicians and factory workers. It was the era in which the very foundations of the Republic — the parties, the state, the authority of the law — came under attack from within.
The strategy of tension
The years of lead began on the right, in a design that Italian observers came to call the strategy of tension. On 12 December 1969 a bomb exploded in the Banca Nazionale dell’Agricoltura in Milan’s Piazza Fontana, killing seventeen people and wounding scores more. The attack was initially blamed on anarchists — a suspect, Giuseppe Pinelli, died after falling from the window of a police station while in custody — but it emerged over the years that the responsibility lay with the neo-fascist far right, and that the bombing had been designed, in the pattern of the whole strategy of tension, to provoke a climate of fear, to blame the left, and to push the country toward an authoritarian, militarised solution to its political crisis. The Piazza Fontana bombing was followed by others — the so-called strage (massacres) of the following years, at Brescia in 1974, on the Italicus train, and finally at the Bologna railway station in August 1980, the worst of all, which killed eighty-five people. The strategy of tension, Mammarella stressed, was the attempt by sectors of the far right, with ambiguous complicities in parts of the state, to overturn the Republic and its democracy through terror.
The Red Brigades and the far left
Against this background of right-wing violence and of the disappointments and limits of the centro-sinistra (centre-left), a terrorism of the far left arose. From the long contestation of 1968 and the worker struggles of the hot autumn of 1969 emerged the Brigate Rosse (Red Brigades), the most formidable armed group of the Italian far left. Formed in the factories and universities of the North, the Red Brigades proclaimed a war on the Italian state and on the capitalist order, and from the early 1970s they kidnapped, wounded and killed their opponents — industrialists, magistrates, policemen, prison officials, and, in the most famous act of the decade, in 1978, the Christian Democrat statesman Aldo Moro himself.
The Red Brigades understood themselves as the vanguard of a revolution, and their actions fed on a climate of social conflict and generational revolt. Yet they never commanded a mass following, and their violence, far from bringing the revolution they dreamed of, served instead to isolate the left and to drive the state and the parties together in its defence. It was precisely the fear that terrorism would destroy the Republic that gave the compromesso storico (historic compromise) its urgency in the mid-1970s.
The state and the crisis of the Republic
The state’s response to the years of lead was a matter of intense controversy. The emergency legislation of the 1970s gave the police and the magistrates new powers, and a special antiterrorist squad was created to hunt the Red Brigades. In the Moro case, the state adopted the linea della fermezza (hard line), refusing to negotiate with the kidnappers, a decision whose consequences were to be debated for decades. There were also the unresolved shadows of the strategy of tension: the accusations of a doppio stato (double state), of dark and deviant sectors within the intelligence services and the apparatus of order, and of the systematic disinformation that had accompanied the right-wing massacres.
For Gentiloni Silveri, the years of lead marked the end of innocence for the Republic — the passage from the comparatively settled order of the 1960s to a decade in which the state’s monopoly of violence, and the trust on which the Republic rested, were called into question as never before. The political violence receded only in the early 1980s, with the collapse of the Red Brigades after the mass arrests of their leadership in 1980–1982 and the movement away from armed struggle on the left. The riflusso (reflux), the return to private life and the reaction of the early 1980s, closed the years of lead. But the Republic that emerged from them was not the Republic that had entered them: the crisis had aged the state, discredited the parties, and left wounds that the collapse of the whole postwar system in Tangentopoli a decade later would reopen.

concepts/authoritative-discourse.title: Authoritative Discourse
concepts/authoritative-discourse.content:
Authoritative Discourse
The authoritative discourse of late socialism — the official language of the party, the press, the schools and the ritual of Soviet public life — is, in Alexei Yurchak’s account, the central object of study for understanding the last Soviet generation. He borrows the phrase from Mikhail Bakhtin: an authoritative discourse is one that is not open to argument or interpretation, that demands to be repeated as it stands, whose very form is inseparable from its authority. The Soviet system was, above all, a discourse of this kind, and Yurchak’s great claim is that its slow internal transformation — the performative shift by which its fixed forms were emptied of their meaning — explains both the durability and the sudden end of the Soviet world.
The constative and the performative
To see what happened, Yurchak distinguishes two functions of language. In its constative function, speech describes the world and can be judged true or false. In its performative function, speech does not describe but acts — it creates the very state it names. When the party press declared that “the Soviet people, led by the CPSU, are building communism,” the sentence might be read constatively, as a claim about reality; or performatively, as an act of participating in the ritual of the system. The first reading asks whether it is true; the second only asks that it be repeated. Yurchak’s argument is that over the decades of late socialism the authoritative discourse shifted decisively from the constative to the performative pole. Its language continued to be reproduced with total fidelity, but the speakers, including many who wrote it, no longer took the sentences as descriptions of the world. The discourse became a form without a content — a hegemonic form, as Yurchak titles his second chapter, whose reproduction no longer required anyone to believe its propositions.
Reproducing the form, not the meaning
This shift is the foundation of everything else. Because the authoritative discourse was performed rather than believed, citizens could reproduce it perfectly and with complete sincerity in the performative sense, while their relation to its meaning was entirely different. The fixed phrases of the system — the slogans, the greetings, the formulaic resolutions, the ritual of the October and May days — were emptied of their constative force and refilled with a new, personal, often ironical meaning that the forms themselves did not dictate. The very fact that the form was invariable, that it could not be changed or argued with, allowed the meaning inside it to drift freely and indefinitely. This is what Yurchak means by the “hegemony of form”: the unchangeable shell of the discourse became the guarantee of a private and shifting interior. The Soviet subject neither accepted the propositions nor rejected them; he inhabited the form, and in inhabiting it, transformed the system from within while keeping its surface entirely intact.
The collapse of the form
The collapse of the USSR, on this account, was above all a collapse of discourse. In the years of perestroika-1985-91 the authority of the CPSU’s language collapsed from within — the “return to Lenin” of the late 1980s, in which reformers sought to strip away the accretions of the Brezhnev years to recover a purer original, only accelerated the disintegration, because it treated the authoritative discourse as a thing whose constative meaning could be recovered and so broke the very performative spell that had held it together. By 1990 and 1991, Yurchak writes, the party had lost its legitimacy, and the fabric of the authoritative discourse fell apart. The system, which had been held up for decades not by belief but by the reproduction of its forms, found itself with forms that were no longer reproduced. The performative shift had prepared this end for a long time: a discourse whose content had been hollowed out could be dissolved with extraordinary speed, and the generation that had reproduced it so faithfully for so long was the very generation most ready to let it go.

concepts/centrismo.title: Il Centrismo (1948-1958)
concepts/centrismo.content:
Il Centrismo (1948-1958)
Il centrismo (centrism) is the name given to the political order that governed Italy in the decade from 1948 to 1958 — the years of the reconstruction, the economic recovery and the consolidation of the Republic under the primacy of the Democrazia Cristiana (Christian Democracy, the D.C.). The term describes both the governing formula and the character of the whole political system: a coalition of the centre parties ranged around the dominant Christian Democrats, committed to anti-communism, to the Atlantic and Western alignment of the country, and to a moderate, reforming social Catholicism. The centrismo was the republic’s first settled political system, the framework in which the institutions born of the referendum of 1946 and the Constitution were consolidated, and the certain majority with which Italy was governed through the 1950s.
The centrist coalition
The political form of the centrismo was the quadripartito (four-party coalition), the alliance of the D.C. with the small parties of the centre — the liberals of the Partito Liberale Italiano (the P.L.I.), the republicans of the Partito Repubblicano Italiano (the P.R.I.) and the social democrats of the Partito Socialista Democratico Italiano (the P.S.D.I.), the party of the moderate socialists who had broken from the socialist left. The quadripartito was the majority with which the D.C. governed: its dominant partner was the Catholic party, which after the landslide of 1948 could rule almost at will, while the smaller centre parties supplied the liberal, republican and social-democratic voices of the coalition. It was a coalition of the centre — excluding alike the communist left and the neo-fascist right — which governed Italy through the reconstruction and the recovery, carrying out the reforms of the centrist decade: the agrarian reform, the foundation of the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno (the Fund for the South), and the programme of economic and social modernisation that set the country on the path to its great growth.
Anti-communism and the conventio ad excludendum
The foundation of the whole centrist system was anti-communism. The centrismo rested on the exclusion of the Partito Comunista Italiano (Italian Communist Party, the P.C.I.) from government — the conventio ad excludendum (convention of exclusion) by which the largest communist party in the West was permanently barred from power. The great confrontation of the election of 18 April 1948, in which the D.C. and its allies defeated the communist-socialist Fronte Democratico Popolare (Popular Democratic Front), fixed this exclusion as the settled fact of the republic. The centrismo was, in consequence, a system built on a negative as much as a positive foundation: it governed not only for its programme but against the communist alternative, and the permanent, disciplined and excluded communist opposition, commanding around a fifth of the electorate, was the shadow against which the whole centrist edifice stood. The centrist coalition could always be held together by the common hostility to the communist left, and its survival was bound up with the Cold War that gave the exclusion its meaning.
The reconstruction and the miracle in gestation
The centrismo was the political frame of the reconstruction and of the beginning of the economic transformation of Italy. Under the centrist governments the country rebuilt its ruined economy with the help of the Marshall Plan, carried out the reforms of the decade, and set in motion the development that was to flower in the miracolo economico (economic miracle) of the late 1950s and 1960s. The political stability of the centrist decade, for all its limits, provided the conditions of this recovery: a country that had entered the postwar world defeated and humiliated emerged, under the centrismo, as a stable, Western and increasingly prosperous republic. The centrist years also anchored Italy in the Atlantic alliance and in the first institutions of European integration, the course set by De Gasperi that was to define the republic’s international place. In the historiography of the reconstruction, the centrismo appears as the political order that carried Italy from the ruin of 1945 to the threshold of its great growth.
The limits of centrism
Yet the centrismo had its limits, which the passing decade made ever more apparent. Its majority, so certain after 1948, was eroded by the failure of the legge truffa (the “swindle law”) of 1953, which robbed the centre of its mechanical guarantee and opened the difficult second legislature. Its reformism, for all its achievements, was judged insufficient by an ever more insistent left — the centrismo proved slow to respond to the pressures for change that mounted in Italian society through the 1950s, to the demands of the industrial workers and the neglected South. The permanent exclusion of the communists, and the limits the system placed on any opening, narrowed the possibilities of Italian politics. By the late 1950s the centrist formula had reached the limits of its capacity for change, and the system began to move toward the new configuration of the centro-sinistra (centre-left), the alliance of the D.C. with the socialists that was to succeed the centrismo and carry Italy into the 1960s.
The system of the 1950s
In the perspective of the Republic’s history, the centrismo stands as the foundational political system of the new democracy — the order in which the institutions of the referendum and the Constitution were consolidated, the anti-communist orientation fixed, and the reconstruction carried through. It was the first and longest phase of Christian Democratic hegemony, the decade in which the D.C. and its centrist allies governed Italy with a security they were never to know again. The centrismo defined the political grammar of the republic for a generation: the dominance of the D.C., the exclusion of the communists, the coalitions of the centre, the Atlantic and Catholic identity of the state. When it gave way to the centro-sinistra, it left to its successor the habits and the limits of the system it had built — the system that was to govern Italy, through all its changes, until the collapse of the party order in the early 1990s.

concepts/centro-sinistra.title: Centro-sinistra (Centre-Left, 1960s-1970s)
concepts/centro-sinistra.content:
Centro-sinistra (Centre-Left, 1960s-1970s)
The centro-sinistra — the centre-left — was the political formula by which the Italian Democrazia Cristiana sought to renew itself and the Republic after the centrismo (centrism) of the 1950s had reached its limits. For the whole first decade of the Republic, the DC had governed with the small lay parties — the Liberals, the Republicans, the Social Democrats — keeping both the extreme left and the far right out of power. By the late 1950s that formula had grown stale, incapable, as Mammarella put it, of responding to the pressures for change building in a rapidly modernising society. The centre-left was the answer: the apertura a sinistra (opening to the left), the admission of the Socialist Party into government beside the DC. It was the defining political project of Italy in the 1960s and the foundation of the Republic’s long subsequent stability.
The apertura a sinistra
The idea of opening to the left was old — it had been debated since the centrist decade — but it was made possible only when the conditions of the Cold War and of Italian politics allowed. The key was the Socialist Party, the Partito Socialista Italiano, and its drift under Pietro Nenni toward a position independent of the Communists. Nenni’s Socialists had suffered defeat in the 1948 elections in alliance with the PCI, and through the 1950s they moved toward a course that would accept the Atlantic alliance and the legitimacy of the Western system while still seeking socialist reform. By the early 1960s the Socialists were ready to enter government, and within the DC a party leader emerged prepared to take the risk: Aldo Moro, who made the opening the central project of his career.
The path was neither straight nor quick. The crisis of the Tambroni government in 1960, which briefly allied the DC with the neo-fascist Movimento Sociale Italiano and provoked riots and violence, discredited the right and made the opening to the left all but inevitable as the only safe alternative. In December 1963 Moro formed his first government, a centre-left coalition of DC, PSI, PSDI and PRI that took office with a programme of reform. The centro-sinistra had arrived — an event that Italian observers of the time understood, and Gentiloni Silveri’s synthesis confirms, as a turning point in the Republic’s history, the moment when the political class chose reform over immobility.
The reforms and their limits
The centre-left governments of 1963–1968 presided over a substantial programme: the nationalisation of the electricity industry in 1962, the beginnings of regional government, the reform of the school system with the introduction of the unified middle school, reforms of pensions and of the housing and health systems, and the first gestures toward economic planning and the reduction of regional inequality. It was the most ambitious attempt at reform the Republic had yet seen, and it was carried out in the years of the economic miracle, when Italian society was being transformed at a speed few governments could manage.
Yet the centre-left was from the outset constrained by its own breadth. The coalition brought together the DC’s right and the Socialist left in a single majority, and the price of holding it together was that it could do less than either partner wished. The DC’s conservative wing resisted the more radical measures; the lay parties feared the DC’s dominance; and the Socialists, having entered government, found themselves obliged to moderate their programme. Mammarella’s judgement was that the centre-left was a political turning point far more than a reformist revolution — an enlargement of the governing class that broadened Italian democracy but whose concrete achievements fell short of its promises. The limits of the formula, and the social pressures the reforms could not absorb, fed directly into the unrest of the late 1960s and the hot autumn of 1969.
The agony of the formula
By the late 1960s the centre-left was already in difficulty, caught between the disappointment of its supporters and the resistance of the right. The years that followed — the autunno caldo (hot autumn) of 1969, the rise of the anni di piombo (years of lead), the economic crisis of the early 1970s — overtook it. The formula staggered through the 1970s, re-formed and re-broken, until it lost all meaning. By the mid-1970s the centre-left as originally conceived was exhausted, and the Republic’s political class was driven to look for a new majority — the search that led, after the elections of 1976, to the compromesso storico (historic compromise) and the PCI’s support for the government. The centre-left had opened the Republic to the left; it remained for the crisis of the 1970s to decide how far that opening would go.

concepts/cohabitation.title: Cohabitation
concepts/cohabitation.content:
Cohabitation
Cohabitation is the name the French gave to the strangest arrangement of the Fifth Republic: the sharing of the executive between a President and a Prime Minister drawn from opposing political camps. It arose from the institutions de Gaulle had conceived — a directly elected President commanding foreign and defence policy, a government answerable to the parliamentary majority — when the two mandates came to be held by different majorities. When the President’s camp lost the legislative elections, he could not remove the Prime Minister the new majority imposed, and so the two halves of the executive were obliged to live together, cohabiter. The result was a division of power never foreseen by the founders of 1958, which nevertheless proved the régime’s greatest proof of adaptability.
The mechanism
The Fifth Republic of de Gaulle had been built on the presumption of a single majority: the President, elected by universal suffrage, was expected to command a parliamentary majority of his own tendency, and the Prime Minister was his subordinate. The cohabitation arose when the logic of the presidential election and the logic of the legislative election diverged. If the electorate returned an Assembly hostile to the President, the Constitution allowed him no choice but to name a Prime Minister from that majority — and, in the practice of the régime, to withdraw from the everyday direction of government. The President kept his constitutional domain, notably foreign affairs and defence, while the government of the opposing camp governed the country.
The three cohabitations
The arrangement was practised three times, each the result of a socialist presidency confronting a conservative Assembly or a conservative presidency confronting a socialist one. The first ran from 1986 to 1988, when François Mitterrand, elected in 1981, confronted a right-wing majority and named Jacques Chirac Prime Minister; the division of the executive was tested and survived. The second, from 1993 to 1995, saw the socialist President Mitterrand share power with the gaullist Édouard Balladur at the head of a right-wing government. The third, the longest, ran from 1997 to 2002, when the conservative President Jacques Chirac, having dissolved the Assembly in April 1997, was answered by a socialist majority and governed with the socialist Lionel Jospin as his Prime Minister. In each case the cohabitation was a period of alternance sans alternative — of change in power without a change of orientation, in which the two camps watched one another and prepared the next election.
The meaning of cohabitation
The cohabitations transformed the Fifth Republic. They broke the presidential reading of the régime, demonstrating that the state could function with a divided executive, and they accustomed France to the idea of alternance as the normal rhythm of its politics. They also stripped the presidency of much of its commanding authority during their periods — the President reduced, in the gaullist reading, to a diminished figure watching his own policy undone. Yet the régime survived all three tests, and each cohabitation ended in a presidential or legislative election that restored a single majority. The concept thus marks the maturity of the Fifth Republic, the proof that the institutions of 1958 could bear the weight of a divided country, and the point at which the gaullisme of the strong executive met its constitutional limit.

concepts/cold-war.title: The Cold War
concepts/cold-war.content:
The Cold War
The kholodnaya voina — the cold war — was the name that came to designate the state of confrontation between the two great blocs into which the world divided in the years after 1945. It was not a war in the old sense, for the armies of the two blocs did not meet in a general European battle, but it was a war nonetheless: a war of ideologies, of espionage, of propaganda, of economic rivalries and of armed conflicts fought by proxies on the peripheries of Europe and of the world. From the breakdown of the wartime alliance of the anti-Hitler coalition to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, the Cold War organised the international order into two camps — the socialist and the capitalist, the East and the West — and imposed its division upon the map of Europe itself.
The rupture of the wartime alliance
The alliance that had won the Second World War did not long survive its victory. The anti-Hitler coalition had been a union against a common enemy, and once the enemy was destroyed the differing purposes of its members came to the surface. In the Soviet reading, the western powers — the United States and Great Britain above all — abandoned the cooperation with the USSR that had marked the war and turned to open enmity and military preparation against the Soviet Union and the countries of people’s democracy. The international conferences of the powers had, at Yalta and Potsdam, sanctioned the division of Europe into spheres of influence; the Soviet Union extended its control far into the centre of the continent, incorporating the Baltic states and exercising control over Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria, which the western allies could no longer contest. The future Germany was carved into four occupation zones, and the line between the Soviet zone and the western zones ran through the middle of the old Reich, along the Elbe, the Werra and the Fulda — a frontier that was to become the very symbol of the division of Europe.
Two lines: war and peace
The opening of the conflict was marked by the famous speech of Winston Churchill at Fulton, Missouri, on 5 March 1946, delivered in the presence of President Truman. In the Soviet account, this speech of “zloi klevety” (malicious slander) against the Soviet Union proclaimed a “crusade” against socialism and a programme of Anglo-American world domination; it was the ideological manifesto of the postwar reaction. To the western mind, the same speech was the sober warning of a statesman that an “iron curtain” had descended across the continent. From that moment the two lines in international politics were drawn: the line of war and aggression on the one side, and the line of peace on the other. The Soviet government, in the interviews of Stalin with western journalists and in the declarations of its delegation at the United Nations, set against the western programme a programme of peaceful coexistence of the two systems — mirnoye sosushchestvovaniye — of the continuation of great-power cooperation, of disarmament and of the strengthening of the United Nations. On the western side, the policy of “containment” sought to halt the extension of Soviet power.
The building of the blocs
The confrontation hardened into institutions. On the western side the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, NATO, founded in April 1949, bound the United States and Western Europe together in an alliance of common defence against the perceived Soviet threat; the western powers carried out the currency reform of June 1948 and pressed on toward the creation of a western German state, the Federal Republic of Germany, founded in 1949. On the eastern side the Soviet Union answered with the Council of Mutual Economic Assistance (Sovet ekonomicheskoy vzaimopomoshchi, Comecon) for the economic cooperation of the socialist states, and ultimately with the Warsaw Treaty of 1955 as the military counterpart to NATO. The confrontation was tested in crises — the Berlin blockade of 1948–49, broken by the allied airlift, the Luftbrücke; the Korean War of 1950–53, in which the two blocs fought by proxy in Asia; and the division of Germany, sealed by the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961, which fixed the Cold War frontier in the heart of Europe.
Détente and its limits
The Cold War was not unrelieved. In the 1950s the Soviet leadership under Nikita Khrushchev carried forward the doctrine of peaceful coexistence and the “thaw” in international relations; the armistice in Korea in 1953 and the Geneva conferences of 1955 eased the tension, and the decade after Stalin’s death opened the prospect of a relaxation. The word that came to describe it was détente — a relaxation of tensions between the blocs. The era of Leonid Brezhnev and the 1970s brought the era of détente in earnest: the Soviet Peace Programme adopted at the XXIV Congress of the CPSU in 1971, the treaties of the new Ostpolitik, the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, which culminated in the Helsinki Accords of 1975, and a series of arms-control agreements. Yet détente was never complete. The ideological struggle continued, the rivalry for the third world sharpened, and the “second Cold War” of the early 1980s, in the years of the confrontation over the deployment of intermediate-range missiles, revived the fears of the earlier era.
The end of the Cold War
The Cold War came to an end with the collapse of the Soviet order in the late 1980s. Under Mikhail Gorbachev’s policy of perestroika (restructuring) and the “new political thinking,” the Soviet Union withdrew from the confrontation, opened its society, and renounced the use of force in the socialist camp. The revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe, the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989, the German reunification of 1990 and the dissolution of the USSR in 1991 dissolved the bipolar world at a stroke. The Cold War had lasted more than four decades; it had organised the international system, divided Europe, and left its mark on the whole of the postwar world. Its end, as the histories of the period note, resolved the German question in freedom and allowed the countries of the East to rejoin the West — the conclusion of what the German historian Winkler calls the “long road to the West.”

concepts/compromesso-storico.title: Compromesso storico (Historic Compromise)
concepts/compromesso-storico.content:
Compromesso storico (Historic Compromise)
The compromesso storico — the historic compromise — was the project, advanced in the 1970s, of a collaboration between the two great popular parties of Italy, the Democrazia Cristiana and the Partito Comunista Italiano, to defend the Republic against the threats of political violence and subversion. For three decades the Cold War had kept the Communists permanently out of the Italian government; the historic compromise proposed, in a moment of acute crisis, to break that taboo. It was the most ambitious political idea in the history of the Republic — and it came to its end in the murder of Aldo Moro in May 1978.
Berlinguer’s proposal
The strategy was announced by the Communist secretary Enrico Berlinguer in the autumn of 1973, in the wake of the coup in Chile, where the elected Socialist president Salvador Allende had been overthrown and killed by the military. For Berlinguer the lesson of Chile was that the democratic left could not govern alone, or even in alliance with the moderate left alone, against the hostility of powerful conservative and military forces — that a socialist transformation in the West could only be carried out with the consent of the great Catholic popular masses. In Italy, that meant the DC, the party of the Catholic majority. Berlinguer therefore proposed a compromesso storico: an alliance, or at least a durable understanding, between the PCI and the DC, the two parties together commanding the loyalty of the great majority of Italians.
It was a sharp departure from the entire logic of the postwar order. It repudiated the idea that the Communists should remain an isolated opposition awaiting the collapse of their rivals, and it accepted the legitimacy of the Christian Democrats as a governing force. It also implied, in Berlinguer’s conception, a transformation of the PCI itself into a party able to govern a Western democracy. The proposal was received with profound scepticism by many on the left, who saw it as an abandonment of the class struggle, and with suspicion by the DC’s right.
Moro’s response and national solidarity
The idea found its Catholic counterpart in Aldo Moro. Moro had spent his career widening the DC’s majority — first toward the Socialists in the centro-sinistra (centre-left), and now, in the crisis of the 1970s, toward the Communists. He pursued the historic compromise in his own key: not as an ideological convergence, which he distrusted, but as a political necessity, the claim that in a time of emergency, with the Republic under assault from terrorism and subversion, the two great popular parties must govern together or at least agree on the Republic’s defence.
The elections of 20 June 1976 gave the strategy its concrete political form. The PCI advanced to within a few points of the DC, its greatest result ever, while the DC, though still the largest party, could no longer govern alone. The result was the government of solidarietà nazionale (national solidarity): a Christian Democrat government under Giulio Andreotti, sustained from outside by the PCI’s abstention, with the Communists supporting the state and its emergency legislation against terrorism without entering the cabinet. It was, as Gentiloni Silveri observes, the high point of the historic compromise — the moment when the great excluded party of the Republic came within reach of power, not as a rival to the DC but as its partner in the defence of democracy.
The crisis of 1978
The project was destroyed in the spring of 1978. Precisely as the negotiations to bring the PCI fully into the government reached their climax — a vote was scheduled for 16 March that would have confirmed Andreotti’s new cabinet with Communist participation — Moro was kidnapped in Rome by the Brigate Rosse (Red Brigades). The Red Brigades had every interest in preventing the historic compromise, which threatened to unite the state’s strongest forces against them; the timing of the kidnapping was widely seen as aimed at the government of national solidarity itself.
In the fifty-four days of Moro’s captivity, the two parties of the compromise held together in the linea della fermezza (hard line) — the refusal to negotiate with the terrorists. Moro’s letters, in which he appealed for a negotiated solution and seemed, to many, to be pleading for his life against the firmness of his own party, tore at the country’s conscience. When Moro was murdered on 9 May 1978, the historic compromise died with him. The project was never renewed. The PCI never entered the Italian government, the solidarity of the two parties dissolved into the political conflicts of the 1980s, and the great opportunity of the 1970s was lost. For many observers, including Gentiloni Silveri, the murder was the funerale della Repubblica — the funeral of the Republic — because the historic compromise had been the Republic’s last, best chance to reform and renew itself, and with Moro’s death that chance passed.

concepts/desarrollismo.title: Desarrollismo
concepts/desarrollismo.content:
Desarrollismo
Desarrollismo — developmentalism — is the name given to the economic growth and the great social transformation of Spain in the 1960s, the process by which the closed and autarkic country that Franco had governed in the 1940s became, within a single generation, a modern urban and industrial society. It is the central paradox of the late franquismo: the development that the dictatorship promoted and that gave it its most tangible justification was the same development that outgrew the dictatorship, creating a society whose mental world and social structure no longer corresponded to the political system that governed it. In Tusell’s account, the desarrollo económico of the 1960s, paired with a deep social transformation of political repercussion, is the key to understanding how the régime, at its very apogee, was already preparing the ground for its own supersession.
The Stabilisation Plan of 1959
The turning point came in 1959, when the régime abandoned the autarky that had produced the “noche oscura” (dark night) of the 1940s — rationing, state interventionism and an economy cut off from the world. The Stabilisation Plan of that year, drafted by the technocratic ministers who had risen to influence in the previous decade, opened the Spanish economy to the international market and dismantled the interventionist apparatus of the old autarky. The plan was the decisive moment of economic liberalisation: it brought foreign exchange, drew Spain into the Western economic system, and laid the foundations for the growth of the following years. The context was the extraordinary expansion of the West in the postwar era, which Spain at last began to share after an exceptional backwardness — a country that had caught the European “miracle” late now grew with it. The political meaning of 1959 was as great as the economic: developmentalism became the régime’s new justification, its claim to legitimacy shifting from the memory of the Crusade to the promise of prosperity.
Growth, tourism and urbanisation
The 1960s were years of rapid and sustained growth — development plans, industrial expansion, rising national income, the end of the isolation of the 1940s in material terms. Among the engines of this growth, tourism was one of the most visible: the Ministry of Information and Tourism, directed from 1962 by Manuel Fraga, cultivated the arrival of millions of European visitors who brought foreign currency, contact with the outside world, and a daily demonstration of the prosperity of Spain’s neighbours. The coastal resorts of the Mediterranean rose in a single decade, drawing a society that had known rationing and penury into the world of consumption. Urbanisation accompanied the growth: the census of 1960 to 1970 records the population rising from thirty to more than thirty-three million, and a demographic modernisation already underway since the 1950s. The great internal migrations of the decade — roughly four million Spaniards changing their residence — carried a rural population to the industrial cities of Madrid, Barcelona and the Basque Country, emptying the countryside and building the great peripheries of the cities.
The social transformation that outgrew the régime
The social change was not merely economic but mental and political. A society of peasants and workers disciplined by order and tradition gave way to a society of industrial workers, clerks and consumers, educated, urban, and connected to Europe. Economic growth modified the closed and authoritarian Spanish society even as the political system seemed to answer to another world, wrestling with the contradictions of modernisation. The new social structure produced new forms of protest — labour conflict and, in the final phase, terrorism — and a growing “oposición social” (social opposition) that outweighed strictly political opposition. The gap widened between a régime whose forms belonged to the 1940s and a population that had entered the 1960s. By the end, the surveys registered the change of mentality: the preference for decisions taken by persons elected by the people rose from 35 per cent in 1966 to 60 per cent in 1974, while conformity values of peace, order and tradition fell from 71 to 55 per cent. The desarrollismo that had given the régime its last great success had created the very society in which the régime no longer fitted — the ground, in the end, on which the transition to democracy was able to be built without rupture.

concepts/detente.title: Détente
concepts/detente.content:
Détente
Détente — the razryadka mezhdunarodnoi napryazhennosti, the relaxation of international tension — was the defining movement of the 1970s in the relations of the blocs. After the nuclear brinkmanship of the Caribbean crisis of 1962 and the trauma of the intervention of 1968, the two superpowers and the two systems turned from confrontation toward a managed accommodation: a decade in which the Cold War was conducted by treaty and negotiation rather than by crisis, in which the frontiers of Europe were recognised and fixed, and in which the two camps, armed beyond any precedent in history, sought to limit the race for the weapons of annihilation. In the Soviet account, expressed in the Peace Programmes of the XXIV and XXV Party Congresses, détente was the triumph of the Leninist policy of peaceful coexistence — the victory of the forces of socialism and peace over the militarism of the imperialist world.
The Peace Programme
The theoretical foundation of détente was the doctrine of peaceful coexistence, mirnoe sosushchestvovanie, which the party held to be the inescapable condition of the atomic age — the recognition that the two social systems, capitalism and socialism, could and must compete and coexist without war. This doctrine, which Khrushchev had made the watchword of Soviet policy after the XX Congress, was elevated under Brezhnev into a comprehensive programme of action. The XXIV Congress of the CPSU in 1971 adopted the Programma mira, the Peace Programme, which set out the struggle for the easing of tension in Europe, for disarmament, for the liquidation of the seats of war and for the security of all peoples; the XXV Congress in 1976 carried it forward as the programme for the further struggle for peace and international cooperation. In the language of the official histories, the Soviet Union pursued a consistent struggle for peace, disarmament and international security against the aggressive circles of the imperialist powers — and the relaxation of tension of the 1970s was its reward.
The architecture of relaxation
The relaxation took concrete form in a chain of treaties and negotiations that fixed the map of Europe and bound the two systems to restraint. The strategic arms talks — SALT, the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks — produced the first treaty on the limitation of strategic offensive arms, signed by Brezhnev and Nixon in Moscow in May 1972, which froze the intercontinental arsenals of the two superpowers and was supplemented by the Anti-Ballistic Missile treaty of the same occasion. The German question, the most dangerous of all the issues of the division of Europe, was settled on the basis of the recognition of the existing frontiers: the treaties concluded by the Federal Republic under the Ostpolitik of willy-brandt — the Moscow Treaty of 1970, the Warsaw Treaty with Poland, the Basic Treaty between the two German states and the Four-Power agreement on Berlin — renounced force and fixed the Oder–Neisse frontier, and were crowned in 1973 by the admission of both German states to the United Nations. And the whole edifice was sealed by the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, which met at Helsinki and whose Final Act of 1 August 1975 recognised the inviolability of the postwar frontiers while declaring the principles of cooperation, sovereignty and human rights. To the East, the Helsinki Act was the great charter of the settlement of Europe; to its critics in the West, the price was the recognition of the division that the Iron Curtain had made permanent.
The limits and the meaning
Détente was never an end to the Cold War but a change in its forms. Even as the treaties multiplied, the two systems continued to compete across the world — in the developing countries, in the arms race that the SALT negotiations did not halt, and in the ideological struggle that neither side renounced. The era of razryadka reached its peak in the first half of the 1970s and then began to ebb: the renewed competition in the Third World, the Soviet build-up of the late decade, and above all the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan in December 1979 brought the second Cold War of the early 1980s and the collapse of the détente of the Brezhnev years. Yet the achievement of the decade was not undone. The settlement of the frontiers of Europe, the habit of summitry and negotiation, the institution of the SALT process and the Helsinki framework all survived the relapse of the early 1980s, and the relaxation of tension prepared the way for the transformations that followed. In the Soviet self-understanding, the razryadka (relaxation of tension) was the vindication of the policy of peaceful coexistence — the proof that the socialist power, while never yielding on the defence of the socialist commonwealth (as the events of 1968 had shown), could conduct its rivalry with the capitalist world within the bounds of peace. The relaxation of the 1970s was the bridge between the confrontation of the age of Khrushchev and the ending of the division of Europe; and the recognition of the status quo that détente enshrined proved, in the end, to be the frame within which that status quo could finally be transformed.

concepts/developed-socialism.title: Developed Socialism
concepts/developed-socialism.content:
Developed Socialism
Developed socialism — развитой социализм — was the official self-description of Soviet society in the era of leonid-brezhnev, the concept by which the party measured the stage its country had reached on the road to communism. The notion arose in 1967, when Brezhnev, speaking in the year of the fiftieth anniversary of the revolution, drew the conclusion that the USSR had built a развитое социалистическое общество (developed socialist society). Over the following decade this observation hardened into a complete doctrine, elaborated at the party congresses from the XXIII to the XXVI and given its most solemn formulation in the Constitution of 1977. It was, in essence, a correction of the ambitions of the preceding age — an acknowledgement, more realistic than the utopianism of nikita-khrushchev, that communism was not to be reached by a fixed date, and that the society of the present was not communist at all, but a mature socialism advancing slowly and securely toward it.
A settled stage
The concept rested on a real fact, the creation in the USSR of the foundations of an industrial society. The party leadership, aware of the utopian character of Khrushchev’s promise to build communism within twenty years, by 1980, quietly moved the goal of communism out of the concrete historical perspective into the indefinite future, and installed in its place a conception of the present as a stable, harmonious stage. Developed socialism, in the teaching of the XXIV, XXV and XXVI Congresses and of the 1977 Constitution, was a society of mature socialist productive forces, of advanced science and culture, in which the welfare of the people was growing and conditions for the all-round development of the individual were being created. Its social relations were held to be fully mature: the classes and social groups had drawn together, the союз рабочего класса, крестьянства и интеллигенции (the alliance of the working class, the peasantry and the intelligentsia) had been consolidated, and a new historical community of people, the советский народ (Soviet people), had taken shape from the brotherly cooperation of all the nations and nationalities, equal before the law and in fact.
The politics of maturity
Out of this description of society flowed a description of the state. Because the working class had become the leading force of a society in which all the toilers had taken up its ideological and political positions, the state of the dictatorship of the proletariat had, in the official theory, grown over into the общенародное государство (all-people’s state) — a state, the first in world history, in which power belonged to the whole people. The Constitution of 1977, drafted by the Constitutional Commission under Brezhnev’s chairmanship after the decision of the XXV Congress, and adopted on 7 October 1977 after an all-people’s discussion in which more than 140 million people took part, was proclaimed the first constitution of the developed socialist society and of the all-people’s state; its sixth article fixed the leading role of the cpsu as the guiding and directing force of Soviet society, and it incorporated into the fundamental law some of the international obligations of the USSR, including the principles of the Helsinki Final Act.
The concept was thus as much a political programme as a description. It gave the regime a doctrine of stability, an ideological warrant for the calm, conservative course of the Brezhnev years — and, as its critics observed, a warrant for complacency. The assertion that Soviet society was homogeneous, that the national question had been finally solved and no significant contradictions remained within it, encouraged the leadership to look upon reality with a certain self-satisfaction, and to postpone the questions the doctrine pronounced already settled. In the judgement of later historians, developed socialism came to serve as the ideological cover of the застой (stagnation), the immobilism that descended on the late Brezhnev years; and it passed from the official vocabulary only in the late 1980s, when the party of yuri-andropov’s successors turned toward the idea of reform that would soon sweep the whole system away.

concepts/east-german-transformation.title: The East German Transformation after 1989/90
concepts/east-german-transformation.content:
The East German Transformation after 1989/90
The word that came to describe what happened to East Germany after the fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 was not Vereinigung, unification, but Übernahme — the takeover. Kowalczuk chose it for the title of his book on the subject, and the choice was deliberate: the East was not so much united with as absorbed into the Federal Republic, folded into an existing order that was presented as the only possible one. The transformation that followed was the most complete social, economic and political remaking of a European society in the century’s second half, and it was conducted on terms set almost entirely by the West. The process of german-reunification-1990 under helmut-kohl was presented as alternativlos, without alternative, so that the question of a genuinely negotiated unity, of a different and longer path, was closed almost before it was asked.
The demand laid upon East Germans was Anpassung, adaptation. They were expected to conform to western institutions, habits, norms and ways of working, and the figure of the Angepasste — the accommodating East German who learned to fit in — became a familiar and quietly humiliating type. The one-sidedness of the demand was itself the point: the West was the norm, the East the deviation that must correct itself. This asymmetry of expectation rested on an asymmetry of perception. East Germans were constructed in the unified republic as die Anderen, the others — a distinct, exotic, often deficient population, measured and found wanting by standards they had never been taught. The failure of the West to understand the East, its Unverständnis, was chronic and mutually felt, and the mutual perception of the two halves never quite met.
Economically the transformation was the story of the collapse and reconstruction told in the Treuhand’s privatisation — the deindustrialisierung, the emptying of the old landscape of work, the birth of mass Arbeitslosigkeit, unemployment, and the permanent class of Verlierer, the losers of the transformation who had built their lives in a system now dismantled around them. The economic collapse was lived, Kowalczuk insists, as a Kulturkampf, a cultural struggle — an assault not merely on livelihoods but on ways of life and on self-respect. The property question, with its Rückgabe vor Entschädigung (restitution before compensation), kept lives and investments in suspense for years, and the Altschulden, the inherited debts of the planned economy, dragged down what might otherwise have survived. The gap between East and West proved stubbornly economic and stubbornly cultural at once, a division written into wages, pensions, unemployment and demography — the permanent westward migration of the young and skilled.
Politically the transformation handed the East a constitution and institutions it had not shaped. The accession proceeded under Article 23 of the Basic Law rather than a new constitution under Article 146, so the new Germany kept the old Basic Law and the East received a democratic order from without. Kowalczuk’s charge of a Demokratie ohne Demokraten, a democracy without democrats, captured the deepest of the transformation’s problems: in 1989 some 87.5 per cent of the GDR population had no personal experience of a functioning democratic state. Only the generation born before 1923 could remember Weimar, and civic democracy had been systematically vilified under both the Nazi dictatorship and the SED state. Eastern Germany therefore inherited democratic institutions without democratic habit — a democracy with the scaffolding but not the inner conviction, which helped to explain the persistently lower electoral turnouts, the distrust of parties, and the later appeal of populism and extremism in the East.
The transformation was, in the end, a society being made anew under conditions it had not chosen. It brought freedom, the Rechtsstaat, and the end of dictatorship — genuine gains that Kowalczuk never denies — but it brought them wrapped in a one-sidedness that left many East Germans feeling they had been acted upon rather than included. The Elitenaustausch at the universities replaced the East’s intellectual elite, East Germans remained almost absent from the leading positions of the economy, politics, media and culture, and the resentment fed the recurring charge of Kolonialisierung, colonisation. Against the boundless hopes with which the East entered 1990, the transformation’s disappointments — for the victims of the communists, the loyal system-goers, the workers, the scientists, the farmers, the civil-rights activists whose counsel was no longer valued — cast a long shadow. The Übernahme is the frame through which that whole history is best read, and its agents, its wounds and its symbols are the treuhandanstalt and the treuhand-privatization-1990-94 that did its economic work.

concepts/economic-and-monetary-union.title: Economic and Monetary Union (EMU)
concepts/economic-and-monetary-union.content:
Economic and Monetary Union (EMU)
Economic and Monetary Union is the project, realised at the turn of the millennium, by which the member states of the European Union surrendered the conduct of monetary policy to a common institution and adopted a single currency. It was the most profound pooling of sovereignty in the history of European integration, a step that carried the Community out of the economics of the common market and into the very substance of the modern state. Its achievement, after three decades of patient monetary cooperation, gave Europe a currency without a nation behind it, and raised with unexampled sharpness the question of how far a monetary union could be sustained without a political one.
From the Werner Report to the snake
The aspiration to monetary union was as old as the Community itself. Its founding document was the Werner Report, published in October 1970, which proposed the gradual development of a single European currency through a three-stage process, with fixed exchange rates, full capital liberalisation and a common monetary authority. The plan was never realised; the collapse of the Bretton Woods system and the monetary disorder of the 1970s overtook it, and the Community’s first practical experiment, the “snake in the tunnel,” failed to stabilise nominal exchange rates and shrank to a core of strong-currency states. Yet the Werner Report, as the Cambridge history insists, was indispensable nevertheless: it established the intellectual pattern of a staged advance to monetary union that all later schemes would follow, and it prepared the way for the European Monetary System. Within the broader process of integration it defined the “economist” pole of the perennial debate — those, above all the Germans, who held that economic convergence must precede and justify any locking of currencies, against the “monetarists,” above all the French, who wished to create the union first and let the discipline of a common monetary framework compel convergence.
The European Monetary System and the Delors Committee
The European Monetary System, established in 1979 under Helmut Schmidt and Valéry Giscard d’Estaing, transformed the prospects of monetary union. It created a zone of exchange-rate stability around the Deutsche Mark, taught the members to live within common monetary disciplines, and revived ideas of a single currency. By the mid-1980s, with the mark acting as anchor currency and the members converging voluntarily around German emphasis on price stability, the system had the de facto support of the participants. The decisive step came with the decision to complete the single market. Jacques Delors, the former French finance minister who had become the activist president of the Commission, saw a monetary union as the logical complement to the Single Market; he was also sensitive to the long-standing French concern with vulnerability to the strength of the mark. In February 1988 the German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher came out in favour of deepening monetary integration and proposed the creation of a European Central Bank. At the European Council of Hannover in June 1988, a committee was established under Delors’s chairmanship, composed of the central bank presidents of the twelve member states.
The composition of the Delors Committee was a stroke of design. By seating the central bankers at the table, the architects of the process ensured that the decisive actors — a core epistemic community since the early days of the Werner Plan — would be committed to the eventual outcome. The committee met at the Bank for International Settlements in Basle, “a bastion of orthodox thinking,” and published its report in April 1989. Like the Werner Plan, it proposed the achievement of monetary union in stages, but without a fixed timetable. A first stage, beginning on 1 July 1990, would see the full liberalisation of capital markets and the participation of all currencies in the exchange-rate mechanism. A second stage would establish a European Monetary Institute, later the European Central Bank, with an independence modelled on and even surpassing the Bundesbank. A third stage would irrevocably fix exchange rates and culminate in a single currency for all participating nations, while distinct national economic policies were retained in the hope that common discipline could be imposed in the process.
The Maastricht design
The Delors report was the blueprint written into the Treaty of Maastricht of 1992. The treaty set the advance to monetary union in three stages, with the final stage dependent on the fulfilment of convergence criteria — sustainable public finances (limits on deficit and debt), price stability, exchange-rate stability and stable long-term interest rates — and fixed the automatic starting date of January 1999 if no earlier date were set. The Maastricht design was, at its core, a compromise between France and Germany. For France it was essential to move quickly and fix a firm timetable; for Germany it was essential first to create convergence, and in exchange for stringent convergence criteria the irreversibility of the move to a single currency was set in stone. The design embedded the German commitment to sound money: the primary objective of the European Central Bank was to maintain price stability, and the bank’s independence, modelled on that of the Bundesbank, was intended as a guarantee that the new currency would not be inflated away. Moravcsik argues that the entire trajectory — from the failure of the snake, through the EMS, to Maastricht — is best explained not by federalist ideas or geopolitical imperatives but by the converging national economic interests of the great states, above all the commercial and financial interests of France and Germany.
The euro and the institutional architecture
The union was realised as designed. On 1 January 1999 the euro was launched, with the exchange rates of eleven currencies irrevocably fixed and the European Central Bank, established in Frankfurt, assuming the conduct of monetary policy for the euro area. On 1 January 2002 the euro was physically introduced, its notes and coins replacing the national currencies. The institutional architecture that accompanied the currency comprised the European System of Central Banks, with the ECB at its apex; the convergence criteria as a gatekeeper of membership; and the Stability and Growth Pact, invented to maintain budgetary discipline — the three-per-cent limit on deficits and the sixty-per-cent reference for debt — once inside the union. The result was an economic union of a particular kind: a single monetary policy, but a fiscal policy that remained in national hands, with coordination between the two a delicate and contested art. This asymmetry, the absence of a fiscal union to stand behind the single currency, was the inherent weakness of the Maastricht design. When the euro area was tested by the great financial crisis of the following decade, the strains that emerged — the difficulty of holding together states with very different economies under a single monetary discipline — would expose the limits of an economic and monetary union that had not been crowned by political union.

concepts/european-integration.title: European Integration
concepts/european-integration.content:
European Integration
European integration is the process by which the states of Europe, above all those of Western and then central and eastern Europe, have bound themselves together since 1945 into an increasingly dense web of shared institutions, policies and law — a process that culminated in the European Union, the most ambitious experiment in the voluntary pooling of sovereignty in modern history. It is at once a historical movement, a legal order, a political system and a set of ideas. It began in the late 1940s with the recovery of a devastated continent and the desire to make war between the European powers impossible; it proceeded through a succession of treaties and enlargements, from the Treaty of Rome to Maastricht and Lisbon; and it created institutions — the European Commission, the Council, the European Parliament, the Court of Justice — that constitute a political system unlike any national one, governing some of the lives of half a billion people without ever becoming a state. The history of European integration is the history of the attempt to answer a single question: whether the nations of Europe, having brought catastrophe upon the world in their rivalries, could learn to govern their interdependence in common. And it is a question that the theorists of integration, and the peoples of Europe themselves, have answered in very different ways.
From the Schuman Plan to the Communities
The decisive founding act came on 9 May 1950, when the French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman, on the advice of the planner Jean Monnet, proposed that France and Germany place their coal and steel industries under a common High Authority. The proposal, addressed to the former hereditary enemy, was the origin of everything that followed: the European Coal and Steel Community of 1951, and then, after the failure of the proposed European Defence Community in 1954, the decision taken at Messina in 1955 to go forward on the economic rather than the military path. The treaty-of-rome-1957 of 1957 established the European Economic Community — a customs union among six states, France, Germany, Italy and the Benelux countries — and Euratom, and set the enterprise on the course of economic integration that was to be its enduring engine. The method, known as the Monnet method or functionalism, was to bind the nations together through common material interests, proceeding step by step and sector by sector, so that war would become not only unthinkable but materially impossible. From these beginnings grew the Community’s distinctive institutions: a Commission to propose and execute policy, a Council of member states to decide, a Parliament to represent the peoples, and a Court to interpret and enforce a law that, by the celebrated rulings of the early 1960s, took direct effect in the legal orders of the member states.
Deepening and widening
The subsequent history of integration is a history of two movements, deepening and widening, which together define the Union’s character. Deepening — the intensification of the common project — proceeded through a series of treaty revisions. The single-european-act-1986 of 1986 relaunched integration after the stagnation of the 1970s, committing the Community to complete its internal market by 1992 and extending qualified-majority voting. The maastricht-treaty-1992 of 1992 transformed the Community into the European Union, adding the single currency and the goal of economic and monetary union, a common foreign and security policy, cooperation on justice and home affairs, and the new citizenship of the Union. The euro-introduction-1999-2002 saw the single currency born in 1999 and the notes and coins of the euro enter circulation in 2002. Widening — the expansion of membership — carried the Community from its six founders to, by the accession of 2007, twenty-seven member states, above all through the eastern-enlargement-2004 of 2004, which reunited the continent after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Each enlargement brought new states, new economic weight and new strains; each deepening brought new competences and new questions of legitimacy. The two movements were never wholly harmonious: the tension between the breadth of the Union and the depth of its integration was to be a permanent theme of its history, and of the crises — the euro-crisis-2010 and brexit-2016 — that tested it in the twenty-first century.
A political system without a state
By the end of the twentieth century the Union had become, in the description of political scientists, a political system in its own right — a “multi-level” polity in which authority was divided between the supranational institutions in Brussels, the national governments, and the regional and local authorities of the member states. Its legal order, built by the Court of Justice, held that Community law took precedence over national law and created rights directly enforceable by individuals. Its institutions, originally technocratic, acquired an increasingly democratic and political character: the European Parliament, directly elected since 1979, gained ever greater powers through successive treaties until it shared legislative authority with the Council on most matters. Yet the Union was not a state, and its members never wished it to become one. It had no government in the national sense, no monopoly of legitimate violence, no final say over the security and identity of its peoples. The editors of the Cambridge History describe it as a political system that governs through the member states — an “inside-out” polity in which the instruments of integration (its money, its policies, its legal culture, its migration regime) shape the continent from within. Whether such a system, lacking the democratic legitimacy of a nation-state, could command the loyalty of its peoples was the question of its age.
Theories of integration
The effort to explain European integration has generated one of the richest bodies of theory in the study of politics, and the theories themselves have shaped the way the process is understood. The earliest grand theory, neofunctionalism, associated with Ernst Haas, argued that integration would proceed through a logic of “spillover” — that integration in one sector would create pressures for integration in adjacent sectors, until a supranational authority acquired a momentum of its own. The rival intergovernmentalist tradition, associated with Stanley Hoffmann, insisted that the nation-state remained the master of the process, and that integration advanced only when national governments chose to advance it. Against both, the American political scientist Andrew Moravcsik proposed liberal-intergovernmentalism, which held that integration was best explained as a series of rational choices by national governments responding to the economic interests of their domestic constituents, to the relative power of states, and to the desire for credible commitments. For Moravcsik the history of the Community, from Messina to Maastricht, was not the work of visionaries or supranational entrepreneurs but the product of converging national economic interests — a claim that located the driving force of integration not in the supranational institutions but in the member states themselves. The debate between these theories was not merely academic: it was a debate about what the Union was, where its power truly lay, and whether its future belonged to the nation-states or to a deeper union.
The Union as a political order
European integration remains, as its historians insist, a work in progress and a question rather than a settled fact. It has been sustained by the great narratives that the Cambridge History traces — of peace, of prosperity, of solidarity, of democracy — and it has been tested by their limits. The peace narrative, built on Franco-German reconciliation, survived the end of the Cold War; the prosperity narrative was strained by the euro-crisis-2010; the narrative of solidarity was tested by the migration crisis; and the promise of democracy faced the persistent complaint that the Union was a technocracy removed from its peoples, a complaint that brexit-2016 carried to its most dramatic conclusion. Yet for all its crises, the Union has proved a durable political order. It has absorbed thirteen new members since its founding six; it has survived the departure of Britain; and in the face of the Russian war in Ukraine it has reasserted the original purpose that had never quite faded — the integration of Europe as the condition of its peace. The process that began with the Schuman Plan has not ended, and it has not become a state. It has instead produced something new in political life: a union of nations that pool their sovereignty without surrendering it, governing their interdependence in common, forever in question and forever in being.

concepts/fifth-republic.title: The Fifth Republic
concepts/fifth-republic.content:
The Fifth Republic
The Fifth Republic is the constitutional régime that charles-de-gaulle founded in 1958 and that has governed France ever since — the longest-lived of the republican constitutions, and the political order built deliberately against the memory of its predecessor. Where the fourth-republic had been an assembly-dominated régime of shifting coalitions, the Fifth was conceived as a strong state: a head of state standing above the parties, a powerful executive, and a constitution written to prevent the return of the ministerial instability that had paralysed France. It is, at once, the realisation of the doctrine the General had proclaimed at Bayeux in 1946 and the product of the crisis of May 1958 that destroyed the old order.
The founding of 1958
The Fifth Republic was born of the Algerian crisis. When Algiers rose on 13 May 1958 and the fourth-republic proved unable either to win the war or to end it, de Gaulle was called to power and entrusted with the drafting of a new constitution. The text, drawn up under Michel Debré through the summer of 1958, rebalanced the powers of the state in favour of the executive and was carried to the country in the referendum of 28 September 1958, adopted by 79.2% of Oui. The régime was completed by the election of the General as President on 21 December and his installation at the Élysée on 8 January 1959. The constitution was thus the institutional expression of gaullisme: the state as arbiter and motor, the President above the parties, the régime des partis set aside.
A presidential régime
The characteristic of the Fifth Republic is the strength of its presidency. In the gaullist design the President of the Republic is the head of the state and its guiding will — the arbiter above the parties who appoints the government, dissolves the Assembly, and holds the exceptional powers of Article 16 in grave crisis. The executive is the motor of the régime, not the servant of a parliamentary majority. The foundation of 1958 was completed in October 1962, when de Gaulle carried by referendum the reform that the parties had refused him: the election of the President of the Republic by universal suffrage. The change, made against the opposition of the parliamentary class, bound the head of state directly to the nation and completed the presidential character of the régime — the man elected by the whole people standing as the supreme authority of the state. It was the second great act in the foundation of the Fifth, and the one that made its presidentialism definitive.
The régime in power
For a decade the Fifth Republic was the régime of its founder. Under de Gaulle it settled the algerian-war-1954-62 with the evian-accords-1962, pursued the effort of economic and social modernisation, and conducted the policy of national independence — the departure from the integrated command of NATO, the visits to Moscow and the East, the pursuit of a Europe européenne. The régime weathered the crisis of may-1968, the greatest general strike of the century, and emerged triumphant in the June elections; yet the crisis aged it, and when de Gaulle staked his authority on a referendum on the reform of the Senate and regionalisation in April 1969, the country answered Non and he resigned. His heir, Georges Pompidou, elected in June 1969, carried the Fifth Republic beyond its founder, tempering the General’s gaullisme into a more pragmatic conservatism while preserving the institutions of 1958.
Evolution and endurance
The Fifth Republic proved durable where its predecessor had been fragile. It was re-founded, in a sense, each time the presidency passed from one party to another — the institutions of 1958 survived the alternation of power that came with the election of the socialist François Mitterrand in 1981 and the cohabitation that followed, when a President of one camp governed with a Prime Minister and a majority of the other. The presidency changed hands through the century — Mitterrand, then Valéry Giscard d’Estaing before him in the 1970s, and the successors who carried the régime toward the twenty-first century — while the constitutional frame of 1958 held firm. Against the sceptics who had seen in the Fifth a temporary expedient of the General, the régime became the settled frame of French politics, its presidentialism adapted to the alternation of the parties. It stands as the institutional legacy of gaullisme, the strong state that the General had sought since Bayeux, made permanent in the life of the nation.

concepts/fourth-republic.title: The Fourth Republic (1946–1958)
concepts/fourth-republic.content:
The Fourth Republic (1946–1958)
The Fourth Republic was the parliamentary régime that governed France from the adoption of its constitution in 1946 to the collapse of May 1958 — twelve years of reconstruction and modernisation shadowed by chronic ministerial instability and by the colonial wars that finally destroyed it. Founded in the ruins of the Liberation and the rejection of de Gaulle’s constitutional ideas, it was denounced by its founder as a régime des partis (regime of the parties), incapable of decision or grandeur. Its history has since been written as a double account: the failure of the régime as a political machine, and the extraordinary successes of the reconstruction and modernisation carried out within it.
The regime of the parties
The constitution of 1946, adopted over the objections of de Gaulle, established a parliamentary régime in which the National Assembly, dominated by the parties — the communists, the socialists and the MRP of the tripartisme, then their successors — held the real power. Government depended on shifting parliamentary combinations, and the régime des partis that de Gaulle had denounced proved unstable indeed: governments rose and fell in rapid succession, twenty and more over the twelve years of the régime, brought down by the defection of their temporary allies. The instability, the immobilisme (immobilism) that gripped the régime in its later years, the difficulty of taking and sustaining decisions — these were the charges brought against the Fourth Republic by the gaullist reading, and the reason its founder’s call for a strong executive above the parties found an ever-wider audience.
The reconstruction within the régime
The political failure obscured a deeper success. Under the Fourth Republic, France carried out the reconstruction of its ruined economy and the modernisation that set the Trente Glorieuses in motion — the nationalisations and the Plan, the rebuilding of industry and agriculture, the demographic and social transformation of the country. The régime founded the European Coal and Steel Community and the first institutions of the Common Market, and gave France its voice in the making of a new Europe. The colonial question proved its undoing: the war in Indochina, lost in 1954, and above all the Algerian war, which the parties could neither win nor end, ground the régime down. The problème algérien was the load the parliamentary machine could not bear.
The collapse of May 1958
The end came in the spring of 1958. The deepening crisis of Algeria, the paralysis of the Assembly, and the threat of the army and the settlers in Algiers brought the régime to its knees. On 13 May 1958 the army and the pieds-noirs rose in Algiers, and the Fourth Republic, which could neither master the war nor find a majority to face it, staggered toward collapse. De Gaulle, who had predicted this end since 1946, was called to power, invested in June, and entrusted with full powers to draft a new constitution. The referendum of October 1958 adopted it, and the Fourth Republic gave way to the Fifth. The régime that had modernised France was buried under its own instability and the war it could not end — the parliamentary republic of the parties defeated at last by the very weakness its founder had always denounced.
