concepts/franco-german-reconciliation.title: Franco-German Reconciliation
concepts/franco-german-reconciliation.content:
Franco-German Reconciliation
At the heart of the building of Europe after 1945 lay a single, improbable reconciliation: that of France and Germany, the two powers whose rivalry had twice in a generation drawn the continent into war. The enmity between them was so old and so bitter that it had its own name in both languages — the hérédité ennemie, the “hereditary enemies”. The great achievement of the postwar years, and the premise of the entire European enterprise, was the replacement of that narrative by another: the couple franco-allemand, the “Franco-German couple”, the engine or motor that drove the Community forward. The Cambridge history of the European Union devotes a chapter to this very narrative of war, peace and memory, tracing the decline of the “hereditary enemies” story and the rise of the Franco-German engine — the deutsch-französische Versöhnung, the Franco-German reconciliation — as the founding tale of integration.
The motor of integration
The reconciliation was not an accident but the deliberate work of statesmen, and it supplied the motor of everything that followed. It was the Franco-German rapprochement, sealed in the coal and steel of the two heavy-industrial regions, that robert-schuman and jean-monnet proposed to make irreversible in the declaration of 9 May 1950; and it was the partnership of Schuman and the German chancellor konrad-adenauer that gave that declaration its force on the German side. Moravcsik’s account, though it stresses the economic interests beneath the surface, does not deny the political purpose: the pooling of French and German coal and steel was designed to make a fresh conflict materially impossible. From the Coal and Steel Community through the treaty-of-rome-1957, the Franco-German understanding was the axis around which the Six turned. It was understood on both sides of the Rhine that Europe could advance only as far as the two great continental powers could agree.
From the Élysée Treaty to the engine of the Community
The reconciliation reached its formal apotheosis in the post-war period with the Élysée Treaty of January 1963, the treaty of friendship signed by konrad-adenauer and charles-de-gaulle. The two old men of Europe — the German chancellor who had staked his reputation on the Western alliance and reconciliation with France, and the French general who had returned to power in 1958 preaching a Europe of states — embraced each other at the Élysée Palace, and the treaty institutionalised a regular machinery of consultation between the two governments. That de Gaulle, the champion of national independence, should have made this the centrepiece of his policy was itself the measure of the change: France and Germany, reconciled, were to be the pivot of a Europe of sovereign states. Thereafter the couple proved the indispensable engine of every advance. Through the empty-chair crisis and the Luxembourg Compromise of the 1960s, through the monetary experiments of the Werner Report and the European Monetary System, through the relaunch of the single-european-act-1986 and the negotiation of the maastricht-treaty-1992 and Economic and Monetary Union, the Franco-German axis — de Gaulle and Adenauer, Giscard and Schmidt, Mitterrand and Kohl — was the motor of the Community and the Union. The Cambridge history notes how the narrative persisted into the present century in the coupling of Merkel and Sarkozy and then Merkel and Macron, the “Merkozy” and “Merkron” media couples of the euro-area and pandemic years. The reconciliation that began as the settlement of a blood feud had become the permanent condition of European construction — the couple without which, as the historians of the narrative observe, the entire edifice would lack its engine.

concepts/francoism.title: Francoism
concepts/francoism.content:
Francoism
Francoism (franquismo) is the political system of the Spain that Francisco Franco ruled from 1939 to 1975 — a personal dictatorship resting on the victory of one half of the country over the other in the Civil War, and one that, in the lifetime of its founder, passed from resemblance to one type of dictatorship to another without changing the man at its head. It is not easily reduced to a single doctrine, for it was less a coherent ideology than a synthesis of authorities and interests held together by the person of the Caudillo: the army that had won the Crusade, the Church that sanctified it, the Falange that furnished its single-party forms, and the conservative and technocratic families that administered it. Because of this synthesis, historians have treated it as a dictatorship without making it a Spanish peculiarity — Franco’s conceptions and behaviour expressed a wider European type of authoritarian rule, distinguished chiefly by its longevity and by the name it took from its founder.
Authoritarianism without a single creed
The régime was a dictatorship in the strict sense — power without constitutional limits, a repressive order that never relaxed its hold on the defeated — yet it never became a totalitarian state on the model of its wartime allies. Its intellectual content was deliberately vague, summed up in the slogan “Una, Grande y Libre” (One, Great and Free): the unity of Spain against the separatism and pluralism that the régime blamed for the national disaster, the greatness of an imperial vocation recovered from the past, and freedom from the disorder of liberal democracy and the menace of communism. Franco was allergic to anything he called “constitutionalisation,” accepting only the weaker word “institutionalisation”; the state’s laws — the Ley de Cortes of 1942, the Ley de Sucesión of 1947, the Ley de Principios del Movimiento — were instruments that barely modified the real power he retained, “constitutional” dispositions designed to offer an appearance of change while preserving the substance of his rule.
The Falange and el Movimiento
The forms of the régime were supplied by the Falange Española, the fascist party founded by José Antonio Primo de Rivera in the 1930s, which Franco incorporated and subordinated after the Civil War. Under the name of the Movimiento Nacional — el Movimiento, the single movement that gathered the régime’s families — the Falange furnished the official party, the sindical organisations that claimed to represent the workers, the youth and women’s organisations, and much of the ceremonial vocabulary of the state. But the Falange was only one family among several. Franco used it instrumentally and yet indispensably, holding the balance among the Falangists, the army, the monarchists, the Catholic and the technocratic groups; the Falangists’ sense that Franco was not one of theirs ran through the régime’s internal history. At the end, the Movimiento stood for the immovable core of the régime, the búnker of those who would concede nothing, opposed to the opening that reformists sought.
National-Catholicism
Beneath the political forms lay the alliance of the régime with the Church, the nacional-catolicismo that identified Spain, the régime and the Catholic faith as one reality. Franco’s was a state that presented itself as Catholic — the Crusade that had defeated the godless Republic was to be followed by the reconsecration of Spain to the faith, expressed in the ceremonies that mixed the military and the religious and in a school and public life saturated with the Church’s teaching. Tusell notes that nacional-catolicismo was more a mentality than a precise theology — a close bond to the state, an “insatiability” that would claim the whole of life. The Concordat of 1953 sealed the alliance with the Holy See. Yet the bond proved the régime’s own undoing in part: deep into the 1950s the hierarchy and Catholics shared the identity of Spain, régime and Catholicism, but the reception of the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s made the Church both a mirror and a motor of change, until much of the Catholic world — and a new generation of priests and laymen — came to stand at a distance from, or against, a régime it had once blessed.
Anti-communism and the political culture
Francoism defined itself above all against communism and the liberal disorder it held responsible for the Civil War. Anti-communism was the régime’s constant article of faith and, after 1945, its indispensable passport to the Western camp: in the Cold War the dictatorship presented itself as the sentinel of the West against the Soviet menace, a claim that reconciled the democracies to its survival and won it the American pacts of 1953. The political culture of the régime was one of order, hierarchy, unity and tradition — a society of conformity in which peace, order and obedience were prized and in which, for the great part of the population, politics meant acceptance of a settled victory rather than participation in any public contest. The slogan “España, una, grande y libre” and the memory of the Crusade gave franquismo its language; the long dictatorship gave Spain its habits of resignation. Yet the same culture, frozen in its certainties, came to answer to another world as the society it governed modernised — a gap between a political system that seemed to belong to an earlier age and a people that had outgrown it, which was already, by the régime’s end, the ground on which its own undoing was prepared.

concepts/gaullism.title: Gaullism
concepts/gaullism.content:
Gaullism
Gaullisme is the political doctrine and tradition that grew up around Charles de Gaulle and outlived him — a conception of France, of the state and of the world shaped by the experience of the man who had summoned the nation to resistance in 1940. It is at once a doctrine of national grandeur and independence, a constitutional idea of a strong executive standing above the parties, and a political movement that has governed France for much of the history of the Fifth Republic. It begins with a certaine idée de la France (a certain idea of France), as de Gaulle put it — a conviction that France could not be France without grandeur, and that the nation must be itself, taking its own decisions in its own name.
The certaine idée de la France
At the heart of gaullism is a conception of France as a great and particular nation. De Gaulle’s France was not one state among many but a power of unique vocation, whose independence was the first of goods and whose voice must be heard in the world. From this flowed the indépendance nationale (national independence) that marked his foreign policy — the refusal to submerge France in an Atlantic bloc, the pursuit of a Europe européenne, a Europe of states rather than a federal construction, and the insistence that France decide for itself on the great questions of war and peace. The doctrine rejected the two blocs of the Cold War and sought for France a place between them, the voice of a Europe from the Atlantic to the Urals.
The strong state above the parties
The constitutional core of gaullism was worked out in the years of the Fourth Republic, which de Gaulle judged a régime des partis (regime of the parties), incapable of grandeur or decision. In the Bayeux speech of 16 June 1946 he set out his alternative: a head of state standing above the parties, a strong executive, a separation of powers that the parliamentary régime conspicuously lacked. This idea, carried against the Fourth Republic’s drafts and embodied in the constitution of 1958 and the referendum of 1962 on the election of the President by universal suffrage, became the foundation of the Fifth Republic — a state whose President was not the servant of the Assembly but the arbiter of the nation, above the conflicts of the parties.
The tradition after de Gaulle
After the General’s departure in 1969, gaullism became a political tradition and a movement, claimed by his heirs and adapted to changing circumstances. Georges Pompidou, his successor, tempered the doctrine — keeping the institutions while abandoning much of the politique de grandeur, opening to Britain and to the European Community. Jacques Chirac carried the heritage into the age of alternance and cohabitation, and Nicolas Sarkozy announced a droite décomplexée that broke with the measured manner of the tradition while still invoking the institutions of 1958. Through all these transformations the essential gaullism endured as a set of habits and convictions — the strong executive, the national independence, the certaine idée de la France — even as the France it addressed grew smaller in the world. The doctrine that had begun as the vision of one man became the enduring centre of gravity of French political life, the tradition against which every President of the Republic has since measured himself.

concepts/german-question.title: The German Question
concepts/german-question.content:
The German Question
The deutsche Frage — the German question — is the question of Germany’s political identity and place in the world that has hung over the nation’s history since the nineteenth century, and in its modern form the question of German unity and the German nation posed by the division of the country in 1945. It is not a single question but a family of questions bound together by the peculiar difficulty of the Germans in settling what and where their nation was. Was Germany a nation of one state, and if so, what were its borders? Was it a nation divided among many states, held together by language, culture and the longing for unity? Or, after 1945, was it a nation condemned to two states, forced to choose between the nation and the peace? The German question in the twentieth century was the open dilemma posed by the division of Germany — a problem that could not be wished away and could not be solved by force, and that was to dominate the politics of the Federal Republic from its foundation until the fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 finally reopened the path to its resolution.
The question of the nation
The German question was modern before it was German. It belonged to the age of nationalism that swept the nineteenth century, but it took in Germany a distinctive and fateful shape. Unlike the nations of the West, which had formed around states, the Germans formed a state around a nation — the “belated nation,” as it was called, whose unity was proclaimed in 1871 at Versailles in the hall of mirrors, after wars against France, in the Reich founded by Bismarck. Even this unification left the question unfinished: it excluded the Germans of Austria and of the lands beyond the borders of the new Reich, and it left unresolved whether the German nation would be bounded by the state or by the language. In the twentieth century the German question was to be answered catastrophically, when the attempt to unite all Germans in an empire of conquest under the Third Reich ended in the catastrophe of 1945 and the division of the country. The question of the nation had become inseparable from the question of peace.
The open dilemma of division
After 1945 the German question took its post-war form: the question of how a nation that had been divided into two states could survive as a nation at all. The founding-gdr-1949 of the East German Democratic Republic, answering the foundation of the Federal Republic in the West, institutionalised the division, and the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961 sealed it. For the Federal Republic the question of unity was written into the Basic Law itself, which declared the German people’s resolve to preserve their national and state unity and which for decades refused to accept the GDR as a foreign state. Yet the practical politics of the Cold War forced a choice. The conservative Chancellor konrad-adenauer answered the question by Western integration, subordinating unity to the alliance; the Social Democratic Chancellor willy-brandt, through his neue Ostpolitik from 1969, sought to preserve the unity of the nation by recognising the existence of the two states — Wandel durch Annäherung, change through rapprochement. Both answers left the question open. The German nation survived its division as a memory and a longing, but the dilemma of how it could be resolved in peace, with the consent of the four powers that occupied Germany and held the two states in their alliances, seemed intractable.
The debate over the nation in the West
The German question was not only a question of diplomacy but a question of self-understanding, fought out in the intellectual life of the Federal Republic. In the later decades the debate was dominated by the Left, which increasingly questioned whether the nation itself was a value worth preserving, and whether the Germans, given their history, should not accept the division as the just price of the catastrophe of 1945. Winkler records this as a debate in which the question of the nation was posed against the memory of National Socialism and the claims of the vergangenheitsbewaeltigung — the coming to terms with the past. For some, the German nation was a burden, the very word a source of danger; for others, the abandonment of the nation’s unity was an abandonment of the Germans’ claim to a normal existence among the peoples of Europe. The essayist and historian Sebastian Haffner, and above all the reflections collected by Joachim Fest, kept the question alive: Fest, whose writings on the German past Winkler draws on, insisted that the Germans could not simply cancel their history, and that the division of the nation left the German question open whether the Germans wished it open or not.
The resolution of 1990
The fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 and the collapse of the GDR reopened the German question as suddenly as the Cold War had closed it, and the german-reunification-1990 answered it. What had seemed an intractable dilemma was resolved in freedom: through free elections, through agreement, and through the assent of the four powers in the two-plus-four-1990 Treaty, the nation recovered its unity without war and without force. The German question was thus answered in the only way the Germans had failed to answer it before — in peace, in freedom, and in community with their neighbours. For Winkler the resolution of 1990 also resolved the question of the nation’s place: the Germans, having settled their borders and their identity, entered the European project as a nation among nations, and the long special path of German history, the sonderweg, came at last to an end.

concepts/glasnost.title: Glasnost
concepts/glasnost.content:
Glasnost
Гласность (glasnost, “openness”) was the policy of publicity and open discussion that, alongside perestroika, came to define the reform programme of Mikhail Gorbachev after 1985. The word itself was an old Russian noun for the quality of being public or open to view; the reform made it the governing principle of the last years of the Soviet system. Where the authoritative discourse of the Brezhnev years had controlled information and shaped public speech, glasnost opened the press, the film and the printed page to questions the regime had once silenced, and in doing so it set in motion a reckoning the leadership could no longer direct.
Openness as policy
In Pikhoya’s account of the politics of power in Moscow, the turn to openness was part of Gorbachev’s bid to break the hold of the conservative apparatus on the party and the state. The disaster at chernobyl-1986 in April 1986, which the authorities could not conceal, became an early and visible proof of the bankruptcy of secrecy: the official silence collapsed before a catastrophe that everyone could see. Thereafter the policy of glasnost gathered force, unshackling the newspapers and the journals, letting the statistics of the past and the crimes of the system into the open, and allowing the suppressed histories of the Stalin years to be told. In Medinsky’s textbook the same arc is drawn: openness that begins as a controlled concession and grows, as the reform deepens, into a torrent the party cannot contain.
Consequences
The policy did not merely inform; it undid. Once the press could print the truth about the past, the legitimacy of the present — the very claim of the party to have led the country aright — came into question. Glasnost fed the growth of independent opinion and, together with the electoral reform and the rise of the nationality question, eroded the control that had held the Soviet system together. It was the precondition of the democratic politics of 1989–1991, the debates that preceded the august-putsch-1991 and the dissolution-ussr-1991, and the medium through which the last Soviet generation came to see its own history with new eyes.

concepts/iron-curtain.title: The Iron Curtain
concepts/iron-curtain.content:
The Iron Curtain
The image that came to stand for the whole division of postwar Europe was that of an “iron curtain” — the zhelezny zanaves — drawn down the middle of the continent. The phrase, made famous by Winston Churchill at Fulton, Missouri, on 5 March 1946, described the frontier that had descended between the Soviet-controlled East and the West. It was not a physical wall, at first, but an ideological and political barrier: a line of demarcation between two systems, two ways of life, two visions of the world, which organised the politics of Europe and the world for more than four decades. Behind the curtain lay the Soviet bloc; before it, the free societies of the West. Its history is the history of the Cold War itself, and its fall in 1989 marked the end of the division of Europe.
Churchill’s phrase
The term had been used before, but it entered the language of the age in the great speech Churchill delivered on 5 March 1946, before an audience that included President Truman, in the American town of Fulton, Missouri. “From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic,” Churchill declared, “an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.” Behind that line, he warned, lay all the capitals of the ancient states of Central and Eastern Europe — Warsaw, Berlin, Prague, Vienna, Budapest, Belgrade, Bucharest, Sofia — subject, in his words, to the increasing measure of control from Moscow. To the western mind, and above all to the British, the speech was the warning of a statesman that the wartime alliance had given way to a new division of the world. To the Soviet government, however, the same speech appeared as a “credo of aggression” — a call for an Anglo-American bloc against the Soviet Union and the countries of people’s democracy, and a programme of war. The two readings of the Fulton speech, each side seeing in it a confirmation of its own fears of the other, marked the moment at which the Cold War may be said to have begun.
The division of Europe
Behind the iron curtain the Soviet Union consolidated its hold on the states of Central and Eastern Europe. Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria, and later the German Democratic Republic established in 1949, became the people’s democracies — countries in which the communists, supported by the presence of the Red Army, took power and built the order of the socialist camp. The division of Germany ran through the heart of the image: the old Reich was split into four occupation zones, and then into two states, the Federal Republic in the West and the German Democratic Republic in the East, with the former capital Berlin divided likewise. The frontier between the two Germanys, and the wall that was built through Berlin in 1961 to stop the flight of East Germans to the West, became the most concrete embodiment of the iron curtain. In the Soviet account the division was the work of the imperialist powers, who had abandoned the agreed German policy and created the western state; in the western account it was the price of Stalin’s refusal to permit free elections and national self-determination in the East. Whatever the assigning of blame, the result was a Europe cut in two.
The two blocs
The iron curtain was not merely a line on the map; it was the organising principle of two blocs and two systems. On the one side lay the socialist camp, bound together by ideology, by the Council of Mutual Economic Assistance (Sovet ekonomicheskoy vzaimopomoshchi, Comecon) and ultimately by the Warsaw Treaty; on the other lay the Atlantic West, the democracies of Western Europe and North America united in NATO and in the project of European economic integration. Each side regarded the other across the curtain with a mixture of fear and contempt. Movement across the frontier was controlled and restricted; trade, travel and information were channelled by the needs of the two systems; and the ideological struggle — the propaganda, the radio broadcasts, the espionage — played itself out along the whole length of the divide. For the peoples of the East, as the German historian Winkler insists, the iron curtain was a lived reality of unfreedom, of a state that controlled not only politics but the very terms of thought; for the peoples of the West it was both a shield and a wall, the frontier of a free world that felt itself threatened.
Détente and the fall
The iron curtain was never, in the strict sense, impassable. The relaxation of the 1950s and the era of détente in the 1970s — the treaties of Ostpolitik, the Helsinki Accords of 1975 with their confirmation of the frontiers of Europe — softened the confrontation and bound the two sides in a web of agreements, yet the curtain itself remained, and the Western powers insisted that the confirmation of the European frontiers at Helsinki must not be taken as the recognition of the permanent division of the continent. It was the crisis of the Soviet system in the 1980s that brought the curtain down. Under the pressures of economic stagnation and the popular uprisings of Eastern Europe, the borders were opened: Hungary’s dismantling of its frontier with Austria, the mass emigration through the Prague embassy, the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig, and finally the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989. “Between Hungary and Austria there was no longer an iron curtain,” as Winkler records; and with the opening of the Wall, the reunification of Germany in 1990 and the dissolution of the USSR in 1991, the iron curtain that Churchill had declared descended across the Continent was at last raised. The division of Europe into two blocs, which had seemed permanent, came to an end — and the peoples of the East rejoined the West.

concepts/last-soviet-generation.title: The Last Soviet Generation
concepts/last-soviet-generation.content:
The Last Soviet Generation
The last Soviet generation is the name Alexei Yurchak gives to those who came of age in the late Soviet period, in the decades from the mid-1950s to the mid-1980s, and whose lives were formed in the years when the great question of the twentieth century was already, to those inside it, a settled fact of daily life. These were the people who grew up inside the system at its most stable and most mature — after the terrors of the Stalin years, after the thaw of Khrushchev, in the long plateau of developed-socialism and the immobilism that came to be called the stagnation. They are the “last” generation because they were the last to be wholly formed by the Soviet order, the last for whom socialism was not a memory or a promise but simply the horizon of an ordinary life; and Yurchak’s book is an anthropology of their experience, the attempt to understand what it meant to be them, and how it was that the system they knew as eternal came to its end.
The paradox of their experience
The formative paradox of this generation, Yurchak insists, is that it perceived the system as eternal while being entirely prepared for its collapse. It did not live in fear or in hope of a different order. It lived in the confident assumption that the Soviet world was permanent, would go on forever — это было навсегда — and in that very confidence it reproduced the system’s fixed forms day after day, year after year. And yet, when the collapse came in the late 1980s and in 1990–1991, it was not experienced as a catastrophe or even as a great surprise. The generation that had believed in the permanence of the system was the same generation that let it go almost without a backward glance. To explain this paradox, Yurchak abandons the familiar oppositions that had governed the study of the USSR — official and unofficial culture, totalitarian and free language, suppression and resistance, public lie and hidden truth — and replaces them with an analysis of the performative shift of the authoritative discourse and the everyday practice of vnenakhodimost.
The way of life of the last Soviet years
In Yurchak’s account, this generation lived out the late Soviet world through a distinctive ethics and poetics. It reproduced the forms of ideology without believing their content — идеология наизнанку, ideology turned inside out — carrying on the ritual language of the party while its meaning drifted away into the private, the personal and the aesthetic. It built for itself a rich inner world that stood beside the official one: the воображаемый Запад (imagined West) assembled from foreign goods, music and images, the records of King Crimson and Deep Purple and Pink Floyd that circulated in the years of “multi-coloured communism,” the dense culture of the Soviet anecdote, the stiob and the necro-aesthetics of a generation that had learned to handle the forms of power as aesthetic objects rather than as beliefs. These were not acts of resistance; they were the texture of an ordinary Soviet life, the way people simply lived. But in being lived, they transformed the system from within, hollowing out the meaning of its discourse while preserving its form.
The passage through perestroika and the collapse
Yurchak’s concluding chapter carries this generation through perestroika-1985-91 and the collapse. As the authority of the CPSU’s language was destroyed from within — the party’s “return to Lenin” of the late 1980s, and the loss of legitimacy that had emptied the authoritative discourse of its power by 1990–1991 — the system’s forms were no longer reproduced, and the whole edifice fell. The last Soviet generation, so long habituated to vnenakhodimost, was uniquely ready for this passage. Because it had for decades inhabited the forms of the system without inhabiting its meaning, it was able to walk out of the collapsing order almost without loss, carrying its inner life intact. The collapse was at once unexpected and inevitable, a surprise and a thing long prepared; and the generation that had lived inside the system while standing a little outside it was the generation that made the end as smooth as it was. When the Soviet world “was forever, until it was no more,” it was this generation, Yurchak argues, that had already ceased, in the deepest sense, to be Soviet long before the flag came down.

concepts/liberal-intergovernmentalism.title: Liberal Intergovernmentalism
concepts/liberal-intergovernmentalism.content:
Liberal Intergovernmentalism
Liberal intergovernmentalism is the theory of european-integration developed by the American political scientist Andrew Moravcsik and set out most fully in his study The Choice for Europe: Social Purpose and State Power from Messina to Maastricht (1998). It is the most influential recent account of why Europe integrated, and the central target of debate for every rival theory that came after it. Its argument is at once simple and unfashionable: European integration is best explained not as the work of visionaries, supranational institutions, federalist ideas, or geopolitical pressures, but as a series of rational choices made by national leaders, responding to the economic interests of powerful domestic constituents, to the relative power of the states in the international system, and to the role of international institutions in making their commitments credible. Against the grand theories that had dominated the field — neofunctionalism, which held that integration acquired a momentum of its own through supranational institutions and “spillover,” and federalism, which saw the goal as a united Europe — Moravcsik argued that the nation-state remained the master of the process throughout, and that the real engine of integration was not the Community’s institutions but the member governments, and behind them the economic and commercial interests of their societies.
National preferences
The first and most distinctive element of liberal intergovernmentalism is its account of how national preferences are formed. Moravcsik begins from a liberal premise: that the state is not a unitary actor pursuing an abstract national interest, but the representative of the interests of its own society, above all of its powerful domestic economic groups. The preferences that governments bring to the negotiating table are formed domestically, and among those preferences the dominant ones are economic and commercial. When France and Germany agreed to the Common Market, when the member states built the European Monetary System, when they completed the internal market and when they created the single currency, what drove them, in Moravcsik’s reading, was not geopolitical ambition or the force of an idea but the concrete economic interests of their producers, exporters, farmers and financial sectors. The term “liberal” in the theory’s name signals this domestic, interest-driven foundation; the “intergovernmentalist” element signals the conclusion that follows — that since national governments represent these preferences, integration advances only when, and because, national governments choose to advance it.
Interstate bargaining and asymmetrical interdependence
The second element is an account of bargaining. Once preferences are formed, the outcomes of the great European negotiations are determined by the relative power of the states, and that power derives from what Moravcsik calls asymmetrical interdependence — the fact that some states need an agreement more than others, and are therefore prepared to concede more to obtain it. The state that can most credibly walk away from the table, because it has alternatives or is least dependent on the cooperation of others, is the state that gets its way. Moravcsik tested this account against the five great negotiations of Community history — the Treaty of Rome, the consolidation of the customs union and the Common Agricultural Policy in the 1960s, the European Monetary System, the Single European Act, and the Maastricht Treaty — and found in each that the bargains struck reflected the distribution of these asymmetries rather than the persuasiveness of supranational entrepreneurs or the pressure of a shared idea. The French and German bargains over agriculture and industry, and the German terms for monetary union, were the products of a field of relative power in which each state’s domestic economic position set the limit of its concessions.
Credible commitment and the role of institutions
The third element explains why governments, having agreed, choose to bind themselves through international institutions. Institutions, in Moravcsik’s account, are not autonomous actors that drive integration forward on their own account; they are instruments by which states make their commitments credible to one another. By pooling or delegating sovereignty — by creating a Court to interpret the treaties, a Commission to propose and monitor, and, in the single currency, an independent central bank — the member states tied their own hands, making their promises to each other more credible and so enabling cooperation that would otherwise have been impossible. The supranational institutions of the Community were therefore not the cause of integration but its consequence and its guarantee: the delegation of power to the Commission and the Court served the purpose of credible commitment, binding the states to the bargains they had struck. This account turned the central claim of neofunctionalism on its head. Where Haas and his successors saw the supranational institutions as an independent force propelling integration, Moravcsik saw them as the servants of the member states — powerful, but powerful only because, and only as far as, the states had chosen to make them so.
The primacy of economics over geopolitics and ideas
What most distinguishes liberal intergovernmentalism from its rivals is its insistence on the primacy of economic interest over the forces that other accounts had stressed. Moravcsik did not deny that the Cold War, the fear of a resurgent Germany, and the visions of a united Europe were present in the minds of the founders; he denied that they explained the outcomes. The weight of his evidence, he argued, showed that commercial and economic motivations dominated national preference formation in every negotiation, and that geopolitical threats, federalist ideology, technocratic imperatives and supranational entrepreneurship played only a secondary role. Nowhere was this claim more provocative than in his treatment of Maastricht. Against the prevailing view that the Treaty on European Union was a response to the geopolitical revolution of 1989 — a French and European effort to lock a newly united Germany into Europe, and a German monetary quid pro quo for unification — Moravcsik argued that the treaty was the culmination of the same converging national economic interests that had produced the Single European Act and the movement toward monetary union, and that it would largely have been concluded even had the Wall not fallen. The choice for Europe, in his phrase, was above all a choice made on economic grounds.
A claim about the nature of Europe
Liberal intergovernmentalism is thus far more than a technical theory of bargaining; it is a claim about the nature of the European Union itself. If Moravcsik is right, the Union is not a supranational federation in the making, and its great institutions are not the advance guard of a United States of Europe. It is a confederation of nation-states, each pursuing its own interests, who have pooled their sovereignty only to the extent that doing so served those interests and made their commitments credible. The theory closes, fittingly, with the words of Jacques Delors — the most supranational-minded president the Commission ever had — insisting that there would never be a United States of Europe and that he sought a federation among strong nation-states; a sentiment that Moravcsik noted brought the great visionary full circle to the view of Robert Schuman with which the book opened. The claim has been fiercely contested — by supranationalists who see the institutions as more than instruments, by historical institutionalists who stress the unintended consequences and path dependence of the institutions, and by constructivists who argue that ideas and identities shaped the interests the theory takes as given. But the debate itself is a measure of the theory’s importance. Liberal intergovernmentalism set the terms on which the explanation of European integration has been conducted ever since, and it remains the standard against which every rival account must define itself.

concepts/ostpolitik.title: Ostpolitik
concepts/ostpolitik.content:
Ostpolitik
Ostpolitik — the Eastern policy — was the great departure in the foreign policy of the Federal Republic after the West treaties of the Adenauer era. Where konrad-adenauer had anchored the republic firmly in the Atlantic and in the European Community, Ostpolitik was the opening toward the East: toward the Soviet Union, toward the states of the Soviet bloc, and above all toward the second German state on the other side of the border that ran through the heart of the nation. It was not a rejection of the Western integration that had made the republic what it was; it rested upon that integration as its secure foundation. But it marked the end of a policy that had left Bonn isolated before the East, and it gave the Federal Republic a diplomacy of its own.
The concept had a prehistory. Its intellectual father was Egon Bahr, the closest adviser of willy-brandt, who in July 1963 gave the new policy its watchword in a speech at the Evangelical Academy of Tutzing: Wandel durch Annäherung, change through rapprochement. The old policy, born of the Hallstein doctrine and the claim of the republic to represent all Germans, had held that the nation’s unity could only be served by refusing to deal with the East as it was. Bahr and Brandt inverted the order: only by drawing near to the Eastern bloc, by recognising the existing realities of the division of Europe and of Germany, could those realities ever be changed. Rapprochement was not the surrender of the national goal but the means to it — the preservation of the unity of the nation by accepting the existence of the two states. The idea matured during the Grand Coalition, in which Brandt as Foreign Minister first tested the ground, and it became government policy when the social-liberal coalition of Brandt and Walter Scheel took office in October 1969.
In practice Ostpolitik unfolded as a chain of treaties. The new-ostpolitik-1969-73 produced the Moscow Treaty of 12 August 1970, renouncing force and respecting the existing frontiers of Europe including the Oder–Neisse line; the Warsaw Treaty of 7 December 1970 with Poland, sealing the recognition of the Polish frontier and witnessed by Brandt’s kneeling gesture before the Ghetto monument; and the Four-Power Agreement on Berlin of 3 June 1972, easing access to the divided city. The design was completed by the grundvertrag-1972 of December 1972, the Basic Treaty with the German Democratic Republic that regulated the relations of the two German states and admitted them to the United Nations. Against the Alleinvertretungsanspruch (sole-representation claim) of the old diplomacy — the insistence that the Federal Republic alone could speak for Germany — Ostpolitik set the recognition of the existence of a second German state, in order, its architects insisted, to keep alive the unity of the nation.
The policy was fought over as fiercely as it was conducted. The parliamentary struggle of 1972 — the defections, the failed constructive vote of no confidence of 27 April, the election of 19 November that became a plebiscite on the treaties — showed how deeply the Ostpolitik divided Germans. Yet it also changed the republic’s place in the world. By conducting active détente itself, the Federal Republic became more “Western”, not less: it differed less from its allies because it no longer stood alone before the East. In the terms of the historian Richard Löwenthal, it overcame the Sonderkonflikt (special conflict) with the Soviet Union and the Soviet bloc, and banished the danger of foreign-policy isolation that had hung over Bonn since the 1950s. Brandt’s own biography — the unshakeable opponent of Hitler, the Mayor of Berlin — lent the policy a moral authority no conservative government could have commanded.
Ostpolitik was not a single settled doctrine but a living strategy that outlived its founder. Under helmut-schmidt and his Foreign Minister hans-dietrich-genscher it was continued and converted into the diplomacy of the second German–German decade — the permanent negotiations, the agreements despite the German Democratic Republic’s policy of Abgrenzung (delimitation), the policy of damage-limitation, and at last the summit in the Uckermark between Schmidt and Honecker in December 1981. It drew the republic into the wider European détente of the 1970s even as, in the second Cold War of the early 1980s, its limits became visible. Its deeper meaning lay in the German question itself: the policy that recognised the two states in order to preserve the nation. When the Wall fell in 1989, the division that Ostpolitik had been designed to render tolerable proved temporary after all — and the Wandel durch Annäherung that had been mocked as a surrender of the national cause was remembered, by those who judged by outcome, as the policy that had kept open the path to unity. concepts/planned-economy.title: Planned Economy
concepts/planned-economy.content:
Planned Economy
The planned economy — плановое хозяйство (the plan economy) — was the economic order of the Soviet Union, the system in which the state, through its planning organs, directed the whole national economy according to a single plan rather than leaving it to the play of the market. It was the economic foundation of socialism as it was actually built: the claim that the socialist state could, by science and by will, balance production and consumption, direct investment, and organise the labour of the whole people toward the goals the party set. At the heart of the system stood the Госплан (Gosplan), the State Planning Committee, the central organ that drew the plans binding on every enterprise and every republic of the Union, together with the great ministries and the Госснаб (Gossnab) through which materials and equipment were allocated.
Gosplan and the five-year plans
The instrument of the planned economy was the plan — above all the five-year plan, the пятилетка (fivе-year plan), the great national accounting into which the whole economic life of the country was gathered. The official history of the USSR describes the fourth (1946-1950), fifth (1951-1955) and sixth (1956-1960) five-year plans as the scientifically grounded, concrete, realistic plans of postwar restoration and development, drawn by the planning organs of the Soviet state on the directives and under the leadership of the Central Committee of the party. The work on the fourth five-year plan, the plan of reconstruction after the devastation of the war, illustrates the system at its fullest reach: begun by Gosplan and the commissariats and the Academy of Sciences as early as 1943, concentrated in Gosplan under its chairman Nikolai Voznesensky, it was debated repeatedly by the Politburo, elaborated by a great army of planners, managers, economists and scholars, and brought into accord with the state budget so that the material and financial expressions of the plan were set against one another. When the plan was confirmed in 1946 its chief economic-political task was to restore the ruined areas, to surpass the pre-war level of industry and agriculture, and then to press on beyond it; and the party mobilised the working class and the broad masses of the toilers in the социалистическое соревнование (socialist emulation) that carried the recovery through in a single five-year term.
A science and a faith
The plan was more than an instrument of management; it was a claim about the superiority of socialism itself. Where capitalism suffered crises and booms, the plan economy promised планомерное развитие (planful, proportional development) — the subordination of production to the needs of society rather than to profit. The confidence in this claim was such that the party leadership of the Brezhnev years, in the shadow of the West’s economic crisis of the 1970s and its defeat in Vietnam, was strengthened in the conviction that the Soviet planned economy was superior. The plan set the wages and the prices, fixed the standards of the goods produced, and reached down into every corner of life — the schedule of the workers, the assortment in the shops, the rhythm of the whole society. And because the state owned the means of production, the plan was enforced not by competition but by command: the ministries transmitted the directives of the centre to the enterprises, and the enterprise fulfilled them.
The problem of reform
Yet the very comprehensiveness of the plan carried within it the difficulty that was to preoccupy the whole later history of the system. Because the plan was imposed from above, it could respond only slowly to the changing needs of the population; the standardised production of an industrial society, fixed by the state plan, increasingly failed to satisfy wants that had grown more various. The shortage became a fixture of Soviet life — дефицит (shortage) — as money accumulated in the hands of the people faster than quality goods reached the shops, and queues formed behind whatever scarce article appeared. The attempt to cure these ills without abandoning the plan became the central economic question of the age. The reform of 1965, associated with alexei-kosygin, sought to make the planned economy work better by loosening its grip: it reduced the number of directives descending on the enterprise, placed the enterprise on хозрасчёт (khozraschyot, economic accountability, the principle that it must cover its own costs), and made profit and sales rather than sheer gross output the measure of success. For a time it worked — the eighth five-year plan of 1966-1970 was the most successful of the late Soviet period — but the centre could not finally surrender its powers, and the reform was wound down.
The debate over how far the plan could be relaxed without ceasing to be a plan ran on through the 1970s and into the 1980s. Economists gathered under yuri-andropov to devise variants of reform that would still keep Gosplan, Gossnab and the other central organs in place; the essentials of the Soviet economic system, including the forms of ownership, were left outside the question. It was in the end a reform from within the plan — the search for a “market socialism” — that the system proved unable to complete, and the contradictions of the planned economy, its rigidity and its shortages, formed the economic ground of the great changes that closed the Soviet period. The planned economy had raised the Soviet Union to the summit of industrial power; it could not, from within itself, be made to satisfy the consumer, and its end came with the end of the system of which it was the foundation.

concepts/sed-state.title: SED State (SED-Staat)
concepts/sed-state.content:
SED State (SED-Staat)
The term SED-Staat — the “SED state” — is the concept by which historians have sought to characterise the true nature of the German Democratic Republic. It rests on a simple but profound observation: the GDR was not a state of its own institutions but the creation and instrument of a single party, the Sozialistische Einheitspartei Deutschlands. The concept insists that to understand the republic one must look past the forms of its constitution — its parliament, its elections, its republic itself — and see the party that stood behind them, directing every office of the state as an agent of its own will. In this sense the GDR was a party-state, a Parteidiktatur (party dictatorship), and the phrase SED-Staat names that fact precisely.
The party behind the state
The concept captures the peculiar structure of rule that the SED built in the Soviet zone and perfected after the founding of the republic in 1949. The party was not content to win office through the state; it absorbed the state, making itself the source of all decisions and reducing the ministries, the courts, the police and the nominal parliament to the executors of its commands. The doctrine of the führende Rolle (leading role), the party’s claim to lead the entire society and state, was written into the republic’s self-understanding and affirmed at every party congress — at the X. Party Congress of April 1981, as Weber records, the party’s leading role was restated as the fixed foundation of the state. The Staatssicherheitsdienst, the stasi, was the sharp edge of this structure, the apparatus that guaranteed that the party’s leading role would never be challenged. To call the GDR an SED state is to say that its constitution was a facade and its real law was the party line.
A one-party dictatorship
Historians use the concept to mark the GDR’s place among the dictatorships of the twentieth century. The SED-Staat was a one-party dictatorship on the Soviet model: a regime in which all power flowed from a single, hierarchically-organised party; in which opposition parties were reduced to satellites; in which the means of coercion and surveillance were deployed systematically against the population; and in which the state and society were organised for the purpose of maintaining the party’s monopoly. Weber describes the founding period as a Stalinisation, an Angleichung an die Sowjetunion (assimilation to the Soviet Union), in which the SED’s dictatorship was consolidated by the coordination of parties, organisations and state apparatus, the purge of the party, and the strengthening of the security machinery. The east-german-uprising-1953, put down with Soviet help, and the building-berlin-wall-1961, which sealed the republic against its own people, mark the two moments in which the dictatorship revealed the coercion on which it rested.
The concept in historical judgement
The phrase carries an analytical and a moral weight. It is used partly descriptively — to identify how power actually functioned — and partly critically, to insist that the GDR cannot be understood as a state like any other, still less as the “democratic” republic its constitution proclaimed. Kowalczuk, who served on the parliamentary Enquete-Kommission of the German Bundestag on the SED dictatorship, treats the concept as the foundation for a broader reckoning with the past: the Aufarbeitung (coming to terms) that followed german-reunification-1990 rested on the recognition that the GDR had been an SED state, a system of domination that ought to be examined, understood, and in some measure condemned. The concept thus bridges the history of the republic and the moral and political questions it left behind. It also directs attention to the party’s members and functionaries — to the ordinary citizens who joined, who adapted, who mitgemacht (went along) — and to the web of accommodation and complicity that made the regime workable, a theme Kowalczuk explores through the biographies of East Germans whose lives mixed conviction and betrayal in ways no simple label captures.
The limits of the concept
No concept is beyond question, and historians who use SED-Staat do so with an awareness of its limits. It can suggest, taken literally, that the state was nothing but the party, when in fact the republic possessed its own institutions, its own experts, its own officialdom, and its own considerable capacity for adaptation and self-assertion among ordinary people. It can flatten the experience of East Germans, who lived not only under the party but within a society that had its own life — its schools and factories, its sports and its friendships — even as that society was constrained from above. And it can obscure the fact that the SED state was also a dependent state, bound to the Soviet Union and sustained by it, its authority resting ultimately on the power of Moscow. Yet for all these qualifications the concept endures, because it names the decisive fact: the German Democratic Republic was governed by the SED, and every structure of that republic was built to serve the party’s leading role. That is what historians mean when they call it an sed-state, and why the collapse of the party in 1989 brought the state down with it.

concepts/sonderweg.title: Sonderweg
concepts/sonderweg.content:
Sonderweg
The Sonderweg — the special path — is the term under which German historians have argued that the political development of Germany deviated from the path of the Western nations, and it is the idea against which Heinrich August Winkler’s history of Germany is written. The concept holds that Germany, unlike Britain and France and the other states of the West, did not develop through the peaceful revolution of a liberal and democratic tradition, but followed a particular course of its own — through the strength of the authoritarian state, the weakness of liberalism, the late and top-down unification by Bismarck, and the absence of a successful bourgeois revolution. On this reading the special path led, by an inner logic, to the catastrophe of 1933 and the Third Reich. Winkler’s two volumes, Der lange Weg nach Westen (“The Long Road to the West”), argue that the German special paths — for he writes of them in the plural, the Sonderwege — at last came to an end, and that in 1990 the Germans achieved the Western normality they had lacked before.
The deviation from the West
The idea of the special path grew out of the peculiar place of Germany in modern European history. While the nations of the West built their states around the principles of the French Revolution — liberty, equality, national sovereignty, constitutional government — Germany’s nineteenth century took a different road. Liberalism failed to impose its revolution in 1848; the unification of 1871 was achieved not from below but from above, by the Prussian state and its iron and blood, in an empire that preserved the power of the crown and the nobility, the army and the bureaucracy. The German middle classes made their peace with this order, gaining economic strength while leaving political power in the hands of the old elites. Against the parliamentarism and democracy of the West, German political thought prized the strong state, the authority of the official, the peculiar freedom of the German conception of the law-governed state (Rechtsstaat). The result, on the argument of the Sonderweg thesis, was a nation modern in economy but pre-modern in politics, whose unresolved tensions were to burst forth in the catastrophes of the twentieth century.
The path through catastrophe
The special path did not end with the empire but led on to disaster. The weak and illiberal republic that the Germans gave themselves at Weimar in 1919 inherited the authoritarian habits of the empire and never won the loyalty of the nation; the attempt of the Third Reich to achieve by conquest and genocide the unity and greatness that had eluded the Germans by peaceful means ended in the catastrophe of 1945. Winkler’s history is written against this shadow: the German self-interrogation of 1945, in which Friedrich Meinecke and Thomas Mann offered their contrasting responses to the catastrophe, was itself a reckoning with the special path. The question forced on the Germans was whether their history was a special path that had led only to ruin, or whether they could, at last, take the road to the West — the road of democracy, liberty and Europe that the nations around them had taken long before.
Westintegration and the new republic
The answer of the Federal Republic was the abandonment of the special path. Under konrad-adenauer Germany chose Western integration (Westintegration) — membership in the Atlantic alliance, in the European Community, in the community of democratic nations — and it grounded its new state in the consciously Western, value-bound constitution of the Basic Law, with its commitment to human dignity and freedom. The republic that emerged, with its social market economy and its firm place among the democracies of the West, represented a break with the German past as deliberate as any in modern history. The politics of the new republic, from the neue Ostpolitik of willy-brandt to the stewardship of helmut-schmidt, unfolded within this Western frame. Yet as long as Germany remained divided, as long as the german-question stood open and a German state lay outside the West under Soviet rule, the special path could not be regarded as fully ended: the nation was still not wholly on the road to the West.
Abschied von den Sonderwegen: the farewell of 1990
The fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 and the german-reunification-1990 completed the journey. Winkler closes his history with an essay titled Abschied von den Sonderwegen (“Farewell to the Special Paths”), in which he draws together the argument of the two volumes: with reunification, with Germany’s firm anchoring in the West and in the European project, and with the resolution of the German question in freedom through the two-plus-four-1990 Treaty, the special German path ended. The Germans achieved at last the Western normality they had lacked before 1990 — a nation among nations, democratic, free, and at peace, its whole territory within the community of the West. The long deviation had come to an end, and with it the sense of permanent anomaly that had shadowed German history. The Germans, Winkler argued, could not claim a special destiny, whether for good or for ill; they were, at last, a normal Western nation.

concepts/sozialmarktwirtschaft.title: Sozialmarktwirtschaft (The Social Market Economy)
concepts/sozialmarktwirtschaft.content:
Sozialmarktwirtschaft (The Social Market Economy)
The economic order of the Federal Republic of Germany bore a name that proclaimed its double purpose: the sozialmarktwirtschaft, the social market economy. It was at once a market economy, committed to the free play of prices and competition, and a social economy, pledged to cushion the inequalities that the market, left to itself, would produce. Conceived by the economists of the Freiburg school and carried into practice by Ludwig Erhard, the social market economy became the institutional soul of the West German economic miracle and the foundation of the prosperity and social peace of the new republic.
The ordoliberal foundation
The doctrine grew out of the school of Ordoliberalismus associated with Walter Eucken and the Freiburg economists of the 1930s and 1940s. Against the two great enemies of the age — the centralised command economy, whether of the Soviet type or of the Nazi war machine, and the ungoverned laissez-faire that had helped destroy the Weimar Republic — the ordoliberals insisted that a free economy was not the natural result of leaving things alone, but the product of a deliberate order. The state’s task was to establish and maintain the Ordnung (order) of the market: a stable currency, guaranteed by an independent monetary authority; open and free competition, protected by cartel law against the concentration that the Germans had always feared; and a legal framework within which free enterprise could flourish. Freedom and order were not opposites but conditions of one another. The market could not flourish without the rule of law, and freedom could not survive without a functioning market.
Market and social policy
The social element of the “social market economy” was as essential as the market itself. Its architects rejected the Laissez-faire conclusion that the market’s outcomes were sacred; the state was to correct the grossest inequalities, to provide for the weak, the old, the sick and the unemployed, and to spread the benefits of growth as widely as possible. Prosperity, in the conception of Erhard and his teachers, was itself the best social policy — a rising tide that would dissolve class conflict and make a decent life accessible to all. Alongside the market stood a welfare state that expanded steadily through the 1950s, a competition policy that protected the small and the new, and a policy of encouraging savings, ownership and consumption. The soziale Marktwirtschaft was thus a “third way” between liberal capitalism and state socialism, a middle path that German history since the Weimar Republic had made almost instinctive: a market, but a market with a conscience and a framework.
The framework of West German prosperity
Erhard proclaimed the social market economy as the economic doctrine of the CDU in the elections of 1949 and, as Economics Minister under Adenauer for fourteen years, made it the working constitution of the Federal Republic’s economy. Its practical instruments were the Währungsreform (currency reform) of 1948, which created the sound money on which the whole edifice rested; the freeing of prices; the liberalisation of trade; and, from the later 1950s, a deepening of the social security system. The result was the great boom of the 1950s, when the social market economy and the economic miracle became virtually interchangeable terms in the public mind. Growth was so rapid and so widely shared that the promise of the doctrine seemed fulfilled: full employment, rising wages, mass consumption, and a social peace in which the old class struggles of German industry were absorbed into a general prosperity.
The social market economy became the common ground of West German politics. The Social Democrats, who had fought the 1949 election on the programme of state planning and socialisation, were driven by the evident success of the market economy to abandon their old orthodoxy at the Godesberg programme of 1959, accepting the market order and the welfare state. Henceforward both great parties governed within the framework Erhard had set. In later decades, as the long boom faded and the costs of the welfare state grew, the balance between the “social” and the “market” in the sozialmarktwirtschaft would be endlessly renegotiated by successors from Helmut Schmidt to Helmut Kohl. But the concept itself — a market economy, constrained and socialised by a framework of law and welfare — remained the settled economic order of the Federal Republic, and the foundation of the prosperity that legitimised the West German state itself.

concepts/stagnation.title: The Period of Stagnation
concepts/stagnation.content:
The Period of Stagnation
The period of stagnation — the период застоя — is the name given to the closing age of the Brezhnev era, the years from the late 1960s to the accession of Gorbachev in 1985, in which the Soviet system, having reached the summit of its power and stability, appeared to stand still. The term is a retrospective judgement, coined not by the men who lived through those years but by those who came after them and looked back — the reformers of perestroika, the historians, and the generations who inherited the mounting, unspoken problems that the era of calm had stored up. It describes an immobility that was at once economic, political and psychological: a system that had ceased to develop in any of the senses that matter, yet held together, stable and self-satisfied, in the certainty of its own eternity. In the school textbooks of the new Russia the question is posed plainly: why is the Soviet political system of 1964-1985 so often characterised by the term застой (stagnation)?
A settled age
The era over which the shadow of stagnation fell had begun in confidence. The removal of Khrushchev in October 1964 had restored what the party called the Leninist norms of party life — an end to the restless reorganisations and voluntarist improvisations of the preceding decade. Under Brezhnev the party proclaimed that Soviet society had entered the mature stage of developed socialism, a harmonious and settled order in which the old contradictions had been resolved and the country could advance without conflict toward communism. The eighth five-year plan of 1966-1970 was the most successful of the late Soviet period; the economy grew, the welfare state expanded, and for the great majority of ordinary people life slowly improved — no wars, no revolutions, no hunger, no upheavals. It was, as the sympathetic historians of the era insisted, in many ways the most favourable time in the whole of the country’s troubled twentieth century.
The hidden immobility
Beneath this settled surface the currents had begun to slow. The reformist vigour of the 1960s faded as the 1970s wore on: the Kosygin reform was wound down, the plans were fulfilled at ever slower rates, and the economy became ever more dependent on the export of raw materials, buoyed by the great oil and gas revenues of Siberia. The campaign to extol Brezhnev had begun, the inflation of the leader’s person into a quiet cult, the portraits and the orders multiplying while the leadership aged around him. A теневая экономика (shadow economy) grew up to fill the gaps left by the failing official distribution, and corruption spread through trade and the apparatus. The party’s confident self-description of a harmonious developed socialism encouraged a complacent view of reality — a willingness to take the pronouncements of the system for its facts. The regime that had opened toward the West in the early 1970s found its hopes of durable détente disappointed by the turn of the decade, and the entry of Soviet troops into Afghanistan in December 1979 brought the relaxation to a close.
The two periods of late socialism
The retrospective literature divides the last decades of the Soviet system into two ages. The first, the оттепель (thaw), was the period of the Khrushchev reforms, a time of opening and experiment. The second was the застой (stagnation), the Brezhnev period — and many observers take the symbolic boundary between them to be the entry of Soviet troops into Czechoslovakia in the summer of 1968. The ethnographic study of the последнее советское поколение (last Soviet generation) treats the whole of this period, from the mid-1950s to the mid-1980s, as поздний социализм (late socialism): a time in which the fixed forms of the system’s authoritative discourse were reproduced ever more faithfully even as their meaning was steadily hollowed out from within. To the subjects of that world, the system felt eternal — это было навсегда (it was forever) — yet they were simultaneously, imperceptibly, prepared for its collapse. The stagnation, in this reading, was not only an economic slowdown but the peculiar quality of a society living inside the ritual reproduction of a discourse whose living content had drained away.
The word and its weight
The term застой carries a heavy, unflattering weight, and its use is not neutral. It was adopted by the reformers to justify the course of perestroika — the claim that a system which had stopped developing must be reformed or perish — and it fixed in the historical memory an image of the late Brezhnev years as a time of grey stagnation against which the new era defined itself. Yet the historians who defend the era point out that it was also a time of genuine stability, of peace and rising welfare, and they resist the unrelieved gloom of the label. The politics of the term is itself part of the history: the naming of the застой was an act of the generation that overthrew it, a way of marking the distance between the stasis of their fathers and the reform they intended to bring. The period closed with the deaths of three successive leaders — Brezhnev in 1982, Andropov in 1984, Chernenko in 1985 — an image of gerontocracy that confirmed the general impression of a system grown old at the summit. And with the election of Gorbachev in March 1985 the age of stagnation passed into the age of reform, and the word застой passed from the description of the present into the memory of the past.

concepts/stiob.title: Stiob
concepts/stiob.content:
Stiob
Стёб — stiob — is the Russian term Alexei Yurchak takes up to name the characteristic irony of the late Soviet generation, a mode of parody so deep it can no longer be told apart from the thing it mocks. The word, which entered the everyday speech of the 1970s and 1980s from youth and bohemian milieux, describes a kind of over-identification with official discourse — a playing with the forms of the authoritative discourse that carries them to such an extreme, so earnestly and so completely, that the boundary between the joke and the sincerity dissolves. Stiob is not satire; it does not stand at a safe distance and point at the absurdity of the system. It inhabits the absurdity so fully that it becomes impossible to say whether the stiobist is mocking the system or loving it, whether the excess is a critique or a devotion.
Beyond dissidence
The significance of stiob, in Yurchak’s analysis, is that it belongs to a world that the old categories cannot describe. It is neither dissidence nor conformity. The dissident stood outside the system and opposed it, speaking a language the official discourse could not absorb; the conformist stood inside and reproduced the forms without question. The stiobist did neither. He was, like all of the last Soviet generation, in vnenakhodimost — simultaneously inside and outside the field of the authoritative discourse — and stiob was the aesthetic expression of that position. It did not challenge the system head-on, because it did not need to; it treated the system’s language as an object, a thing to be handled aesthetically, carried to extremes and made strange. In stiob the authoritative discourse was no longer believed, but it was also no longer fought. It had become material for play, and a thing played with is a thing already partly dead.
Necro-aesthetics and the anecdote
Yurchak locates stiob within a wider family of late-Soviet practices that he groups together as the irony of vnenakhodimost — некроэстетика (necro-aesthetics), the aesthetic fascination with old books, images and forms, and the Soviet anecdote, the immense oral genre of the everyday joke. The rock group Laibach, with its dead-serious performance of totalitarian pomp, stands in Yurchak’s text as the purest emblem of the stiobist position: a band from Ljubljana that so completely over-identified with the iconography and rhetoric of power that its allegiance became radically undecidable, equally legible as fascist kitsch and as a devastating critique. What united these practices was their refusal of the binary of belief and opposition. The anecdote, endlessly retold, took the slogans of the system and turned them into shared property of laughter without ever confronting them as propositions. Stiob worked the same way on a grander, more aestheticized scale: it was the irony of a generation that had so thoroughly internalized the exterior of the authoritative discourse that its parody and its sincerity were the same gesture.
The meaning of the over-identification
The power of stiob, Yurchak argues, lay precisely in its ambiguity. Because the stiobist could not be distinguished from the true believer, stiob operated from inside the system’s own forms, transforming their meaning without ever declaring war on them. It was the aesthetic counterpart of the performative shift of the authoritative discourse itself: just as the official language shifted from constative truth to performative reproduction, so stiob shifted from opposition to over-identification, reproducing the forms of power so completely that power could no longer tell its friend from its parodist. In doing so, stiob became one of the ways the last Soviet generation lived out the end of the system before the system itself knew it had ended — a mode of speech that had already ceased to believe in its object, and so was already, in its very form, a preparation for the collapse.
