concepts/strategy-of-tension.title: The Strategy of Tension — Strategia della tensione
concepts/strategy-of-tension.content:
The Strategy of Tension — Strategia della tensione
The strategia della tensione, the strategy of tension, names the theory and the practice of using violence to bend the political life of Italy toward a reaction. At its heart lay a calculated wager: that a wave of bombings attributed to the far left would so alarm the country that a frightened and divided public would turn toward the right, discredit the parties and movements of the left, and open the way to an authoritarian order. Whether such a coherent design truly directed the bombs — or whether what appeared was rather the convergence of subversive groups, rival secret services and a general climate of paranoia — is a question the historians have never been able to settle with certainty. What is beyond dispute is that from December 1969 the bombs of the extreme right and the shadowy forces behind them filled an entire phase of Italian life with dread, and helped to produce the crisis of the state that in Italy would be called the years of lead.
Piazza Fontana and the opening of the spiral
The strategy of tension is conventionally dated from the worst of the early attacks, the bombing of the Banca dell’Agricoltura in Piazza Fontana, Milan, on 12 December 1969. The explosion of a high-powered bomb caused a veritable massacre: sixteen dead and ninety wounded. On the same day three other bombs exploded in Rome, wounding sixteen, and another was found unexploded at the Banca Commerciale of Milan. The episode of Piazza Fontana and the days of December 1969 marked the opening of a spiral of violence destined to last for many years and to characterise an entire phase of national life. The technique and characteristics of the attack linked it to those that followed — Piazza della Loggia in Brescia, the Italicus train, the station of Bologna — all of them, in the language of the time, of matrice nera, of the black matrix, the stamp of the far right.
In the two years that followed the bombings continued with impressive insistence: no fewer than 271 dynamite explosions were counted in the first half of 1972 alone. Around the attacks gathered a train of unresolved deaths — the anarchist Giuseppe Pinelli, who fell from a window of the Milan police station where he was being interrogated for the massacre; the publisher Giangiacomo Feltrinelli; the commissioner Luigi Calabresi, assassinated in 1972 — cases in which the real responsibilities were never clarified, giving credit to the hypothesis of a violence nourished by conspiracies of subversive groups, by secret services in conflict among themselves, and even of a strage di stato, a massacre of state.
The reactionary logic
Mammarella, weighing the evidence with care, judges that it is still impossible to give a documented and definitive verdict on the origins and responsibilities of the wave of violence. On the basis of the later findings, however, he considers it justified to place the greater part of the episodes of this first phase within the framework of the response of conservative forces to the economic and political ascent of the working class, and of the reaction of terrorist groups of the extreme right directed at striking the democratic institutions and creating the conditions for a change of regime. This was the strategia della tensione of which the subversive groups of the right were the interpreters: by spreading the fear of a revolutionary danger, the forces behind the bombs hoped to provoke a reaction that would consolidate order and push the state toward authoritarian remedies. The climate was that of a country under siege — the daily confrontation of demonstrations and counter-demonstrations, the stillicidio of violence, the ideologised dissension spreading from the universities through every environment of society, shaking the church and the family themselves.
The ambiguous years
The strategy of tension ran through the most dramatic years of the Republic, from 1969 into the middle of the next decade. It was shadowed always by the suspicion that sectors of the state — above all the secret services — had played a part, either by tolerating the far-right violence or by deliberately steering the investigations away from its true authors. The inquest into the Bologna massacre of 1980 would revive these fears: the SISMI, the military intelligence service, was suspected by the press of having depistato, deflected, the investigations of the Bolognese judges, in a way that seemed to accredit the disquieting hypotheses about the role of the secret services in the strategy of tension. Gentiloni Silveri, for his part, sets the whole experience within the frame of the “end of innocence” — the long 1968 passing into political violence and terrorism — and the crisis of the democratic institutions that the years of lead inflicted on the Republic. The strategy of tension was, in its political aim, a failure: the country did not fall to an authoritarian order, and in the end the democratic state, painfully and imperfectly, reasserted itself. But the wounds it left — the unsolved massacres, the shattered confidence in the state — long outlasted the bombs.

concepts/tangentopoli.title: Tangentopoli — Bribesville
concepts/tangentopoli.content:
Tangentopoli — Bribesville
The word tangentopoli — Bribesville — was coined in the spring of 1992 to name what the investigating magistrates of Milan had uncovered: a diffuse and deeply rooted system of corruption that bound together the parties, the politicians and the great contractors of the Italian Republic. It was, in the phrase of the time, the city of the tangente, the bribe — a hidden, tolerated and consolidated illegality that had financed the machinery of the parties and enriched the administrators of the state for years. The exposure of this system, in the investigations known as Mani pulite, Clean Hands, detonated a political earthquake that swept away the entire governing class of the postwar Republic.
The system
The corruption laid bare was not a matter of isolated rogues but a network of behaviour and constraint — a genuine cultura dell’illecito, a culture of the unlawful, that had marked conduct, mentalities and attitudes toward the state and its institutions. Its heart lay in the awarding of public works: the metro, the airport, the motorways, the public buildings that had been constructed in Italy over the previous two decades had all fed what observers called a tangentocrazia, a rule of the bribe. Politicians and contractors exchanged favours, privileges and sums of money in the sectors of public contracts and in the financing of parties in search of support. All the principal parties were involved in some measure — the Democrazia cristiana and the Partito socialista most heavily — while only the MSI, the Greens and a few formations without positions of local power stood aside.
The explosion of Mani pulite
The trigger was apparently trivial. On 17 February 1992, in Milan, the socialist Mario Chiesa, president of the Pio Albergo Trivulzio old people’s home, was caught red-handed receiving a mazzetta of seven million lire from a supplier of the institution. The investigations, conducted with scrupulous patience by a young magistrate, Antonio Di Pietro, and his collaborators of the Milan prosecutor’s office, revealed an extraordinarily dense web of corruption and complicity. Dozens of holders of local power — including two former mayors of Milan, Paolo Pillitteri and Carlo Tognoli — fell into Di Pietro’s net, and the connivance between politicians and the great entrepreneurs who paid the bribes in exchange for public works emerged in full. The scale appeared enormous from the start, measured in tens of billions of lire paid into the coffers of the parties and further billions deposited in the Swiss accounts of corrupt administrators. Within months the investigations spread from Milan to other cities of north and south, revealing the national dimensions of the phenomenon.
The season of inquests, which Gentiloni Silveri calls a rivoluzione dei giudici, the revolution of the judges, moved with dizzying speed. The pool of Mani pulite, led by the head of the Milan prosecutor’s office Francesco Saverio Borrelli, distributed dozens of judicial notices almost daily; by the end of 1992 more than fifteen per cent of parliamentarians stood under investigation. Over the course of the long season, the figures grew enormous: seventy prosecutors’ offices conducted proceedings against more than twelve thousand people, with 25,400 avvisi di garanzia issued, 4,525 arrests and 1,233 convictions. Six ministers resigned after receiving notice of investigation; in less than five months of 1993 every secretary of the governing parties abandoned his post. The scandals extended into industry and finance, drawing in the FIAT, the ENI and the Montedison and their leading men, and into the state’s own secret funds and even the magistracy itself.
Reactions and victims
The affair split the country. Some sought to limit its meaning, circumscribing corruption to well-defined milieux — the mele marce, the rotten apples — or drawing a subtle distinction between those who enriched themselves individually and those who had merely financed their party in a system where the cost of politics had never been regulated by law, the defence taken up by Craxi. Others pressed for a clean break in the name of a regained legality, convinced that everything could change quickly. The public’s hunger for purification found its hero in Di Pietro and its symbol in the clinking of handcuffs. The spectacle had its victims: the socialist deputy Sergio Moroni, the former ENI president Gabriele Cagliari and the industrialist Raoul Gardini took their own lives, and the PSI administrator Vincenzo Balzamo died of a heart attack. The referendum of April 1993, in which a huge majority voted for the majority system and against the public financing of parties, marked the first verdict of the people against the old order.
The collapse of the party system
Gentiloni Silveri identifies three interlocking planes that brought down the Republic: the inquests of Tangentopoli revealing a corruption that had guaranteed consents, visibility and positions of power; the new regional leagues of the North threatening the bond between centre and periphery; and the end of the Cold War that had inscribed the whole postwar Italian parabola. The international collapse of 1989 proved in the end the most conditioning of all. Whatever its deeper causes, Tangentopoli delivered the death blow to the Republic of the parties. The Democrazia cristiana dissolved in June 1993, its secretariat announcing the end of the party and the beginning of its diaspora; the socialists crumbled; and out of the ruins rose the new formations — and above all the movement of Silvio Berlusconi — that would contest the elections of 1994 in the shape of a new party system.

concepts/trente-glorieuses.title: The Trente Glorieuses
concepts/trente-glorieuses.content:
The Trente Glorieuses
The Trente Glorieuses — the “thirty glorious years” — is the name given, long after the fact, to the exceptional period of French growth and modernisation that ran from the end of the Second World War to the great crisis of the mid-1970s. The expression was coined by the economist Jean Fourastié in 1979 to describe the révolution invisible (invisible revolution) of 1946 to 1975, the quarter-century in which France was transformed from a rural and traditional country into a modern industrial society of mass consumption. It is a retrospective name: contemporaries, Fourastié insisted, did not live these years as “glorious,” only as the ordinary passage of time. The term has since become the emblem of the postwar golden age — and, as the historian’s reading of the era insists, a myth to be interrogated as much as a period to be celebrated.
Reconstruction and the Plan
The era opened with the reconstruction of a France left in ruins by the war. Industry and agriculture had collapsed, and the will to reform the structures of the economy animated the Liberation. Between the state and the market arose the Plan — the planification that set the objectives of national production — and the great nationalisations of the immediate postwar years. The working of the Marshall Plan and the discipline of reconstruction set the country on the road of the état de croissance, the “growth state,” in which the modernising state drove the transformation of the economy. France, which had entered the war an agrarian power, emerged from the first decade of the era as an industrial nation in full expansion.
The transition modernisatrice
The historian’s phrase for the era is the transition modernisatrice (modernising transition), the transformation of the 1950s and early 1960s that remade French society. It was the age of the génération modernisatrice, of the grands aménagements du territoire — the great reshaping of the national territory with its dams, motorways and towns — of a demographic and social revolution carried by immigration and by the mass entry of women and the salaried into the workforce. The working world was increasingly fragmented, salarisation, tertiarisation and féminisation reshaping a society that had once known only the peasant and the artisan. Alongside the old France of the paysan, a new France of the factory and the office was being born.
Consumption and the welfare state
The Trente Glorieuses were the years of mass consumption and of the welfare state. The household equipment that was to become the furniture of ordinary French life — the refrigerator, the automobile, the television — spread through the population, celebrated and mocked at once by the writers and artists of the age, from Boris Vian’s Complainte du progrès to Jacques Tati’s Mon oncle. Advertising, credit and the new distribution remade the everyday, while the civilisation du loisir — the civilisation of leisure — opened with the tourist and the paid holiday. The state built the État-providence, the social security and public services that underwrote the new prosperity. It was a period, in Fourastié’s phrase, of invisible revolution — a transformation so complete that those who lived it barely perceived it as change at all.
The end of the glorious years
The Trente Glorieuses came to an end with the crisis of the early 1970s, the turn of 1973 that broke the long expansion. The consciousness of a durable economic crisis, of unemployment as a permanent horizon, replaced the certainties of growth, and it was then that the phrase took on its retrospective glow — the Trente Glorieuses shining, in the historian’s image, “like the light of a lost paradise.” The era left France the modern country it had become: the industrial society, the welfare state, the mass culture and the consumer abundance that subsequent decades would inherit, and against which they would measure their own disappointments. The Trente Glorieuses stand in the history of France as the foundation of everything that followed, the golden age whose memory shaped the nation’s sense of its own decline.

concepts/vergangenheitsbewaeltigung.title: Vergangenheitsbewältigung
concepts/vergangenheitsbewaeltigung.content:
Vergangenheitsbewältigung
Vergangenheitsbewältigung — literally, the mastering or coming to terms with the past — is the German name for the confrontation with the Nazi past, and it names one of the central themes of the history of the Federal Republic. The word combines Vergangenheit, the past, with Bewältigung, the act of mastering, coping with, or overcoming something. It denotes the burden laid on the Germans by the crimes of the Third Reich: the demand that the nation confront, acknowledge and answer for what had been done in its name between 1933 and 1945. Winkler’s history of divided Germany rests on the premise that the years 1933-45 shaped everything that followed so deeply that the history of the two Germanies is in large part a history of coming to terms with the deutsche Katastrophe — the German catastrophe. Vergangenheitsbewältigung was not a settled achievement but a running confrontation, an unfinished labour of memory and responsibility that ran through the whole life of the old Federal Republic.
The legacy of the catastrophe
The catastrophe of 1945 confronted the Germans with a past they could neither deny nor easily bear. The Third Reich had ended not in liberation but in ruin, and with it had collapsed the state that had committed crimes of a kind unprecedented in the history of nations — the murder of the European Jews, the extermination of whole peoples, the war of annihilation in the East. The self-interrogation of 1945, in which Friedrich Meinecke and Thomas Mann offered their contrasting responses to the catastrophe, marked the beginning of the reckoning. Yet for the Federal Republic the past was not a subject of free contemplation but a wound that would not close. The memory of what had been done, the guilt of those who had done it and of those who had looked away, the presence among the citizens of the new republic of the generation that had lived under Hitler — all this made the Nazi past a living political question, to be revisited again and again as the republic sought to define what it was.
The republic’s struggle with the past
The relationship of the Federal Republic to the past was a struggle carried on at every level — legal, political, intellectual and personal. The republic prosecuted at Nuremberg and then in its own courts the crimes of the Third Reich, but it also had to live with the continuity of elites who had served the dictatorship, and it faced, in the early years, the temptation to let the past be past. The 1950s saw the republic’s founders, above all konrad-adenauer, insisting on the rehabilitation of the state, the integration of former followers, the restitution owed to the victims of the Jews — and yet also a marked reluctance to press the reckoning too far. As the decades passed the confrontation grew more insistent. The 1960s brought the great Auschwitz trials in Frankfurt and the student movement of 1968, whose demand that the older generation account for its past under Hitler broke the silence that had settled over the republic. The past returned again and again, in the Filbinger affair, in the debate over the historians’ interpretation of the Holocaust, in the questions asked of the republic’s institutions and its leaders. Vergangenheitsbewältigung was not a single act of penance but a perpetual demand that the republic answer for what the Germans had done.
Memory, responsibility and the nation
The coming to terms with the past was bound up with the other great questions of German identity — the german-question and the sonderweg. For many Germans the memory of the catastrophe seemed to discredit the nation itself; the very longing for unity, for a normal national existence, was shadowed by the suspicion that the Germans, having once surrendered to the worst, could not be trusted with the claims of nationhood. The debates of the late Federal Republic turned on this tension: whether the Germans, weighed down by the past, could claim a normal place among the peoples of Europe, or whether the memory of the crimes must forever forbid them the consolations of the nation. Winkler’s own argument is that the Germans could not simply cancel their history — that a nation which had no Western normality before 1990 could claim no permanent anomaly either, and that without clarifying their national identity the Germans could not contribute to the project of Europe. The reckoning with the past was thus not the renunciation of the nation but the condition of it: the Germans could recover a normal existence only by first owning the catastrophe that had made them abnormal.
The unfinished labour
After reunification, Vergangenheitsbewältigung took on a new and expanded meaning. The german-reunification-1990 added to the reckoning with the Nazi past the reckoning with the dictatorship of the East — the confrontation with the SED regime and the crimes of the GDR, which the unified republic pursued through the opening of the Stasi files and the official labour of Aufarbeitung (working through). The confrontation with the past, which had begun as the burden of the West, became the burden of the whole nation. Yet the essential character of Vergangenheitsbewältigung remained what it had been throughout the history of the Federal Republic: an unfinished labour of memory and responsibility, in which each generation must ask anew what its country has done and what it owes. The word itself — the attempt to master a past that cannot be mastered, only confronted — captures the paradoxical task at the heart of the German republic: to live with a history it could not undo, by refusing ever to forget it.

concepts/vertical-of-power.title: Vertical of Power
concepts/vertical-of-power.content:
Vertical of Power
The vertikal’ vlasti (вертикаль власти), the “vertical of power”, was the governing idea of the Russian state in the first years of the presidency of vladimir-putin — the rebuilding of the hierarchy of command through which the centre would once again rule the whole of the country. The term named a structure and a project at once. A vertical of power is a chain of subordination running from the top of the state to the localities; the phrase became the slogan of a policy that set out to repair the broken chain, to make the decisions of the federal centre run downward to the regions and to bind the regions back to the centre. In the official school textbook it is defined plainly: an hierarchical system of the subordination of the local organs of power to the central ones. The project of building it — stroitel’stvo vertikali (строительство вертикали) — was announced by the new president as the first priority of his government, and the historian Pikhoya made it the very title of his account of the first Putin years: full throttle up the vertical (gazuyem po vertikali, газуем по вертикали).
The problem it answered
The vertical was built to answer the disintegration that the 1990s had bequeathed. From the late years of perestroika the “parade of sovereignties” (parad suverenitetov, парад суверенитетов) had set the republics and regions of Russia upon their own paths, and the tendency persisted through the Yeltsin years. The constitutions of the republics within the Russian Federation and the charters of the territories and regions frequently contradicted federal law; the organs and institutions of federal power in the regions were often uncoordinated; and the old institution of presidential representatives had proved unable to impose unity. The Soviet vertical of command — the nomenklatura (номенклатура), the apparatus of appointment from above and dependence of the lower upon the higher — had collapsed with the USSR, and in the decade that followed the regions elected their own governors, who no longer depended upon Moscow. The task of the new policy was to restore, by new instruments, the authority that the old hierarchy had once exercised by appointment.
The federal districts and the plenipotentiaries
The first and most famous instrument was the division of the country into seven federal districts (federal’nyye okruga, федеральные округа) by the decree of May 2000 — the Central, North-Western, Southern, Volga, Ural, Siberian and Far Eastern districts, each gathering together republics, territories and regions, and each placed under a plenipotentiary representative (polnomochnyy predstavitel’, полномочный представитель) of the President. The decree declared its aim to be the realisation by the President of his constitutional powers, the raising of the efficiency of the federal organs of power, and the improvement of the system of control over the execution of their decisions. The plenipotentiary was to represent the President within his district, to organise the implementation of the state’s internal and external policy, to ensure control over the execution of federal decisions, to carry out the President’s personnel policy, and to report to the Kremlin on the political, social and economic condition of his district and on matters of national security. A new tier had been inserted into the machinery of the state. The elected governors, who had been almost free of central control, now found themselves watched and disciplined by an apparatus answerable to the President.
The instruments of pressure
The administrative machinery was reinforced by law. In June 2000 the State Duma adopted a measure that for the first time allowed the President to dissolve a regional parliament and dismiss the highest official of a subject of the Federation where their activity obstructed the realisation of federal powers. The breadth and vagueness of the formula put the heads of the regions at the mercy of the President. Their last shield had been their membership, by right of office, of the upper house of parliament — the Federation Council — where, with the speakers of the regional assemblies, they could form a “regional fronda” (regional’naya fronda). But the President reached even there, bringing in a law to change the formation of the Federation Council so that governors and speakers could no longer sit in it as senators; henceforward each region was to be represented by delegates chosen from its legislature and from its administration. The governors lost both their immunity and their institutional voice. The Kremlin was further girded by the creation of the State Council in 2000, a consultative body, and by a law on political parties in 2001 that imposed strict requirements for registration — measures that began the reshaping of the party landscape around the “party of power” that would come to dominate the Duma.
The state restored
The vertical of power was inseparable from the state’s recovery of its means. The favourable movement of world oil prices, which tripled Russian crude from the depths of 1998, filled the treasury and gave the restored state the resources with which to govern — to pay pensions and salaries, to run budget surpluses, to build up reserves. And the vertical was inseparable from the discipline imposed on the great private fortunes. At the summer meeting of 2000 with the leading businessmen, Putin proclaimed the principle of “equidistance” (ravnoudalennost’): the state would hold all the oligarchs at an equal distance from power. Those who treated the warning lightly — the media magnates Gusinsky and Berezovsky, later the oil baron Khodorkovsky — were broken or driven abroad, and their empires passed to the state. The relationship of society and power was transformed as well. The people, exhausted by fifteen years of uncertainty and want, had looked to the new leader to stop the disintegration of the state, and through his first term the polls recorded rising trust. By the presidential address of 2001 Putin could declare that the period of the “sprawling” of the state was past and that the disintegration of the country had been halted.
The meaning of the vertical
The vertikal’ vlasti was more than a set of administrative reforms; it was the doctrine by which the Russian state reconstituted itself after the decade of collapse. Its builders presented it as the restoration of unity, order and law — the means by which the constitution of the country would at last be obeyed from the Baltic to the Pacific. It answered a real disorder, and it was received by a society that longed for an end to chaos. It also concentrated power decisively in the presidency, subordinating the regions, disciplining the elites, and remaking the relationship between the governors and the governed. The project reached its fullest form in the consolidation of Putin’s first two terms, and it defined the political order of Russia for the era that followed. It stands, in the history of the post-Soviet state, as the deliberate and successful reversal of the centrifugal motion of the nineties — the rebuilding of the single chain of command that the collapse of the Soviet Union had broken.

concepts/vnenakhodimost.title: Vnenakhodimost
concepts/vnenakhodimost.content:
Vnenakhodimost
Вненаходимость — vnenakhodimost, “being-outside-ness” — is the term Alexei Yurchak gives to the singular position occupied by the last Soviet generation, the way of living at once within and without the field of the system’s authoritative discourse. It names a place that the familiar maps of late socialism cannot contain, because it belongs to neither side of the great binary that used to divide the Soviet world into rulers and ruled, official and unofficial, true believers and hidden dissenters. The Soviet person of the late years was neither a loyal subject nor a secret enemy, neither a conscious dissident nor an unconscious dupe; he stood, rather, in a relation to the whole that Yurchak describes as simultaneously inside and outside, a positioning that allowed him to reproduce the system’s forms faithfully while the meaning of those forms drifted far from anything the system intended.
Neither support nor opposition
The concept was not born of ideology but of practice, and Yurchak draws it from the philosophy of Mikhail Bakhtin, who used the word for the peculiar vantage that allows an author to stand beside his own creation. In the late Soviet everyday, this external-inside position became an entire way of life — a образ жизни (a way of life), the very title of Yurchak’s fourth chapter. It was a mode of being that did not take the system as an object of belief at all, whether for or against. The citizen who lived in vnenakhodimost did not pretend to believe in the ideology he repeated, for the distinction between a real belief and a pretended one had ceased to organize his speech. He neither supported the system nor opposed it. He simply stood a little apart from the whole question, inhabiting the forms of the authoritative discourse as one inhabits a well-worn house — without asking what the house means, without doubting it, occupying it as the given frame of an ordinary day.
Spaces of vnenakhodimost
This outward position could be found, Yurchak argues, wherever the fixed forms of the system were carried on but had been emptied of their constative force. It was lived in the воображаемый Запад (the imagined West) that took shape in Soviet everyday life through foreign goods, music and images — the plastic bag printed with the address of a New York laundromat, the smuggled vinyl of a Western rock band — a space of symbolic otherness that stood beside the official world without challenging it, because it did not even speak its language. It was lived in the “multi-coloured communism” of the late years, in which the young listened to King Crimson and Deep Purple and Pink Floyd, absorbing a foreign world that had nothing to do with the party’s claims and so neither confirmed nor contradicted them. It was lived in the irony of the Soviet anecdote and the stiob of the late-Soviet stage, forms that played with the authoritative discourse as a thing already dead, already an object of aesthetic handling rather than belief.
The engine of transformation
The deepest consequence of vnenakhodimost is that it was not a withdrawal from the system but a mode of its reproduction. Because the last Soviet generation reproduced the forms of the authoritative discourse faithfully without believing their content, it kept the outward shell of late socialism intact while the meaning inside the shell quietly transformed. The very act of living in vnenakhodimost thus changed the system from within — an internal shift that Yurchak takes as the central mechanism of the period. It explains the great paradox of the collapse: that a system perceived as eternal could fall, and that its fall was experienced not as a shocking rupture but almost as a natural transition. The people who had lived out vnenakhodimost were already prepared for the end, because they had long since ceased to inhabit the system’s meaning — they inhabited only its form, and when the form gave way, nothing of their inner life gave way with it. The system perished, Yurchak concludes, when it was no longer reproduced from within, and the generation that had so long stood inside and outside its field was the generation for whom that passage was easiest of all.

concepts/wirtschaftswunder.title: Das Wirtschaftswunder (The Economic Miracle)
concepts/wirtschaftswunder.content:
Das Wirtschaftswunder (The Economic Miracle)
To the world that looked on in the 1950s, the recovery of West Germany seemed almost a miracle — a nation that in 1945 had lain in ruins, its cities rubble, its currency worthless, its factories dismantled and a defeated population living on rations and black markets, was within a decade the most prosperous state in Europe. The Wirtschaftswunder, the “economic miracle,” was the name given to that astonishing recovery, and it became the founding legend of the Federal Republic: the proof that the new state worked, the reward of the free market, and the social foundation upon which Adenauer’s republic and the social market economy rested.
The ruins of 1945
The starting point was catastrophe. The Germany of 1945 had lost a war and been destroyed in the process: its great cities bombed flat, its industry in ruins or dismantled by the victors, millions of refugees and expellees flooding in from the East, and its currency so debased by the inflation and the price controls of the war and occupation that money had almost ceased to function. People traded by barter — cigarettes, coffee, and the goods of the black market — and lived on the ration and the relief of the occupying powers. The immediate years of occupation were a time of hunger and hopelessness, in which the Western zones seemed condemned to stagnation. It was precisely from these depths that the recovery would astonish the world.
The leap of 1948
The turning point was the Währungsreform (currency reform) of 20 June 1948, when the Western zones abandoned the worthless Reichsmark for the new Deutsche Mark. Almost in the same breath Ludwig Erhard, the director of the economy in the Bizone, freed prices and ended rationing against the wishes of the Allied authorities. The effect was immediate and dramatic. Shops that had stood empty for years filled overnight with goods that had been hoarded and hidden; production surged; and within months the visible signs of the recovery — the filled shop windows, the rebuilt workshops, the returning bustle of commerce — were everywhere. The sound currency, the freed market and the pent-up demand of a whole population combined into a growth that was to prove self-sustaining.
The boom of the 1950s
Through the 1950s the miracle compounded itself. West German industry, its equipment rebuilt and modernised, found an insatiable world market for its machinery, its chemicals, its cameras and above all its cars — the Volkswagen, exported across the world, became the emblem of German quality and the German recovery. The Cold War and the Korean War boom of the early 1950s fed the demand for German goods, while a large and disciplined labour force, swelled by refugees from the East, kept wages competitive and production rising. Growth rates of the kind that would later seem impossible were achieved year after year; unemployment, which stood in the millions at the start of the decade, fell away to what the age called full employment; and the Federal Republic overtook Britain to become the strongest economy in Western Europe.
Export-led growth and the consumer age
The miracle was export-led — German industry earned its prosperity by selling to the world — and it transformed the lives of ordinary Germans. The Konsumgesellschaft, the consumer society, arrived: the automobile in the garage, the holidays by the Mediterranean, the well-stocked kitchen, the television in the living room. Erhard promised that mass prosperity would dissolve the conflicts of the class society, and in the boom years it seemed to do so; the Wirtschaftswunder became the badge of a new West German identity, a prosperity that legitimised the state and bound its citizens to the West. The growth was not evenly felt — the first years were hard, and the refugees and the workers at the bottom waited longest — but the tide rose so strongly and so visibly that the miracle carried nearly everyone.
The legend and its meaning
The Wirtschaftswunder was more than an economic phenomenon; it was a political and cultural idea. It was claimed by Erhard and the CDU as the fruit of the social market economy, the reward of economic freedom, and the refutation of both the Nazi planned economy and the state socialism offered by the East — and the comparison with the sluggish economy of the German Democratic Republic became one of the great arguments for the West. The miracle gave the Federal Republic its self-confidence and its claim to be a success story in a century of German catastrophe. It rested, of course, on circumstance as much as on doctrine — the sound currency, the recovery of Europe, the labour of the East, the luck of the boom — but as a legend it endured. When the boom slowed in the 1960s and the economies of later chancellors from Helmut Schmidt to Helmut Kohl met harder times, the memory of the miracle remained the standard against which German prosperity, and German political legitimacy, were measured.

concepts/world-socialist-system.title: World Socialist System
concepts/world-socialist-system.content:
World Socialist System
The world socialist system — мировая система социализма (the world system of socialism) — was the community of socialist states that came into being in the years after the Second World War, when the peoples of eastern Europe and, in Asia, of China and beyond threw off the rule of the old order and set out to build socialism. For the Soviet party and its official historians the formation of this system was a great historical acquisition of the peoples, second in significance for the fate of humanity only to the October Revolution itself. The emergence of a second world, standing opposed to the capitalist system, had transformed the international relations of the globe.
The formation of the socialist community
The victorious conclusion of the Great Patriotic War freed the peoples of central and eastern Europe from fascist tyranny, and in the years that followed the peoples’ democratic revolutions carried them out of the capitalist system and onto the path of socialist construction. The victory of the peoples’ democratic forces — народная демократия (people’s democracy) — in Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia and the German Democratic Republic, and then in Asia, where the Chinese People’s Republic was proclaimed in 1949 and the Democratic Republic of Vietnam and the Korean People’s Democratic Republic took shape, created the conditions for a unified socialist world. In the account of Soviet diplomacy the formation of the world socialist system signified a fundamental turn in international relations: it changed the correlation of class and political forces in the world decisively in favour of socialism, and the socialist states began to exert an ever-growing influence on international development.
Comecon and the Warsaw Pact
The economic foundations of the socialist bloc were laid in 1949, when, at a conference in Moscow, the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance — Совет экономической взаимопомощи, the СЭВ (Comecon) — was formed. Its founding members were the USSR, Bulgaria, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Czechoslovakia; in the years that followed they were joined by Albania (which left in 1961), the German Democratic Republic, Cuba, Mongolia and Vietnam. The aim of the Council was the development of mutually advantageous and steadily deepening социалистическая экономическая интеграция (socialist economic integration) among the socialist countries; its decisions were taken collegially, and within it the Soviet Union continued to render great assistance to its socialist partners. The economic bloc of the East was completed by its military counterpart: only after the creation of NATO in 1949 did the Soviet Union make its answering step, and on 14 May 1955, with the participation of the east European states, the Organization of the Warsaw Treaty — Организация Варшавского договора (the Warsaw Pact) — was established as a defensive alliance of the socialist states.
The socialist community
The relations between the socialist countries, in the official conception, constituted a new type of international relations, conforming entirely to the nature of socialism. They rested on friendship and mutual assistance, on пролетарский интернационализм (proletarian internationalism), and they combined the interests of each country with those of the socialist commonwealth as a whole — the социалистическое содружество (socialist community). The friendship and mutual help between them, the official histories insisted, made possible the rapid and planful development of each economy and of the whole world economic system of socialism; the fraternal relations between the ruling communist and workers’ parties stood at the centre of this cooperation. The path was not without its difficulties — the schism with Yugoslavia after 1948, and later the national deviation that carried the leaderships of China and Albania into conflict with the other socialist states — but these were judged passing errors, subordinate to the essence of genuinely socialist relations.
In Western usage this community was more often called the “socialist camp” (соцлагерь, the social camp), a term the Soviet world itself adopted to describe the bloc at its height — a bloc of states bound together by ideology, economic integration, military alliance and the leadership of the cpsu and the Soviet Union. The leonid-brezhnev years saw the community’s consolidation as a political fact of the first order, the framework within which the Soviet Union pursued the Programme of Peace and the detente of the 1970s, and the collective organisation in whose name Moscow acted in the crises of the age. The world socialist system reached its widest extent in the 1970s; and it was dismantled in the space of a few years at the end of the 1980s, when Comecon and the Warsaw Treaty Organization were formally dissolved in 1991, and the second world, as a single system, ceased to exist.

entities/adolfo-suarez.title: Adolfo Suárez (1932–2014)
entities/adolfo-suarez.content:
Adolfo Suárez (1932–2014)
He was the most unlikely of architects. When the King appointed Adolfo Suárez president of the government in July 1976, the appointment was received with astonishment and contempt by the very reformers who had expected to be chosen — manuel-fraga and José María de Areilza, both better known and better placed, were left indignant and surprised by the elevation of a young provincial politician of the Movimiento. Yet it was precisely the obscurity and the régime provenance of Suárez that fitted him for the task. He was a man the franquista political class trusted, young enough to represent the future, and ambitious enough to risk it; and it was he, the creature of the régime, who set about dismantling it from within.
The choice of the king
His selection among the three young reformist ministers of the Arias government was a calculation of biography. Suárez carried a career wholly formed inside the institutions of francoism — a falangist youth, service in the official movement, the directorship of state television — and this very provenance was his credential. The Law for Political Reform had to pass through the régime’s own Cortes and the National Council, bodies of the old order, and no one identified with the democratic opposition could have persuaded them. Suárez, speaking the language and carrying the credentials of the franquista world, was the man most likely to secure franquista approval for a measure that would dissolve the system that had created him. Judgments on him, Tusell noted, have shifted sharply within a quarter-century; there are two Suárezes separated by the cardinal date of 1979. Mere origin and charm are not enough to explain the historical protagonist; it was the calculation of the King and of Torcuato Fernández Miranda, the president of the Cortes and of the Council of the Kingdom, that placed him where biography and opportunity met.
The political reform
His great work was the Law for Political Reform, drafted through the summer of 1976 by Fernández Miranda’s team and presented to the senior military commanders on 8 September. The law, offered as a reform de la ley a la ley (from the law to the law), provided for free elections to a constituent Cortes while appearing to respect the continuity of the régime’s legality — a paradox by which the old order was persuaded to vote itself out of existence. In the referendum of December 1976 the country approved the law by an overwhelming margin, and Suárez measured the two stages of the reform with an assurance that was his finest hour: first the passage of the law through the régime’s Cortes, then free elections for a constituent assembly. Between the referendum and the elections of June 1977 the process passed through weeks in which terrorism and military pressure could have aborted it; it was held together by the Spanish will for democratic coexistence and by the government’s careful timing, which deliberately delayed a harsh economic programme that might have derailed the political calendar.
The constituent elections and the UCD
In the general election of 15 June 1977 Suárez’s Union of the Democratic Centre (UCD), a coalition assembled hurriedly around the premier, emerged as the largest party in the new constituent Cortes, defeating the socialist left that had expected victory. Suárez became the first prime minister of the democracy and the presiding figure of the constituent process that produced the constitution-1978. His government shepherded the legalisation of the parties and the extraordinary settlement of the national question, and carried the consensus that made the constitution possible. It was a role without a clear rival: the unitary opposition organisms that had led the fight against Franco lost the initiative once Suárez reached the presidency, and the new party system configured itself around him.
The fall
The ruin was as rapid as the rise. His first error, Tusell judged, came already in the investiture debate after the 1979 elections, and his decline accelerated through 1980. From the summer of that year the polls placed the socialist felipe-gonzalez and the PSOE ahead, and Suárez’s own party began to disintegrate around him — the UCD, which had filtered the conflicts of the Transition within itself to spare the country open confrontation, could not contain the strain once its unifying purpose was spent. Personal and party exhaustion followed the constituent years; an acrimonious struggle developed within his own ranks. In January 1981 Suárez, weary and besieged, resigned both the premiership and the presidency of his party. His departure was the prelude to the great crisis of 23-f-coup-1981, and the UCD he had built collapsed altogether, disappearing in the election of psoe-victory-1982. A man who had played a transcendental role in the Transition ended his political life as the leader of a party that could not survive the passing of the circumstances that had called it into being.

entities/alcide-de-gasperi.title: Alcide De Gasperi (1881-1954)
entities/alcide-de-gasperi.content:
Alcide De Gasperi (1881-1954)
No single figure presided so completely over the birth of the Italian Republic as the Trentino statesman Alcide De Gasperi. A man formed in the Habsburg borderlands of the old Austro-Hungarian Empire, a Catholic politician who had served his apprenticeship in the underground years of fascism, he emerged after the war to lead the Democrazia Cristiana (Christian Democracy, the D.C.) and to govern Italy without interruption from the Liberation to 1953. He was the architect of the reconstruction, of the decisive anti-communist alliance of 1948, and of the anchoring of the new republic in the Atlantic and in the making of a united Europe — the role that was to earn him a place among the padri fondatori, the founding fathers of European integration.
From Trentino to the leadership of the D.C.
De Gasperi was born at Pieve Tesino in the Trentino, then part of the Austrian Empire, and entered politics as a deputy to the Viennese parliament before the First World War. After 1918 he was a member of the Partito Popolare (People’s Party), the Catholic political movement founded by Luigi Sturzo, and its secretary at the moment the fascist regime came to power. He refused the compromise that would have kept him inside the fascist system, was arrested in 1927, and spent the years of dictatorship in the shadowy survival of a Catholic politician deprived of open politics — a preparation that marked him with a deep distrust of ideological extremism and a devotion to measured, parliamentary government. With the fall of fascism in July 1943 and the resumption of political life, the Catholic party was reborn under a new name, the Democrazia Cristiana, and De Gasperi, returned to active politics, rose quickly to its leadership.
The premiership of the reconstruction
After the war De Gasperi became the central figure of the first governments of the democratic republic. From December 1945 he headed a succession of cabinets through the constituent phase and the first years of the Republic, prime minister almost without interruption from 1945 to 1953. It was a premiership that spanned the most perilous moment of Italian reconstruction: the formation of the Constituent Assembly and the referendum of 1946, the negotiation of the peace treaty that left Italy humiliated and diminished, the economic recovery from the devastation of war, and the mounting pressure of the Cold War as it arrived on Italian soil. De Gasperi’s governments carried the country from the ruin of 1945 through the choice of the republic, the writing of the Constitution, and the setting of Italy’s international course, when the country — caught between the blocs, with the largest communist party in the West — was obliged to choose its side.
The turn of 1947 and the election of 1948
The decisive moment came in 1947, when De Gasperi dismissed the communist and socialist ministers and reconstituted his government without them, ending the tripartismo of the postwar coalition. The rupture, driven by the deepening Cold War and the May 1947 expulsion of the communists from government in France, set the terms of Italian politics for decades. It was followed in April 1948 by the great electoral confrontation in which De Gasperi and the D.C. stood against the Fronte Democratico Popolare (Popular Democratic Front) of the communists and socialists. The election of 18 April 1948 delivered the Christian Democrats an absolute majority in the Chamber of Deputies, a landslide that fixed the republic’s orientation against the left and confirmed De Gasperi as the indispensable man of the centrist order. From that victory the centrismo — the D.C.-centred coalition of the centre parties — was built and sustained under his premiership.
Atlanticism and Europeanism
De Gasperi’s foreign policy set Italy firmly within the Western camp. He carried the country into the North Atlantic Treaty in 1949, an Atlanticism that followed from the same anti-communist necessity that had shaped the domestic coalition. Alongside it he pursued a European vocation that was both political and Catholic in inspiration: Italy was a founding member of the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) and of the treaties of Rome (1957) that created the Common Market. With Robert Schuman, Konrad Adenauer and others of his generation, De Gasperi belongs to that circle of postwar statesmen who, from the Catholic political tradition of the continent, built the first institutions of a united Europe — a Europeanism born of the ruins of the war and of the shared hostility to its divisions, and one rooted in the reconciliation of the old continental powers.
The limits of his premiership
The premiership came to an end in 1953, in the aftermath of the failure of the legge truffa (the “swindle law”), the majority-bonus electoral law that De Gasperi’s government had pressed through and then seen fail to deliver its intended majority in the elections of June 1953. The rejection deprived the D.C. of its certain majority and opened the difficult second legislature of the centrist decade. De Gasperi, who had held power so long, did not survive the setback long as leader; he died in 1954. He left behind the structure of the Italian Republic he had helped to found — the Christian Democratic hegemony, the Atlantic alignment, the European commitment — and a reputation, in the historiography of the reconstruction, as the moderate and Catholic statesman who, in the name of measured government, had carried Italy out of the war and the shadow of fascism into the democratic order of the West.

entities/aldo-moro.title: Aldo Moro (1916-1978)
entities/aldo-moro.content:
Aldo Moro (1916-1978)
No figure of the Italian Republic stands so completely at the centre of its two great projects and its darkest hour as Aldo Moro. A professor of law from Bari, a Catholic intellectual formed in the Federazione Universitaria Cattolica Italiana (the Catholic university federation) and the youth of the Democrazia Cristiana, Moro rose in the party as a man of the centre who believed the Catholic world must at last meet the modern democratic left. His life’s work was a series of openings — to the Socialists, to the Communist party, and finally to a Europe beyond the Cold War — each one an effort to give the Republic a majority broad enough to govern and stable enough to endure. It was the last of these openings, the compromesso storico (historic compromise) of the 1970s, that carried him to the Via Fani and the tragedy that came to mark, for the generation that lived through it, the funerale della Repubblica (funeral of the Republic).
The architect of the apertura a sinistra
Moro belonged to the generation of Christian Democrats who judged that the centrismo of the 1950s, for all its stability, had reached its limits — that a party of government committed to reform could no longer govern alone or with the small lay partners of the old four-party coalition. He became the principal architect of the apertura a sinistra (opening to the left), the patient and repeatedly deferred project of bringing the Socialist Party into government alongside the DC. As party secretary and as the mind behind the strategy, Moro argued that the Republic could not forever exclude a party that represented a large part of the working class, and that the Cold War’s veto on the left must be relaxed — at least to the point of the Socialists, who had broken with the Communists and accepted the Atlantic alliance.
In December 1963 Moro formed his first government, presiding over the fourth legislature, 1963–1968, as the centro-sinistra (centre-left) finally came to power. The governments he led through the mid-1960s carried the programme of the opening: the nationalisation of electricity, the beginnings of regional government, the reform of the school system and of pensions, and the first gestures toward a planning of the economy. Yet the coalition was never easy. The DC’s right distrusted the alliance with the Socialists, the lay parties resisted the DC’s dominance, and the very breadth of the majority Moro had built limited what it could do. The opening, Mammarella observed, was a political turning point more than a revolution of reform — a broadening of the governing base whose fruits were real but whose promise outran its delivery.
The years of the compromesso
The centre-left formula exhausted itself in the turmoil of the late 1960s and the 1970s, and Moro, who had been the architect of the first opening, became the architect of the second. In the climate of the anni di piombo (years of lead), with political violence on the right and the left and the Republic itself seemingly under assault, Moro turned toward the project of the compromesso storico — an understanding between the DC and the Partito Comunista Italiano to defend democracy. It was a strategy he pursued in his own key: less the ideological convergence proposed by the Communist secretary Enrico Berlinguer than a political necessity, the claim that in a time of emergency the two great popular parties must govern the country together, or at least agree on its defence. When the elections of 20 June 1976 brought the Communists to within a few points of the DC, Moro and Berlinguer negotiated the solidarietà nazionale (national solidarity), the arrangement by which the PCI sustained the government from outside.
Through 1977 and into 1978 Moro was working to consolidate this new majority — to give the Communist participation a stable institutional form. It was in the midst of that labour, on the very eve of the vote that would have brought the PCI into a government headed by his long-time colleague Giulio Andreotti, that Moro was seized by the Red Brigades.
The kidnapping and death
On the morning of 16 March 1978, in Via Fani in Rome, the Brigate Rosse (Red Brigades) ambushed Moro’s escort and carried him off, murdering his five bodyguards. He was held prisoner for fifty-four days in a “people’s prison,” while the state, led by the man who would have been his ally in the government of national solidarity, refused to negotiate. The linea della fermezza (hard line) held that the Republic could not bargain with terrorists. Moro’s letters from captivity, in which he argued for his own release and appealed to the DC, were published by his captors and threw the country into a crisis of conscience; his plea for a negotiated solution, for his life, was set against the principle that the state must not yield.
On 9 May 1978 his body was found in the boot of a red Renault in Via Caetani, in Rome, halfway between the headquarters of the DC and that of the PCI. The two parties he had laboured to bring together were joined, in that moment, by his death. For Gentiloni Silveri the murder was not merely a crime but the supreme wound of the Republic — an act that came to be called the funerale della Repubblica, the funeral of the Republic, because the old order of parties and the old certainties of the Cold War never fully recovered from it. Moro’s name remained a shadow over Italian politics, a reference point for every subsequent reflection on the state and the democracy he had given his life to widen.

entities/alexei-kosygin.title: Alexei Kosygin (1904-1980)
entities/alexei-kosygin.content:
Alexei Kosygin (1904-1980)
For sixteen years Alexei Kosygin governed the Soviet economy while others governed the party. As Chairman of the Council of Ministers (Председатель Совета Министров), the prime minister of the USSR from 1964 to 1980, he stood at the head of the government as leonid-brezhnev rose to dominate the party. He was, in the words of the official party history, one of those leading figures who had resisted the anti-party group of 1957 alongside Brezhnev and the others — a seasoned administrator of the Soviet system, remembered above all for the reform that carries his name, the Kosygin reforms of 1965.
His long service ran back through the war itself. It was Kosygin who had served as deputy chairman of the evacuation council in the terrible summer of 1941, when the Soviet state moved its industry and its people eastward out of the reach of the German armies; under his hand, in the account of the party historians, more than ten million people and over 1,360 large enterprises were evacuated between July and November of that year. He was a man of industry and supply, of figures and tonnage, formed in the ministerial machinery of the Stalinist state. In 1946 he took his place as a deputy chairman of the Council of Ministers under Stalin, and in the decades that followed he remained a constant presence at the summit of Soviet government while the First Secretaries changed around him.
The October 1964 Plenum and the two-headed leadership
When nikita-khrushchev was removed in October 1964, charged with волюнтаризм и субъективизм (voluntarism and subjectivism), the Plenum of the Central Committee chose to separate the two supreme offices that Khrushchev had united in his own hands. Brezhnev became First Secretary — from 1966 General Secretary — of the party, while Kosygin was appointed Chairman of the Council of Ministers. The division was deliberate, a restoration of what the party called the ленинские нормы партийной жизни (Leninist norms of party life), an end to the concentration of the party leadership and the head of government in a single person. For a time it produced a genuine partnership: the party under Brezhnev, the government and the economy under Kosygin. It was the moment of the Soviet Union’s collective leadership, and Kosygin was its economic face.
The Kosygin reforms of 1965
Kosygin’s name was fixed to the economic reforms of 1965, which sought to raise the efficiency of the planned economy by giving the enterprise a measure of independence. The agrarian reform of that year raised the procurement prices paid to the farms, fixed the state procurement plan for ten years, and paid a 50 per cent premium for above-plan sales. The industrial reform, adopted at the September 1965 Plenum, was the more ambitious undertaking: it sought to reduce the number of directives descending from above, to place the enterprise on хозрасчёт (khozraschyot, economic accountability, the principle that an enterprise must cover its own costs), and to make profit and sales, rather than sheer gross output, the measure of success. The party historians of the 1980s described the aim as the перестройка хозяйственного механизма (restructuring of the economic mechanism) and the линия на интенсификацию производства (line toward the intensification of production) — the hope of making the planned economy work better by relaxing its grip from the centre.
The reform was real, and for a time it appeared to work. The eighth five-year plan (1966-1970), the plan that ran alongside it, was the most successful of the late Soviet period, and the national income rose to nearly 290 billion rubles by 1970. But the reform carried within it a contradiction. The party state could not permit the autonomy it had promised; the central planners, the ministries, and the party itself were reluctant to give up their powers, and the reform was gradually wound down rather than carried through. By the later years of Kosygin’s premiership the line on intensification had slowed, the plan discipline that the reform had loosened was being reasserted, and the совершенствование планирования (improvement of planning) that the congresses still called for was admitted to be proceeding медленнее, чем намечалось (more slowly than planned). The reform had shown that the command economy could be questioned from within; it had not shown that it could be remade.
The limits of the partnership
Kosygin’s authority, like his reform, faded as Brezhnev’s consolidated. The two-headed leadership of 1964 gave way through the 1970s to the unmistakable ascendancy of the General Secretary, whose name attached itself to the foreign policy — the Программа мира (Programme of Peace) proclaimed at the XXIV Congress was Brezhnev’s, delivered in the Central Committee’s report, while the разрядка (détente) that followed was pursued by the party leadership as a whole. Kosygin’s own diplomacy was not insignificant — his visits to France, where in December 1966 the joint Soviet-French statement acknowledged that разрядка напряженности (the easing of tension) was the first necessary stage in the development of relations between European states — but the great initiatives of the era were increasingly the General Secretary’s. By 1980, ill and eclipsed, Kosygin was relieved of the premiership. He died that December, the administrator of the Soviet economy who had governed longest and reformed most, whose name marked both the high point of the planned economy’s self-confidence and the demonstration of how hard it was, from within, to change.

entities/andrei-gromyko.title: Andrei Gromyko (1909–1989)
entities/andrei-gromyko.content:
Andrei Gromyko
Андрей Андреевич Громыко (Andrei Andreevich Gromyko, 1909–1989) was the Soviet foreign minister for nearly three decades, from 1957 to 1985, and the enduring face of Soviet diplomacy through the whole arc of the Cold War — the man Western diplomats called Mister Nyet for the stubbornness with which he defended Soviet positions. He is also, in this corpus, one of the two editors (with Б. Н. Пономарев) of the official История внешней политики СССР that documents the Soviet view of that diplomacy from the postwar settlement to 1980.
The long tenure
Gromyko rose through the diplomatic service under Stalin and held the ambassadorship in Washington during the war, then served as deputy foreign minister before taking the foreign ministry itself in 1957. From khrushchev-secret-speech-1956 through the cuban-missile-crisis-1962, the prague-spring-1968, the SALT talks and the detente of the 1970s, he was the constant figure at the Soviet side of the East–West table. In the leadership after the fall of Khrushchev he anchored the conservative continuity of the state, and under Brezhnev he personified the immobility of the late period: patient, immovable, and in command of every file. In 1985 Gorbachev, marking the new course, set him aside as foreign minister in favour of Eduard Shevardnadze; Gromyko moved to the largely ceremonial chairmanship of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet until his retirement in 1988.
The historian’s chair
Within this knowledge base Gromyko matters as well for the official history that bears his name. The История внешней политики СССР he edited with Ponomarev is the authoritative Soviet account of the postwar settlement, the German question, the Korean and Indochinese wars, disarmament, decolonisation and détente — the lens through which the Soviet state read its own policy. His figure thus connects the personal history of Soviet diplomacy with the documentary record that this wiki draws upon.

entities/bettino-craxi.title: Bettino Craxi (1934-2000)
entities/bettino-craxi.content:
Bettino Craxi (1934-2000)
The man who broke the long custom of the Italian Republic was a Milanese socialist who rose through the party of Nenni and then bent it entirely to his own ambition. Bettino Craxi took the secretariat of the Partito socialista italiano (the Italian Socialist Party, the PSI) in 1976, at a moment when the party seemed condemned to the margins, and he turned it into the pivot of the governing coalition — winning at last, in August 1983, the prime ministership that no socialist had ever held. His was the longest single tenure at Palazzo Chigi in the history of the Republic, a run of years that his admirers called craxismo and his critics denounced as a presidential drift toward personal rule. A decade later the same man, accused in the great corruption inquests, fled into self-imposed exile in Tunisia, and died there, unrepentant, in the year 2000.
The reconstruction of the PSI
Craxi’s project was to release the socialists from the shadow of the Partito comunista and to make his own party the decisive force at the centre of the political system. For decades the PSI had wavered between the alliance with the communists and the governing collaboration with the Democrazia cristiana. Craxi chose the latter road with ruthless clarity, and the party’s long climb began in earnest in the 1970s and 1980s, fed by a growing suffrage that carried it steadily upward through the middle years of the decade. By the early eighties the socialists had recovered their strength, and the crippling rivalry between Craxi and the Christian Democratic leader became the central drama of Italian politics — the two giants of the pentapartito (the five-party governing coalition) locked in a duel that, as the years wore on, gave the whole system the air of a war of attrition.
Il primo socialista a Palazzo Chigi
The elections of June 1983 delivered the decisive blow to the relative-majority party. Humiliated, the Democrazia cristiana was forced to surrender the presidency of the Council for the first time, and the task of forming a government fell to Craxi. For the socialist leader and his party it was a historic goal — the first government under socialist direction in the history of Italy. Yet the manner of its coming, not through a great electoral victory but through the defeat of the majority party, sharply reduced the weight of the new premier and his room for manoeuvre. He reconstituted the pentapartito coalition, with two sitting party secretaries in the cabinet, and he was immediately squeezed between a Partito repubblicano that considered itself the true victor and a Democrazia cristiana loath to accept even the loss of the presidency. The greatest danger, however, came from the communist opposition, which saw in Craxi not merely a formidable electoral rival but a man bent on changing the rules of the political game — through institutional reform and a new method of government designed to relegate the PCI to a role of pure opposition. The communists went so far as to accuse him of preparing an authoritarian turn.
His programme was hemmed in from the start by a disastrous financial situation. The state deficit, which had stood at 80,000 billion lire in 1982, threatened to pass 100,000 billion, eighteen per cent of GDP, in 1984, and Craxi made the containment of public spending his first priority — a pledge to hold the deficit within 80,000 and then 90,000 billion lire through cuts and new levies, with the aim of reducing inflation to ten per cent. In the autumn of 1983 he announced a package of measures, mixing cuts to health, defence and family allowances with new taxation and a much-criticised condone for illegal building, that was meant to reduce the state’s financial requirement by more than 40,000 billion lire. The condone was blocked by the so-called franchi tiratori (the snipers) of his own majority, an early sign of the frailty of his coalition.
Decisiveness and personal government
What set the Craxi years apart was a readiness to act where his predecessors had hesitated. He drove the containment of the deficit, brought a new decisiveness to the offensive against organised crime, and pursued a foreign policy of unaccustomed dynamism — standing with the European partners against the American landing in Grenada, pressing the long-stalled negotiations on the British contribution to the Common Market, and presiding over the installation of the cruise missiles at Comiso despite the opposition of the peace movement. He completed in 1984 the long-gestating revision of the Concordat with the Church, abolishing the principle of Catholicism as the official religion of the state and ending the confessional order. His manner of governing, by direct confrontation and personal command, delighted his supporters and alarmed his opponents, who saw in the concentration of power in one man the erosion of the collective leadership of the parties.
The great reformist pretensions and the collapse
The later Craxi years were marked by pretensions that never quite became programmes. He spoke of a great reform of the institutions and of the rules of the game, of a grande riforma that would carry Italy beyond the immobilism of the old parties, yet the results lagged far behind the rhetoric. The Duelli senza vincitore, the duels without a winner that Gentiloni Silveri discerns in the decade, left the country politically paralysed even as the public debt mounted and the machinery of the state groaned. Meanwhile the very system Craxi had mastered was sustained, as the investigations would later reveal, by a diffuse and long-tolerated corruption — the funding of the parties through bribes and kickbacks that would come to be known as tangentopoli. When the magistrates of Milan struck, the PSI, and above all its leader, stood at the centre of the storm.
In February 1993, after seventeen years of unchallenged power at the head of the party, Craxi abandoned the secretariat of the PSI, struck by successive avvisi di garanzia from several prosecutions and accused of corruption and of violating the law on the public financing of parties. He had tried to dismiss the whole affair as the work of a single delinquent — the mariuolo, the petty rogue, as he called Mario Chiesa — and to distinguish those who enriched themselves individually from those who had merely financed their party in a system where the cost of politics had never been regulated by law. The distinction found few takers in a country hungry for a reckoning. The Chamber of Deputies refused in April 1993 to authorise proceedings against him, a decision that appeared to many a last desperate defence of privileges the palace could no longer defend. Pursued by the inquests, Craxi withdrew to his refuge in Hammamet in Tunisia rather than face the courts. He died there in January 2000, defiant to the last, leaving behind a movement that had crumbled to 2.2 per cent of the vote and a verdict on his career that the historians of the Second Republic still debate.

entities/boris-yeltsin.title: Boris Yeltsin (1931-2007)
entities/boris-yeltsin.content:
Boris Yeltsin (1931-2007)
The man who was to bring down the Soviet Union first rose to prominence inside it. Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin, born in 1931 in the Ural region, was a construction engineer and party organiser of the Sverdlovsk oblast who was brought to Moscow by the reforming leadership of the mid-1980s as one of the new men. He became First Secretary of the Moscow city committee of the party, a full member of the Politburo, and for a time the very emblem of the fresh, blunt, energetic official that mikhail-gorbachev claimed to be promoting. Yet his impatience was greater than his patron’s. His public criticism of the slowness of the reform, and of the privileges of the party elite, made him an outcast within the leadership, stripped of his Moscow post and his Politburo seat in 1987 — and, in his fall, the darling of a public that had begun to tire of the party altogether. From that expulsion his whole later career unfolded, as the rebel against the system became the man who would stand against the system’s last leader and preside over its end.
The return as the Russian leader
The political earthquake of 1989–1990 delivered Yeltsin his platform. Elected to the new Congress of People’s Deputies of the USSR in 1989, and then, in a stunning result, to the Congress of People’s Deputies of the RSFSR in 1990, he was elected Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the Russian Federation in May 1990. Pikhoya, who as chief state archivist lived through the making of these documents, traces the rise of what he calls the “Russian factor” — the appearance of the RSFSR, the largest republic, as a political actor in its own right against the Union centre. Under Yeltsin’s chairmanship the Russian Congress adopted the Declaration of State Sovereignty of Russia on 12 June 1990, asserting the primacy of Russian law over Union law; the ensuing война законов (voyna zakonov, ‘war of laws’) between Moscow and the Kremlin of the USSR paralysed the centre; the foundation of the Communist Party of the RSFSR, a Russian party distinct from the CPSU, divided the communists themselves. Yeltsin pushed the radical “500 Days” programme for the transition to a market economy, which Gorbachev first welcomed and then abandoned. Through 1991 the Russian President’s authority grew as the Union’s shrank — and the centre, watching the secession of the republics it could no longer control, began to see in him the gravest threat to its survival.
The stand against the putsch
The summer of 1991 brought the confrontation to its crisis. On 12 June 1991, in the first direct popular election in Russian history, Yeltsin was elected President of the RSFSR, a legitimacy no Soviet leader possessed. When the hardliners of the ГКЧП (GKChP, the State Committee for the State of Emergency) seized power on 19 August 1991 and held Gorbachev at Foros, Yeltsin became the visible centre of resistance. From a tank outside the White House, the seat of the Russian parliament, he called on the people of Moscow and of Russia to defy the coup; barricades rose around the building; and in three days the putsch collapsed before a resistance that had rallied around the Russian flag. Pikhoya’s account of those days — Foros, the Kremlin, the White House, the tragedy in the tunnel of Kalinin Prospekt — records how the failure of the coup destroyed the Union’s organs of power and the CPSU itself, and how the authority that survived belonged to the Russian President. It was Yeltsin who took the leadership of the country in the autumn of 1991, suspended the Communist Party, and set in motion the reconstruction of the Russian state.
The end of the USSR and the new Russia
With the Union beyond saving, Yeltsin completed its dissolution. On 8 December 1991 he met the leaders of Ukraine and Belarus in the forest of Belovezhskaya Pushcha and signed the accords declaring the Soviet Union at an end and establishing the Commonwealth of Independent States. On 25 December, with Gorbachev’s resignation and the lowering of the red flag, the USSR ceased to exist, and Yeltsin became President of the Russian Federation. The new Russia he inherited was broken and friendless — the economy in collapse, the Soviet system of supply disintegrating, the old order’s certainties gone. He drove the country into the market, freeing prices and opening privatisation, reforms whose cost in popular suffering was enormous and whose authors he would both justify and blame. His presidency of the 1990s, the Russia that Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook treats as the hard road of the post-Soviet decade, was a decade of constitutional crisis — the confrontation with the Supreme Soviet that ended in the shelling of the White House in October 1993 — of war in Chechnya, of the financial default of 1998, and of the ruinous exhaustion of the population. Pikhoya calls the late years “tired Russia”. In the last hours of 1999, with his health and his popularity gone, Yeltsin resigned and handed the presidency to vladimir-putin, the man he had chosen as his heir. He left behind a Russia that had been remade in his image — sovereign, independent, and free of the Soviet past, at the price of an enormous and unresolved national reckoning.
