entities/carlos-arias-navarro.title: Carlos Arias Navarro (1908-1989)
entities/carlos-arias-navarro.content:
Carlos Arias Navarro (1908-1989)
Carlos Arias Navarro was the last president of the franquista governments, the man who presided over the régime’s final year and the first months of the succession, and the last to embody the spirit of the Movimiento in office. He came to the head of the government in the twilight of Franco’s life, the product not of any programme of reform but of the definitive rise of the family circle around the dying dictator; and his tenure, first as president under Franco and then briefly as the first president of the new monarchy, has become the type of the reformism that could not be carried out — what Tusell calls the reformismo imposible (the impossible reformism).
The spirit of the Movement
Arias Navarro was a lawyer of the régime, a man formed in the apparatus of the Franco state rather than in the armed struggle of the Civil War generation. His name was bound to the hard interior ministry of the 1950s, when he served as director-general of security during the years of the dictatorship’s greatest repression, before the reassessment of his career took him through the municipal government of Madrid and eventually, in 1965, to the Ministry of the Interior. He stood for a certain reading of franquismo — the reading that held that the Movimiento, the single political movement that gathered the families of the régime, was not to be dismantled but to be prolonged, that the institutions Franco had built were to outlast their founder. When the appointment came at the end of 1973 and the beginning of 1974, after the assassination of Admiral Carrero Blanco, Arias was chosen precisely because he represented continuity, the immovable core of the régime, at the moment when its head was visibly dying.
The last franquista government
The almost only continuity between Carrero’s government and the government of Arias Navarro was Franco’s irremediable physical decline. The appointment of Arias was testimony to the definitive rise of the family circle in régime politics — the circle of Nieto Antúnez and Arias himself, in which Carrero had never had much standing. The new cabinet was gestated without consulting the prince Juan Carlos, a sign of how far the change put the succession itself in doubt. Inside the government the tendencies pulled in different directions: the minister of information, a reformist current gathered around the idea of an apertura that might open the régime cautiously toward the future, confronted the hard core of the búnker, the immovables who would concede nothing. Arias governed in the shadow of both, a man of the old order asked to manage the end of the order itself. The programme he announced — a limited, guarded liberalisation, freedom of association within the strict bounds of the Movimiento — satisfied no one: too little for the reformers, who saw in it no real transformation, and already too much for the búnker, which saw the beginnings of the end.
Continuity at Franco’s death
When Franco died in November 1975, the king Juan Carlos confirmed Arias Navarro at the head of the government — a choice of continuity, of reassurance to the régime’s supporters that the succession would not turn overnight into a rupture. The new monarchy thus began under a president who was the living emblem of the old order. But the task required of a president in those first months was not continuity but change: the establishment of the king’s supreme responsibility and the opening of a road toward a democratic order. Arias’s reformism proved impossible from its origins. He was not the man to carry the transformation, and the régime he embodied was not the vehicle for it. The government became what one contemporary called a “colchón” (mattress or cushion) between two periods — the cushion on which the transition could be arranged before it was set aside.
The failure to reform
The crisis of the “semestre Arias” — the Arias semester — exposed the incoherence of the government and the limitations of its president. Public-order conflicts, the economic crisis and the wave of strikes of early 1976, above all in Madrid, overwhelmed a government that could neither govern in the old manner nor embrace the new. Political demands alone could not mobilise mass protest, yet the sense of release among organised workers extended the conflictivity across the country. The king, needing to establish that the supreme responsibility lay with the monarchy and not with the continuismo of the franquista presidency, secured Arias’s resignation in the summer of 1976. His substitution was engineered through the control of the Council of the Kingdom by Torcuato Fernández Miranda, who presented the tern of candidates — Silva Muñoz, Adolfo Suárez and López de Letona — from which Suárez was chosen. Arias Navarro thus left the stage at the very moment when the transition that he had failed to begin, and that his own government had for a season cushioned, was about to become reality. He remains in the history of the period as the last franquista president, the man of the Movimiento whose impossibility to reform was, in the end, the measure of the régime he served.

entities/charles-de-gaulle.title: Charles de Gaulle (1890–1970)
entities/charles-de-gaulle.content:
Charles de Gaulle (1890–1970)
The long shadow that fell across the whole of postwar France was cast by the man who had summoned the nation to resistance from London on 18 June 1940. Charles de Gaulle, the soldier of the armoured division who had led the Free French, entered the Liberation as the undisputed head of the provisional government — and then, at the moment of his apparent triumph, chose to abandon power. His departure on 20 January 1946, a sudden resignation from the head of the GPRF, was not the retirement of a defeated man. It was the opening of a patient wait, a traversée du désert (crossing of the desert), from which he would return twelve years later to remake the French state in his own image.
The withdrawal and the Bayeux declaration
De Gaulle had presided over the Liberation and the reconstruction of the republic from the ruins of Vichy, but he found himself increasingly at odds with the parties that dominated the Constituent Assemblies — the communists, the socialists and the MRP. He left office in January 1946, resentful of a régime he judged delivered over to what he called the régime des partis, the rule of the parties. From his retreat at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises he did not fall silent. On 12 May 1946 he spoke on the tomb of Clemenceau, and on 16 June he delivered at Bayeux, the first town liberated in 1944, the great statement of his constitutional doctrine — a head of state standing above the parties, a strong executive, and a separation of powers that the Fourth Republic’s draft constitution conspicuously lacked. He campaigned openly against the successive drafts, denouncing them in declarations of 27 August, 19 September, 9 October and 1 November 1946, and at Épinal on 29 September, until the constitution was adopted over his objections in October.
The Rassemblement du peuple français
His answer to the Fourth Republic was a movement of his own. At Bruneval on 30 March 1947 he launched the Rassemblement du peuple français (Rally of the French People, the R.P.F.), a gathering meant to transcend the parties and rally the nation to his programme of a strong state, national grandeur and social reconciliation. The years 1947 to 1953 saw the General on the road — Strasbourg, Bordeaux, Lille, Rennes, Lyon, Vincennes, Algiers, Marseille, Nevers, Verdun — and before the press at the Maison de la Résistance and the Palais d’Orsay. The R.P.F. swept the municipal elections of 1947 and stood at the height of its strength, a great rassemblement (rally) poised at the edge of power. Yet it never commanded a majority, and the party system the movement had sworn to break proved more resilient. After the decision of 1953 to suspend the R.P.F.’s active electoral politics, the movement faded, and de Gaulle entered the years of silence.
La traversée du désert
From 1954 the General withdrew once more, speaking only rarely — the great press conference of 30 June 1955 at the hôtel Continental, the allocution at Cerdon in 1956 before the monument to the maquis of the Ain, the address at Saint-Cyr-Coëtquidan to the officer cadets. It was a traversée du désert in earnest, a decade of waiting through the collapse of French power in Indochina, the beginnings of the Algerian war, and the ministerial instability of the Fourth Republic that he had always predicted. The communiqué of 12 September 1957 on the framework law for Algeria closed this period on the very eve of his return.
The return of 1958
The Algerian crisis, which had broken the parties that could neither win the war nor end it, brought him back. When the army and the settlers of Algiers rose on 13 May 1958, and the Fourth Republic staggered toward collapse, de Gaulle was called to the Palais d’Orsay, invested by the National Assembly in June, and entrusted with full powers to draft a new constitution. He returned as the arbiter above the parties he had always claimed to be. In September 1958 he carried the new constitution to the country in a referendum — the discours from the place de la République in Paris, and the journey to Madagascar, Dakar and Constantine with its programme of development for Algeria. On 21 December 1958 the college of grands électeurs elected him President of the Republic; he was installed at the Élysée on 8 January 1959 with Michel Debré as his Prime Minister.
The Fifth Republic and the Algerian settlement
As President he set about ending the war he had inherited and remaking France’s position in the world. The self-determination offer of September 1959, the semaine des barricades of January 1960, the generals’ putsch of April 1961, the Évian negotiations — through all of it de Gaulle drove a policy that would at last settle the Algerian question, confirmed by the referendum of 8 April 1962. Against the empire he had once defended he set decolonisation, granting independence to the states of the Community as they asked it. And in the autumn of 1962 he altered the institutions themselves, carrying by referendum the election of the President by universal suffrage, the change that completed the Fifth Republic he had conceived at Bayeux.
The policy of national independence
His foreign policy was a doctrine of indépendance nationale (national independence). France, he insisted, must be itself — a great nation that took its own decisions. He vetoed Britain’s entry into the Common Market in January 1963 and signed the treaty of friendship with Germany; he pursued a Europe européenne, a Europe of states rather than an Atlantic vassal. In 1966 France withdrew from the integrated command of NATO, and in June of that year de Gaulle travelled to Moscow in the grandest of the great visits that marked his second term. He spoke for a Europe from the Atlantic to the Urals, and of a France that played its part between the two blocs rather than inside one of them. Re-elected against François Mitterrand in December 1965, he pursued the effort of industrial and social modernisation at home while carrying the voice of France to Latin America, to the East, and to the French of Quebec.
May 1968 and the resignation
The upheaval of May 1968 struck the foundations of the regime. The greatest general strike of the century and the revolt of the students brought the General, for a moment, to the edge of disappearance — on 29 May he was briefly and famously absent from Paris. He returned to dissolve the Assembly, appeal to the nation, and win the June elections in an unqualified victory. But the crisis had aged the regime, and de Gaulle chose to stake his authority on a referendum on the reform of the Senate and regionalisation. On 27 April 1969 the country answered Non. On 28 April he resigned — the last text of the five tomes of his Discours et messages — and retired to Colombey, where he died in November 1970. He left behind a republic built to his measure, and a political tradition, gaullisme, that was to shape France long after the General himself had withdrawn to the silence from which he had twice returned.

entities/cpsu.title: Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU)
entities/cpsu.content:
Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU)
At the heart of the Soviet system stood a single institution: the Kommunisticheskaya partiya Sovetskogo Soyuza (the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, the CPSU). It was, by its own account and in its own legal definition, the leading and guiding force of Soviet society, the avangard (vanguard) of the working class and of the whole people. The party claimed the direction of every sphere of national life — the economy, the state, the armed forces, the unions, the Komsomol, culture and ideology — and the brief history of the postwar Soviet Union is inseparable from the history of its congresses and its leadership. From the XIX Congress of 1952, which gave the party its modern name, to the great congresses of the developed-socialism era, the CPSU was the nervous system of the country.
Structure and leading role
The organisation of the party rested on the principle of democratic centralism — demokraticheskii tsentralizm — elected bodies from the primary organisations, the pervichnye organizatsii of factories, farms and institutions, upward to the congresses, while the decisions of the higher organs bound all below. Between the congresses supreme authority resided in the Central Committee, the Tsentralnyi Komitet (the CC), whose plenary sessions — plenumy — in turn elected the directing organs: the Politburo (reconstituted as the Presidium of the Central Committee after the XIX Congress, and again as the Politburo in 1966) and the Secretariat under the General Secretary. From 1953 to 1964 that post was held by Nikita Khrushchev; from 1964 by Leonid Brezhnev. Within the party lay the whole career of the country’s elite, the nomenklatura of appointed posts through which the leadership bound together party and state. Its strength grew without interruption: from over five and a half million members in 1946 to more than seventeen million communists by the beginning of 1981, drawn from the working class, the collective-farm peasantry and the intelligentsia.
The XIX Congress and the renaming
The XIX Congress, held in Moscow from 5 to 14 October 1952, was the first to meet after the victory in the Great Patriotic War, and the first since the establishment of the people’s democracies and the world socialist system. It gathered 1,359 delegates representing nearly 6.9 million communists, with the delegations of the communist and workers’ parties of the socialist countries present as guests. The congress heard the report of the Central Committee delivered by Georgy Malenkov, adopted the directives for the fifth five-year plan of 1951–1955 and a new Party Statute, and decided on the change of name: the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks), the VKP(b), became the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. It was this congress that reconstituted the Politburo as the Presidium, a reorganisation whose full import was only realised after Stalin’s death the following March.
The XX Congress and de-Stalinisation
The XX Congress of February 1956 marked a watershed. Convened amid the struggle for the succession after Stalin’s death, it heard Khrushchev’s secret report on the cult of the personality and set the party on the course of restoring what it called the Leninist norms of party and state life — leninskiye normy partiynoy i gosudarstvennoy zhizni. The Congress advanced the theory of peaceful coexistence and of the many forms of transition of different countries to socialism, while in internal affairs it opened the campaign to overcome the cult of the personality and its consequences. The July 1953 Plenum had already condemned the violations of Leninist norms and insisted on the collectivity of leadership as the highest principle of the party; the XX Congress carried that programme forward, tied the blame for the repressions to Stalin, Beria and Yezhov, and set in motion the rehabilitation of victims of the 1930s. The shock of the revelations reached far beyond the party’s own ranks, unsettling the communist movement abroad and provoking the first alienation of the Chinese and North Korean parties from Moscow.
The XXII Congress and the third Programme
The XXII Congress of October 1961, meeting in the new Palace of Congresses in the Kremlin, was the largest yet — more than 5,200 delegates representing 9.7 million members, with delegations from eighty foreign Marxist-Leninist parties. It adopted the third Programme of the CPSU, which declared that the country had entered the period of the full-scale building of communism, razvyortnutoye stroitelstvo kommunizma, and set the construction of the communist society for 1980. The Programme and the Congresses of the decade fixed the party’s claim to lead the advance of the world socialist system and to determine the main direction of world development.
The congresses of developed socialism
With the fall of Khrushchev in 1964 and the election of Leonid Brezhnev, the party entered the period of “developed socialism” — razvitoy sotsializm. The XXIII Congress (1966) restored the title of General Secretary and the name of the Politburo; the XXIV (1971) adopted the Peace Programme in foreign policy and oversaw the opening of the era of détente; the XXV (1976) approved a further programme for peace and international cooperation; and the XXVI Congress of 1981, gathering the party at its full strength of seventeen million members, consolidated in the Constitution of 1977 the principle of the party’s leading role and set the course of the early 1980s. The party that had carried the country through revolution, war and reconstruction presented itself, at the summit of its power, as the political vanguard of the whole Soviet people — the institution around which the entire history of the USSR, and of the Cold War, was organised.

entities/erich-honecker.title: Erich Honecker (1912-1994)
entities/erich-honecker.content:
Erich Honecker (1912-1994)
The man who succeeded Walter Ulbricht was, by upbringing and instinct, the very model of the party soldier. Erich Honecker was born in 1912 in the Saarland, the son of a coal-miner and an old communist, and entered the movement as a boy; in the years of the Third Reich he worked illegally for the party and was imprisoned for a decade in the penitentiaries of Brandenburg-Görden, a credential that gave him an unshakeable standing in the republic of the antifascists. Released in 1945, he rose through the youth organization of the Soviet zone, the Free German Youth, and into the upper ranks of the Socialist Unity Party, until in 1958 he entered the Politburo as the party’s secretary for security and the army. For a decade he stood at Ulbricht’s right hand as the guardian of the apparatus, the discreet and loyal executor of the system’s discipline — until 1971, when he was raised to supplant his own patron and carry the German Democratic Republic through the last two decades of its existence.
The succession
The change of leadership came on 3 May 1971, when the Central Committee deposed Ulbricht and chose Honecker as General Secretary of the party. Weber places the event in the context of a wider Anpassung an die UdSSR, an adaptation of the GDR to the Soviet Union: the replacement of the aging, self-glorifying Ulbricht, whose independence had grown inconvenient to Moscow, opened the way to a closer alignment of the East German state with the USSR. The paradox, as Weber stresses, was that this very subordination was what made the new course possible at all. Honecker, less brilliant than Ulbricht but more pliant, carried through the adjustment that permitted the Federal Republic’s Ostpolitik to bear fruit — the intra-German treaties and the Grundlagenvertrag of 1972, by which the two German states recognized one another within the framework of Willy Brandt’s new Eastern policy. For the first time the GDR was acknowledged as a state, and Honecker could claim the diplomatic recognition that Ulbricht had never won.
Einheit von Wirtschafts- und Sozialpolitik
Honecker gave his programme a watchword that was to define his long tenure: the Einheit von Wirtschafts- und Sozialpolitik, the unity of economic and social policy. Reversing some of Ulbricht’s more austere experiments, he set out to bind the loyalty of the population by raising consumption — building housing, subsidizing prices, expanding welfare — on the assumption that the socialist economy could be made to deliver the standard of living that East Germans would otherwise seek in the West. The policy answered a genuine need of the regime: with the border sealed since the building of the Wall, the state had to govern without the safety-valve of emigration, and so it sought to buy the acquiescence of its citizens with material comfort. For a time the strategy worked, and the early and mid-seventies were the most confident years of the republic, as Honecker pursued his “unity” of promise and provision at home and the party’s absolute commitment to the Soviet Union abroad.
Abgrenzung and the crisis of the eighties
The reverse of Honecker’s rapprochement with the West was a deliberate Abgrenzung, a delimitation of the GDR from the Federal Republic. Winkler describes how the policy sought to consolidate the republic’s separate identity, insisting that the East German state was a distinct socialist nation whose citizens owed it their whole allegiance. Yet the material foundations of the “unity of economic and social policy” were never secure. From the mid-seventies the economy stalled under the burden of its promises; the late seventies brought renewed crisis and a tightening of the system, the expatriation of the dissident singer Wolf Biermann in 1976 and the wave of protest that followed. In the early eighties, as the second Cold War intensified, Honecker pressed the party’s leading role and its absolute loyalty to Moscow at the X. Party Congress of 1981, while a conspicuous personality cult gathered about his own person — a man who had risen as the enemy of Ulbricht’s cult now presiding over a cult of his own.
The fall
By the late eighties the contradictions had become unbridgeable. The republic Honecker had consolidated against the West proved unable to withstand the new pressure from the East, as Mikhail Gorbachev’s reforms in Moscow undermined the ideological ground on which the SED stood. Kowalczuk records the terminal crisis of the autumn of 1989, when the republic celebrated its fortieth anniversary on 7 October in a hollow pageant while its citizens fled through the opening in Hungary and filled the squares of Leipzig. Days before, on 18 October 1989, the Politburo had deposed Honecker, replacing him with Egon Krenz — the man who had built the Wall and personified the state’s separation from the West was cast aside to save the regime that was already beyond saving. Within weeks the Wall itself fell, and the republic collapsed around its fallen leader. Honecker, indicted for the shootings at the border, took refuge first in Moscow and then in the Chilean embassy in Moscow, was eventually extradited to a reunified Germany and tried for manslaughter and the “shooting order,” and died in exile in Chile in 1994 — the last head of the SED state surviving to see his creation dissolved in the fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 and its absorption into the Federal Republic.

entities/felipe-gonzalez.title: Felipe González (b. 1942)
entities/felipe-gonzalez.content:
Felipe González (b. 1942)
He was, in Tusell’s judgment, the historical protagonist who gives unity and coherence to the whole socialist era — a figure so central that the period of his governments is commonly named for him. Leader of the PSOE at thirty-two and president of the government at forty, Felipe González was the representative of a new political generation, born after the Civil War, formed in the opposition to the dictatorship, and entirely the counterfigure of the Caudillo against whom his youth had been spent. A generation that had known Francoism as its own memory and its own grievance rose to power with him in October 1982 and was to govern Spain for fourteen years.
The making of the leader
He came to politics through the Catholic organisations of the opposition — militancy in the JOC and the HOAC, the young workers’ and adult workers’ Catholic movements — and through the teacher Jiménez Fernández, who first opened his political horizons. An Andalusian lawyer, he joined the inner resistance to francoism and rose rapidly in the underground PSOE, which he led from 1974 as its general secretary. His leadership was conquered early and revalidated in the crisis of 1979, and it was not seriously contested again until the electoral defeat of 1996. Against the burden of the radical ideology the party had carried through its opposition years, González imposed a pragmatism that chose moderate reformism in the fundamental decisions — a man who, as Tusell put it, was far below Azaña in intellectual capacity yet knew far better than Azaña how to set the calendar, the priorities and the content of a reforming action once in power.
The reformation of the party
The transformation of the PSOE into a party fit to govern was the decisive internal drama of the Spanish left. The party of the opposition, theoretically radical, could only connect with majority Spanish society by renouncing its most doctrinaire positions. At the congresses of 1979 González proposed to drop Marxism as the party’s exclusive ideological principle — a proposal that threw the rank-and-file into chaos, the gran novatada, and led to his resignation after re-election when only the radical Bustelo was willing to succeed him. An extraordinary congress in September 1979 restored him with a reduced and controllable delegate body, and the party emerged remade: reformist, electable, and positioned as the natural government alternative to the dying centrism of adolfo-suarez. The agony of the UCD opened the path, and in the psoe-victory-1982 of 28 October 1982 González carried the party to a landslide, becoming prime minister of a government with a comfortable parliamentary majority.
The Socialist governments
His governments governed with stability and a durable team through the 1980s, their economic portfolios always in the hands of specialists long connected to the administration — the greatest continuity with the past, which explains why the essential line of economic policy did not change. The arrival of the Socialists met genuine yearnings for governmental stability and answered a very negative judgment of the UCD; the involucionist dangers of the Transition disappeared in the Socialist stage, and the democratic regime consolidated around the new majority. The great project was European integration: democratisation had been equated with Europeanisation and homologation with the Western world, and it was under González that the long-delayed entry into the European Economic Community was finally accomplished in 1986, ending the external isolation the Transition had only begun to break. At home his governments built the state of the autonomies, developing Title VIII into the quasi-federal organisation of the state, and presided over a decade of economic and social modernisation that carried Spain to eighth in the world by GDP by the mid-1990s. Against that record stood the great unresolved failure of the age: the terrorism of ETA and the state’s dark answer to it in the GAL, the anti-terrorist groups whose consequences were judged among the greatest blots on the socialist governments.
The long hegemony and its erosion
Through the first half of the 1980s the PSOE commanded a voting intention of thirty to forty per cent, with satisfaction with González running extraordinarily high, while the right could average no more than fifteen per cent outside campaign periods. Even from 1986 to 1992 the party kept its lead, though the absolute majority was lost in 1993. The decisive change of opinion came from 1991, when the PSOE began definitively to lose the hegemony it had enjoyed; by that year a majority of Spaniards judged they paid too much tax for the services they received, and identification with the centre-left was declining. The long tenure, renewed election after election, wore on into scandal and fatigue, until the general election of 1996 brought the era to an end and delivered power to the right. González had governed longer than any democratic prime minister of the age, and in doing so had turned the democratic regime of the Transition from a fragile achievement into a settled, ordinary part of Spanish political life.

entities/francisco-franco.title: Francisco Franco (1892-1975)
entities/francisco-franco.content:
Francisco Franco (1892-1975)
The man who ruled Spain for nearly four decades was born at El Ferrol in 1892, in a naval family of six generations, and entered the Toledo Military Academy in 1907 as the youngest cadet of his promotion only after the destruction of the Spanish fleet had closed the naval path that his brother Nicolás had taken. From that beginning in arms — the hard school of the Moroccan campaigns that made his name — he rose through the Civil War to the head of the Spanish state, and he remained there, under the title of Caudillo, from the last war bulletin of 1 April 1939 until his death in November 1975. His dictatorship passed in his own lifetime from resemblance to one type of authoritarian rule to another without any substantial change of the man at the head — which is one reason historians have chosen to name the whole régime by the man who personified it.
The victor and the new state
The Franco who entered Madrid in the spring of 1939 was the product of the Crusade, the Cruzada that his propagandists made of the Civil War. The Victory parade of 19 May 1939, with its 120,000 soldiers and the grand cross of San Fernando, and the religious ceremony of 20 May in Santa Bárbara, where Franco stood beneath the palio and deposited his sword before the Cristo de Lepanto, mixed the military, the political and the religious as in a medieval warrior society. Against the tendency to reduce his long rule to a psychological portrait of its founder, the regime’s own power structure mattered as much as his temperament: he was a general who had won a war, and he built a state on the victory of one half of Spain over the other. From the first days the repression fell on the defeated — the thousands in exile across the Pyrenees, the hundreds of thousands more who remained under the weight of the victors’ order.
The fascist temptation, 1939-1951
From the end of the Civil War to the summer of 1940, when the German victory over France made the defeat of the old democratic order seem decided, Spain drifted toward homologation with the Axis. Against the later claim of franquista propaganda that Hitler had pressed and Franco resisted, the German triumph produced an absolute identification of the Spanish leadership with the Axis cause, prolonged with nuances into 1944. The Falangist press greeted the fall of France as the great occasion awaited for decades — the moment for a repartition of Europe and of French colonial possessions in which Spain hoped to share. The internal struggle over the interventionist temptation of 1940-42 was fought out within the régime, between the Falange’s revolutionary pretensions and a more cautious realism, but Spain’s pretensions never had a real chance of success, for Hitler’s Germany was far from the vision the Spanish leaders projected onto it. When the war turned, Franco was carried on a hesitant path toward genuine neutrality — favoured by events as much as by any single decision of his own.
The close of the world war brought the régime its gravest simultaneous dangers: uncertainty of internal course, an opposition aiming at rupture or peaceful transition, and external isolation born of its wartime stance. Franco early discovered the need to show an appearance of institutional change — “constitutional” dispositions such as the Ley de Cortes of 1942 that barely modified the real power he retained. The Ley de Sucesión and the other cosmetic measures of the late 1940s offered an apparently democratising image while he kept the substance. Through the isolation he survived: Spain was not invited to the San Francisco conference that founded the United Nations, and the world’s democracies kept the dictatorship at arm’s length. Behind the façade lay the “noche oscura” (dark night) of autarky and rationing, an economic management lamentable beyond the circumstances of Spain and the world. When the European environment changed, the political system did not; it adapted only cosmetically.
The years of consensus, 1951-1965
By 1951 the worst immediate pressure of the postwar had passed, and the régime entered its period of plenitude. The Cold War conjuncture was of first-order importance for the dictatorship’s survival: with the Korean conflict of 1950, Spain began a rapid rehabilitation culminating in 1953, when the Concordat with the Holy See and the pacts with the United States broke the isolation at a stroke. The American embrace was a pure recognition of Spain’s admission to the international community, while the Concordat confirmed the bond of the state with the Church. The ration book ended in 1951, national income began to grow, and Spain began to catch the European postwar “miracle” after an exceptional backwardness. Passive social acceptance could now be called a consensus — a dictatorship stable enough that a great part of society came to live with it, even as the opposition was dismantled by repression and the exile from which the survivors of the old parties never fully returned.
Franco governed in these middle years as an arbiter among the political “families” of the régime — the Falange, the army, the Church, the monarchists, the technicians. The ministerial change of 1951 was one of the most complete in the régime’s history, a counterweight of tendencies under his arbitration. He used the Falange instrumentally and yet indispensably; he was allergic to anything called “constitutionalisation,” accepting only the weaker word “institutionalisation.” After 1956 a new interior opposition arose, not derived from the prewar or exile groups but from among the victors or from those who had been absent from national political life — the germ of what late franquismo called the oposición moderada.
Developmentalism and tardofranquismo, 1966-1975
The last decade was dominated more than any earlier phase by Franco’s own person in decline, as the succession and the accumulating crises of the régime concentrated on the aging dictator. Yet even as the political system answered to another world, economic growth was modifying the closed and authoritarian Spanish society. The desarrollismo of the 1960s — the Stabilisation Plan of 1959, the growth of tourism, the urbanisation and the internal migrations that carried roughly four million Spaniards from the countryside to the cities — created a social transformation the régime could not contain. In the years of the apertura (1965-1969) Franco tolerated a loosening of controls — the new Press Law associated with the minister Manuel Fraga — a loosening that was not a transformation of the régime but that signalled its growing uncertainty of course. He could still act decisively, as in October 1969 when he formed the monocolor government around Admiral Carrero Blanco, and in 1969 he confirmed the succession of the young prince Juan Carlos, installed at the Zarzuela since 1963, over whom he demanded “identificación absoluta.”
The late tardofranquismo was defined not only by physical decline but by the lack of a clear course, by public-order problems, by the fragmentation of the political class into antagonistic leaderships, and by paralysis before the most urgent questions. Foreign visitors left portraits of an old man who scarcely spoke; his daily routine was to receive dozens of people while barely articulating a word, sedentary before the television, his mind fixed on the Moroccan wars that had made his youth. In 1974 he suffered a thrombophlebitis, and had to relearn to speak and to walk by narrating the campaigns of the Rif. He was senile, inarticulate, tearful — “escuchaba, pero no oía” (he listened, but he did not hear), as Fraga put it. Yet he obstinately remained in power until the end, through the assassination of Carrero in December 1973, the appointment of the last franquista government under Arias Navarro, the terminal decolonisation of the Sahara, and the pathos and esperpento of the final year. He died on 20 November 1975, and with him the régime that was named for him. Sociologically it already represented less and less of the society that had outgrown it, and the succession to the young king that he had chosen was already opening the road to the transición that would undo his work.

entities/francois-mitterrand.title: François Mitterrand (1916–1996)
entities/francois-mitterrand.content:
François Mitterrand (1916–1996)
For nearly a quarter of a century François Mitterrand was the lodestar of the French left and then, for fourteen years, its master of the state — the man who led the socialists out of opposition, carried them to the first alternance of the Fifth Republic, and presided over France through the deepest transformations of its recent history. He was a politician of extraordinary patience and will, who had failed twice for the presidency and won it on his third attempt, in 1981, at the head of a left united for the first time since the Liberation.
The long opposition
Mitterrand had entered politics under the Fourth Republic, a minister in its governments and a figure of the centre-left, before the founding of the Fifth Republic left him in the wilderness. The gaullisme of 1958, which he denounced as a personal and authoritarian régime, became the object of his life’s political work. He built the union of the left — the Programme commun of government signed with the Communist Party in June 1972, the reconstituted Parti socialiste born of the congress of Épinay in 1971, with its slogan Changer la vie (change life) drawn from Rimbaud. He carried the banner of the united left into the presidential elections of 1974, where he lost narrowly to Giscard d’Estaing, and again in the face of a left divided. The union, at once forged and strained by the alliance with the communists, held through the 1970s.
The victory of 1981
On 10 May 1981 Mitterrand won the presidency, defeating the incumbent Giscard d’Estaing — the first time in the history of the Fifth Republic that the left had taken the Élysée, and the first peaceful alternance of the régime. The état de grâce (state of grace) of the first months carried an extraordinary programme. The new President dissolved the Assembly and obtained a socialist majority, and the government of Pierre Mauroy set about a reform of extraordinary ambition: the nationalisations that had haunted the left since the war, a great social programme of the minimum wage and the retirement age, the abolition of the death penalty, the grands travaux — the Grand Louvre, the pyramid of Ieoh Ming Pei, the new Bastille opera house — and the decentralisation that remade the relationship of the state to its communes. It was the programme of the Changer la vie of 1972 at last attempted from power.
The tournant de la rigueur
The great gamble failed against the constraints of the world. The reflationary relance of 1981–1982 ran into the reality of the global economy, the pressure of the markets and the defence of the franc, and the government was forced to choose. In March 1983 Mitterrand abandoned the socialist programme of growth for a policy of austerity — the tournant de la rigueur (turn of rigour), the moment when the left in power renounced its Keynesian ambitions and accepted the discipline of the European Monetary System rather than leave it. It was the decisive turn of his presidency, the acceptance of a constraint that redefined the French left in power for a generation. The nationalisations remained, but the momentum of transformation was spent.
The two presidencies
The fourteen years of Mitterrand in the Élysée divide into two distinct mandates, and each into the alternating rhythm of presidential and cohabitation government. The first septennate, 1981–1988, saw the great reforms of the first years and then the turn of rigour and the recovery of the 1980s, and ended with his re-election in 1988 over the gaullist candidate. The second, 1988–1995, was spent in large measure in cohabitation with a right-wing government — from 1986 to 1988 with that of Jacques Chirac, and from 1993 to 1995 with that of Édouard Balladur — a constitutionally strange arrangement in which a socialist President shared power with conservative Premiers, and which proved the Fifth Republic could function with an executive divided against itself. The end of his presidency was darkened by the affair of his concealed wartime past and by his illness; he left office in 1995, the longest-serving President of the Republic.
Mitterrand’s legacy is double. He gave the French left its first real exercise of power under the Fifth Republic and remade the urban and cultural face of France with his grands travaux; but he also presided over the abandonment of the programme commun and the acceptance of the market constraint that came to define the left after him. In the history of the Republic he stands as the great adapter — the man who brought the left into the institutions of 1958 and then bent both the left and the institutions to the demands of a changing world.

entities/franz-josef-strauss.title: Franz Josef Strauß (1915–1988)
entities/franz-josef-strauss.content:
Franz Josef Strauß (1915–1988)
The pole of the right in West German politics was occupied for a generation by a Bavarian of formidable intelligence and ambition who divided the country as no other figure of his time. Franz Josef Strauß, born in 1915 in Munich, had been an early enemy of the Nazi regime and a soldier in the war, and had risen in the politics of Bavaria to lead the Christian Social Union, the CSU — the Bavarian sister-party of the CDU that he built into the regional bastion and, through him, into a force in national politics. For years he was the embodiment of the conservative opposition to the governments of the left — the sharpest, the most feared, and for his enemies the most dangerous voice in the republic.
Strauß had already been a national figure in the Adenauer era, as defence minister and as a champion of the West’s rearmament and of the strong anti-communist front. He stood for the polar opposite of the ostpolitik that willy-brandt conducted after 1969: where Brandt offered the East Wandel durch Annäherung (change through rapprochement), Strauß argued for firmness and warned that the recognition of the division of Germany would consecrate it. He was the standard-bearer of those who saw in the Eastern treaties a capitulation, and the guarantee that the treaties’ passage through the Bundestag — survived by a hair in the vote of no confidence of April 1972 — was fought to the last vote.
In the Schmidt years, Strauß became the leader of the right’s assault on the social-liberal coalition. He stood for a strategy of confrontation — what his critics called the Konfrontationsstrategie (confrontation strategy) — against the more conciliatory course preferred by the CDU chairman helmut-kohl. Where Kohl favoured a konstruktive (constructive) opposition that kept the door open to cooperation, Strauß pressed for a harder line and for the candidacy of the strongest challenger. He played a decisive role in the Union’s politics of the late 1970s, pushing his party toward the confrontational course, testing the ground for his own ambitions, and raising, to the alarm of many and the delight of his supporters, the spectre of Strauß ante portas — Strauß at the gates.
His greatest moment came with his Inthronisierung (enthronement) as the Union’s candidate for the chancellorship. The CDU/CSU, after years of internal quarrels over personnel and programme, finally crowned Strauß as its candidate for the federal election of 1980. The contest set him against helmut-schmidt in what the press called the Duell der Giganten (duel of the giants) — the two most forceful and the two most polarising men in German politics, face to face. The campaign was the hardest-fought and most bitter of the era. Yet the duel ended in a resounding defeat for Strauß: Schmidt and the social-liberal coalition won decisively, and the candidacy that had been meant to carry the right to power delivered instead its most crushing disappointment. The failure of 1980 confirmed what the longer history of the republic had suggested — that Strauß, however great his gifts, was too divisive a figure to command the confidence of a majority of Germans.
After 1980 Strauß’s national hopes were spent. He retired to the summit of his Bavarian domain, serving as Minister-President of Bavaria — the office in which he consolidated the CSU’s dominance of its home state and remained, until his death in 1988, one of the weightiest and most controversial voices in the republic. In the years of the second Cold War he spoke for the hard anti-communist line; his very presence, and the campaign of 1980, were proof of how deep the polarisation ran in the Federal Republic — how the republic’s politics, for all its consensus, were anchored at both ends by men as unyielding as the chancellor of the left and the master of the CSU. Strauß was the great alternative to the social-liberal order, the man who embodied the right pole of West German politics, never reaching the chancellorship he had so long sought, yet leaving on the republic the imprint of his ambition and his warning.

entities/georges-pompidou.title: Georges Pompidou (1911–1974)
entities/georges-pompidou.content:
Georges Pompidou (1911–1974)
The man who succeeded General de Gaulle was in many ways his opposite — a former professor and banker rather than a soldier, a discreet servant of the state who rose through the corridors of the Élysée and Matignon rather than through the battles of the Liberation. Yet Georges Pompidou became the indispensable lieutenant of the General, the head of his government through the hardest years of the Fifth Republic, and in 1969 the heir who carried the new régime beyond the departure of its founder.
The discreet rise
Pompidou came to power from outside the party arena. He had served de Gaulle in the years of shadow and the early Fifth Republic, and in April 1962 the General turned to him to head the government — a choice that astonished a political class accustomed to the tribunes of the parties. As Prime Minister he steered the consolidation of the new institutions, presiding over the great changes of the era: the settlement of the Algerian war, the October 1962 referendum on the election of the President by universal suffrage, the ambitious industrial and social policy of the effort, and the re-election campaign of December 1965 that confirmed the General for a second term.
Prime Minister of the Fifth Republic
Under Pompidou’s hand the Fifth Republic acquired its administrative mastery. The technocrat of Matignon managed the everyday machinery of the state that the General, on the heights of national and foreign policy, was content to leave to him. He was the steady partner through the years of national independence, of the departure from the integrated command of NATO in 1966, and of the great visits to Moscow and the East — the trusted manager who held the régime together while its founder pursued the grand design of a Europe européenne and an independent France.
The crisis of May 1968
The greatest test came in May 1968, when the student revolt and the general strike of the century threatened to sweep the régime away. While the General — absent, famously, from Paris on 29 May — deliberated over his own disappearance, it fell to Pompidou to negotiate with the unions at the Grenelle agreements and to hold the government together. He emerged from the crisis as the indispensable man, the one who had steadied the state when its architect seemed to falter. The distance between the two men widened thereafter, the heir apparent grown too strong for the founder.
President of the Republic
When de Gaulle resigned on 28 April 1969 after the defeat of his referendum, Pompidou was the natural successor. Elected President in June 1969, he succeeded where the General had chosen to fall — but his presidency tempered the gaullisme he inherited. Where de Gaulle had pursued the politique de grandeur and independence from the blocs, Pompidou opened a pragmatic path: the entry of Britain into the Common Market that de Gaulle had vetoed, the pursuit of relance and industrial modernisation, the choice of a France anchored firmly in the Atlantic alliance and the European Community. The policy of national independence softened into a realism of growth and stability, the great industrial projects of the Trente Glorieuses continuing under his hand.
The passing of the heir
His presidency, marked by a serious illness that he long concealed, was cut short by his death in April 1974 — the first President of the Fifth Republic to die in office, and the second man of the régime, after the General himself, to leave a vacancy at the heart of the state. He bequeathed to his successors the very different gaullisme he had reworked: a modern, managerial conservatism that preserved the institutions of 1958 while abandoning much of the General’s manner. In the arc of the Fifth Republic he stands as the bridge — the lieutenant who became the master, the man who made the régime durable after its founder had gone.

entities/giulio-andreotti.title: Giulio Andreotti (1919-2013)
entities/giulio-andreotti.content:
Giulio Andreotti (1919-2013)
The man they called the Divo Giulio — the divine Julius, after Caesar — was the most durable political figure of the Italian Republic, a presence at the heart of power from the first governments after the war to the collapse of the party system in the 1990s. Giulio Andreotti, born in Rome in 1919, entered the Democrazia Cristiana as a young Catholic militant, rose in the party under Alcide De Gasperi, and for half a century held almost every office the Republic could offer — minister across the decades, seven times prime minister, and for long stretches the master of the quiet arts by which the DC actually governed. He was the emblem both of the Republic’s extraordinary stability and of the web of compromise, patronage and unresolved secrets on which that stability came to rest.
The rise to the centre of power
Andreotti’s apprenticeship was in the first years of the Republic, in the inner circle of De Gasperi, and he came of political age with the centrismo of the 1950s. A figure of the DC’s right, prudent and reserved, he moved through the ministries — Interior, Treasury, Foreign Affairs, Defence — accumulating the detailed knowledge of the state that was his hallmark. His manner was famously elliptical; his wit dry; his answers to questions deliberately ambiguous. Over the decades he came to embody what the country knew as correnti (factions) and sottogoverno (the “sub-government” of boards and agencies through which the DC distributed its influence), the machinery of a party that had become the permanent mainstay of Italian rule.
He reached the premiership for the first time in 1972, and presided over the difficult governments of the early 1970s, a period shaped by economic crisis and the mounting violence of the anni di piombo (years of lead).
The strategy of tension and its shadows
Andreotti’s long career was entangled, in ways that were to be contested and never fully resolved, with the darker currents of the period. The strategy of tension — the series of bombings, beginning with the Piazza Fontana massacre of 1969, that seemed designed to blame the left and push the country toward an authoritarian solution — hung over the Republic throughout his years in power. Questions that were to pursue him for the rest of his life concerned the state’s knowledge of those plots, the toleration of the far right, and the ambiguous dealings with which, his critics charged, the permanent party of government preserved its hold. Andreotti himself, with his gift for remaining above every controversy, tended to survive the storms that broke others. His defence, repeated to the end, was that the true history of those years would never be known, and that the secrets he carried were the Republic’s own.
The years of the compromesso and national solidarity
It was Andreotti who gave the compromesso storico (historic compromise) its institutional form. In 1976, in the wake of the Communist advance at the elections of 20 June, he formed the government of solidarietà nazionale (national solidarity) — a Christian Democrat cabinet sustained by the abstention of the Partito Comunista Italiano, with Enrico Berlinguer’s party supporting from outside. It was on the point of bringing the Communists fully into the government, in the spring of 1978, that the project was shattered by the kidnapping of Aldo Moro. In the fifty-four days of Moro’s captivity Andreotti led the state’s linea della fermezza (hard line), refusing to negotiate with the Brigate Rosse (Red Brigades) even as Moro’s own letters from prison pleaded for a negotiated solution. Moro was murdered on 9 May 1978. The decision to hold firm was and remains among the most debated acts of the Republic; Andreotti, who had been Moro’s friend and who would have headed the government Moro was seeking to create, carried its weight for the rest of his career.
The fall in Tangentopoli
The 1980s saw Andreotti return repeatedly to the premiership, the last of them from 1989 to 1992, a long season in which the postwar order — the DC’s dominance, the exclusion of the Communists, the Atlantic anchoring of the state — began to give way. The end of the Cold War removed the very reason for the political system’s existence, and in 1992 the Tangentopoli (“Bribesville”) investigations of Mani pulite (Clean Hands) exposed the systematic corruption that had sustained the parties for decades. The DC, the party Andreotti had embodied, collapsed. Andreotti himself was indicted, charged with colluding with the Mafia and with involvement in the murder of a journalist; he was tried, convicted and acquitted in a long legal saga that ended only with the statute of limitations. He never returned to power, and the era he had personified was buried with him. When he died in 2013, aged ninety-four, he was remembered both as the guardian of the Republic’s stability and as the living monument of everything the Republic’s crisis had swept away.

entities/guy-mollet.title: Guy Mollet (1905-1975)
entities/guy-mollet.content:
Guy Mollet (1905-1975)
The secretary of the section
He came out of the industrial north, a schoolteacher from the Pas-de-Calais who had risen through the federation of the Section française de l’Internationale ouvrière — the S.F.I.O., the old French socialist party — through the Resistance and the long years of militant apprenticeship. By the middle of the nineteen-fifties Guy Mollet had become the party’s general secretary, the keeper of its machine, a man whose patience and organisational grip mattered more than any eloquence. When the Fourth Republic lurched from one ministry to the next, it was to men of his patient sort that the assemblies turned, half in despair, to form a government. He formed one in February 1956, at the head of a coalition known as the Front républicain, and held power for nearly sixteen months — a longevity remarkable in a régime where ministries rarely outlived the seasons.
The moment of the Front républicain
Mollet came to the Hôtel Matignon on the strength of an electoral promise of peace. His coalition had campaigned on ending the war in Algeria, on negotiation, on the modernisation of the economy and of social life. The general election of 2 January 1956 had returned a majority that seemed to speak for change; Mollet himself had stood on a platform that promised to settle the Algerian question by political means. He visited Algiers in the first weeks of his premiership, and there the European crowd of the capital — the pieds-noirs, the settlers of a million and more who had made Algeria a French department — gave him a reception so violent, so hostile to any gesture toward the rebels, that the new premier turned. The government of negotiation became a government of war. Special powers were voted, the army was given its head, the conscript army of the Republic was sent across the Mediterranean in force, and the émeutes and their repression set the pattern of what contemporaries were already beginning, though with reluctance, to call the guerre d’Algérie. The socialist who had promised peace presided over the escalation.
The immobilism of the régime
Mollet’s ministry was the Fourth Republic’s clearest demonstration of its own paralysis. It was a government of the centre-left that could do nothing decisive either way — it could neither bring itself to negotiate seriously with the nationalists nor confess that it was waging an all-out colonial war; it could neither reform the régime nor defend it. His colonial minister, Robert Lacoste, governed Algeria through the army and the administration of maintenance of order, the maintien de l’ordre, which everyone understood to be a war that no one would name. The weakness of the executive, the sway of the parliamentary groups, the dependence of every ministry on the shifting combinations of the Assembly — all the features that contemporaries denounced under the name of the régime des partis — were concentrated in his tenure. To the critics of the régime, above all to the gaullists watching from the wings, Mollet’s government was the proof that the Fourth Republic could neither finish its colonial wars nor govern.
The voice from Colombey
From his retirement at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises, Charles de Gaulle watched this dissolution with a patience he had made a doctrine. His pronouncements of the middle fifties — the press conference of 30 June 1955, the rare communiqués of 1956 and 1957 — returned again and again to the theme that the régime was incapable of settling the Algerian question, incapable of governing, incapable of saving the state. The last text of his volume of the years of waiting, the communiqué of 12 September 1957 on the framework law for Algeria, was a direct intervention in the Mollet inheritance: the General pronounced on a question the government had failed to master. When the crisis of May 1958 came — the army in Algiers in revolt, the Republic without authority — the very failure of Mollet’s generation of parliamentarians opened the way for the return of the man who had denounced them. Guy Mollet, who had been a minister in the government of the Liberation and a loyal servant of the Republic, found himself on the wrong side of history as the régime he had embodied crumbled and the Fifth Republic rose in its place. He lived on as a figure of the old order, the socialist of the S.F.I.O. whose name was bound up with the Fourth Republic’s last, unhappy years.

entities/hans-dietrich-genscher.title: Hans-Dietrich Genscher (1927–2016)
entities/hans-dietrich-genscher.content:
Hans-Dietrich Genscher (1927–2016)
No German politician of the era governed so long in the same office, or so successfully made his party indispensable, as the Free Democrat who stood for nearly two decades at the head of the foreign ministry. Hans-Dietrich Genscher, born in 1927 in Reideburg in the province of Saxony, had fled the Soviet zone as a young man in 1952 and risen through the ranks of the FDP, the Free Democratic Party, to become its leader and the architect of its place in the German political order. He was the maker of the FDP’s balance of power — the party that, too small to govern alone, held the key to which of the great parties would rule, and that used that position to keep itself in government for virtually the whole life of the republic.
Genscher’s first great step was taken in 1969, when he was general secretary of the FDP: the party’s decision to enter the social-liberal coalition with the SPD of willy-brandt rather than continue the old alliance with the CDU. It was Genscher who stood in 1969 for the Koalitionsaussage (coalition declaration) that turned the Free Democrats toward the left. In 1974 he reaped the reward. When the affair of Guillaume brought down Brandt in May 1974, Genscher succeeded Walter Scheel — who became Federal President — as Foreign Minister and chairman of the FDP; and when the succession passed to helmut-schmidt, Genscher remained at his side in the first Schmidt/Genscher cabinet. In the murky business of the Guillaume affair Genscher had himself been entangled — as interior minister he had received the early warnings and had passed on the disastrous advice to keep the spy in the Chancellery — but he could not resign without bringing down the coalition, and he carried the responsibility in silence.
As Foreign Minister, Genscher became the guarantor of the continuity of the ostpolitik. The Eastern policy inaugurated by Brandt was carried on under Schmidt by Genscher, who made it the common ground of the social-liberal coalition and, later, of every coalition of his long tenure. In the era of détente he conducted the Federal Republic’s relations with the Soviet Union, the multilateral détente of Europe, and the bilateral policy toward Eastern Europe; he steered the German–German diplomacy of the second decade — the permanent negotiations, the agreements despite the German Democratic Republic’s policy of Abgrenzung (delimitation), the policy of damage-limitation that sought to hold the German–German relationship together through the estrangement of the late 1970s and the second Cold War of the early 1980s. In foreign policy he was the embodiment of the republic’s diplomatic weight, cultivating at once the American alliance, the European Community and the détente with the East.
At home, Genscher’s task was the survival of his party and of the coalitions that rested upon it. Through the Schmidt years he steered the FDP’s difficult course between the larger coalition partner and its own liberal independence — the liberale Eigenständigkeit (liberal independence) that was both its claim and its vulnerability. As the coalition with the SPD wore thin in the early 1980s, over the economy and over the nuclear question, Genscher and the FDP moved toward the Union. The break of 1982 was his work as much as any man’s. The social-liberal coalition fell in October 1982, and Genscher, at the side of the new Chancellor helmut-kohl, carried the FDP into a Christian-liberal coalition — a Wende (turning-point) that restored the old alliance of the Free Democrats with the CDU/CSU and ended fourteen years of social-liberal rule.
Genscher’s distinction was to serve as Foreign Minister through both changes of government — first under the Social Democrats, then under the Christian Democrats — and to hold the office without interruption from 1974 until 1992. He outlasted Schmidt and came to outlast much of the era itself, becoming in the last years of his tenure a symbol of the republic’s continuous and unwearied diplomacy. In the autumn of 1989, when the refugees streamed out of the German Democratic Republic through the West German embassy in Prague, it was Genscher who went to the balcony to tell the crowds they could leave — an image of the Foreign Minister of the Wende standing at the hinge of the reunification he had done so much, across two decades, to keep possible.

entities/helmut-kohl.title: Helmut Kohl (1930-2017)
entities/helmut-kohl.content:
Helmut Kohl (1930-2017)
He was the man who came to power late, long after the generation of the founding fathers had passed, and who left the stage as the longest-serving Chancellor of the Federal Republic and the architect of the country’s unity. Helmut Kohl, born in 1930 in Ludwigshafen am Rhein, in the Palatinate, had grown to manhood in the ruins of the Third Reich and in the consciousness of the catastrophe of 1945 that weighed on all German politics. He carried that history not as a burden spoken aloud but as a fixed point of orientation: Germany belonged in the West, and the German question, the question of the nation divided, was the unfinished business to which everything else ultimately returned. For sixteen years in the Palais Schaumburg and the new Chancellery he pursued those two aims — the anchoring of Germany in Europe and the West, and the recovery of national unity — and he saw both accomplished in the momentous year of 1990.
The Palatinate and the road to the chancellorship
Kohl was a provincial by origin and temperament, a Rhinelander and a Palatine who rose through the Christian Democratic Union, the party of konrad-adenauer. He entered the Rhineland-Palatinate parliament young, became the state’s Minister-President in 1969, and over the following decade established himself as a national figure in the CDU — a man of formidable organizational patience, remembered by his enemies for his political cunning and by his friends for his capacity to hold a coalition together. He led the party from 1973, through the years in opposition to willy-brandt and helmut-schmidt, waiting out the long rule of the social-liberal coalition. When the coalition finally broke apart in the autumn of 1982, over the intractable questions of the economy and the budget, Kohl was the man the Free Democrats chose to turn to. In October 1982 he was elected Chancellor by a constructive vote of no confidence — the Wende (the change of course), as the new government called it, from the social-liberal era to the conservative-liberal era that he was to preside over for the next sixteen years.
The Wende and the government in Bonn
The change of 1982 was carried through in the interest of the republic’s stability, yet it rested on a constitutional device — the constructive vote of no confidence — that Kohl was obliged to confirm at the polls in 1983. He won that election, and the victory settled his authority. His government combined the Christian Democrats and the Free Democrats, pursued a policy of continuity in the alliance with the West, of steadiness in the Atlantic community, and of friendship with France that grew into the motor of European integration. For most of the 1980s Kohl appeared to many observers a figure of consolidation rather than of historical destiny — a Chancellor of management, of the economic upswing, of the middle classes. Yet beneath the surface of the Kanzler der Mitte (Chancellor of the middle) ran the fixed conviction, which he voiced repeatedly, that the division of Germany was not a permanent condition, that the German question remained open, and that the nation’s unity would one day be recovered in peace and freedom.
The Chancellor of unity, 1989-90
The events of 1989 overtook every political calculation. When the crisis of the GDR broke in the autumn of that year — the flight of its citizens through Hungary and the Prague embassy, the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig, the collapse of the erich-honecker regime — Kohl moved with a boldness that surprised even his own supporters. His Ten-Point Programme of 28 November 1989, set out in the Bundestag before a reunified Germany was yet a credible prospect, sketched a path toward a confederation and beyond; the programme drew criticism from abroad, from neighbours who feared a new German giant, but it placed Kohl at the head of the national question. He grasped that the moment demanded decision. In the fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 and its aftermath he spoke for the cause of unity in freedom, and as the chancellor of the Federal Republic he came to stand, by the measure of the day, as the figure of German unity rather than his rival of the Social Democrats. It was Kohl who drove the german-reunification-1990 forward — the free elections in the GDR in March 1990, the economic and monetary union of July 1990, and the accession of the GDR to the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990.
The two-plus-four and the restoration of sovereignty
The recovery of German unity was inseparable from the recovery of full sovereignty, and that was the work of the two-plus-four-1990 negotiations. Kohl conducted them in concert with his Foreign Minister, Hans-Dietrich Genscher, and with the allies of the wartime coalition that had occupied Germany in 1945 — the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. He won the assent of Moscow and of the other powers to a Germany that would remain in NATO and in the European Community, would renounce the possession of weapons of mass destruction, and would recognise the Oder-Neisse border. The Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany, signed in Moscow in September 1990, restored to the reunited Germany its full sovereignty. What remained of the Bismarck Reich after two world wars, as Winkler put it, had been reunited — and reunited in freedom, through free elections and agreement rather than through force.
Europe and the monetary union
Kohl’s vision of a united Germany was bound up from the first with the vision of a united Europe. He had always insisted that the two belonged together — that the German question could only be settled within a European framework, and that the weight of a restored Germany must be borne by a stronger European community. In the same years in which he pursued unity he pressed forward with the construction of European union, and above all with the creation of the single European currency. At Maastricht in December 1991 the member states agreed to the treaty that carried Kohl’s European project forward, and the European monetary union was to become the crowning and most contested achievement of his chancellorship — a commitment that bound the reunited Germany irrevocably into the West, even as it divided opinion at home over the surrender of the Deutschmark.
The longest chancellorship
Kohl remained Chancellor until 1998, sixteen years in all, longer than any of his predecessors — outlasting konrad-adenauer, the other great architect of the Western republic. The later years were shadowed by the mounting costs of unity, the strains of the transformation in eastern Germany that the historian kowalczuk-die-uebernahme-wie-ostdeutschland-teil-der-bundesrepublik-wurde-2019 would analyse with such critical force, and by the scandals of party financing that broke around him as he left office. Yet the verdict of history that formed during his lifetime rested on the two great acts of his statesmanship: the reunification of Germany in freedom, and the anchoring of that reunited Germany in the West and in Europe. He died in 2017, mourned as the Kanzler der Einheit (Chancellor of Unity), the man to whom, by his own measure and that of his country, the recovery of the nation’s wholeness in peace had been entrusted and by him accomplished.

entities/helmut-schmidt.title: Helmut Schmidt (1918–2015)
entities/helmut-schmidt.content:
Helmut Schmidt (1918–2015)
The man who governed the Federal Republic through its deepest economic and security crises in the 1970s was a figure of an entirely different temper from the chancellor he succeeded. Helmut Schmidt, born in Hamburg in 1918, had served as an officer in the war and had made his reputation as the hardest-headed of the Social Democrats — an administrator and crisis-manager rather than a visionary, a man of the Senate of Hamburg, of the defence ministry and, from 1972, of the finance ministry, where he had managed the republic’s money through the first storms of the oil crisis. When willy-brandt fell over the affair of Guillaume in May 1974, Schmidt was Brandt’s own choice as successor, and on 16 May 1974 he formed the first Schmidt/Genscher cabinet with the Free Democrat hans-dietrich-genscher.
His government’s programme was summed up in its slogan: Kontinuität und Konzentration (continuity and concentration). The foreign policy of the ostpolitik was to continue without interruption; the task of the hour was to concentrate the state’s energies on the crisis of the world economy that the oil-price shock of 1973 had unleashed. The years of the great boom were over. The Federal Republic entered the deepest recession since its founding; unemployment and inflation rose together, and the confident reform politics of the Brandt years gave way to the sober management of decline. Schmidt’s authority rested on his mastery of this crisis-management — on his command of economic detail, his rhetorical force, his capacity to present the republic’s interest in a world of rising prices and faltering growth. The model of firm, expert, pragmatic government that he embodied came to be called the Modell Deutschland (model Germany), a name that carried both the pride and the anxieties of the republic in those years.
The 1976 federal election confirmed him. Helmut Kohl led the Union into the contest as its candidate, but Schmidt — by then celebrated, in the coinage of the press, as a Superstar — carried the coalition to victory, and the second Schmidt/Genscher cabinet took office. Yet the years that followed were the republic’s hardest trial. The domestic-political history of the era was marked by the polarisation between the governing coalition and an opposition that developed the Neue Soziale Frage (new social question), by the growing alienation of the FDP from reform politics, by the citizens’ protest against nuclear energy that drew the ecological movement and the Greens onto the stage, and above all by terrorism. The RAF, rebuilt after its near-destruction, carried out a campaign of murder — the Federal Prosecutor Siegfried Buback in 1977, the banker Jürgen Ponto — that culminated in the Deutscher Herbst (German Autumn) of 1977, the german-autumn-1977.
The autumn of 1977 was Schmidt’s ordeal. After the kidnapping of the employers’ president Hanns Martin Schleyer, Schmidt created crisis staffs unknown to the constitution and pursued a strategy of delay founded on the Kontaktsperre (contact ban) that isolated the imprisoned terrorists; when the Lufthansa jet Landshut was hijacked, he authorised the counter-terrorist unit GSG 9 to storm it at Mogadishu, saving the hostages but sealing Schleyer’s fate; and when Baader, Ensslin and Raspe took their own lives in Stammheim, he bore the weight of the decision that had made their deaths a weapon against the state. Schmidt spoke before the Bundestag of the tragedy of having to choose, and of the government’s refusal to be blackmailed. The crisis hardened his standing: he emerged from the German Autumn confirmed as the guarantor of the republic’s capacity to act.
The later years brought new fronts. In foreign policy Schmidt’s era was one of stabilisation and crisis-management — the stabilisation of the world economy, the founding of the European Monetary System, the European direct elections of 1979, and the continuation of the German–German diplomacy under the roof of the grundvertrag-1972, pursued through permanent negotiations and a policy of damage-limitation against the German Democratic Republic’s policy of Abgrenzung (delimitation), and crowned by his meeting with Honecker in the Uckermark in December 1981. But the 1980s opened the strains of the second Cold War, and the co-ordination difficulties with the United States over the nuclear question — the stationing of new American missiles in Europe — divided his own party and brought the coalition under growing stress.
The contest of 1980 set him against the most feared figure of the right, the CSU leader franz-josef-strauss. The Duell der Giganten (duel of the giants), as the press called it, ended in a resounding victory for Schmidt. Yet the triumph masked the decline that followed. The economy faltered again; the coalition partners quarrelled; and the Free Democrats, under hans-dietrich-genscher and the economics minister Otto Graf Lambsdorff, drifted toward the Union. The break came in 1982. The social-liberal coalition, sick and exhausted by the strains of its last cabinet, collapsed over the fundamental disagreement on economic policy; on 1 October 1982 the Bundestag elected Helmut Kohl Chancellor in a constructive vote of no confidence, and Schmidt’s era came to an end. From a social-democratic minority cabinet the republic passed to a Christian-liberal coalition — the Wende (turning-point) of 1982 that ended fourteen years of social-liberal rule.
Schmidt’s was the government that held the republic together through the crisis of the oil age, through the trial of the German Autumn, through the first genuine economic depression since the war. He had governed with a pragmatism that some found cold and many found reassuring, and he left the republic a legacy of firmness, of continuity in foreign and German policy, and of an unwillingness to be moved by the storms of the age.
