entities/italian-christian-democracy.title: Italian Christian Democracy (1943-1994)
entities/italian-christian-democracy.content:
Italian Christian Democracy (1943-1994)
The Democrazia Cristiana (Christian Democracy, the D.C.) was the party that governed Italy from the birth of the Republic to the collapse of the old party system in the 1990s — a Catholic party, formed in the spring of 1943 on the ruins of the pre-fascist Partito Popolare (People’s Party), that grew in a few years into the largest party of the country and the fixed centre of every governing coalition. It was the party of the centrismo, the anchor of the anti-communist republic, and, in its internal life, a party of permanent factional struggle — the celebrated correnti (currents) that divided its leadership and apportioned its offices. For nearly half a century the D.C. held power without interruption, and the Italian political system, from 1948 to the early 1990s, was in its essence the system of the Christian Democratic hegemony.
The formation of the Catholic party
The D.C. was founded in 1943, as the fascist regime fell and the resumption of political life began, by Alcide De Gasperi and the Catholic politicians who had worked in the interwar years under the shadow of the regime. It revived in new form the political tradition of the Partito Popolare of Luigi Sturzo, which the fascists had suppressed, but it was conceived as a broader and more modern party: a party that sought to gather the Catholic masses and, with them, a wider centre of the nation, transcending the old divisions and offering a political home to all those who opposed both the communist left and the residue of the old order. Its inspiration was Catholic and interclassist — a party of social harmony rather than of class struggle, which aspired to stand at the centre of the nation and to reconcile the country with itself. From its foundation it was the great rival of the Partito Comunista Italiano for the soul of the Italian people, and the two mass parties of the left and the centre were to divide the country between them for half a century.
The party of the reconstruction
The D.C. entered the postwar governments of the reconstruction as a principal partner, and under De Gasperi it rapidly became the dominant force of Italian politics. In the election of the Constituent Assembly in 1946 it emerged as the largest party, ahead of the socialists and the communists. In 1947 De Gasperi expelled the communists and socialists from the government and reconstituted the cabinet without them — a rupture that set the D.C. at the head of the anti-communist coalition. In the election of 18 April 1948, standing against the Fronte Democratico Popolare of the left, the D.C. won an absolute majority of the Chamber, the decisive triumph of the republic’s early years. From that victory the party became the fixed centre of the centrismo — the coalition of the centre parties, the quadripartito of the D.C., the liberals, the republicans and the social democrats, that governed Italy through the 1950s. It was a position the party would never lose: the D.C. was in every Italian government from 1944 to the early 1990s, its primacy the cardinal fact of the republic.
The correnti: a party of factions
The internal life of the D.C. was defined by its correnti (currents), the organized factions into which the party divided itself from early on. These were not mere tendencies of opinion but organized groups with their own leaders, their own press and their own followers, which competed within the party for the direction of policy and the distribution of power. The correnti — of the left and right of the party, of the trade-unionist and the conservative wings, the currents of the various notabili (notables) and rising leaders — made the D.C. a party of permanent internal negotiation. Every congress was a test of strength among them, every government a balance of their claims. The correntismo (factionalism) gave the party its extraordinary stability — for it was held together by the common interest of its leaders in keeping the D.C. in power and its offices in their hands — while making it at once deeply divided within and immovable without. It was a system of power in which the party’s leadership rotated among its currents, and in which a rising politician of the party, from the era of the centrismo to the later generations, made his career as much by the management of the factions as by the appeal to the voters.
The conventio ad excludendum and the anti-communist system
The very foundation of the D.C.’s hegemony was its exclusion of the communist opposition. The party’s government was built on the conventio ad excludendum (the convention of exclusion), the tacit and fundamental understanding that the Partito Comunista Italiano — the largest communist party in the West — could never be admitted to government. The republic’s coalition system was a system of the centre parties ranged against the excluded communist left; the D.C. was the pivot of this arrangement, able to govern always at the centre, and able to turn left or right within the spectrum of the centre as the moment required. The exclusion was the condition of the centrismo and the source of the D.C.’s permanent centrality: so long as the communists were barred, every alternative majority was unthinkable, and the Christian Democratic supremacy was safe. The party could and did experiment with its allies — from the centrist quadripartito to the later openings toward the socialists of the centro-sinistra — but never with the communists, whose admission would have dissolved the system the D.C. had built.
The long supremacy and its end
For decades the D.C. dominated the republic. It supplied nearly every Prime Minister — De Gasperi, then his successors through the centrismo and the centro-sinistra — and governed through every phase of Italian postwar history, the reconstruction, the economic miracle, the social and political struggles of the 1960s and 1970s. Its primacy was built on its vast Catholic and popular following, its organization, its identification with the state itself, and the effective exclusion of its great rival. The system endured until the early 1990s, when the end of the Cold War removed the very foundation of the conventio ad excludendum, and the collapse of the party system — the Tangentopoli corruption investigations and the annus horribilis of 1992 — swept the D.C. from power and into dissolution. The party that had governed Italy for half a century vanished from the political map, its place taken by the transformed parties of the 1990s, but the republic it had shaped and dominated remained stamped with its long rule.

entities/italian-communist-party.title: Italian Communist Party (1921-1991)
entities/italian-communist-party.content:
Italian Communist Party (1921-1991)
The Partito Comunista Italiano was the largest communist party in the Western world, a force that for half a century organised a third of the Italian electorate, dominated the culture of the working class and the intelligentsia, and yet was perpetually barred from the government of the Republic. Born in 1921 out of a split from the Socialists, it was forged underground under fascism and in the Resistance, and after the war it stood at once as the heir of that anti-fascist epic and as the great excluded of the Cold War order. Its history was the history of an anomaly — a mass party of the left, loyal to Moscow in origin, that evolved into a party of national reform and eventually into the principal challenger to the Democrazia Cristiana and the permanent governing system the DC had built.
The via italiana and the great exclusion
The party that emerged from the Resistance was a mass organisation under the leadership of Palmiro Togliatti, who returned from Moscow in 1944 and set the party on its distinctive course. Togliatti’s strategy was the via italiana al socialismo (the Italian road to socialism) — the claim that socialism could be reached through the Republic’s own institutions and parliamentary democracy, rather than by revolution. He was the architect of the svolta di Salerno (the Salerno turn), the choice to collaborate with the other anti-fascist parties in the national unity governments of 1944–1947 and to accept the monarchy’s decision, in the service of the national struggle against fascism. It was Togliatti who pushed for the party’s inclusion in the writing of the Constitution and who secured the church’s cooperation, a gamble on legality and national unity.
The Communist party was nonetheless cast out of government in the crisis of 1947, when the Christian Democrats, under the pressure of the Cold War and the split of the world into blocs, expelled the left from the coalition. From the elections of 18 April 1948, which the DC won overwhelmingly over the Communist–Socialist Fronte democratico popolare (Popular Democratic Front), the PCI stood permanently in opposition. For four decades it remained the great excluded, condemned by its ties to the Soviet Union and by the logic of the Atlantic alliance never to enter the government of the Republic.
The long opposition and the new course
Under Togliatti, and after his death in 1964 under his successors, the party sought to combine its role as a mass movement of the working class with a claim to be a party of national reform. It grew ever more distant from Moscow — Togliatti’s famous Memoriale di Yalta of 1964, his last testament, set out the vision of a polycentric communism no longer obedient to a single centre — and it came to represent, as Mammarella stressed, a form of left that was both part of the Western political tradition and, by its own account, beyond it.
The party’s great moment came in the 1970s under Enrico Berlinguer, its secretary from 1972. Faced with the anni di piombo (years of lead) and the subversive threat of the strategy of tension, Berlinguer proposed the compromesso storico (historic compromise) — an alliance of the two great popular parties, the PCI and the DC, to defend Italian democracy. He advanced also the eurocomunismo (Eurocommunism), a declaration of independence from Moscow in common with the French and Spanish communist parties. At the elections of 20 June 1976 the PCI advanced to within a few points of the DC, its greatest result, and entered the years of solidarietà nazionale (national solidarity), sustaining the government of Giulio Andreotti from outside. The project was cut short by the kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro in 1978, and the party’s long advance was never resumed.
The end of a party
The 1980s saw the PCI hold its great strength in the regions it governed and in the trade unions, but its moment of power had passed, and the party’s raison d’être — the Cold War exclusion it had both suffered and, in part, derived its identity from — began to dissolve. When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, Berlinguer’s successor led the party toward its transformation: in 1991 the Partito Comunista Italiano dissolved itself and was reborn as the Partito Democratico della Sinistra (Party of the Democratic Left), a party of the democratic left that abandoned the name and symbol of communism. The largest communist party in the West had, in the end, chosen to end itself rather than to outlive the cause it had been created to serve. For Gentiloni Silveri, the story of the PCI is inseparable from the story of the Republic itself — the excluded party whose very exclusion defined the political order, and whose transformation marked the closing of that order’s long season.

entities/jacques-chirac.title: Jacques Chirac (1932–2019)
entities/jacques-chirac.content:
Jacques Chirac (1932–2019)
No politician embodied the gaullisme of the long term after the General more completely than Jacques Chirac, the man who carried the gaullist tradition through the alternances and cohabitations of the Fifth Republic and finally brought it back to the presidency. His career was one of extraordinary patience and resilience — a young Prime Minister under Giscard d’Estaing, the founder of a reconstituted gaullist party, twice Prime Minister in cohabitation with a socialist President, and at last, on his third attempt, President of the Republic. Through it all he was the standard-bearer of the movement that had founded the régime, and its survivor into the age of a changed France.
The young prime minister
Chirac rose within the gaullist majority of the Fifth Republic, a young and energetic minister who became Prime Minister in 1974 under the newly elected Giscard d’Estaing. The collaboration was brief and tense; the two men of the majority, the reformist centrist and the impatient gaullist, fell out, and Chirac resigned in 1976 to build his own instrument. He founded the Rassemblement pour la République, the R.P.R., a movement that claimed the heritage of de Gaulle’s R.P.F. and set itself against the moderate course of the Giscard presidency — a gaullism of the street and of the militants, deliberately hard in its language.
Prime minister of the cohabitation
The R.P.R. and its allies won the legislative elections of March 1986, and since the socialist François Mitterrand remained President, France entered its first cohabitation — a divided executive in which a gaullist Prime Minister governed while a socialist President watched from the Élysée. Chirac presided over the first cohabitation of 1986 to 1988, a period of privatisations and economic liberalisation that tested the strange arrangement of the new régime, and he was the defeated candidate of the right when Mitterrand won re-election in 1988. He had failed for the presidency once; he was to fail again, in 1995 running his final campaign.
The presidency
In May 1995 Chirac at last won the presidency, elected over the socialist candidate on a programme of healing the fracture sociale (social divide) that the years of crisis had opened. His first term was marked by the confrontation with the great strikes of December 1995 — the grève par procuration in which the nation seemed to protest by proxy against the reforms of the government of Alain Juppé — and by the decision that redefined his presidency: the dissolution of the Assembly in April 1997, which produced a left-wing majority and drove him into a long cohabitation with the socialist Lionel Jospin that was to last until 2002. The second term, opened by the extraordinary re-election of 2002, saw him at the height of his authority — the President who had rallied the nation against the far right and who presided over the France of the early twenty-first century.
The re-election of 2002
The election of 2002 was the strangest and most decisive of his career. The first ballot on 21 April 2002 eliminated the socialist candidate and left Chirac facing Jean-Marie Le Pen of the Front national in the second round — a shock that rallied the whole of the political class to the incumbent as the guardian of the Republic. Re-elected with a crushing majority, Chirac emerged as the arbiter of a France that had recoiled from the far right, and his second term carried the republic into the age of the enlarged Europe. He left office in 2007, the longest-serving President after Mitterrand, the man who had carried the gaullisme of his youth through every twist of the Fifth Republic and outlived them all.
Chirac’s career was a mirror of the post-gaullist right — at once the heir of de Gaulle’s movement and its adapter, the champion of the fracture sociale and the architect of cohabitation governments, the man who had campaigned against the Europe of Maastricht and yet led France into the euro. He stands in the history of the Republic as the survivor, the gaullist who held the tradition together through the alternances of the age.

entities/jacques-delors.title: Jacques Delors (1925–2023)
entities/jacques-delors.content:
Jacques Delors (1925–2023)
If the founding of the Community belonged to the visionaries of 1950, its relaunch in the 1980s belonged to an architect — and the architect was Jacques Delors. Born in Paris in 1925, Delors came to the presidency of the European Commission in 1985 from a career at once syndicalist and technocratic, formed in the Christian trade union movement and in the service of the French state. He had been a banker at the Banque de France, a planner, a minister of economy and finance in the early years of the Mitterrand presidency, and one of the few French socialists of his generation who carried a reputation for fiscal discipline and economic realism. His ten years at the head of the Commission, from 1985 to 1995, were the most consequential of any president’s: the years in which the European Community, after the stagnation of the previous decade, resumed the forward march that carried it through the single-european-act-1986 to the maastricht-treaty-1992.
The relaunch and the single market
Delors took office at a moment when integration appeared to have run out of breath. The previous decade had been one of difficulties — the monetary turbulence of the 1970s, the “eurosclerosis” of the early 1980s, a Community whose project had narrowed and stalled. Delors’s Commission proposed to break the impasse with a great programme of completion: the abolition of the remaining barriers to the free movement of goods, services, capital and labour so as to create a genuine internal market by the end of 1992. The programme was given treaty form in the Single European Act of 1986, which extended qualified-majority voting and set the deadline of 1992. Moravcsik’s chapter on the relaunch treats the internal-market programme less as the Commission’s own creation imposed upon the governments than as the response to a convergence of national commercial interests, above all the preference of the French, German and British governments for market liberalisation. Yet whatever the deeper causes, it was Delors who gave the project a face and a deadline, and the revival of confidence that followed was inseparable from his presidency.
From the single market to Maastricht
The momentum of the internal market carried the Community further than its authors had first promised. Under Delors the monetary ambitions that had flickered since the Werner Report of 1970 were revived, and in 1989 his committee, the Delors Committee, produced the report that gave the design of Economic and Monetary Union — the three stages, the convergence criteria, the independent central bank, the single currency. The negotiations of 1990–91, concluded in the Maastricht Treaty agreed in December 1991, built upon that design a union at once monetary and political: the Community enlarged into a European Union of three pillars, with EMU at its heart, a modest common foreign and security policy, and cooperation in justice and home affairs. Moravcsik, again against the common geopolitical reading that Maastricht was above all the locking-in of a reunited Germany after 1989, argues that the treaty crowned the same converging national economic interests that had produced the earlier negotiations; the Cambridge history likewise presents Maastricht as the founding act of the EU. Through it all Delors remained the motor, the man who drove the governments forward and who articulated, in the phrase with which Moravcsik closes his study, that Europe should never become a “United States of Europe” but rather “a federation among strong nation-states” — a formula, the historian notes, that brought the most distinguished visionary of the 1980s back to the very view of robert-schuman with which the story had begun.

entities/jean-monnet.title: Jean Monnet (1888–1979)
entities/jean-monnet.content:
Jean Monnet (1888–1979)
Of all the figures who stood behind the building of Europe after 1945, none was more elusive than the man who disclaimed being the author of anything. Jean Monnet, born at Cognac in 1888 into a family of brandy merchants, was not a politician, not an elected deputy, not a professor. He was a planner, an organiser, a man of committees and commissariats, who preferred the anonymity of the administrator to the light of the tribune. Yet it was his hand that shaped the method by which Europe was actually put together — not through great federations proclaimed in one stroke, but through the patient, sector-by-sector pooling of sovereignty that came to be called functional integration. His contemporaries and the historians who followed have both called him one of the founding figures of the Community, and the Cambridge history of European integration counts him among the “visionaries” out of whose heads the architects of later decades built.
A planner, not a tribune
Monnet’s formation was the world of supply and coordination rather than of party politics. In two world wars he had served the cause of allied cooperation as an economic organiser — a commissioner of the Franco-British supply machinery in the first war, and the man who, after the fall of France in 1940, pressed the abortive project of an Anglo-French union upon Churchill. It was this wartime experience of pooled resources and joint planning that became his model. In the Liberation he produced the Plan de modernisation et d’équipement, the Monnet Plan for the reconstruction of France, and presided over its Commissariat général. The state, he believed, could guide the economy by planning; and the same conviction he carried onto the European stage. Where others dreamed of a United States of Europe, he proposed something more modest and, in his view, more workable: the creation of concrete institutions that would make war materially impossible by binding the economies of former enemies together.
The Schuman Plan and the Coal and Steel Community
It was as the invisible author of the most famous proposal of the early European movement that Monnet did his decisive work. On 9 May 1950 the French foreign minister robert-schuman read to the press the declaration, drafted in Monnet’s office with his collaborator, which proposed to place the coal and steel production of France and Germany under a common High Authority open to the other countries of Europe. The plan bore Schuman’s name and his authority, but its conception was Monnet’s — a way, as he saw it, to transcend the Franco-German conflict at its most sensitive point, the heavy industries of war. Out of it came the European Coal and Steel Community, the first of the Communities, whose High Authority Monnet himself led as its first president until 1955. The principle it enshrined, that sovereignty over a limited sector should be delegated to a supranational body, was the method that would define the whole subsequent course of integration. Moravcsik, whose study of the choice for Europe opens with a quotation from Monnet — “to succeed, always choose the path of least resistance” — treats the Community less as the fruit of federalist vision than as the product of converging national interest; but whatever weight one gives to the economic causes, it was Monnet who supplied the institutional form.
The method of the Community and the Action Committee
After leaving the presidency of the High Authority, Monnet withdrew from the institutions he had helped to create, but not from the cause. He established the Comité d’action pour les États-Unis d’Europe, the Action Committee for the United States of Europe, a pressure group of parties and trade unions through which he continued to push for further integration — from the relaunch of the 1950s that culminated in the Treaties of Rome to the later projects of the 1970s. Even as the Community grew, he insisted on the necessity of the method he had invented: integration advanced by small, technical, cumulative steps, each creating a new centre of decision whose existence made the next step necessary. In his famous phrase, Europe would be built through concrete achievements that first created a de facto solidarity. He died in 1979, having seen the Coal and Steel Community give way to the wider Common Market of the treaty-of-rome-1957, and having supplied the template that later architects of the single-european-act-1986 and the maastricht-treaty-1992 would still draw upon.

entities/joseph-stalin.title: Joseph Stalin (1879–1953)
entities/joseph-stalin.content:
Joseph Stalin (1879–1953)
The man who had commanded the Red Army to Berlin and taken the salute at the victory over Germany stood, in 1945, at the summit of a power such as no Russian ruler had ever held. Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin — Generalissimo of the Soviet Union, General Secretary of the Central Committee, Chairman of the Council of Ministers — ruled a country that had lost some twenty-seven million of its people in the Great Patriotic War yet emerged as one of the two great victors of the world conflict. The official biography of 1948, closed to his cult, declared him the disciple and successor of Lenin, “Stalin is Lenin today,” and in that formula the personality and the party had become one. His last eight years would be the years of reconstruction at home and of the opening of the Cold War abroad.
The postwar leader
Victory had brought the Soviet Union to a position of unprecedented prestige and reach. It had annexed the Baltic states, western Ukraine and Belorussia, extended its frontier westward, and planted its influence across the states of Central and Eastern Europe that had fallen under the Red Army’s shadow — the future people’s democracies of the mir sotsialisticheskoi sistemy (the world socialist system). Stalin presided over the passage of the country from war to peace: the demobilisation of the army, the repatriation of millions of Soviet citizens, and the laying down of the fourth five-year plan, the chetviortaya pyatiletka (fourth five-year plan) of 1946–1950, whose task he defined as the restoration of the ruined regions and of the prewar level of industry and agriculture, and then the surpassing of that level. The economy, its priority still heavy industry and the fuel, energy and metallurgical base, recovered with a speed that outran the plan; by 1947 the prewar volume of production had been regained, and by 1950 the target was exceeded. The personality cult, kult lichnosti, reached its height in these years, and Stalin’s word stood as the measure of all doctrine in the sciences and the arts alike.
The leader of the socialist camp
In foreign affairs Stalin stood at the head of the camp of peace against the “imperialists.” The wartime coalition of the anti-Hitler alliance broke apart as the western powers, in the Soviet reading, turned to open enmity and military preparation. The Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan and the North Atlantic Treaty appeared to the Soviet government as the stages of an “aggressive” policy of encirclement, answered by the consolidation of the eastern bloc — the formation of the Council of Mutual Economic Assistance (Sovet ekonomicheskoi vzaimopomoshchi, Comecon) and, in Stalin’s last years, the armed confrontation in Korea, where the Soviet Union supplied the Korean People’s Army and the Chinese volunteers and sent its air divisions to shield the north-east of China. Stalin, through his interviews with western journalists in 1946, pressed the language of peaceful coexistence and cooperation between the great powers, while the “cold war,” kholodnaya voina, hardened the division of Europe into two camps along the line that the western zone of Germany and the Soviet zone had carved through the old Reich.
The last years
The final years of his rule were marked by a renewed turn inward. The XIX Congress of the party, held in Moscow in October 1952, renamed the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Kommunisticheskaya partiya Sovetskogo Soyuza, the CPSU) and adopted a new Party Statute, though Stalin’s death forestalled the reforms that the reorganisation of the party organs had seemed to portend. He died on 5 March 1953, at the very opening of a new era of which he would not be part. The Kratkaya biografiya of 1948 had fixed the portrait of the model leader, teacher and Generalissimo; within three years of his death his successors would begin the great work of dismantling the very cult that had sustained him, and the name of Stalin would become the contested memory around which the whole subsequent history of the Soviet Union, and of the Cold War, would turn.

entities/juan-carlos-i.title: Juan Carlos I (b. 1938)
entities/juan-carlos-i.content:
Juan Carlos I (b. 1938)
He had been raised for a destiny he chose to enlarge. When the Cortes swore him in as King of Spain on 22 November 1975, two days after the death of the Caudillo who had designated him successor, Juan Carlos de Borbón inherited a dictatorship without its dictator. He was a young man of thirty-seven, unknown to the country he now ruled, a prince educated under the tutelage of the régime and married to a granddaughter of the old Pretender. No one could then be certain what he would make of the monarchy — least of all the franquista political class that had placed him on the throne in the expectation that he would be the caretaker of a continuation. That he chose instead to be the pivot of the democratic transicion-democratica-1975-78 is the fact on which the entire Spanish settlement turned.
The designated successor of francoism
He came to the throne as the very product of the system he would dismantle. Under the Law of Succession of 1947 and the designation of 1969, Franco had chosen the grandson of Alfonso XIII precisely because the prince’s education and loyalties seemed to offer the safest guarantee that the régime would survive its founder. Juan Carlos spent his formative years in Spain under the watch of the Movimiento, groomed at the military academies and tutored in the doctrine of the Estado. His father, Don Juan, the Pretender who stood for the restoration of the traditional liberal monarchy, had been passed over in his favour — a choice that divided the monarchist world. The prince who took the oath of allegiance to the Leyes Fundamentales at his proclamation was, in the eyes of the old guard, one of their own. That same training was precisely what fitted him for the part he came to play: a king raised inside the régime could command the confidence of its institutions, and turn that confidence to ends the old guard had never intended.
Choosing to be a great king rather than a small Caudillo
From the first moment, Tusell observed, Juan Carlos chose to be a great king rather than a small Caudillo. Where a timid monarch might have entrenched himself behind the franquista inheritance, this one perceived that the monarchy’s only future lay in anchoring the legitimacy of a state that was ceasing to be Franco’s. The monarchical institution became a distinctive and irreplaceable trait of the Spanish Transition. Its function was not decorative: in any transition the gravest danger is the break of legitimacy between the vanished dictatorship and the democracy not yet consolidated, and the Crown supplied the instrument to bridge that gap — without parallel in the other Mediterranean transitions of the third wave. Juan Carlos deployed his authority to set the reform in motion, replacing a prime minister who would not move and installing the man who would. In the summer of 1976 he engineered the resignation of Arias Navarro and, guided by Torcuato Fernández Miranda, appointed adolfo-suarez — a young reformist minister of the régime whom the franquista Cortes would accept — to carry the political reform forward.
The crisis of 23 February 1981
The full measure of the monarchy’s utility was revealed at the moment of gravest danger, the 23-f-coup-1981 of 23 February 1981. When Colonel Antonio Tejero seized the Congress of Deputies with a squad of Guardia Civil officers, and the coup spread to the Captaincy-General of Valencia under Milans del Bosch, the fate of the young democracy hung on the king. That night Juan Carlos, in uniform, broadcast to the nation, refusing the conspirators the cover of his authority and commanding the loyalty of the armed forces to the democratic order. The intervention was decisive: the conspiracy collapsed when it could not claim the king, and the institutions survived. The defeat of the coup strengthened rather than weakened the regime — dissatisfaction with the democracy, already low, fell further in its wake, and the monarchy emerged from the crisis with its prestige at its height, identified henceforth with the defence of the constitutional order it had helped to create.
The reign’s arc
For a decade and more he presided over the consolidation of the new democracy, a constitutional king under the constitution-1978 who had shepherded the country from the death of the dictator to membership in the democratic West. The prestige he earned in the Transition, and above all in the hours of 23-F, was real and long-lived. It was a capital spent slowly over the decades that followed, as the reign passed from the exaltation of the constitutional years into a longer, unheroic maturity — a monarchy increasingly separated from the democratic legitimacy it had once personified, its standing eroded by the political and personal scandals that would eventually, in the second decade of the new century, drive him into abdication and exile. The king who had chosen greatness at the moment of the Transition remained, in the historiography, the indispensable hinge of the Spanish settlement — the prince raised to preserve Francoism who instead gave the country over to the democracy the dictator had feared.

entities/kgb.title: KGB (Committee for State Security, 1954-1991)
entities/kgb.content:
KGB (Committee for State Security, 1954-1991)
The Committee for State Security — Комитет государственной безопасности, in its initials the КГБ (KGB) — was the sword and shield of the Soviet state, the agency that guarded the revolution’s gains against enemies within and without. Created in 1954 in the reorganisation that followed the death of joseph-stalin, it was the successor to a long line of organs of state security that ran back to the Cheka of the revolutionary years; and it stood, in the architecture of the system, as the guardian of the political order of the cpsu and the collector of the information on which the leadership governed. Its mandate was enormous: foreign intelligence, counter-intelligence, the protection of the state frontier, the fight against subversion, the surveillance of that small but persistent current of opinion the authorities judged hostile to the state.
The organ and the system
In the Soviet idiom the KGB was most often called simply органы (the organs), a name that conveyed both its place at the heart of power and its diffused, quietly omnipresent character. It was a ministry-like structure of committees and territorial directorates, a professional bureaucracy of officers whose reach extended across the whole society. Under the long chairmanship of yuri-andropov from 1967 to 1982, the Committee acquired its mature, imposing form — an agency that was at once a vast security establishment and, increasingly, an instrument for the renewal of the party itself. Andropov, ambassador to Hungary during the events of 1956 and a man of exceptional intelligence and severity, made the KGB an arm of the leadership’s discipline, in foreign affairs and at home alike.
The Committee’s work was not only clandestine. A note of 11 October 1972 from the chairman of the KGB and the Procurator General of the USSR to the Central Committee described in plain, administrative language the preventive labour the organs performed: the exposure and профилактика (prevention) of groups of a “politically harmful character” organised by nationalists, revisionists and other anti-Soviet elements. Over the five preceding years, the note reported, some 3,096 such groupings had been uncovered across Moscow, the Baltic and Caucasian republics and beyond, and thousands of those drawn into them warned against the consequences of continuing. It proposed that the organs be empowered to issue official written cautions in the name of the authorities, demanding the cessation of politically harmful activity. This was the security state speaking in its own calm, bureaucratic voice: the defence of the social order was conceived as a labour of administration as much as of punishment.
Security and everyday life
The place of the organs in late Soviet life was more subtle and more pervasive than the catalogue of denunciations might suggest. The ethnographic observer of the last Soviet generation records that for most people the KGB was not a looming terror but a constant, half-felt presence woven into ordinary existence. In the café culture of Leningrad, the Сайгон (Saigon) and its milieu, the habitués knew that an undercover officer might sit at the next table — and, by and large, did not greatly mind, since those who neither spoke of politics nor acted did not fear the attention. The state, indeed, both enabled and bounded such spaces: the Leningrad rock club of 1981 was established under the patronage of the Komsomol and the quiet oversight of the organs, which treated the rock milieu as a lens through which to observe the moods of the young. Even the guide at the state tourist agency Интурист (Intourist) found that the идеологический отчёт (ideological report) she filed after escorting foreign guests had to be written in a special room deep in the building — in effect, a small station of the Committee — yet the officials she dealt with were bureaucrats, and her encounter with them, however distasteful, was a formality of the system rather than a sentence. The KGB was feared, respected, resented and shrugged at, all at once: a fixture of the Soviet world as ordinary as the queue, as fixed as the plan.
The Committee at the summit
By the last years of leonid-brezhnev the organs had risen to the very summit of the state. Andropov, at the head of the KGB for fifteen years, succeeded Brezhnev as General Secretary on his death in November 1982, carrying the discipline of the security service into the renewal he attempted — the struggle against the shadow economy and the corruption of the trading and distributive network, greeted by the population with sympathy. The Committee had grown from a guardian of the system into a path to its leadership. In the Soviet order the KGB stood as the final guarantor of stability, the organ charged with protecting the revolution’s achievements; and when that order came to an end in 1991, it was the Committee for State Security that dissolved with it, its great buildings and its immense archive passing, along with the system itself, into history.

entities/konrad-adenauer.title: Konrad Adenauer (1876–1967)
entities/konrad-adenauer.content:
Konrad Adenauer (1876–1967)
When the Federal Republic of Germany was brought to life in the summer of 1949, the man summoned to preside over it was already in his seventy-third year — a Catholic Rhinelander, a former Lord Mayor of Cologne, a politician who had survived the Weimar Republic, the Nazi seizure of power and the wreck of 1945 to become, almost by the force of his own obstinacy, the architect of West Germany. Konrad Adenauer, who had sat in the Prussian Herrenhaus under the Kaiser and had been dismissed from his Cologne office by the Nazis in 1933, carried into the office of Federal Chancellor a generation of experience, a deep attachment to the Rhineland and to the Catholic West, and an unshakeable conviction about the direction his new state must take: out of the middle of Europe and into the West.
The father of the republic
Adenauer’s rise to the chancellorship was the outcome of the peculiar circumstances of the occupation years. Restored as Lord Mayor of Cologne by the Americans in 1945 and then deposed again by the British, he threw himself into the founding of a new party, the Christlich-Demokratische Union (Christian Democratic Union), which was to unite Catholics and Protestants across the old confessional divide. In the parliamentary council that drafted the Grundgesetz (Basic Law) he presided as its president, and in the first Bundestag election of August 1949 he led the CDU to a narrow plurality. On 15 September 1949, by a majority of one vote over the Social Democratic candidate, the Bundestag elected him Federal Chancellor. The father of the Bundesrepublik, the man who had done more than any other to shape the Basic Law, now took command of it.
Westintegration
Adenauer’s governing idea, which dominated the fourteen years of his chancellorship, was the Westbindung — the binding of the Federal Republic to the West. Germany, he held, could not float in the middle of Europe, torn between East and West; only by tying itself firmly to the Atlantic community and to Western Europe could it regain sovereignty, security and standing. This meant a policy of unhesitating alignment with the United States and with France, an acceptance of the division of Germany as the price of that alignment, and a turning of the back upon the temptations of neutrality and of a reunited but unattached Germany. It was a policy pursued with a single-mindedness that infuriated his critics — the Social Democrats and their leader Kurt Schumacher, who warned that Western integration would cement the division of the nation — but Adenauer held his course, convinced that German unity could be won only through the West and in freedom, and not at all in the meantime.
The social market economy and the Western alliance
The economic foundation of this project was the sozialmarktwirtschaft (social market economy) entrusted to his Economics Minister ludwig-erhard, whose currency reform and liberalisation of prices had already unleashed the recovery that came to be called the economic miracle. Politics and economics worked in the same direction: prosperity bound West Germans to the new state and to the West. Adenauer’s diplomacy sealed the alliance in a series of great treaties. The Federal Republic entered the Council of Europe, and in 1951 became a founding member of the European Coal and Steel Community alongside France, Italy and the Benelux states — the first step in the construction of a united Europe that the Chancellor embraced as the surest anchor for his country. Adenauer, as Andrew Moravcsik observes, was a European because Europe was the vehicle of Germany’s return; he conceived the German interest and the European interest as one and the same.
Reconciliation with France
Nowhere was Adenauer’s Westpolitik more consequential than in the reconciliation with France. Against the ancient enmity of the two nations he set a personal partnership with robert-schuman, the French foreign minister who proposed the pooling of coal and steel, and with the architect of that plan, jean-monnet. The Deutsch-französische Freundschaft was sealed in January 1963 in the Élysée Treaty, signed with General de Gaulle in Paris — a treaty of friendship and cooperation that crowned a decade of Franco-German partnership and made the two former enemies the motor of European construction. Adenauer, the Rhinelander, looked West across the Rhine as naturally as he distrusted the East.
Sovereignty and rearmament, 1955
The culmination of Westintegration came in 1955. With the ratification of the Paris Treaties the occupation statute was lifted and the Federal Republic acquired the sovereignty of a normal state; in the same year it joined NATO, and rearmament — the Wiederbewaffnung — began within the framework of the Western alliance. Adenauer had been obliged to watch the failure of the European Defence Community in 1954, which had been designed to rearm the Germans within a European army; its defeat by the French National Assembly forced the alternative, a German contribution to NATO, which he accepted. In the words that defined his diplomacy, sovereignty was won, in his view, not by the four powers alone but by the strength and loyalty of the West. Germany was to be rearmed, but rearmed as a member of a community that would keep it safe from itself and from the East.
The later years and the European vision
By the end of the 1950s Adenauer’s grip on the chancellorship was contested. His age, his authoritarian style, and the Spiegel affair of 1962 eroded his standing, and in October 1963 he was obliged at last to hand over the office to his Economics Minister, Ludwig Erhard. He retired to his villa at Rhöndorf above the Rhine, where he died on 19 April 1967 at the age of ninety-one. He left behind a state that bore his stamp as completely as the Fifth Republic bore that of de Gaulle: a Federal Republic firmly anchored in the West, reconciled with France, committed to Europe and to the Atlantic, and prosperous under the social market economy he had entrusted to Erhard. To his successors — Willy Brandt, Helmut Schmidt, Helmut Kohl — the path he had chosen remained the given of German politics. The Alte, the “Old Man” of German politics, had made the long road to the West the founding direction of the Federal Republic.

entities/konstantin-chernenko.title: Konstantin Chernenko (1911-1985)
entities/konstantin-chernenko.content:
Konstantin Chernenko (1911-1985)
The interlude between the stern reformer Andropov and the young Gorbachev was filled by a man of the old guard, a career apparatchik who had spent his life in the shadow of Leonid Brezhnev and who came to power only when the Soviet leadership, hesitating at the threshold of change, reached once more for a known and settled face. Konstantin Chernenko was General Secretary of the Central Committee for barely a year. The historians who recorded his brief tenure wrote that he was distinguished by firmness and consistency in making decisions, yet left no serious trace in history — he came to the supreme post too old and too ill, and remained at the head of the party too short a time to do more than preside over the passage between two ages.
The servant of the machine
Chernenko’s origins lay deep in the ordinary life of the country. He was born in 1911 in a peasant family in Siberia, and his whole career was made within the party apparatus. For many years he served as a close assistant to Brezhnev, one of those figures of the inner circle who work beside the leader without stepping before him. In 1976 he was elected a secretary of the Central Committee, and his rise was bound to that of his patron: when Brezhnev died in November 1982, Chernenko became the second man in the leadership of the party, standing behind the new General Secretary Andropov. He embodied the conservatism and continuity of the Brezhnev generation — a man of the machine through and through, trusted by the apparatus precisely because he promised no surprises.
A year at the summit
After the brief rule of Andropov, who died in February 1984, Chernenko was elected General Secretary of the Central Committee and then Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet, head of state as well as of the party. His tenure was a holding action, a return to the settled, cautious ways of the age that was already passing. He was not the man to carry forward the momentum of reform that Andropov had begun to set in motion; the economists and the search for ускорение (acceleration) continued beneath him, but the impetus was blunted. Yet even in the immobility of that year a decisive current was at work. It was during Chernenko’s rule that the reformist wing of the leadership finally crystallised and strengthened, and its leader was the young Secretary of the Central Committee, Gorbachev — a man who stood for the future against which Chernenko’s appointment had, for a moment, seemed a bulwark.
The succession
Chernenko died on 10 March 1985, his illness expected by all who watched the ageing leadership. Less than a day later the Plenum of the Central Committee elected Gorbachev head of the party. The brevity of Chernenko’s tenure, and the sequence of deaths that had struck the Soviet leadership through the first half of the decade — Brezhnev in 1982, Andropov in 1984, Chernenko in 1985 — laid bare the crisis of succession at the heart of the system, the gerontocracy of the stagnation that had left an entire generation to grow old at the summit. Chernenko was the last of that generation. His death cleared the way for the youngest and most vigorous leader the party had chosen in years, and for the course of reform that was to sweep the system away. In the memory of the era he is the caretaker, the man of the interregnum, remembered above all for having been succeeded.

entities/leonid-brezhnev.title: Leonid Brezhnev (1906-1982)
entities/leonid-brezhnev.content:
Leonid Brezhnev (1906-1982)
For nearly two decades Leonid Brezhnev stood at the head of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, the longest tenure of any General Secretary save Stalin himself. The party historians who recorded his epoch set his life against the great transformation of his country: born in 1906 in the working-class family of a metallurgist in the industrial town of Kamenskoye on the Dnieper, he came of age in the labour of the factory and the fury of the civil war, joined the Komsomol in 1923 and the party in 1931, and rose through the ranks as the Soviet state built socialism, fought the war, and remade the world after it. He was, in the words of the official history, a man of the generation that built the Soviet system — and he came to personify its maturity, its confidence, and at last its weariness.
The rise and the October 1964 Plenum
Brezhnev’s ascent ran through the party machine itself. After the war he rose to prominence as a party secretary in the restored Ukraine and in the Central Asian and eastern regions; he shared in the great political struggles of the age, standing alongside alexei-kosygin and the others against the anti-party group of 1957, and entering the top leadership under nikita-khrushchev. When Khrushchev was removed in October 1964, charged with волюнтаризм и субъективизм (voluntarism and subjectivism) for his improvident reorganisations, the Plenum of the Central Committee elected Brezhnev First Secretary of the party — from 1966 General Secretary — while Kosygin took the premiership. The arrangement restored what the party called the ленинские нормы партийной жизни (Leninist norms of party life), an end to the concentration of both supreme offices in one pair of hands. Those who sat in the hall remembered the relief of that moment: a warm, kindly man with thick brows had taken the helm, and promised the party an orderly, settled life after the restless upheavals of his predecessor.
The era of developed socialism
Under Brezhnev the party proclaimed that Soviet society had entered the stage of развитой социализм (developed socialism), a mature socialist society in which the old contradictions had been resolved and the country could advance without conflict toward communism. The claim rested on real foundations — the powerful industrial economy built in the preceding decades, the achievement of a society that in the official account had grown socially homogeneous, with a new historical community of people, the советский народ (Soviet people). The XXIII, XXIV, XXV and XXVI Congresses marked the course, and the Constitution of 1977, adopted under Brezhnev’s chairmanship of the Constitutional Commission, enshrined the developed socialist society in the fundamental law, fixing the leading role of the cpsu and proclaiming the общенародное государство (all-people’s state). Economic development continued apace — the eighth five-year plan of 1966-1970 was the most successful of the late Soviet period — and in industry the Kosygin reform of 1965 sought to make the planned-economy work more efficiently by loosening its grip from the centre.
The Peace Programme and detente
Brezhnev’s foreign policy was written into the party’s programme as the Программа мира (Programme of Peace), proclaimed at the XXIV Congress in 1971 and carried forward by the XXV and XXVI Congresses. It was a policy of мирное сосуществование (peaceful coexistence) pursued from a position of strength: by the late 1960s the Soviet Union had achieved военно-стратегический паритет (military-strategic parity) with the United States, and the leadership judged the correlation of forces in the world to have shifted in favour of socialism. On this basis Moscow pursued the разрядка (détente) that eased the confrontation between the blocs. Brezhnev signed the SALT I treaty with President Nixon in Moscow in May 1972, the first arms-limitation agreement in history, and with it the agreement on the prevention of nuclear war; the 1973 visit to Washington, and the accords that followed, marked a turn from confrontation toward relaxation. The culmination came on 1 August 1975 at Helsinki, where Brezhnev, with the heads of thirty-three European states and of the United States and Canada, signed the Final Act of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, a great codification of the principles of inter-state relations. Meanwhile the Soviet Union, carrying out the Programme of Peace, supported the national-liberation struggles of the developing world — the decolonisation of the Portuguese empire in Africa, the friendship treaty with India, the solidarity with the peoples fighting for their independence — strengthening the world-socialist-system of which it stood at the head.
The stagnation of the late period
The long Brezhnev years carried within them a growing immobility. From the late 1960s the campaign to extol Brezhnev had begun, the inflation of his person into a quiet cult that the party apparatus itself promoted; he accumulated honours, and the portraits and orders multiplied while the leadership aged around him. The reformist vigour of the 1960s faded as the 1970s wore on: the Kosygin reform was wound down, the plans came to be fulfilled at slowing rates, and the economy, buoyed by the great oil and gas revenues of Siberia, grew ever more dependent on the export of raw materials. The party’s self-description of a harmonious developed socialism encouraged, in the judgement of its critics, a complacent view of reality. The regime that had opened toward the West in the early seventies found its hopes of durable detente disappointed by the turn of the decade; the late period is remembered in the historical literature by the term застой (stagnation). Brezhnev died on 10 November 1982, still in office, and was succeeded first by yuri-andropov, the long-time chairman of the kgb. He left behind a state that had reached the summit of its power and its global reach — and one that had begun, almost imperceptibly, to stand still.

entities/ludwig-erhard.title: Ludwig Erhard (1897–1977)
entities/ludwig-erhard.content:
Ludwig Erhard (1897–1977)
The prosperity of the Federal Republic had a single, unlikely author: a corpulent, cigar-smoking Bavarian economist, trained in commerce and in the statistical offices of the Nuremberg industry, who had spent the war years in a private institute thinking about money, prices and the reform of the German economy. Ludwig Erhard was the architect of the sozialmarktwirtschaft (social market economy) and the man whose name became inseparable from the economic miracle. Where Adenauer gave the new state its politics and its place in the West, Erhard gave it its wealth.
The currency reform of 1948
Erhard’s moment came in the summer of 1948, before the Federal Republic existed. As director of the administration for the economy in the Anglo-American Bizone, he prepared the great monetary operation that was to cut through the dead weight of the Reichsmark — a currency so debased by the inflation and black market of the post-war years that the economy had sunk into a barter of cigarettes and coffee. On 20 June 1948 the Western allies introduced the Währungsreform (currency reform): the old currency was called in and replaced by the Deutsche Mark, each citizen receiving a small allocation of the new money and the savings and fortunes of the past sharply devalued in the process. Against the express orders of the Allied authorities, who still favoured rationing and control, Erhard simultaneously declared the freeing of prices and the end of rationing in the following day. It was an act of audacity — a bet that, given sound money and freed prices, German enterprise and German workers would respond with a flood of production. The gamble, as the recovery of the following months showed, paid off.
The Economics Minister
When the Federal Republic was founded in 1949, Erhard entered the cabinet of Konrad Adenauer as Economics Minister, a post he was to hold for fourteen years. His doctrine, elaborated from the ideas of the Ordoliberalen — the Freiburg school of Walter Eucken and its insistence on a market order guaranteed and policed by the state — held that the market, not the plan, was the instrument of both prosperity and freedom. The state’s task was not to direct the economy but to create and enforce the Ordnung (order): stable money, open competition, and the legal framework within which free enterprise could flourish. Against the Keynesian temptations and the dirigiste habits of the age, Erhard preached the soziale Marktwirtschaft — a market economy, but one with a social conscience, tempered by competition policy and by the social measures that would cushion the weak.
The Wirtschaftswunder
The years that followed made Erhard’s reputation as the Vater des Wirtschaftswunders, the father of the economic miracle. The recovery exceeded all expectations: within a decade the Federal Republic had overtaken its pre-war output, unemployment fell to levels the occupation years had made unthinkable, and the German economy became the strongest in Europe, exporting machinery, cars and chemicals across a world hungry for them. The new currency, the freed market, the inflow of refugees and labour from the East, and the demand of the Korean War boom combined into a surge of growth that transformed West German society. Erhard’s claim that prosperity would dissolve the conflicts of the class society seemed, in the 1950s, to be borne out: the consumer’s world of the Wirtschaftswunder — the Volkswagen, the holidays abroad, the full shop window — became the daily proof that the Federal Republic worked.
The Chancellor, 1963–1966
Adenauer, who had never fully trusted his unconventional minister, resisted Erhard’s candidacy for the succession, but public opinion forced the change. In October 1963 Erhard became Federal Chancellor, the most popular man in the country and the very emblem of its success. The chancellorship proved harder than the ministry. The long boom began to cool, the costs of the welfare state rose, and the easy growth of the miracle years gave way to the first rumblings of recession and of the Konjunktur problems of the late 1960s. Erhard, a man of ideas rather than of party intrigue, was ill-suited to the rough management of coalition politics, and in December 1966 he was obliged to resign, displaced by the Grand Coalition of the CDU and the SPD under Kurt Georg Kiesinger. He died on 5 May 1977, remembered above all as the economist who had given the Federal Republic its prosperity and its self-confidence — the minister who, by the courage of a single June day in 1948, had set the miracle in motion.

entities/manuel-fraga.title: Manuel Fraga Iribarne (1922-2012)
entities/manuel-fraga.content:
Manuel Fraga Iribarne (1922-2012)
Manuel Fraga Iribarne was the most intellectual of the franquista politicians and the one whose career most fully spanned the régime and the democracy that followed it. As minister of information and tourism from 1962 to 1969 he was the principal voice of the apertura, the cautious opening of the régime toward the modern world, and the author of the new Press Law that loosened the censorship. In the Transition he sought to channel the franquista right into a democratic party, founding Alianza Popular, and he went on to a long public life as minister, party leader and president of the Junta of Galicia. His trajectory — from architect of a limited opening under Franco to founder of a democratic right — makes him a revealing figure of how the personnel of the old régime made their way into the new order.
The man of the apertura
Fraga belonged to the generation of franquista administrators formed after the Civil War, better managers and men of more bureaucratic formation than the old Falangist ideologues — precisely the type that the régime, in the 1960s, increasingly promoted. Appointed to the Ministry of Information and Tourism in 1962, he set about modernising the image of the régime abroad and loosening its grip at home. The great instrument of this policy was the Press Law of 1966, which replaced the system of prior censorship with a regime of responsibility in which the press could publish subject to punishment after the fact — a genuine opening, though one whose limits the ministry could still enforce. Fraga understood that a régime seeking to survive the development of its own society had to allow the cultural world a margin; the apertura he personified was a loosening of controls without a substantial transformation of the régime. It was in these same years that the cultural and journalistic world began, in the space that opening created, to advance Spain in a modernising sense.
The technocratic and political struggles
The years of the apertura were also years of internal struggle within the régime, and Fraga was at its centre. His November 1965 remarks to the foreign press — remarks that seemed to question the direction of the régime and were remembered against him — entangled him in the factional quarrels that the aging Franco arbitrated. The arrival of October 1969 and the monocolor government grouped around Carrero Blanco marked the triumph of the technocratic current over the reformist and Falangist voices; Fraga left the ministry and the immediate circle of power. In the late régime he remained a figure of the moderate right, his name spoken among the reformists who sought an exit from a dictatorship that had lost its course, while the búnker distrusted his liberalism and the opposition doubted his sincerity.
Fraga in the Transition
At Franco’s death, Fraga was a minister in the first government of the king — the government of Arias Navarro, whose impossible reformism Fraga’s own restless energy could not save. He was one of the ministers surprised and indignant when the substitution of the summer of 1976 passed over him and Areilza in favour of the younger Adolfo Suárez. Out of office, he set about organising the democratic right. Alianza Popular, founded in 1976, gathered the franquista heirs and the conservative notables around his leadership, seeking to convert the continuity of the old right into a legitimate force within the new democracy. Through the constituent years and the consolidation of the régime of 1978, AP was the principal right-wing alternative, though it laboured under the weight of its franquista origins and the memory of the régime’s repressive past. Fraga’s own electoral fortunes waxed and waned — he lost the presidency of the party after the disappointments of the early 1980s, and returned to prominence as the long president of the Junta of Galicia, the old Africanist and minister at last a democratic regional leader. In the verdict of the historians, he stands as the figure who tried to make a modern conservative party out of the material of franquismo — the reformist who opened the régime and, when it fell, helped carry its inheritance into the democracy without ever fully escaping the shadow of the years in which his political formation was made.

entities/mikhail-gorbachev.title: Mikhail Gorbachev (b. 1931)
entities/mikhail-gorbachev.content:
Mikhail Gorbachev (b. 1931)
The man who set out to reform the Soviet Union and ended by presiding over its dissolution came to the summit of power in March 1985 as the youngest leader the Kremlin had known since Stalin. Mikhail Sergeyevich Gorbachev, born in 1931 in the village of Privolnoye in the Stavropol region, was a child of the collectivised countryside, a man formed in the party itself — a graduate of the law faculty of Moscow State University, a party secretary in Stavropol, a Central Committee secretary, and from 1982 a member of the Politburo under the ailing old guard that preceded him. He arrived proclaiming not the abandonment of the system but its renewal, and he spoke to a country that, after the long застой (zastoy, stagnation) of the Brezhnev years, was ready to listen. Few of those who watched him in the first months, and fewer still among those he would set against the old structures, could have foreseen the direction his перестройка (perestroika, ‘restructuring’) would take — or where it would end.
The new course and uskorenie
Gorbachev’s first impulse was acceleration, not demolition. The watchword he carried to the party in 1985 was ускорение (uskorenie, ‘acceleration’) — a quickening of the economic and social development of the country within the existing system. On his trip to Leningrad in May 1985 he spoke openly, and the country was startled by the new frankness; the leaders were to tell the people the truth, and the people were to work harder. He launched a dramatic struggle against drunkenness, the great social scourge of the last years, as the first of his campaigns, and he swept away the old men who had surrounded Brezhnev, bringing in his own generation — the foreign-affairs official Eduard Shevardnadze, the economist Nikolai Ryzhkov. The XXVII Party Congress of 1986 endorsed the course. But the economy did not respond to exhortation, and the young team in the Kremlin found that the machine it had inherited could not be made to accelerate. The remedies attempted within the old frames failed; the reform was to be pushed further and deeper than anyone had planned, and within a year the word on every lip had changed from uskorenie to perestroika.
Glasnost and the road to democratisation
The decisive turn was the opening of speech. The demand that the country should be told the truth became гласность (glasnost, ‘openness’), and glasnost proved to be a force the party could not confine to economics. It let the accumulated lies of the past be spoken — the history of the system, the crimes of its leaders, the failures of its plans — and it allowed, for the first time in two generations, genuine political life. Pikhoya, writing as both historian and witness of the age, records how the managed democratisation of 1987–1989 slid into a democratisation the authorities could no longer manage. The manifesto of Nina Andreyeva, an early cry against the reform, was answered and buried; Yeltsin’s letter of protest to Gorbachev and the scandal at the plenum of 1987 split the leadership in public; the question of Nagorny Karabakh and the republics’ cry of “вплоть до выхода” (vplot do vykhoda, ‘up to secession’) brought the nationality question, long suppressed, roaring into the centre of politics. In 1989 Gorbachev created the Congress of People’s Deputies of the USSR, the first genuinely contested elections in Soviet history, and the cameras of the First Congress brought the arguments of the deputies into every home. Glasnost, Pikhoya concludes, was the point of no return — the moment at which the reform of the system became the unmaking of it.
The end of the Cold War and the collapse of authority
Abroad, the new course dismantled the confrontation of forty years. Gorbachev proclaimed новое мышление (novoye myshleniye, ‘new thinking’) in foreign policy — the recognition that in the nuclear age the old categories of class struggle could no longer govern the world, and that the security of all was the security of each. He withdrew from the ideological export of revolution, accepted the revolutions in Eastern Europe in 1989 without firing a shot, and presided over the reunification of Germany and the end of the Cold War. The statesmen of the West honoured him for it; at home, the recognition of defeat corroded the regime’s authority further. By 1990 he had replaced the old party supremacy with the office of President of the USSR, elected by the Congress, hoping to anchor his authority in the state rather than the party; he assembled the Russian reform programme of the “500 Days” and then abandoned it; he faced the election of boris-yeltsin as President of the RSFSR in June 1991 and the rise of the Russian factor he could no longer contain. Pikhoya, a leading archivist of the age, argues that the party had been the core of the political system, and that once its authority and its monopoly were broken, the union of republics it had held together could not stand. Yurchak, the anthropologist of the last Soviet generation, saw in these same years the destruction from within of the authoritative discourse of the party — the very speech by which the system had once constituted itself suddenly emptied of belief.
The putsch and the resignation
In August 1991 the old guard struck. The State Committee for the State of Emergency, the ГКЧП (GKChP), attempted to seize power while Gorbachev was held under house arrest at his holiday dacha at Foros in the Crimea. The coup collapsed in three days before the resistance of Yeltsin and the crowds of Moscow; Gorbachev returned to a Kremlin whose authority had been destroyed, and whose power now lay with the Russian President. He struggled to preserve a union, to keep something of the Soviet state alive, but the republics had ceased to believe in him or in the centre. On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus met at Belovezhskaya Pushcha and declared the Soviet Union at an end; on 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned as President of the USSR, and the red flag was lowered over the Kremlin. The reformer who had intended to renew socialism had instead presided over its end. To the historians of his own country he remains a figure of deepest controversy — to some the man who freed the nations of the empire, to others the destroyer of a great power — and the story of his perestroika is inseparable from the story of perestroika-1985-91 itself.

entities/nicolas-sarkozy.title: Nicolas Sarkozy (1955– )
entities/nicolas-sarkozy.content:
Nicolas Sarkozy (1955– )
The President who took the Élysée in 2007 announced a break with the entire manner of his predecessors. Nicolas Sarkozy, the Minister of the Interior who had made his reputation on firmness toward the banlieues, presented himself as the man who would finally break with the immobilism of the old right — the standard-bearer of a droite décomplexée (an “uninhibited” right), unashamed of its language and its programme. His presidency, the first quinquennat (five-year term) under the shortened mandate adopted by referendum in 2000, was to be consumed in large part by the world financial crisis that broke upon Europe within months of his taking office.
The right “uninhibited”
Sarkozy came to power at the head of a reconstituted majority, the Union pour un mouvement populaire, the U.M.P., that had carried the gaullist and centrist right since 2002. He was a man of energy and of rupture, the political heir who set himself deliberately apart from the measured gaullisme of Jacques Chirac. His election in May 2007 over the socialist Ségolène Royal promised a presidency of movement — of work, of authority, of a France restored to the first rank of the world. The sarkozysme of those first months was that of a right determined to govern without embarrassment, to speak plainly, to shake the settled order of the state.
The presidency and the crisis
The promise of rupture ran headlong into the crise of 2008. The financial crisis that broke in the autumn of 2008, spreading from the American banks to the whole world economy, struck France as it struck its neighbours, and the presidency was redefined by it. Sarkozy, who had proclaimed a break with the old ways, found himself the crisis manager of a state called upon to support its banks, to hold its people against unemployment, to negotiate a European response to a storm that no single country could master. The loi des marchés (the law of the markets) that pressed upon the French state in this era made the President of the Republic, for all his energy, seem at once indispensable and powerless.
The end of the quinquennat
His presidency, absorbed by the management of the crisis and by a style that divided the country, ran its five-year course to the election of 2012. The quinquennat had shortened the office de Gaulle had conceived for seven years, and the rhythm of the presidential election now governed French politics more tightly than ever; the break with the gaullisme of the long mandate was itself a marker of the age. Defeated in 2012 by the socialist François Hollande, Sarkozy left the Élysée as the symbol of a right transformed — the “uninhibited” conservatism of the early twenty-first century, the presidency overtaken by the great crisis of the globalised economy that his own language of rupture had promised, but could not command.
Sarkozy’s place in the Fifth Republic is that of the rupture announced and then undone by circumstance. He broke the settled manner of the gaullisme he inherited, shortened and quickened the presidency, and governed France through the worst economic crisis since the Trente Glorieuses ended — the man of the droite décomplexée at the helm of a state besieged by the markets.

entities/nikita-khrushchev.title: Nikita Khrushchev (1894–1971)
entities/nikita-khrushchev.content:
Nikita Khrushchev (1894–1971)
The man who was to inherit Stalin’s power was in many ways his most faithful servant. Nikita Sergeyevich Khrushchev — born in 1894, a locksmith of the Donbas pits and mines, a fervent Stalinist who had led the Moscow party organisation and the Central Committee of the Ukrainian Communist Party through the terrible purges of 1937–1938 — rose in the last years of Stalin’s life to the innermost circle of the succession. It was Khrushchev who, within three years of Stalin’s death, would tear down the cult he had once served, and who would give his name to an entire decade of Soviet and world history: the ottepel (the thaw).
The road to the leadership
Stalin died on 5 March 1953. In the struggle for the succession the first round went to Georgy Malenkov, who became Chairman of the Council of Ministers, and to Lavrenty Beria, the head of the security organs, who was arrested in June 1953 and shot as an “enemy of the party and the Soviet people” — an arrest organised, significantly, at the instigation of Khrushchev himself and Malenkov. The fall of Beria, whose “criminal encroachment” on party leadership of society was the heart of the accusation, cleared the way for the party apparatus that Khrushchev represented. In September 1953 he was elected First Secretary of the Central Committee of the CPSU. From that base he pressed the attack on Malenkov, who was removed as head of government in February 1955 and replaced by Nikolai Bulganin, and then on the “anti-party group” of Malenkov, Molotov and Kaganovich, defeated at the June 1957 Plenum. In March 1958 Khrushchev added the chairmanship of the Council of Ministers to the First Secretaryship, concentrating in his own hands the two supreme posts of party and state.
The XX Congress and the secret speech
The event that marked the era was the XX Congress of the CPSU, held in Moscow in February 1956. On the night of 25 February, in a closed session, Khrushchev delivered his report “On the Cult of the Personality and its Consequences,” O kulte lichnosti i ego posledstviyakh — the famous “secret speech.” He set the blame for the repressions, which he tied to the specific deeds of Stalin, Beria and Yezhov, while insisting that the cult had not changed the nature of socialism nor turned society from the correct path to communism. The report was never published; it was read aloud to party and Komsomol meetings, and its boundaries were fixed by the Central Committee resolution of the summer of 1956 on overcoming the cult of the personality and its consequences. The shock was enormous, in the Soviet Union and across the world. The communist parties of China and North Korea condemned the criticism as revisionism and began to distance themselves from the new leadership of the CPSU. De-Stalinisation — destalinizatsiya — and the rehabilitation of victims of the political repressions of the 1930s, begun with the amnesty of 1953 that freed nearly half of all prisoners, became the defining work of the period.
The thaw and its reforms
Khrushchev’s decade was one of restless, often improvised reform. In agriculture he launched the great campaign for the osvoyeniye tseliny (the virgin lands), opening from 1954 more than forty-five million hectares of the steppe of Kazakhstan and Western Siberia to the plough, while raising state purchase prices and abolishing the tax on private household plots. He reorganised the machine-tractor stations, the MTS, and set the ambition of catching up with and surpassing America in the production of foodstuffs per head. In industry he swept away the branch ministries in favour of regional economic councils, the sovnarkhozy, in a decentralising reform that pleased the provinces and alienated the central apparatus. He reduced the armed forces, loosened the cultural controls of the Stalin era, and opened the prison camps of the Gulag. The XXII Congress of 1961 adopted the third Programme of the CPSU, the Programma KPSS (the Programme of the CPSU), which proclaimed that the country had entered the period of the razvyortnutoye stroitelstvo kommunizma (the full-scale building of communism) and set the building of the communist society for the year 1980.
The fall
The very energy of his rule undid him. The failure of his agricultural campaigns, the half-remembered enthusiasm of the “dosing” of democracy, the turmoil of repeated reorganisations and loud campaigns left the apparatus, the military and the intelligentsia weary. In October 1964 he was charged with volyuntarizm i subyektivizm (voluntarism and subjectivism), removed from the leadership of party and state and sent into retirement. Leonid Brezhnev was elected First Secretary (from 1966 General Secretary) of the Central Committee, and Alexei Kosygin became Chairman of the Council of Ministers. Khrushchev lived on in obscure retirement until his death in 1971, leaving behind a country he had opened to the world and to itself — the ottepel that would outlast him, and the memory of the first and most audacious of the attempts to reform the system he had inherited.
