entities/palmiro-togliatti.title: Palmiro Togliatti (1893-1964)
entities/palmiro-togliatti.content:
Palmiro Togliatti (1893-1964)
For the whole of the Italian Republic’s first two decades, the man who commanded the largest communist party in the Western world was Palmiro Togliatti. A founding figure of the Italian Communist Party (Partito Comunista Italiano, the P.C.I.), formed in the split of Livorno in 1921, Togliatti spent the years of fascism in exile in Moscow, where he worked inside the structures of the Comintern and earned the confidence of Stalin. He returned to Italy in 1944, at the head of the party, and for the next two decades shaped the strategy of the Italian left — the partito nuovo, the policy of collaboration, and the celebrated via italiana al socialismo (Italian road to socialism) that set the P.C.I. apart from the rigid orthodoxy of the Eastern parties. He was the great adversary of the Democrazia Cristiana and the man who, more than any other, defined the political field against which the centrismo and the D.C. governments were constructed.
Exile and the return
Togliatti was among the founders of the P.C.I. in 1921, a leading Communist organizer and intellectual. With the establishment of the fascist dictatorship and the party driven underground and into exile, he became its principal figure abroad, resident in Moscow for much of the interwar period and an important functionary of the Comintern, the Communist International. In 1944, as the war moved toward its end and the Allies advanced up the peninsula, Togliatti returned to Italy — landing at Naples in March 1944 — and took command of the party’s reconstruction. He returned as the disciplined and authoritative leader of the P.C.I., marked by his Moscow years but a formidable and autonomous politician in his own right, intent on making the party a mass force at the centre of Italian national life.
The Salerno turn and the partito nuovo
Togliatti’s first great act on his return was the celebrated “Salerno turn,” the policy announced at Salerno in 1944 by which he steered the party into collaboration with the royal government and the other anti-fascist forces, postponing the institutional question of the monarchy in the name of national unity and of the Resistance against the German occupier. It was the signature of his strategy: a party that sought its legitimacy inside the national democratic process rather than at its margins. From this he built the partito nuovo (the “new party”), a mass party of the Italian working people organized on the national territory — a party of workers, peasants and intellectuals, with an extensive network of sections, a daily press and a vast popular following, the largest such organization of the Italian left. The partito nuovo was conceived not as the clandestine revolutionary vanguard of the interwar years but as a great legal and popular party competing for influence within the new democratic republic.
The communists in the postwar coalition
The Salerno turn brought the communists into the postwar governments. Togliatti was minister of justice in the early cabinets of the reconstruction, a member of the Constituent Assembly and one of the principal authors of the republican Constitution of 1948, contributing to the social and labour provisions it enshrined. The communists sat in the tripartito government with the Christian Democrats and the socialists until 1947, when De Gasperi, under the pressure of the Cold War, expelled them from the government. The rupture of 1947 consigned the P.C.I. permanently to opposition. From that point Togliatti led the party in the electoral confrontation of 1948, when the communists and socialists stood together in the Fronte Democratico Popolare (Popular Democratic Front) against the Christian Democrats — and suffered the decisive defeat of 18 April 1948, the landslide that fixed the republic’s anti-communist orientation.
The permanent opposition and the via italiana al socialismo
For the remaining years of his leadership Togliatti presided over a party that, as the largest communist party outside the Eastern bloc, commanded a vast and stable share of the Italian vote — around a fifth of the electorate in the centrist decade — yet was excluded from power by the very structure of the political system. He developed the doctrine of the via italiana al socialismo (Italian road to socialism), the claim that in Italy the advance to socialism could and must proceed along a national and democratic path, within the framework of the republican Constitution and the democratic institutions, rather than by the revolutionary and Soviet model. It was a strategy of an opposition both implacable and constitutional — the P.C.I. a permanent and disciplined adversary of the D.C.-centred centrismo, yet committed to the republic and the popular front politics of collaboration with the socialists. The party under Togliatti became a pillar of Italian political life, its isolation a defining fact of the republic, and its eventual claim to share responsibility in the state a question that hung over the whole system. Togliatti died in 1964, at a moment when the centro-sinistra (centre-left) was just opening the alliance of the D.C. with the socialists — an opening from which the communists, under his successors, would be excluded as they had been throughout his life.

entities/pierre-mendes-france.title: Pierre Mendès France (1907-1982)
entities/pierre-mendes-france.content:
Pierre Mendès France (1907-1982)
The radical and the Cassandre
He was of the generation that came to politics through the École libre des sciences politiques and the law, a Radical deputy from the Eure since 1932, a young man marked by the rigour of a technical mind. At the Liberation he had served in the Provisional Government under General de Gaulle, minister of the national economy, and he had made himself the apostle of an austere orthodoxy — devaluation, a clean budget, the refusal of the easy money that financed the inflation of the day. He resigned rather than accept what he considered the soft economic course of his colleagues, and from that moment he carried the reputation of a man who spoke the language of truth when others flattered. Contemporaries called him a Cassandre, the prophet whom no one wished to hear: his warnings on Indochina, on the war that could not be won, were uttered for years before events forced the country to listen.
The voice of truth in Indochina
By the spring of 1954 the war in Indochina had become the great haemorrhage of the Republic — the expeditionary corps bogged down against the Viet Minh, the treasury drained, the empire sliding away. The catastrophe of Dien Bien Phu in May 1954 broke the government and brought Mendès France to the Hôtel Matignon at the head of a ministry of radical initiative. He took office in June with a promise that gave him thirty days to make peace or resign — a fixed term, a deadline, a style of government the Assembly was unaccustomed to. He went to Geneva, met Zhou Enlai, negotiated the end of the Indochina war, and came back to a country that had tasted for the first time in years the sensation of being governed. It was the style Mendès France: the language of rigour, the directness, the refusal of the parliamentary circumlocutions that had made the régime a byword for indecision.
Modernity without a sequel
The mendésiste moment was the Fourth Republic’s best hope of reforming itself, and its clearest demonstration of why that hope failed. Mendès France governed through the autumn of 1954 and into 1955 — he settled the Tunisian question, set the terms for what would become Moroccan independence, tried to bring the same resolution to the assembly of the Republic that he had brought to the conference table. His manner divided opinion savagely: the modernisers, the jeunes loups of the administration and the press, saw in him the man who could break the immobilisme; the parliamentary old guard saw a moralising outsider who treated the Assembly as an obstacle. He fell in February 1955, overthrown on a secondary question, and the régime returned to its accustomed shuffle. The constitutional reform he proposed — the very reforms of the executive that de Gaulle had demanded since Bayeux — went nowhere. Serge Berstein’s judgement that the Fifth Republic valorised itself by diabolising its predecessor finds its most poignant illustration in Mendès France: the modernisation politique remained introuvable, unfindable, precisely because the régime could not keep at its head the one man who might have carried it out.
The general’s measure
For de Gaulle, watching from Colombey, Mendès France was an ambiguous figure — a man of capacity who nonetheless remained a prisoner of the régime. The General’s constitutional ideas, set out at Bayeux in June 1946 and never abandoned through all the years of the traversée du désert, demanded a strong executive standing above the parties; Mendès France was a parliamentarian of genius, but he was still a parliamentarian, operating within the very system de Gaulle condemned. When the mendésiste experiment failed, it confirmed the gaullist reading that the régime of the parties could not reform itself from within. Mendès France himself drew the bitter lesson of 1958 differently: he opposed the return of the General, voted against the new constitution of the Fifth Republic, and remained thereafter a republican critic of the presidential régime — the moderniser who had failed to save the Fourth, refusing to consecrate the Fifth. He ended his political life as a voice for another left, a moral reference rather than a power, the incarnation of a republic that had been, briefly and brilliantly, on the point of governing.

entities/robert-schuman.title: Robert Schuman (1886–1963)
entities/robert-schuman.content:
Robert Schuman (1886–1963)
The statesman whose name was given to the founding declaration of European integration was, by origin, a man of the disputed frontier that the new Community was meant to pacify. Robert Schuman was born at Clausen, near Luxembourg, in 1886, a subject of the German Empire, educated in German as well as French; his family belonged to Lorraine, that region which had changed hands between France and Germany so often that he seemed to embody the very problem he would one day be called upon to solve. He entered French politics in the interwar years, served as a minister after the Liberation, and by 1948 had become one of the most respected figures of the French government, a man of sober Catholic conviction whose moderation won him the presidency of the Council of Ministers. The Cambridge history of European integration numbers him among the “visionaries” — the small company of founding figures, with jean-monnet, konrad-adenauer and de Gasperi, who stood at the birth of the Community.
Foreign minister and the May 1950 declaration
It was as French foreign minister, in the unstable ministries of the Fourth Republic, that Schuman made his historic move. The year 1950 opened with the question of Germany pressing upon the governments of Europe: how to bind the new Federal Republic, rearming and recovering within the Atlantic alliance, into a framework that would make a repetition of the old conflict impossible. The answer Schuman brought forward on 9 May 1950 was startling in its brevity and its audacity. In a declaration drafted in his ministry — the conception, by his own account and that of the historians, owed much to jean-monnet — he proposed that France and Germany place their production of coal and steel under a common High Authority, open to the other states of Europe. The pooling of the two industries, the sinews of war, would make conflict between the former enemies not merely undesirable but materially impossible. As he put it in the text that Moravcsik sets at the head of his study, “our European states are a historical reality” that no juridical construction could wish away — the task was not to abolish them but to bind them into a larger unity.
The father of the Coal and Steel Community
Out of that single declaration grew the European Coal and Steel Community, signed at Paris in April 1951 and ratified over the following year. The negotiation was rapid, the language of the declaration deliberately spare, and the outcome a genuinely supranational institution — a High Authority empowered to act upon the industries of the Six over the heads of their governments. Schuman, having launched the project, left office in 1952, but his name had become permanently attached to the cause. Along with the declaration of 9 May, remembered thereafter as “Schuman Day”, he stood as one of the two or three acknowledged fathers of European integration. When, in the chapter that closes his study, Moravcsik returns to jacques-delors’s post-Maastricht insistence that he sought “a federation among strong nation-states” rather than a United States of Europe, he observes that the most distinguished visionary of the 1980s had thereby come full circle to the view of Schuman, whose words opened the book. It was Schuman, the devout Catholic of the borderlands, who had first posed the question that the whole later edifice would answer: how to reconcile the historical reality of European states with the peace that only their union could secure.

entities/rpf-rassemblement-du-peuple-fra.title: R.P.F. (Rassemblement du peuple français)
entities/rpf-rassemblement-du-peuple-fra.content:
R.P.F. (Rassemblement du peuple français)
The Rassemblement du peuple français (“Rally of the French People”, the R.P.F.) was the movement launched by Charles de Gaulle at Bruneval on 30 March 1947 as his answer to the fourth-republic. Deliberately a rassemblement (a rally) rather than a party, it was meant to gather the nation above the parties to his programme of a strong state, national grandeur and social reconciliation — the political embodiment, in the years of his retirement, of what would later be called gaullism.
The campaign against the régime des partis
The R.P.F. was built in open war against the parliamentary republic that de Gaulle had denounced at bayeux-speech-1946. Its platform fused the call for a stronger executive with a nationalism of grandeur and a sharp anti-communism, positioned to stand between the parties and against the growing Communist presence in French politics. Its early years were a sustained electoral assault. The movement swept the municipal elections of 1947, when it took some of the great city halls, and stood at the height of its strength in the late 1940s, poised at the edge of power. The years 1947 to 1953 saw the General on the road — Strasbourg, Bordeaux, Lille, Rennes, Lyon, Vincennes, Algiers, Marseille, Nevers, Verdun — and before the press at the Maison de la Résistance and the Palais d’Orsay, in the speeches and press conferences collected in the second tome of his Discours et messages.
Decline and suspension
For all its early strength, the R.P.F. never commanded a majority in the country, and the party system it had sworn to break proved more resilient than the rally. Gaullist deputies drifted into alliance with the parties of the régime, and the movement’s edge was dulled. After the decision of 1953 to suspend the R.P.F.’s active electoral politics, the rally faded, and de Gaulle entered the long silence of the traversée du désert. When he returned to power in may-1958-crisis he came as the arbiter above the parties, not as the leader of a party — the very posture the R.P.F. had been designed to achieve, but achieved at last through the institutions of the fifth-republic rather than through the rally.

entities/sed.title: SED (Socialist Unity Party of Germany)
entities/sed.content:
SED (Socialist Unity Party of Germany)
The Sozialistische Einheitspartei Deutschlands — the Socialist Unity Party of Germany — was the instrument through which the German Democratic Republic was governed from its founding until its collapse. It was born not of a natural union of equals but of a forced merger, imposed from Moscow in the wreckage of the Soviet occupation zone, and it held power with the patience and ruthlessness of a machine built to endure. For four decades the SED was the state: it is the thread that runs through the whole of the GDR’s history, the party whose “leading role” (führende Rolle) the constitution of the republic was written to confirm.
The forced unification of 1946
The party’s origin lay in the spring of 1946, when the Soviet occupation authorities under the Sowjetische Militäradministration in Deutschland (Soviet Military Administration in Germany, the SMAD) brought pressure to bear on the two working-class parties of the Soviet zone. The Kommunistische Partei Deutschlands (KPD), licensed first and under strict Soviet control, and the Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands (SPD) were driven to unite, under duress that few could resist. The merger was proclaimed in Berlin in April 1946, welding the communists and the social democrats into a single party that claimed to heal the old breach of the workers’ movement while in truth delivering it into communist hands. Weber’s documents record how the party line was imposed and then, when inconvenient, quietly rewritten — even the founding articles of its own leaders were mutilated in later collected editions to fit the current doctrine. The SED inherited the membership of both parties but not their freedom: it was a party of the Soviet model, its internal life governed by the principle of demokratischer Zentralismus (democratic centralism), which meant in practice that decisions flowed downward and dissent was a crime against the party.
A state party in the making
In the years of the occupation zone the SED prepared the ground for the state it would rule. It directed the Bodenreform (land reform), the expropriation of large estates, and the nationalisation of industry, and it drove the zone toward the volksdemokratische (people’s-democratic) system that culminated in the proclamation of the German Democratic Republic on 7 October 1949. With the founding of the state the party completed its transformation: from 1949 the SED no longer competed as one party among several but governed as the sole arbiter, reducing the other licensed parties and mass organisations to satellite bodies that existed to affirm its direction. Weber marks the years after 1949 as the period of the “Stalinisation” of the GDR, the Gleichschaltung (coordination) of parties, organisations and the state apparatus on the Soviet model, accompanied by purges within the party itself and the steady strengthening of the security machinery that guarded its power.
The Stalinization and the leading role
The party’s absolute claim found its symbol in the uprising of 17 June 1953, when East German workers rose against the leadership and were put down only with the intervention of Soviet troops — a shock that forced the SED under walter-ullbricht to retreat, for a time, into a Neuer Kurs (New Course) of softer measures. Under Ulbricht’s long dictatorship the party nonetheless consolidated its grip through the fifties, weathering its internal struggles and closing off the republic’s last escape by the building of the Berlin Wall on 13 August 1961. It was the Wall that gave the SED the stability it craved: with the border sealed, the party could pursue its model experiments of the sixties — the Neues Ökonomisches System (New Economic System), the abortive rivalries with the reform communism of Prague — without fear of being emptied from within. After 1961 the führende Rolle of the party, its leading role, became the settled doctrine of the state.
Honecker and the party’s high tide
The change of leadership in 1971, when erich-honecker displaced Ulbricht, marked the party’s turn toward a closer alignment with the Soviet Union — a paradox that, as Weber stresses, made détente with the Federal Republic possible at all, since Moscow trusted a leadership that had bound itself to the bloc. Honecker’s SED proclaimed the Einheit von Wirtschafts- und Sozialpolitik (unity of economic and social policy), the promise that rising consumption and rising production would advance together, and through the seventies it oversaw the Grundlagenvertrag (Basic Treaty) of 1972 and the GDR’s hard-won international recognition. Yet this was also the period of the party’s tightening grip on dissent, marked by the expatriation of the singer and poet Wolf Biermann in 1976 and the wave of protest that followed. The party that ruled through its network of informers, its mass organisations, and above all its secret police, the stasi, demanded from its citizens a conformity it was increasingly unwilling to tolerate as broken.
The SED state
The party structured the state to its own measure. Membership was the route to advancement in a society where the party controlled employment, education and the media; the SED’s structure ran parallel to and above the state’s, its Politburo and Central Committee making the decisions that the ministries and the Volkskammer, the nominal parliament, merely enacted. Weber’s collection shows the party’s own self-conception in its congresses — the X. Party Congress of April 1981, which reaffirmed the party’s leading role and its “unity of economic and social policy” at home and its absolute loyalty to the Soviet Union abroad, while Honecker’s personality cult grew ever more conspicuous. It was, in the historian’s phrase, a Herrschaftsverband (structure of domination) of the Soviet type, a one-party dictatorship in which the distinction between party and state dissolved. This is the sense in which historians speak of the GDR as an sed-state: a state defined not by its own institutions but by the party that created and controlled them.
The party’s end
The SED proved unable to outlast the crisis that gathered around it in the 1980s, when the republic’s economic troubles, its mounting debts, and the mass emigration that would eventually empty it combined with the collapse of the Soviet patronage that sustained it. When the Wall fell on 9 November 1989, the party’s monopoly dissolved with it; by german-reunification-1990 the SED had been stripped of its leading role, renamed in an attempt to shed its past, and reduced to the remnant of the force that had governed the GDR for four decades. The party that had been born of a forced union in 1946 and had built a state around its own authority found, in the end, that it could not survive the loss of that authority. Its name remains shorthand for the regime it created, the sed-state that ruled eastern Germany until the autumn of 1989.

entities/silvio-berlusconi.title: Silvio Berlusconi (1936-2023)
entities/silvio-berlusconi.content:
Silvio Berlusconi (1936-2023)
The most consequential entry into Italian politics since the founding of the Republic was made not by a party man but by a businessman who had built a private television empire in the deregulated years of the eighties. Silvio Berlusconi, the cavaliere of Arcore, rose from property speculation in the new satellite city of Milano 2 to control the three main private television networks of the country, and then, in the vacuum left by the collapse of the old parties, transformed himself into the dominant figure of a new political order. His “descent into the field” (discesa in campo) in January 1994 and his victory in the elections of March of that year marked the passage of Italy to what would be called the Second Republic.
The builder of the media empire
The making of Berlusconi was inseparable from the transformation of Italian broadcasting. From the launch of Tele Milano in the mid-seventies, a cable channel serving the satellite city he had himself built and financed, he pushed outward — from local to regional to a national horizon, challenging the monopoly of the state broadcaster Rai from an antenna installed on the grattacielo Pirelli in Milan. Between 1976 and 1980 viewing figures quadrupled; more than ten million spectators were drawn to the offer of a television that was “light and engaging,” a commercial television that entered the homes of Italian families alongside the public service. In the early eighties the quiz Sogni nel cassetto hosted by Mike Bongiorno created the conditions for the launch of Canale 5, and Berlusconi then strengthened his position by acquiring Italia 1 and Rete 4 in sequence from Edilio Rusconi and the Mondadori group. The Fininvest group became the largest private conglomerate in the country after that of the Agnelli family.
Gentiloni Silveri reads this as a turning point verging on the anthropological: the arrival of a new cittadinanza diretta passing through television, a “popolo di teledipendenti,” a people of the addicted, built on advertising, entertainment and simplified, direct messages. The political class, convinced it could profit from a tolerated deregulation, failed to regulate. Instead the vacuum of rules favoured a lottizzazione, a spartizione of the public network among the parties, and a perverse tangle of interests between industry, finance and politics. The loggia massonica P2, which numbered leading figures of the information world among its members, cast a dark shadow over the era. The law Mammì of 1990, which gave concessions for national broadcasting, did little more than sanction a condition that had grown up in a legal void, leaving the dyad of public Rai and the Berlusconi system to dominate the ether.
The discesa in campo
The collapse of the old political order after tangentopoli-1992 left Berlusconi suddenly exposed. The disintegration of the Partito socialista and the personal ruin of his old protector Bettino Craxi robbed the Fininvest empire of a powerful shield, and the prospect of an electoral victory of the left appeared to him a serious danger to his possessions. These reasons — together with his personal convictions, founded on economic liberalism and a fierce hostility to the parties of the left, and the vacuum left at the centre by the crisis of the Democrazia cristiana and the PSI — drove him to enter politics. Pragmatic in politics as in business, the cavaliere was confident of gathering around himself a vast movement of moderate opinion. In November 1993 he came out in support of Gianfranco Fini, the leader of the post-fascist MSI, then a candidate for the mayoralty of Rome, and declared his own entry into politics “to prevent the victory of the left.”
On 26 January 1994 he confirmed his candidacy and announced the birth of a new movement, Forza Italia. Built with remarkable speed — largely on the staff and clients of his own companies, whence its label of partito aziendale, the company party — and backed by the mobilisation of his television networks, the movement was credited with a strong showing before the ballot. Almost simultaneously Umberto Bossi’s Lega Nord allied with him, and Fini relaunched the old MSI as Alleanza Nazionale with a new profession of democratic faith. Out of this emerged not one but two coalitions: the Polo delle Libertà between Bossi and Berlusconi in the North, and the Polo del Buon Governo between Berlusconi and Fini in the South, with the CCD of former Christian Democrats and the Liberals present in both.
The victory of March 1994
The message he broadcast in January 1994, recorded and aired simultaneously on both broadcasting giants, was a masterpiece of televisual politics — the image of an orderly white study, family photographs, a vase of flowers, a bookcase without books, the reassuring spot of an entrepreneur who promised that “L’Italia è il paese che amo.” The elections of 27 and 28 March 1994 returned a clear victory for the Pole. Forza Italia, founded barely a month before the vote, emerged as the first national party with twenty-one per cent of the proportional vote; Alleanza Nazionale, with thirteen and a half per cent, became the third party and triumphed in the South; the Lega, holding its ground, won a great haul of seats thanks to Berlusconi’s generosity in ceding it the representation of a large number of constituencies. The left was routed: the Partito democratico della sinistra won 20.3 per cent, Rifondazione comunista six, the Partito Popolare eleven, while the old Partito socialista collapsed to 2.2 per cent. Berlusconi, as the recognised leader of the winning party, was the natural candidate for the presidency of the Council, and he formed a government sworn in on 11 May 1994.
The three premierships and the transformation of politics
The first Berlusconi government proved short-lived, lasting barely a summer before the withdrawal of the Lega brought it down in December 1994. Yet the transformation he had wrought in the political system proved durable. The coalitions of the right and the left that took shape under the new electoral law, and the alternation of centre-right and centre-left governments that followed, defined what Gentiloni Silveri calls the “mancata transizione” — the transition that never quite arrived — to a bipolar order. Berlusconi returned to the premiership in 2001, this time with a stable coalition that held power for the full legislature, and again in 2008. Through three terms as prime minister he dominated Italian public life for two decades, the perpetual point of reference for the country’s politics — the living embodiment of the new media politics, of the fusion of private power and public office, and of the questions of conflict of interest that the Republic never resolved. He died in June 2023, having remade Italian politics in the image of his own restless enterprise.

entities/stasi.title: Stasi (Ministry for State Security)
entities/stasi.content:
Stasi (Ministry for State Security)
The Ministerium für Staatssicherheit — the Ministry for State Security, known everywhere by its short name, the Stasi — was the sword and shield of the SED state. Founded in 1950 on the model of the Soviet security apparatus, it grew from a small political police into one of the most comprehensive surveillance machines ever built, a parallel state that watched the citizenry of the German Democratic Republic, both at home and abroad, on a scale its founders could hardly have imagined. For the sed-state the Stasi was not a mere instrument but an essential organ of rule: the institution that gave meaning to the party’s demand for conformity, and whose files would outlive the state itself.
The foundation and the Soviet model
The ministry was established in February 1950, in the period of Stalinisation that followed the founding of the GDR, and it was from the first a creature of the Soviet system. Its officers were trained in the methods of the Soviet secret police, and it answered to the party leadership even as it watched over the party itself. Its early task, in Weber’s account, was the consolidation of the SED’s dictatorship — the hunt for opponents, the intimidation of the population, the purge of the state apparatus — and it played its part in the repression that made the Stalinisation of the republic a reality. The uprising of 17 June 1953, when workers rose against the party and were suppressed with Soviet help, was a demonstration of the limits of the Stasi’s strength against a genuinely popular revolt; but in the years that followed it built itself into something far more pervasive.
The instrument of the SED state
Under Walter Ulbricht and then erich-honecker the Stasi became the state’s principal means of control. It maintained a dense network of informers — the Inoffizielle Mitarbeiter (unofficial collaborators, the IMs) — who reported on their neighbours, their colleagues, and even their families, recruited across every level of society in a system that blurred the line between the watchers and the watched. The ministry’s Hauptverwaltung Aufklärung (Main Administration for Reconnaissance) ran espionage abroad, while its domestic divisions tracked dissent, emigration attempts, the churches, and the arts. It was the Stasi that dealt with the regime’s critics after the expatriation of Wolf Biermann in 1976, and it was the Stasi that pursued the civil-rights and peace movements of the 1980s, cataloguing their members and their meetings in files that grew to an extraordinary scale. For a population that could trust almost no one, the uncertainty of whether one’s acquaintance was an IM was itself a form of control.
The surveillance of society
Kowalczuk, himself an East German and a leading historian of the security apparatus, describes the Stasi’s reach across the whole of GDR society — an apparatus that aspired to know everything about everyone, and whose methods shaped the daily experience of the republic. It monitored letters and telephones, planted agents in every institution, and operated an economy of reward and coercion that bound the informers to the system even as they served it. The ministry’s size and budget grew steadily through the seventies and eighties, far beyond the needs of any plausible opposition, because its function was not merely to crush resistance but to pre-empt it, to make dissent seem futile before it could begin. In this the Stasi was the logical extreme of the sed-state’s logic: a party that could not tolerate any space outside itself created an apparatus that filled that space with observation.
The files and the reckoning
When the GDR collapsed in the autumn of 1989 the Stasi, alone among the institutions of the state, prepared to defend itself — its officers stood ready to destroy the files that were its true monument, and only the occupation of its offices by the citizens of the republic in the winter of 1989–90 saved the archives from the flames. Those files became, in Kowalczuk’s account, the centrepiece of the Aufarbeitung (coming to terms with the past) that followed reunification: the Gauck authority opened the Stasi’s records to the citizens who had been watched, and the revelation of who had informed on whom — including those who had informed on themselves — became one of the most painful and defining experiences of the new Germany. The Stasi thus passed from being the instrument of rule to being the symbol of it, its files the enduring evidence of how thoroughly the sed-state had sought to know its own people.

entities/treuhandanstalt.title: Treuhandanstalt
entities/treuhandanstalt.content:
Treuhandanstalt
When the old GDR economy was handed over to the new order after the fall-of-berlin-wall-1989, there was no market waiting in the East to receive it — only the immense bureaucratic body of a state that had owned nearly everything. The instrument devised to dissolve that body was the Treuhandanstalt, the trustee agency, born in the last months of the GDR and carried over into the Federal Republic as the single most powerful shaper of the first half of the 1990s. Its task, stated plainly, was to take the Volkseigene Betriebe, the people’s enterprises that the SED state had gathered under its wing, and turn them into something the market economy could own. What that meant in practice was the largest privatisation ever attempted, and for eastern Germany a social upheaval whose scars never quite healed.
The agency’s name spoke of a Treuhand, a trust held on behalf of others — as if the property of the people were being entrusted to a neutral manager who would hand it back to them in better form. The reality was harsher. In the breathless months after 1990 the Treuhand presided over the fate of roughly eight thousand enterprises, and of them only a portion was sold off as going concerns to new owners. The rest were liquidated outright, their machines auctioned and their workers dismissed, or gesundgeschrumpft, “shrunk to health” — trimmed down to a profitable core by shedding the labour and the product lines that the old economy had carried. The word that did the work was Privatisierung, privatisation, but for the hundreds of thousands who lost their places it read as something closer to dissolution.
The cost was paid in employment. The GDR had counted 9.7 million people at work in 1989; by the end of 1993 that figure stood at 6.2 million. A third of the eastern German workforce passed through unemployment, into the new and unfamiliar condition of Arbeitslosigkeit, joblessness — an experience the East had never really known, since the planned economy had guaranteed everyone a place. The Treuhand closed the factories that could not find buyers, and it sold many that did find buyers on terms that left the new owners free to rationalise, which almost always meant to shed workers. The Reichsbahn strike, when the railwaymen of the East walked out, announced the arrival of a new kind of conflict in which the state no longer guaranteed the job but faced a workforce defending it.
Beyond the plant closures lay the Eigentumsfrage, the property question, which the Treuhand and the whole state apparatus took on with enormous administrative labour and enormous social cost. The principle adopted was Rückgabe vor Entschädigung, restitution before compensation — the return of property to those who had been expropriated under the GDR and the Nazi era before it, in preference to paying them for the loss. Every claim had to be examined, every file opened, and the slow grind of that machinery cast its shadow over investment and over the lives of those who waited, often for years, uncertain whether the house or the shop or the factory in which they lived and worked would be taken from them. The burdens of the old system were visited on the new: firms inherited debts, the Altschulden, that had piled up under the planned economy, and found themselves dragged toward bankruptcy in a market that showed no mercy for the past.
The Treuhand was never merely an economic instrument, and its name has come to stand in eastern German memory for the whole one-sided character of the transformation. The small businessman like Dieter, who greeted the fall of the Wall with renewed energy and then watched his firm collapse under inherited debt and the privatisation regime, ending bankrupt and privately liable — such stories gave the agency a dark emblematic weight. It was the agent of an Übernahme, a takeover, in which the economy of the East was not nursed into the new order but subordinated to it. Where the GDR had organised work around full employment, the market organised it around profit, and the Treuhand was the institution that made the change with a hard, administrative finality. It remains, for those who lived through it, the symbol of what the East lost as well as of what it was meant to gain — the lever by which the people’s enterprises were handed over, and the engine of the deindustrialisation that emptied the old industrial landscape. For its history in the transformation see treuhand-privatization-1990-94; for the wider process see east-german-transformation.

entities/valery-giscard-destaing.title: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing (1926–2020)
entities/valery-giscard-destaing.content:
Valéry Giscard d’Estaing (1926–2020)
The third President of the Fifth Republic belonged to a generation that had come of age under the new institutions rather than in the battles of the Liberation. Valéry Giscard d’Estaing, the young énarque and finance minister who had served de Gaulle and Pompidou, embodied the reformist, managerial centrism of a France that wanted to move beyond the founding gaullisme without abandoning its institutions. Elected in 1974, at forty-eight the youngest President of the Republic, he set out to modernise the state from within — and found himself, seven years later, the man swept aside by the political alternance that changed the history of the régime.
The heir of the majority
He came to the presidency out of the conservative majority that had governed the Fifth Republic since 1958. As Minister of the Economy and Finance under both de Gaulle and Pompidou he had become the trusted voice of French monetary orthodoxy, the man of the franc and of budgetary discipline. The death of Pompidou in April 1974 opened a vacancy that the majority could not fill without a contest, and Giscard stood against the gaullist candidate as the standard-bearer of a modernised, centrist right — a break with the strict succession of the gaullisme he nevertheless carried. He won the second ballot on 19 May 1974 against François Mitterrand, the candidate of the united left.
The reformism of the Giscard years
His presidency was that of a reformer confident that the institutions of 1958 could serve a social and cultural liberalism. Giscard proclaimed the advent of a society at once modern and generous, the société libérale avancée (advanced liberal society), and set his hand to the everyday life of the French rather than to the grand drama of the state. The majorité of the young President lowered the age of majority to eighteen, liberalised the laws on contraception and divorce, and set in motion a policy of social measures — while the crisis that had begun in 1973 darkened the horizon of all that he attempted. It was under his presidency that the consciousness of a durable economic crisis hardened, and the unemployment that the Trente Glorieuses had seemed to banish returned as the permanent horizon of French life.
The crisis and the challenge of 1981
The years 1975 to 1981 were those of an economic turn that no political majority could command. The crisis, first read as conjoncturelle (conjunctural) and then recognised as structurelle, mounted through the second half of the 1970s; the first measures against unemployment came only in 1977, as the political directors of the state grasped, tardily, the durable character of the new poverty of work. Against this background Giscard’s modernising centrism wore thin, and the united left of François Mitterrand, carrying the Programme commun of 1972 into the presidential campaign, gathered the discontent of a decade. In the election of 10 May 1981 the French chose change, and Giscard became the first President of the Fifth Republic to be defeated in his bid for re-election — the first alternance, the peaceful passage of power from the majority that had founded the régime to the left it had always excluded.
He left the Élysée as the symbol of a reformism overtaken by the crisis, the man who had modernised the manners of French power — the filmed strolls through the streets, the lunches with ordinary citizens — without being able to master the economic turn that undid him. The Giscard years stand in the history of the Fifth Republic as the bridge between the gaullisme of its foundation and the alternances that followed, the moment when the institutions of 1958 proved able to change their masters and survive.

entities/vladimir-putin.title: Vladimir Putin (b. 1952)
entities/vladimir-putin.content:
Vladimir Putin (b. 1952)
The man who came to the Kremlin at the close of the twentieth century was, by the standards of Russian political life, almost an unknown. Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin (Владимир Владимирович Путин), born in Leningrad in 1952 into a working family, had spent his adult life out of the public eye. He was a career officer of the Committee for State Security, the KGB, an intelligence man rather than a party tribune. He served in the 1980s, then, after the fall of the Soviet state, became a devoted aide of the democratic mayor of Petersburg, Anatoly Sobchak, working first as his assistant and later as chairman of the city government’s Committee for External Relations. When Sobchak lost the gubernatorial election of 1996, Putin left Petersburg and made his way to Moscow — into the Presidential Administration, then to the head of the Main Control Directorate, then, in 1998, to the directorship of the Federal Security Service. From these corridors of the state he was drawn, in the autumn of 1999, into the blinding light of supreme power. His rise was the answer to a question the country had been asking for a decade: what was to come after the disorder of the nineties?
The making of a premier
The appointment that launched him came as the second Chechen war was breaking. On 9 August 1999 President boris-yeltsin proposed to the State Duma that the head of the Federal Security Service, Vladimir Putin, be confirmed as Chairman of the Government. The choice fell on a man who had never stood before the electorate and who was barely known to the Moscow political world. Yet he came to the premiership at a moment of crisis, when the war on the Caucasus had resumed, and he made that war his own. Under his direction the Chechen fighters who had invaded Dagestan were pushed back and the federal forces reopened their campaign on the territory of Chechnya. In a country sick of the humiliations of the nineties, the image of a premier who spoke of waging war to the end and who promised to chase the bandits “in the outhouse” (в сортире) answered a deep hunger for order. Through the second half of 1999 his popularity rose without pause.
The transfer of power and the election of March 2000
Yeltsin, who had long sought a successor to whom he could hand the state, saw in the young premier the guarantee of his own security and of continuity. The arrangement was sealed in the elections of 19 December 1999, when the pro-government bloc “Unity” (Единство), of which Putin was the informal leader, finished within a fraction of a point of the Communist Party. The two then merged with the former opposition bloc “Fatherland–All Russia”, and for the first time since 1993 the State Duma was loyal to the government. On 31 December 1999 Yeltsin astonished the country: in his televised New Year address he announced his resignation and named Putin acting President. The succession was prepared and executed with care — the preemstvennost’ vlasti (преемственность власти), the continuity of power, that the outgoing president had set himself to guarantee. On 26 March 2000 Putin was elected President of the Russian Federation in the first round of voting. He took office declaring that Russia was becoming a modern democratic state and that the peaceful transfer of power was the vital element of political stability.
The building of the vertical
Putin’s presidency was defined from its first months by a single project: the restoration of the state’s control over its own territory. The condition of the country was alarming. The “parade of sovereignties” of the perestroika years persisted in milder form — the constitutions of the republics and the charters of the regions contradicted federal law, the local organs of power followed their own paths, and the presidency’s representatives in the regions had proved unable to impose unity. In May 2000, by decree, Putin divided the country into seven federal districts (федеральные округа) and placed over each a plenipotentiary representative of the President. A law of June 2000 gave the President the right to dismiss the heads of regions and dissolve their parliaments where they obstructed federal power. The upper house, the Federation Council, was reformed so that governors no longer sat in it by right of office, taking from the regions their last institutional shield against the centre. This was the vertikal’ vlasti (вертикаль власти), the “vertical of power” — the reconstruction of the chain of command that the nineties had shattered.
The taming of the elites
The restoration of the state’s authority was carried out no less firmly against the great businessmen — the oligarkhi (олигархи) — who had grown rich and politically powerful in the privatisation of the Yeltsin years. In the summer of 2000 Putin summoned the leading magnates to the Kremlin and declared the principle of “equidistance” (ravnoudalennost’): the state would keep them all at an equal distance from power, and would not tolerate their interference in politics. Those who had financed Yeltsin’s re-election campaign of 1996, who controlled the great television channels, treated the young president’s warning lightly. They were disabused quickly. The media magnate Vladimir Gusinsky, whose channel NTV had been critical of the war in Chechnya, saw his company raided, was arrested, and fled abroad; his media empire passed into the hands of the state-owned Gazprom. Boris Berezovsky, once the great manipulator of Kremlin politics, resigned his Duma mandate in protest and eventually took refuge in London. Mikhail Khodorkovsky, head of the oil company YUKOS, who had financed a liberal foundation and seemed to harbour political ambitions, was prosecuted and convicted; his associates were jailed or driven abroad. In a short space — one or two years — the President had made plain that no private fortune could stand beside the state.
The consolidation of power to 2005
The strengthening of the state rested on a fortunate economic wind. From the collapse of oil prices in 1998 the price of Russian crude, which had sunk to some seven dollars a barrel in December of that year, tripled by 2000 and by 2004–2005 reached heights never seen before. The windfall filled the treasury: the budget ran surpluses from 1999, gold and currency reserves swelled beyond 160 billion dollars, a stabilisation fund was built, and after a decade of decline the gross domestic product began to grow. Putin could pay the pensions and salaries that the state of the nineties had left unpaid, and could present himself as the man who had stopped the disintegration of the country. In his address to the Federal Assembly in 2001 he could say that the period of the “sprawling” (расползание) of the state was over, that the disintegration of which he had warned had been halted.
The consolidation expressed itself in elections as well. In the Duma elections of 2003 the pro-presidential party “United Russia” (Единая Россия), formed in 2001 from the merger of Unity with its former rivals, won 306 of the 447 seats, while the liberal parties of the right failed even to cross the barrier into parliament. In March 2004 Putin was re-elected to a second term. Sociologists charted the change in the mood of the country: a people exhausted by the uncertainty, hardship and instability of fifteen years looked to him, across all social layers, as the leader who would restore the integrity of the state. Where earlier governments had been judged by the endless catalogue of their failures, the new one was trusted — in a vote of confidence given almost before he had acted — to embody the state itself, standing above parties and above private interests. By 2005 the vertical of power was largely built, the elites were disciplined, and Russia had found in one man the symbol of its reasserted unity.

entities/walter-ullbricht.title: Walter Ulbricht (1893-1973)
entities/walter-ullbricht.content:
Walter Ulbricht (1893-1973)
The man who built the German Democratic Republic and ruled it for two decades came from a Leipzig carpenter’s household, a joiner by trade who had entered the Communist Party of Germany in its earliest years and risen through its hardest school. Walter Ulbricht, the son of the Saxon working class, belonged to that generation of communists for whom exile, prison and the Comintern’s discipline were the ordinary curriculum of political life. Fleeing Hitler in 1933, he spent the years of the Third Reich in Prague, Paris and Moscow, and returned to Germany in 1945 in the baggage of the Red Army to help fashion the Soviet zone. From that moment until his seventieth year he was the architect, the clerk and finally the patriarch of the East German state — the man whose patient accumulation of every office and every lever of power made him, in the words of Hermann Weber, the embodiment of the “Stalinization” of the GDR.
The apprenticeship of power
Ulbricht was among those KPD functionaries who landed in Germany behind the Soviet lines, and within the Soviet Military Administration’s zone he set at once to constructing the political order that Moscow required. He was a central figure in the forced merger of the Social Democrats with the Communists that produced the Socialist Unity Party in 1946, the instrument through which the Soviet zone was to be remade. In the last chapter of his memoir he recalled that in 1946 he had still spoken of a “special German path” to socialism — a thesis that, as Weber notes, was later mutilated out of the official selections of his works once it no longer fitted the line. What Ulbricht actually believed mattered less than what the party line required; his genius lay in identifying the line, executing it, and removing those who stood in his way. Through the late forties he rose through the party apparatus, mastering the Stalinist arts of organization, demagogy and intrigue, until by the founding of the GDR he stood ready to take the new state in hand.
The head of the SED state
When the German Democratic Republic was proclaimed on 7 October 1949 in response to the founding of the Federal Republic, Ulbricht did not take the most visible offices. The presidency of the new state went to the old Communist Wilhelm Pieck, and the premiership to Otto Grotewohl of the Social Democrats; but Ulbricht held the decisive post, that of General Secretary of the SED, the party whose “leading role” was written into the constitution of the party state. From that command post he directed the Gleichschaltung, the forced coordination, of the parties and mass organizations, the purges of the party itself, and the strengthening of the security apparatus that made the years 1949 to 1953 a deliberate Angleichung an die Sowjetunion, an assimilation to the Soviet model. Weber identifies in this relentless Stalinization the prelude to the catastrophe of 17 June 1953, when the workers’ uprising against the party leadership shook the regime to its foundations.
The uprising and the consolidation
Stalin’s death in March 1953 briefly endangered Ulbricht’s position. In Moscow the new Soviet leadership favoured a “New Course” and flirted with replacing the dogmatic Saxon; for a moment, as the party wavered, Ulbricht seemed expendable. Yet when the workers of East Berlin and the industrial towns rose on 17 June 1953 against the increased work norms, the revolt was crushed with Soviet help, and the frightened leadership of the Soviet Union chose to keep the man who could hold the state down. Ulbricht survived the crisis and the “thaw” that followed, beating back the inner-party opposition groups that the changed climate had encouraged. Through the later fifties he drove the forced collectivization of agriculture and the nationalization of industry, and presided over an economy that bled its population westward — until the hemorrhage of emigration threatened to empty the state.
The Wall and the model experiments
On the night of 13 August 1961 Ulbricht ordered the sealing of the border in Berlin, the building of the Wall that at once ended the mass flight and, with it, the last open wound through which the East German state had leaked its citizens and its legitimacy. It was Ulbricht’s most decisive and most consequential act: the Wall, however it may have been judged abroad, gave the regime the stability it had never known. In the years that followed Ulbricht pursued what Weber calls his Modellversuche, his “model experiments” — the economic reforms of the Neues Ökonomisches System (New Economic System), an attempt to build a distinctive, technically confident socialism of the GDR under his own leadership. In 1968, when the reform movement in Prague threatened to spill across his borders, he stood at the head of the confrontation with the “Prague Spring,” the most loyal of Moscow’s clients against the heresy next door. The same period saw the beginning of his extraordinary self-glorification, the mounting personality cult that alarmed even his own party.
The removal
By 1970 Ulbricht’s independence had become inconvenient. His refusal to subordinate the GDR’s course wholly to Moscow, and his obstruction of the Soviet push toward a settlement with the Federal Republic, set him against the Soviet leadership and against the younger men in his own Politburo. On 3 May 1971 the Central Committee, in an operation prepared in agreement with Moscow, relieved him of his posts in favour of Erich Honecker. The old man was given the empty honorific of chairman of the state council’s successor institution and pensioned into obscurity, dying in 1973 in the very republic he had built, watched over and so nearly bled dry. Winkler, measuring him against the West German founders of the same years, saw in Ulbricht the very type of the party functionary who had staked everything on a state that his successors, and eventually history, would discard. He left behind a German Democratic Republic that bore his impress in every institution — a state so thoroughly his creation that its later, more flexible masters could never quite escape the pattern he had set.

entities/willy-brandt.title: Willy Brandt (1913–1992)
entities/willy-brandt.content:
Willy Brandt (1913–1992)
The most significant chancellor of the Federal Republic after konrad-adenauer, and the man who changed its face more deeply than any of his immediate predecessors, was a refugee from the Germany of the catastrophe. Willy Brandt, born Herbert Frahm in 1913 in Lübeck, had fled the country in the 1930s as an opponent of Hitler and had spent the war years in exile in Norway and Sweden, from where he had returned after 1945 bearing the mark of the emigrant and the active anti-fascist. He had belonged in his youth to the Socialist Workers’ Party; his biography — the enemy of Nazism, the man who had left Germany rather than serve it — was to prove, decades later, one of the decisive instruments of his greatest political achievement.
His road to the chancellorship ran through Berlin. As Governing Mayor (Regierender Bürgermeister) of West Berlin from 1957, Brandt had stood at the edge of the abyss of the city in the years of crisis, and it was he who personified the defiant republic of the divided metropolis in the summer of 1961, when the Wall was built and the Western powers left him, in his own judgment, largely alone. His profile was at once national and Western: the mayor of the besieged city who was nonetheless trusted in Washington and London. It carried him into the grand coalition of Kurt Georg Kiesinger as Vice-Chancellor and Foreign Minister, and to the leadership of his party, the SPD. On 21 October 1969 the Bundestag elected him Federal Chancellor at the head of a social-liberal coalition with the FDP of Walter Scheel — the first Social Democratic chancellor since 1930, and the first government of the republic to be led from the moderate left.
The policy with which Brandt’s name is permanently joined was the neue Ostpolitik, the ostpolitik of the opening toward the East. The intellectual design had been laid down by his closest adviser Egon Bahr in the phrase Wandel durch Annäherung (change through rapprochement): only by drawing near to the East and recognising the realities of the division of Europe could those realities be changed, and only by accepting the existence of the two German states could the unity of the nation be preserved. As Chancellor, Brandt turned this insight into the chain of treaties that made up the new-ostpolitik-1969-73: the Moscow Treaty of 12 August 1970, the Warsaw Treaty of 7 December 1970, the Four-Power Agreement on Berlin of 1972, and the grundvertrag-1972 with the German Democratic Republic in December 1972. No moment captured the moral authority of the policy so completely as his gesture in the Polish capital on the day of the Warsaw Treaty’s signature, when he knelt before the monument to the victims of the Warsaw Ghetto uprising — a Kniefall (kneeling gesture) that went round the world as an image of the German taking upon himself a guilt that was not his own.
The policy made him an international figure. In 1971 the Nobel Committee awarded him the Peace Prize — the first time in its history the prize went to a German chancellor — in recognition of the Ostpolitik’s contribution to the relaxation of tension in Europe. At home, however, the treaties were fought over with an intensity that brought the republic to the edge of constitutional crisis. The defections of 1972 and the first constructive vote of no confidence of 27 April 1972, in which Rainer Barzel fell two votes short of unseating him, were survived; the election of 19 November 1972, advanced to resolve the deadlock, became a plebiscite on the Ostpolitik and delivered the greatest triumph of Brandt’s life. The SPD emerged as the largest party in the Bundestag for the first time since 1949, and Brandt was re-elected Chancellor on 14 December 1972.
The fall came swiftly and with an almost tragic irony. The reform programme of the second term fell short of the expectations it had raised; the government struggled with inflation and the first stirrings of economic crisis; and Brandt, his great foreign-policy goal achieved and no new challenge to command him, sank into exhaustion and recurrent depression. The catastrophe was of a kind that seemed to belong to another world. Günter Guillaume, a trusted official of the Chancellery who had accompanied Brandt on his travels and had access to his secrets, was unmasked in April 1974 as a spy of the East German Ministry for State Security — an agent who had entered the republic in 1956 disguised as a refugee and risen, under the very government that conducted the Ostpolitik, into the Chancellor’s immediate circle. The responsibility was shared and murky, reaching into the offices of the interior minister and the head of the security service; but the political burden fell on the Chancellor. On 6 May 1974 Brandt resigned, taking political responsibility for the negligence surrounding the affair of Guillaume. “I take over the political responsibility for negligence in connection with the agent affair Guillaume,” ran his letter to the Federal President. The resignation was a sensation throughout the world — the involuntary work, as the historian observed, of the German Democratic Republic, whose secret service had not intended to bring down the architect of détente with the East. Brandt’s successor was his Finance Minister helmut-schmidt.
Brandt’s historical rank was by then removed from the contest of parties. He had been the most important chancellor since Adenauer. In his years in office the face of the Federal Republic had changed more thoroughly than under his predecessors Erhard and Kiesinger: the Umgründung der Republik (refounding of the republic) after 1968, the opening to the East, the overcoming of the special conflict with the Soviet bloc that had threatened the republic’s isolation. The foundation of Western integration laid by Adenauer had been the secure ground on which Brandt performed the opening toward the East between 1969 and 1973. He had made the Federal Republic, within the limits of the possible, a normal Western state — and the deep trace he left was on foreign policy, in a diplomacy of which the whole of divided Europe was the field.

entities/yuri-andropov.title: Yuri Andropov (1914-1984)
entities/yuri-andropov.content:
Yuri Andropov (1914-1984)
For fifteen years Yuri Andropov stood at the head of the Committee for State Security, the Комитет государственной безопасности, the sword and shield of the Soviet system; and then, in the last two years of his life, he was called from that guardian’s post to the summit of the party itself. The man who succeeded Leonid Brezhnev in November 1982 was in many ways his opposite — where Brezhnev had been warm, kindly and reassuring, Andropov was a figure of formidable intelligence and reserve, a politician with a reputation for the двойное дно (double bottom), for the hidden second meaning that Brezhnev conspicuously lacked. He came to power already gravely ill, yet in his brief tenure he stirred the stagnant calm of the Brezhnev years with a campaign of discipline, and gathered about himself the men and the ideas that were to carry the country toward reform.
The making of a chairman
Andropov’s biography ran through the apparatus of the young Soviet state. Born in 1914 in the family of a railwayman and a music teacher, he threw himself into Komsomol work from his youth, then into party work, and rose through the ranks of the machine. He was Soviet ambassador to Hungary during the events of 1956, and the memory of that upheaval — of the Soviet state obliged to defend the socialist commonwealth from within — marked his whole understanding of politics. In 1967 he took the chairmanship of the Committee for State Security, a post he was to hold for fifteen years, until 1982. Under his hand the organs acquired their mature and imposing form: a vast security establishment and, increasingly, an instrument for the renewal of the party itself. He entered the Politburo in 1973, alongside the Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko, and over the years of Brezhnev’s decline his authority grew, his reputation for severity and intellect setting him apart from the ageing leadership around him.
The discipline of the organs
Andropov’s tenure at the head of the KGB fixed the character of his later rule. He was a man of exceptional intelligence, political talent and personal modesty, who knew how to draw people to him and command respect; and he was, in equal measure, an experienced, hard and purposeful politician. The security service under his direction was not only a machine of surveillance but a guardian of the moral and economic order of the system. In the language of the official histories, the party of the developed socialist society waged a steady struggle against corruption, speculation and the shadow economy that grew up around the shortages of the late Soviet order — and Andropov, who knew the extent of that shadow world better than any man in the leadership, was its most implacable enemy.
The campaign of discipline
When Brezhnev died on 10 November 1982, Andropov was elected General Secretary of the Central Committee and head of state. He stood, in his own words, for the preservation and renewal of the Soviet system — not for its dismantling, but for its cleansing and strengthening. His first measures were aimed at the теневая экономика (shadow economy) and at the corruption that had grown up in the sphere of trade and the distribution of social goods. These efforts were greeted by the population with sympathy; the people, who lived daily with the shortages and the privilege, saw in the severity of the new leader a long-awaited justice. The discipline he imposed reached down into the everyday — into the workplace, the trading floor, the whole texture of a society grown accustomed to ease and slackness — and for a time the country felt itself being drawn up short, held to a stricter standard than it had known in years.
Andropov also encouraged Soviet scholars to seek the optimal recipes of reform, including on the basis of foreign experience. A circle of economists — Shatalin, Anchishkin, Zaslavskaya, Aganbegyan — worked on variants that would seriously transform the role of the state in managing the economy. In 1983 work began on a programme of ускорение (acceleration) of socio-economic development, a word that was to enter the political vocabulary and pass on to his successors. Two models of modernisation were considered: reform carried out under the firm political control of the state, the path then being pursued in China; and the transition of the whole economy to a market basis alongside political reform. Neither was fully resolved — no single, coherent programme of reform had been created by the mid-1980s — but the ground was being prepared.
The unfulfilled tenure
Andropov’s rule was cut short. In February 1984 he died, having been at the head of the party for little more than a year, much of it spent in illness. He had come to the summit already seriously ill, and the reformer’s energy he embodied was never permitted to reach full expression. His significance lies in what he began rather than what he completed: the discipline campaign that was remembered with sympathy, the call to the intellectuals, the shaping of a current of opinion that would find its voice after him. He left the party to Konstantin Chernenko, and then to the younger man whom Andropov’s circle had already singled out, Mikhail Gorbachev. In the historical literature he stands as the bridge between the immobilism of Brezhnev and the reforms of perestroika — the one leader of the early eighties who understood, at the summit of the security state, that the system he had guarded for fifteen years could not stand still.

events/23-f-coup-1981.title: The Coup Attempt of 23 February 1981 (23-F)
events/23-f-coup-1981.content:
The Coup Attempt of 23 February 1981 (23-F)
On the afternoon of 23 February 1981, as the Congress of Deputies gathered to vote on the investiture of the new prime minister, Leopoldo Calvo-Sotelo, the doors of the chamber burst open and a squad of Guardia Civil officers under Lieutenant-Colonel Antonio Tejero poured in, firing into the air and seizing the entire parliament hostage. In the same hours the Captain-General of Valencia, Jaime Milans del Bosch, brought his troops into the streets in the name of the coup. Spain, five years into its democracy, confronted the moment the army had always threatened: the armed forces of the régime that had inherited the Transition rose against it. The event, known to every Spaniard as el 23-F, was the gravest crisis of the transicion-democratica-1975-78 — and it ended in the defeat of the conspirators and the consolidation of the regime they had tried to destroy.
The army as enemy of the Transition
The coup was the culmination of a long threat. The military had been the principal structural enemy of the Transition, an institution inherited from the dictatorship that the new monarchy and civilian government had to manage without rupture. Through the constituent years successive conspiracies and pressures had run beneath the surface of Spanish politics; the armed forces, formed under francoism, regarded the democracy, and above all the legalisation of the communists, as a betrayal of everything they had fought for. The governments of the Transition had moved cautiously around this danger, and the discontent was fed by the perceived weakness of the state in the face of terrorism and the national question. On 23 February the conspiracy that had been building burst into the open, with the seizure of the Cortes as its dramatic centrepiece.
The king’s intervention
The crisis was resolved by the monarchy. As the deputies lay on the floor of the chamber and the coup spread to Valencia, juan-carlos-i — the Captain-General of the armed forces, the man to whom the army’s loyalty was owed — acted decisively. That night the king appeared on television in uniform, refusing the conspirators the cover of royal authority and ordering the armed forces to hold to their constitutional duty. The intervention was decisive: the soldiers who had waited to be told that the king was behind them were instead told that he was against them, and the conspiracy collapsed. Tejero surrendered his hostages the following morning, and Milans del Bosch was arrested. The coup that had seemed to hold Spain’s fate in its hands dissolved within a day, defeated less by force than by the authority of the Crown.
The consolidation of democracy
The failure of 23-F proved a turning point. The defeat of the conspiracy strengthened rather than shook the democratic regime: the Spanish people had seen the democracy’s mortal enemy, and had seen it beaten, and the regime emerged from the crisis with its legitimacy enhanced. Tusell recorded the change in the mood of the country — dissatisfaction with the democratic regime, already limited, fell from about nine per cent before February 1981 to about five per cent by the time of the 1982 elections. The episode foreclosed the involucionist danger for good: the army, once its coup had failed and the king had declared for the constitution, ceased to be a living threat to the order it had so nearly overturned. Calvo-Sotelo, the man whose investiture the coup had interrupted, took office shortly after, and the democracy went forward to its decisive test and settlement in the election of psoe-victory-1982. The constitution-1978 had survived the gravest assault upon it, and the Transition was politically complete.

events/algerian-war-1954-62.title: Algerian War (1954-1962)
events/algerian-war-1954-62.content:
The Algerian War (1954-1962)
On the night of 1 November 1954, on the feast of All Saints — the Toussaint rouge — a series of coordinated attacks across Algeria announced to the metropole, in the language of fire, that the long tutelage over French Algeria was being torn apart from within. The insurrection had begun, and France, across the Mediterranean, would spend the better part of the next eight years fighting a war it had never formally declared.
A Territory of Two Peoples
To understand what was at stake, the shape of the land itself had to be seen. Algeria was not a colony in the manner of Tunis or Morocco but, in the legal fiction of the Republic, three départements of France. Nearly a million people of European origin lived there in 1954 — the great majority, over eighty percent, born in Algeria itself — cohabiting with nearly nine million Algériens musulmans who had been excluded from full political rights. This was the society the insurgents struck at: a colonial order woven into the fabric of the Republic, defended not as an overseas possession but as French soil.
The Insurrection and the War
The National Liberation Front, the Front de libération nationale (FLN), waged its campaign of terror and guerrilla war, and the French state answered with a policy of maintien de l’ordre — the “maintenance of order” — which was, without ever saying the word, a war. Pierre Mendès France, before the Assembly in the days after the Toussaint attacks, declared that the first duty of the government was to devote every necessary means to the restoration or maintenance of public order; the re-establishment of order had become the priority of all parties and of opinion itself.
The war was not only fought in the mountains and djebels of the bled but in the language used to describe it. The terms themselves carried contested weight — pieds-noirs for the Europeans of Algeria, Français musulmans d’Algérie for the colonised, guerre d’Algérie for the conflict — each a small symbolic battlefield on which the very meaning of the struggle was disputed.
The Settler Factor and the Republic’s Wounds
The settlers, the pieds-noirs, formed the immovable mass at the centre of the crisis, and their pressure radiated into metropolitan politics. They had a long tradition of resistance to reform from Paris, and as the war deepened they became a force that could bring down governments. It was in part the Algerian question, unresolved through the ministries of Edgar Faure and Guy Mollet, that hollowed out the fourth-republic from within — its régime des partis seemed incapable of either winning the war or ending it. The colonial question, long the blind spot of the national conscience, had become a wound the Republic could not stanch.
The Winding Road of Charles de Gaulle
The crisis of 13 May 1958, born in Algiers of settler and army revolt, swept the General back to power. On 4 June 1958, from the balcony in Algiers, charles-de-gaulle spoke the words that thrilled the crowd and bound him ambiguously to the settlers: “Je vous ai compris” — “I have understood you.” At the height of his return he still appeared to stand for Algérie française; his government proclaimed a programme of economic and social development for Algeria, set out in the Constantine Plan of October 1958, which promised to make of the territory a land of modern prosperity.
But the road de Gaulle actually travelled bent steadily away from the settlers’ hopes. From the outset of his presidency he treated Algeria not as a department to be defended at all costs but as a question to be resolved, and the solution he came to favour was one he alone could impose. He understood that France’s future — its place in Europe, its economy, its standing in a decolonising world — demanded that the war end.
Self-Determination and the Barricades
In the autumn of 1959, in a broadcast allocation of 16 September, de Gaulle offered Algeria the choice of self-determination — a dramatic shift that put the future of the territory, for the first time, in the hands of the population themselves. The settlers and the partisans of Algérie française reacted with fury. In January 1960, a week of barricades shook Algiers as the extreme right and the army’s settlers rose against the President’s policy; de Gaulle answered on the airwaves, reaffirming his authority and his course.
The war, meanwhile, was reaching its cruelest stage. The French army, having nearly defeated the FLN militarily by 1959–60, found itself drawn into methods — torture, internment, the brutalisation of the countryside — whose moral and political costs ate into the nation’s conscience. In April 1961, a group of generals, led by figures who saw de Gaulle’s abandonment of Algérie française as betrayal, staged a putsch in Algiers. It failed within days, as the conscripts refused to follow and the nation rallied to the President, but it revealed how close the army itself had come to the precipice.
Toward the End
The referendum of January 1961 approved the principle of self-determination, and the negotiations toward it were opened with the FLN. But the conflict was not yet finished, and its last phase was the most terrible of all. As the end approached, the settlers and the army officers who would not accept it gathered into the Organisation armée secrète (OAS), which turned to bombing and assassination in both Algeria and the metropole, trying by terror to derail the course de Gaulle had set. The pieds-noirs saw their world collapsing around them, and the OAS spoke for their despair.
The war ended in March 1962 with the signing of the evian-accords-1962, and the referendum of 8 April 1962 ratified them overwhelmingly. But the fureur of the OAS continued into the spring, and the peace that finally fell over Algeria was preceded by a last convulsion. For the pieds-noirs it was the end of a world: nearly the whole of the European population of Algeria would leave, in an exodus that emptied a society in the space of a year. France, the General told the nation, had taken its decision, and the nation had chosen.
The Algerian war left scars that would not close — on the army, on the political right, on the conscience of the Republic, on a million displaced French Algerians, and on the memory of the Français musulmans who had served France and been left behind. It destroyed the fourth-republic and, in a strange turn of history, made the man who ended it the founder of the fifth-republic. It was the matrix out of which the France of the Trente Glorieuses emerged, and the wound that, decades later, still fed French politics.
