events/august-putsch-1991.title: August Putsch (19-21 August 1991)
events/august-putsch-1991.content:
August Putsch (19-21 August 1991)
In August 1991 the Communist Party of the Soviet Union made its last attempt to save the state it had created, and destroyed it. On the morning of 19 August, while President mikhail-gorbachev was away at his holiday residence at Foros on the Black Sea, the hardliners of the Soviet leadership seized power in Moscow. A self-appointed State Committee for the State of Emergency — the Государственный комитет по чрезвычайному положению, the ГКЧП (GKChP) — announced that the President was incapacitated and that they had taken control of the country, and sent tanks into the streets of the capital. The coup was meant to stop the reform and to prevent the signing of the new Union Treaty that would have loosened the bonds of the Soviet republics. In three days it collapsed, broken against the resistance of the Russian President boris-yeltsin and the people of Moscow — and in its collapse it swept away the organs of the Union and the party that had created them, and opened the road to the end of the USSR.
The origins and the seizure of power
The putsch had been brewing through the crisis-ridden months of 1991, as Gorbachev’s attempts to hold the union together faltered and the republics, led by Russia, asserted their sovereignty. The State Committee united the leaders of the forces that stood to lose most from the reform: the Vice-President, the heads of the security organs, the army command, the industrial and party establishment. On 19 August, with Gorbachev cut off at Foros and held incommunicado, the Committee announced that power had passed into its hands and deployed troops in Moscow and the major cities. Pikhoya, who as a witness to the age recorded the events as they unfolded, stresses how carefully the coup was prepared and how completely it failed in its essentials — the leadership that seized power did so without a plan for how to govern, without the loyalty of the troops, and without reckoning on the one man in the country who possessed both legitimacy and courage: the elected President of Russia.
Yeltsin’s resistance and the crowds of Moscow
The centre of resistance was the White House, the seat of the Russian parliament, and the man at its head was Yeltsin. On the morning of the 19th he climbed onto a tank outside the building and called on the people of Russia to disobey the putsch and defend the constitution; barricades rose around the Russian parliament as Muscovites streamed out to defend it. Through the days of 20 and 21 August the crowd held the White House against the threat of a storm that the army was never willing to carry out. Pikhoya’s account — the place of action at Foros, at the Kremlin, in and around the White House, the commanders Grachev and Lebed and their refusal to turn the army on the people, the tragedy in the tunnel of Kalinin Prospekt where three young men were killed — reconstructs the fragility and the triumph of the resistance. By the 21st the putsch was collapsing of its own weight: the troops withdrew, the Committee’s members fled or were arrested, and Gorbachev returned from Foros to a capital in which the authority was no longer his. The failure of the coup had made Yeltsin, in effect, the ruler of the country.
The collapse of the CPSU and the road to dissolution
The consequences of the failed putsch were immediate and total. In the days that followed, Yeltsin suspended the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and seized its assets; the party that had ruled the country for seven decades collapsed with barely a struggle, its members abandoning it by the million. The whole edifice of the Union’s central organs of power self-liquidated, as Pikhoya titles the chapter. Gorbachev returned to find the Soviet state stripped of the party that had been its nervous system and of the authority of the centre; the republics, emboldened by the exposure of the Union’s weakness, moved rapidly toward independence, and the negotiations that might have produced a renewed Union Treaty foundered on the fact that the centre no longer commanded the trust of the republics. Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook treats the August events as the decisive rupture that made the collapse of the USSR all but inevitable. From the failure of the putsch the road ran straight to the Belovezhskaya accords of December and to dissolution-ussr-1991 — the end of the Soviet Union that the generals and party chiefs of the ГКЧП had taken power to prevent.

events/bayeux-speech-1946.title: Bayeux Speech (16 June 1946)
events/bayeux-speech-1946.content:
Bayeux Speech (16 June 1946)
The speech in the first liberated town
On 16 June 1946, two years after the first town of the metropole was liberated, General de Gaulle stood in the streets of Bayeux to set out the constitutional doctrine on which he was prepared to stake his political life. The occasion was a ceremony of remembrance, but the address was an act of politics. Out of power since his resignation of 20 January 1946, de Gaulle used the sacred setting of the Liberation to define, once and for all, the institutions he believed France required — and to measure them, publicly and unanswerably, against the draft constitution that the parties were then preparing for the Fourth Republic.
The head of state above the parties
The heart of the Bayeux declaration was a demand for a strong executive rooted in the nation rather than in the parliamentary game. De Gaulle called for a head of state who would be the arbiter of the political struggle, standing above the parties, invested with the authority to embody the state, to govern with the assent of the nation, and to hold the continuity of the country through the vicissitudes of the party system. Against the doctrine of the sovereign Assembly, which reduced the executive to the creature of the chamber, he set the separation of powers and a government that could actually govern. The nation, he insisted, was one and indivisible; its destinies could not be left to the shifting majorities of a parliamentary assembly alone. This was the doctrine he had been taught by the débâcle of 1940 — that the weakness of the executive had delivered France to catastrophe — and it was the programme from which he would never waver, through the years of the traversée du désert (crossing of the desert) and on to the constitution of 1958.
The measure of the Fourth Republic
The Bayeux speech was a sword pointed at the Fourth Republic before the Republic even existed. It was delivered while the first Constituent Assembly, elected in October 1945, was drawing up a constitution that ran directly counter to de Gaulle’s demands — a régime of the primacy of the Assembly, the régime des partis (rule of the parties) that he denounced. He campaigned against the successive drafts with declarations through the summer and autumn of 1946 — 27 August, 19 September, 9 October, 1 November — and in the speech at Épinal on 29 September, urging the rejection of a constitution that institutionalised the weakness he had condemned. When the country adopted the constitution of October 1946 against his advice, de Gaulle retired to the opposition, and Bayeux became the fixed star of his long wait.
A programme deferred, not abandoned
For twelve years the Bayeux doctrine lay dormant, sustained by the R.P.F. and then by the silence of the traversée du désert, as the Fourth Republic confirmed his every prediction of ministerial instability. When the crisis of 1958 brought him back to power, the constitution of the Fifth Republic that he carried to the referendum of September 1958 was in its essentials the constitution of Bayeux — a strong president as arbiter, a government that could govern, a nation confirmed as the source of power. The speech of June 1946 thus stands at the origin of the régime that replaced the Fourth Republic, the founding text of gaullisme and of the Fifth Republic, pronounced in a small Norman town twelve years before the institutions it described were realised.

events/berlin-blockade-1948-49.title: Berlin Blockade and Airlift (1948–49)
events/berlin-blockade-1948-49.content:
Berlin Blockade and Airlift (1948–49)
In the spring of 1948 the future of Germany, and with it the future of Europe, was decided in a city 200 kilometres behind the line that divided the Soviet zone from the Western zones — and decided not by diplomats at a conference table but by the endurance of a besieged population and the courage of the airmen who fed it. The Berlin Blockade, which closed every road, rail and water route into the Western sectors of the city, and the great airlift that broke it, marked the moment when the wartime alliance of the four occupying powers finally hardened into the two blocs of the Cold War, and when the division of Germany into two states became almost inevitable.
The currency dispute and the division of the zones
The blockade grew out of the breakdown of four-power cooperation over Germany. The occupying powers had agreed at Potsdam in 1945 to treat Germany as a single economic unit, but the Western powers — and above all the Americans, under the impulse of the Marshall Plan — were coming to see the reconstruction of a Western Germany as essential to the recovery and security of Europe. The Soviet Union, for its part, suspected the West of seeking to draw a revived Germany into its own camp. The immediate precipitant was the currency: when the Western allies prepared a currency reform for their zones in the spring of 1948, the Russians saw a decisive step toward the creation of a separate West German state. On 20 June 1948 the Western authorities introduced the Deutsche Mark in the Western zones and the Western sectors of Berlin, three days after which the Soviet military government announced a reform of its own in the East. Berlin, a city of four-power status surrounded by Soviet territory, became the testing ground.
The blockade and the airlift
On 24 June 1948 the Soviet authorities closed all land and water communications between the Western zones and Berlin — the Blockade — cutting off food, fuel and every necessity from two and a half million people in the Western sectors. The Western response, born partly of necessity and partly of determination, was the Luftbrücke, the “air bridge”: an enormous airlift in which American and British aircraft flew round the clock into the airports of Tempelhof and Gatow, carrying coal, flour, dried potatoes and the staples of daily life into the blockaded city. At its peak in the spring of 1949 the planes were landing at intervals of little more than a minute, delivering up to 13,000 tons a day. The Russians had calculated that the West would not sustain so enormous an effort, or would negotiate away its rights in Berlin; instead the airlift became a demonstration of Western resolve and of American power, and the besieged Berliners, defying the Soviet threats and the lures of the Eastern ration cards, became for the West the heroic defenders of freedom.
A cold-war division hardened
The blockade had the opposite of its intended effect. Rather than driving the Western powers out of Berlin, it drove them to fuse their occupation and, eventually, to rearm in the face of the Soviet threat; rather than preventing a West German state, it made one certain. The eleven months of the blockade crystallised the hostility of the two camps. In the West it hardened the conviction that Germany must be reconstructed, armed and integrated into the Western alliance; in Berlin itself it bound the Western sectors and their population indissolubly to the West. The contest became the emblem of the Cold War — a confrontation in which the fate of a city stood for the fate of Europe.
The founding of the two German states
The blockade was lifted on 12 May 1949, when the Soviet authorities at last reopened the land routes, the Western powers having agreed at a conference in New York to raise their own counter-measures and to discuss Berlin at the Council of Foreign Ministers. The airlift continued for some weeks to build up stocks, and was formally ended in September 1949. The siege had, however, already done its work. During the months of the blockade the Western powers had pressed ahead with the constitution for a West German state — the Grundgesetz (Basic Law) drafted by the parliamentary council — and the Soviet zone with its own preparations. Within months of the lifting of the blockade, in May and October 1949 respectively, the Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic were proclaimed. The city that had been blockaded and kept alive by the airlift remained divided, an island of the West in the East and the sharpest symbol of the division of Germany and of Europe — the division that was to be sealed thirteen years later by the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961.

events/bologna-massacre-1980.title: The Bologna Massacre (2 August 1980)
events/bologna-massacre-1980.content:
The Bologna Massacre (2 August 1980)
The deadliest attack of the years of lead struck Italy on 2 August 1980, at the height of the summer holidays, when much of the country was in motion toward the places of its villeggiatura. A dynamite bomb tore down a wing of the railway station of Bologna, turning the second-class waiting room into a scene of massacre: eighty-three dead and more than two hundred wounded among the travellers who had crowded there at the beginning of August. It was a new act of terrorism whose technique and characteristics linked it directly to those of Piazza Fontana, of Piazza della Loggia and of the Italicus train — all of them, in the parlance of the age, of matrice nera, the stamp of the far right.
The attack
The station of Bologna was a natural target at that moment of the year — the great junction of the national rail network, the gateway between the north and the centre of the peninsula, packed with families bound for the beaches and the mountains. The explosion in the waiting room of the second class, in the late morning of a Saturday, caught the crowd unawares. The collapse of a whole wing of the building buried dozens beneath the rubble, and the work of rescue, carried on for days, was among the most harrowing the Republic had known. The toll of eighty-three dead made it the gravest single act of terrorism in the entire history of the Italian Republic.
The inquest and the deflection
The magistracy followed the neo-fascist trail from the start and in a short time appeared to come to grips with the responsible parties. But neither the first nor the second trail indicated by the military intelligence service, the SISMI — trails that led to a group of German terrorists who would have acted on the mandate of the Italian neo-fascists — withstood verification and more thorough investigation. Indeed, the press came to suspect the SISMI of having deflected the investigations of the Bolognese judges, for purposes that seemed to accredit the disquieting hypotheses that were being formed about the role played by the secret services in the strategia della tensione. A year and a half after the beginning of the inquest all the suspects of the massacre were released, and four years later the proceeding closed with nothing achieved, leaving this new crime of the black terrorism unpunished. Only the appeal process, concluded in 1988, identified the guilty — but not the mandanti, the instigators who had ordered the massacre.
The place of the massacre
The Bologna massacre stood at the tail of the darkest sequence of the years of lead, coming at a moment when the state was at last gaining the upper hand over left-wing terrorism. The general Carlo Alberto Dalla Chiesa and his carabinieri, reorganised and better equipped, had gone over to the counter-offensive and were dismantling the apparatus of the Brigate Rosse; the confessions of the first pentiti had begun. In this context the bomb at Bologna served to underline that the black terrorism, and the shadowy forces behind it, remained an unsolved and unconfessed crime — a wound in the body of the Republic. Gentiloni Silveri sets it within the frame of the continuing crisis of the state and the years of political violence that, together with the murder of Aldo Moro, had brought the institutions of the country to their most difficult hour. The massacre remained, for decades, a symbol of the impunity that could still shelter the perpetrators of political violence in Italy.

events/brexit-2016.title: Brexit (2016)
events/brexit-2016.content:
Brexit (2016)
The referendum of 23 June 2016, in which the people of the United Kingdom voted by 51.9 per cent to 48.1 per cent to leave the European Union, was the first time in the history of european-integration that a member state had chosen, by popular vote, to depart. It ended a British relationship with the continent that had been marked, from its beginnings, by distance and hesitation — a relationship that the historian of the Union would read against the grain of what was once called “British exceptionalism.” Britain had joined the Community only in 1973, after two applications had been vetoed by charles-de-gaulle; it had won for itself a succession of opt-outs from the Union’s deeper projects, from the single currency to the Schengen area; and it had stood, in the decades since, as the member most persistently at odds with the federal direction of the enterprise. The vote of 2016 was the culmination of that long ambivalence — the moment at which the British, offered the choice between membership and sovereignty, answered with departure. The departure itself took more than four years to complete, and it was to test the Union almost as severely as the euro crisis had done, forcing on it a question it had never been designed to answer: how a member state could leave.
A half-hearted member
Britain’s exceptionalism was real, but it was not, as its own mythology liked to claim, the expression of a nation that had simply never wished to join. Britain had sought membership eagerly in the 1960s, and had been refused; it had entered in 1973, confirmed its membership in a referendum in 1975, and remained a powerful and influential member for four decades. Yet the relationship was marked throughout by a distinctive unease. Britain had come late to the Community, and it had never fully accepted the Community’s deepest premise — that its member states were bound together in a union that pooled their sovereignty. It kept its own currency, its own borders, and its own sense of a destiny that lay as much across the Atlantic as across the Channel. The opt-outs Britain negotiated at maastricht-treaty-1992 — from the single currency and from the social chapter — were the badges of this half-membership. In the Cambridge account, the British relationship was a story of an awkward but durable partner whose exceptionalism lay less in a refusal of Europe than in a refusal to accept the logic of a union of ever-closer integration.
The referendum of 2016
The referendum was called by a British prime minister, David Cameron, who had promised it in 2013 under pressure from the eurosceptic wing of his own party, and who expected to win it. It was fought, in a summer of extraordinary political ferment, over the question of membership itself — the first such choice since 1975. The campaign was dominated not by the institutional arcana of the Union but by the two great anxieties of the age: sovereignty and migration. The Leave campaign argued that the British people could not govern themselves while laws were made in Brussels, and that the free movement of people had made the country’s borders meaningless; the Remain campaign warned of the economic and political cost of departure. On 23 June 2016 the country answered. The result divided the United Kingdom as nothing had divided it in living memory — by generation, by class, by education, and by nation, with England and Wales voting Leave while Scotland and Northern Ireland voted Remain. The prime minister who had called the vote resigned the next morning, and the Union entered the most uncertain period of its existence.
The long departure
The decision to leave, once taken, proved far easier to vote than to execute. The task of negotiating the terms of departure fell to a succession of British governments over more than four years, through two general elections, the resignation of two prime ministers and the convulsions of a country struggling to define what “taking back control” actually meant. The Union, for its part, negotiated as one: the twenty-seven remaining member states, drawn together by the crisis, delegated the task to the Commission and refused, with remarkable discipline, to be divided among themselves. The Withdrawal Agreement eventually reached set the terms on which Britain left, and the subsequent Trade and Cooperation Agreement defined the future relationship — but it was the question of the border between Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom, and the Republic of Ireland, part of the Union, that proved the hardest, and that was resolved only by a protocol that left the United Kingdom, in the eyes of its own Unionists, partially inside the Union’s customs and single market. On 31 January 2020 Britain left the European Union. The departure was accomplished, but the questions it raised — about the unity of the United Kingdom itself, about the meaning of sovereignty in an interdependent world, and about the limits of national exceptionalism — were not.
The limits of exceptionalism
Read against the grain of British exceptionalism, Brexit was not the reassertion of an exceptional Britain but the demonstration of its limits. The departure, the Cambridge account suggests, was less the triumph of a nation that had always stood apart than the exhaustion of a particular way of being European — the last act of a member that had never quite accepted the rules of the union it had joined. And the Union survived the departure as it had survived the euro crisis. The removal of its most awkward member, far from bringing the enterprise to an end, allowed the twenty-seven to pursue integration more coherently; Britain’s long dissent had, paradoxically, constrained the Union’s federal ambitions, and its departure removed a brake. The euro crisis had tested the Union’s centre; Brexit tested its periphery. Both passed through the crucible, and by the time of the next crises — of migration, of Covid-19, of the Russian war in Ukraine — Britain was gone, and the Union faced them as a body of twenty-seven. Brexit thus marked both the end of a national project of exceptionalism and the confirmation that european-integration, however contested, was a durable fact of the continent’s life.

events/building-berlin-wall-1961.title: The Building of the Berlin Wall (13 August 1961)
events/building-berlin-wall-1961.content:
The Building of the Berlin Wall (13 August 1961)
In the early hours of Sunday, 13 August 1961, the soldiers and police of the German Democratic Republic moved into the streets of Berlin and sealed the border between the eastern and western halves of the city. Barbed wire was unrolled along the sector boundary, the streets were torn up and barricaded, the trains and tramways of the S-Bahn were halted where they crossed the line. Within days the wire grew into a wall of concrete, and within months into the fortified barrier of watchtowers, guards and death strips that was to divide Berlin, Germany and the world for twenty-eight years. The building of the Berlin Wall closed the last open border between the socialist and the capitalist world — and, with it, the last escape from the German Democratic Republic. It was at once an admission of failure and a turning point: the moment the regime confessed that it could keep its people only by force, and the moment from which, sealed and stabilized, it began its long consolidation.
The flight that emptied the state
The Wall was the answer to a hemorrhage that threatened to destroy the republic. Since the founding of the GDR in 1949, hundreds of thousands of East Germans — the young, the skilled, the enterprising — had voted with their feet against the regime, walking out through the open border in Berlin, where the Soviet and the western sectors met and the barrier between East and West had not yet been built. The flight was the great weakness of the state: the collectivization and industrial drive of the fifties had made it a drain of labour and talent, and by 1961 the emigration had reached flood-tide. Weber records how the mass flight in the summer of 1961 — tens of thousands in a single month — confronted Ulbricht and the party with a choice between sealing the border and watching the republic bleed to death. The regime had long denied any such intention; only days before, at an international press conference, Ulbricht had answered a question on the subject with the claim that “nobody has the intention of building a wall” (niemand hat die Absicht, eine Mauer zu errichten). The denial was the prelude to the deed.
The sealing of the border
The operation on the night of 13 August was prepared in secret, in agreement with Moscow, and carried out with sudden, overwhelming efficiency. The GDR’s armed forces and its police, the Volkspolizei, moved into position in the early hours, while the Soviet Union, which alone could guarantee the action, lent it the weight of its authority. The border was closed without warning, the crossings reduced to a handful of checkpoints, and the inhabitants of the East woke to find the partition of their city become concrete. The western allies protested and sent patrols to the line, but they did not interfere; the frontier of Berlin was a line the West accepted rather than fight for. Within weeks the provisional barricade was replaced by the permanent Wall, the antifaschistischer Schutzwall (“antifascist protection rampart”) of the regime’s official language — a name that inverted the truth of what it did: it existed not to keep danger out but to keep the GDR’s own people in.
The turning point
The building of the Wall was a watershed in the Cold War and in the history of the two German states. For the GDR it was a strange paradox. On the one hand the Wall was a confession of bankruptcy — a state that had to wall in its citizens could claim no legitimacy over them. On the other hand it was, as Weber emphasizes, the foundation of the republic’s stability: with the border closed, the regime was at last freed from the constant drain of emigration, and could begin the Festigung, the consolidation, of the state that had eluded it since 1949. The years after 1961 were the most settled of the GDR’s existence, the era of the Neues Ökonomisches System and of the “model experiments” under Ulbricht. For the Western world and especially for the Federal Republic, the Wall hardened the division of Germany into permanence: Winkler treats it as the culmination of the confrontation of the two systems, the moment the partition of Europe and of Germany, so long provisional, was made solid, and the hope of a quick reunification was abandoned. The Wall, erected to stop the East German exodus, became the symbol of the Cold War itself — a symbol that would stand for nearly three decades, until the opening of the border on 9 November 1989 and the fall of the Wall at last brought down what the regime had built to contain its own people.

events/chernobyl-1986.title: Chernobyl Disaster (26 April 1986)
events/chernobyl-1986.content:
Chernobyl Disaster (26 April 1986)
On the night of 26 April 1986, at the nuclear power station at Chernobyl in Ukraine, seventy miles north of Kiev, the reactor of the fourth generating unit exploded during a test, hurling a plume of radioactive material into the atmosphere and beginning the worst nuclear accident in history. The disaster — чернобыльская катастрофа (chernobylskaya katastrofa, the Chernobyl catastrophe) — burned out of control for days, forced the evacuation of the city of Pripyat and then of hundreds of thousands of people, and spread contamination across Ukraine, Belarus and far beyond into Europe. Its human and environmental toll was enormous and, in the immediate years, impossible to measure. But in the history of the Soviet Union the significance of Chernobyl reaches well beyond the reactor itself: the disaster struck at the very outset of perestroika-1985-91, and the way the system first hid and then half-revealed it became a turning point in the story of glasnost — an event that broke the credibility of the regime and exposed, before the eyes of the world, the costs of the secrecy and the false reports on which the old order had been built.
The accident and the first silence
The test that destroyed the reactor was conducted in the early hours of Saturday 26 April, during the shift of engineers carrying out a safety experiment on the turbine. A surge of power out of control, an explosion that tore the roof from the building and set the graphite of the core on fire — within minutes the station was a ruin pouring smoke and radioactivity into the night. The authorities of the USSR, heirs of a system in which bad news was suppressed as a matter of state, responded at first with silence. The nearby town of Pripyat was not evacuated until the following day; Moscow issued a terse announcement two days later that spoke of an “accident” at the station and of measures being taken. For days the government denied the scale of the catastrophe. Pikhoya’s account of the disaster situates it within the first years of the reform: the accident occurred while the leadership was still pursuing the old reflex of concealment, and the gap between what the world could measure with its own instruments — the radiation cloud detected across Scandinavia within days — and what Moscow was willing to say became a scandal that the new policy of openness could not ignore.
Glasnost and the exposure
Chernobyl became, in effect, the test that forced glasnost into being. The Scandinavian states detected elevated radiation within days and demanded explanations; the Soviet public, cut off from the details of the catastrophe in its own territory, learned of it from abroad; the official news machine, caught in contradiction, was compelled to publish what it had sought to conceal. Under the pressure of the new spirit of openness that Gorbachev himself was promoting, the regime began at last to tell the truth — and the contrast between the old silence and the new revelation did incalculable damage to the authority of the state. The disaster, Pikhoya argues, was one of the great events that broke the faith of the people in the system’s competence and honesty; it discredited the party’s claim to rule, exposed the poverty of the technology and the administration on which the superpower rested, and demonstrated that the country could no longer hide its failures either from its own citizens or from the world. Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook treats Chernobyl among the decisive shocks of the perestroika period, an event whose consequences for the spiritual and political climate of the country were profound.
Consequences for the regime
The immediate toll of Chernobyl was appalling — the dead and the radiation-sick among the firemen and the liquidators who fought the fire at the cost of their own health, the mass evacuations, the contamination of vast agricultural lands, the birth defects and the illness that followed for decades. The political consequences were no less real, and they rippled outward through the whole course of the reform. The catastrophe undermined confidence in the scientific and technological claims of the state and fanned the growth of public concern, in Ukraine and Belarus, that would feed the rising national movements of the late 1980s. It forced the leadership further along the road of openness that was consuming it, and it accelerated the erosion of the party’s legitimacy that Yurchak describes as the destruction of the authoritative discourse from within. In the history of the Soviet Union’s end, Chernobyl stands as one of the first great cracks in the edifice — a catastrophe that the system could neither prevent, nor conceal, nor survive untouched, and whose consequences belonged as much to the collapse of dissolution-ussr-1991 as to the silent steppe around the ruined reactor.

events/constitution-1978.title: The Constitution of 1978
events/constitution-1978.content:
The Constitution of 1978
On 6 December 1978 the Spanish people, voting in referendum, ratified the constitution that was to govern the new democracy — a text of eleven titles and 169 articles, with additional and transitional dispositions, that fixed the form of the Spanish state for the age to come. It was not the work of a single majority, but the product of a deliberate consenso (consensus) among the principal parliamentary forces, the shared settlement by which the political classes of the transicion-democratica-1975-78 agreed to make their common ground the foundation of the state. Drafted after the constituent elections of June 1977, through a long and patient elaboration, the constitution was at once the culmination of the Transition and the institution-building act of the young democracy.
The long road to the text
The constituent work opened in the Cortes elected on 15 June 1977. The drafting fell to a small committee of the principal parties — representatives of the governing centrists of adolfo-suarez, the socialist left, the communist party and the national forces — charged to reconcile what the Civil War and the dictatorship had divided. The road was long. The consensus demanded that the constitution be a text no major force would reject, and this requirement governed every article: the form of the state, the catalogue of rights, the place of the Crown, the organisation of the territory all had to be settled in language all could accept. Tusell described it as a consensus politics pursued through a long drafting path; the result was a settlement that enshrined the compromises of the Transition in fundamental law.
The content of the settlement
The constitution established a parliamentary monarchy, placing the Crown of juan-carlos-i within a democratic order whose sovereignty resided in the Spanish people. It proclaimed a comprehensive catalogue of rights — the rights of the person, of expression, of association, of political participation — guaranteed against the state. It created a Cortes of two chambers, a government responsible to the parliament, an independent judiciary, and a title on constitutional reform to give the settlement durability. Its most contested and most consequential provision was Title VIII, on the territorial organisation of the state: the constitution transformed Spain from the centralised state of the dictatorship into a Estado de las autonomías (state of the autonomies), recognising the regions — above all the historic nationalities of the Basque Country, Catalonia and Galicia — as communities entitled to self-government. The national question, the great question the Transition had left pending, was answered in the constitution by a flexible and open framework whose concrete content was still to be specified, and which the Socialist governments would develop into the quasi-federal structure of the modern state.
The referendum and the balance
Approved by referendum in December 1978, the constitution entered into force as the common ground of all Spaniards, an instrument of “what unites us all.” Institutionally it closed the Transition — the democracy of the Spanish state was henceforth fixed in law. Yet the constitutional settlement was not the whole of the achievement, nor the end of the difficulties. The nationalisms and terrorism of the Basque and Catalan tracks, the great unresolved question beside the constitutional settlement, would press upon the new democracy for decades. And the settlement itself would be tested within little more than two years, when the army rose at 23-f-coup-1981 against the order the constitution had created. The constitution survived that crisis as it had survived the passage from dictatorship to democracy, and remained the enduring frame within which the political life of the new Spain — the socialist era of felipe-gonzalez, the autonomies, the entry into Europe — was to unfold.

events/constitution-fifth-republic-1958.title: Constitution of the Fifth Republic (1958)
events/constitution-fifth-republic-1958.content:
The Constitution of the Fifth Republic (1958)
The constitution that founded the Fifth Republic was written in a summer of crisis and carried to the country in a climate of urgency that had no equal since the Liberation. Drafted between the investiture of charles-de-gaulle in June 1958 and the referendum of autumn, it was the instrument by which a man who had spent twelve years denouncing the constitution of the fourth-republic at last gave France the institutions he had conceived at Bayeux in 1946. The constitution of 4 October 1958 abolished the régime of the parties and replaced it with a state built around a strong executive.
The drafting
The text was drawn up under the direction of Michel Debré, the minister of justice and the General’s most devoted constitutional jurist, together with the other members of the government charged with the task. Debré, who had defended de Gaulle’s constitutional doctrine through the years of opposition, translated the Bayeux design into a workable instrument. The drafting was carried out with a deliberate haste that was itself a political act: the crisis of May 1958, born in Algiers, had shown that the state must not again be left at the mercy of an assembly-dominated régime and an army it could not command. The new constitution gave the President of the Republic the standing of an arbiter above the parties, a strengthened executive, and the means to govern — the strong state that the General had demanded since his return.
A strong executive
The heart of the constitution was the rebalancing of the powers of the state. Where the Fourth Republic had been dominated by the National Assembly and its shifting coalitions, the Fifth gave the President the power to appoint the government, to dissolve the Assembly, and in moments of grave crisis the exceptional powers of Article 16. The executive, no longer the prisoner of the parliamentary majority of the day, was to be the motor of the régime; the régime des partis that de Gaulle had condemned since 1946 was set aside. In the gaullist reading the constitution restored to France the authority of a state that the parties had, in the years of ministerial instability, hollowed out from within. The choice of the uninominal majority two-ballot scrutiny for the elections of November 1958, a scrutiny that weakened the role of the parties, completed the design.
The referendum of 28 September 1958
De Gaulle carried the constitution to the country in September with all the weight of his authority. He addressed the nation from the place de la République in Paris, travelled to Madagascar, Dakar and Constantine with a programme of development for Algeria, and staked the future of the new régime on the verdict. On 28 September 1958 the referendum adopted the constitution by a large majority — 79.2% of Oui in the metropole, with 15.06% abstentions. The choice was, in de Gaulle’s framing, a choice between the state and the disorder of the old régime. France answered with the largest vote for a new order that the Republic had seen.
The new régime begins
The constitution took effect on 4 October 1958. On 21 December the college of grands électeurs elected de Gaulle President of the Republic, and on 8 January 1959 he was installed at the Élysée with Michel Debré as his Prime Minister. The Fifth Republic had begun — the régime of the strong executive that de Gaulle had sought since the Bayeux declaration of 1946, realised at last through the crisis of May 1958 and ratified by the referendum of September. The constitution of 1958 was to prove the most durable of all the French republican constitutions, the frame within which the effort of modernisation, the settlement of Algeria, the policy of national independence and the crises of the late 1960s would all unfold. It was the founding text of the régime that the General would complete four years later with the referendum of October 1962 on the election of the President by universal suffrage.

events/cuban-missile-crisis-1962.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)
events/cuban-missile-crisis-1962.content:
The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)
For thirteen days in October 1962 the world stood at the brink of a war that neither side could survive. The confrontation that the Soviet histories call the karibskii krizis — the Caribbean crisis — was the closest the Cold War ever came to the nuclear abyss: the confrontation over Soviet missiles on the island of Cuba, ninety miles from the coast of the United States, in which the two superpowers tested each other to the edge and then, at the last moment, drew back. It arose from the most dangerous of all the perils of the atomic age — the rivalry of the blocs armed with weapons capable of destroying mankind — and it ended in a settlement that showed both sides the price of going further. In the Soviet reading, the crisis was the work of the aggressive policy of the United States against revolutionary Cuba, and its resolution a victory for the firmness of the Soviet Union and the cause of peace.
The missiles and the blockade
Revolutionary Cuba, under Fidel Castro, had been the first socialist state in the Western hemisphere, and the United States had never reconciled itself to its existence. The fiasco of the Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961 and the open threats and plots that followed convinced the Soviet leadership that the island, unprotected by its own power, stood in mortal danger. In 1962 the Soviet government secretly placed medium- and intermediate-range ballistic missiles on Cuban soil, ready to defend the fraternal republic and to redress the balance of a strategic relationship in which the United States, ringed with bases around the Soviet Union, held an overwhelming advantage. When American reconnaissance aircraft discovered the missile sites on 14 October 1962, the United States responded with the utmost severity. President Kennedy went before his people on 22 October to announce a naval quarantine of Cuba, a blockade of the island to halt the further shipment of offensive weapons, and demanded the withdrawal of the missiles already there. Soviet ships steamed toward the quarantine line; the world held its breath, and the two superpowers faced each other across the Caribbean with their full arsenals armed.
The thirteen days
The days that followed were the most perilous of the nuclear age. Soviet ships approached the line and then, under orders from Moscow, turned back or stood off rather than force the confrontation; the American blockade held, and the pressure on both sides mounted to the point of breakdown. Khrushchev and Kennedy exchanged messages of mounting gravity — some of them public, some of them conducted through secret channels — as the United States prepared its forces and the Soviet Union warned that it would not be intimidated. The crisis reached its peak when an American U-2 aircraft was shot down over Cuba and the world learned that the local commanders had acted on the edge of the abyss. Then, in the final days of October, the settlement was reached. In exchange for the withdrawal of the Soviet missiles from Cuba, the United States gave its undertaking not to invade the island and, in a less public concession, to remove its own missiles from Turkey. On 28 October Khrushchev announced that the Soviet Union would dismantle and remove its missiles, and the quarantine was lifted. The karibskii krizis (Caribbean crisis) was over; the ships turned away, the missiles went home, and the two powers, having looked into the furnace, resolved never to look again.
The consequences
The Cuban missile crisis was a watershed of the Cold War. Its lesson, drawn on both sides, was the imperative of the razryadka, the relaxation of tension, that was to dominate the following decade. It led directly to the establishment of the “hot line” between Moscow and Washington, the direct link by which the two leaders could speak instantly in a moment of crisis; to the partial test-ban treaty of 1963, which forbade nuclear tests in the atmosphere; and to the opening of the long series of arms-control negotiations. For the Soviet Union the outcome was a sobering demonstration of the consequences of strategic inferiority — a demonstration that impelled the vast build-up of Soviet strategic forces that was to give the USSR, by the era of the Brezhnev leadership, nuclear parity with the United States. And for the wider world the crisis fixed the image of the two superpowers as masters of life and death, whose restraint had preserved the peace — an image that lent urgency to the drive for détente and the disarmament negotiations that followed. The official Soviet histories drew from October 1962 the vindication of the policy of peaceful coexistence: the socialist power had defended revolutionary Cuba, the aggression had been repelled, and the world had been saved by the reasonableness of the Soviet leadership from the madness of imperialist brinkmanship.

events/dissolution-ussr-1991.title: Dissolution of the USSR (December 1991)
events/dissolution-ussr-1991.content:
Dissolution of the USSR (December 1991)
In the last days of December 1991 the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the state built by the Bolshevik revolution of 1917 and extended across a sixth of the earth’s land surface, ceased to exist. The process that ended it had run through the whole of perestroika-1985-91 and reached its climax in the autumn, after the august-putsch-1991 had destroyed the authority of the central organs and the party that sustained them. Its formal act came on 8 December 1991, when the leaders of the three Slavic republics — Russia, Ukraine and Belarus — met in the forest of Belovezhskaya Pushcha, the Беловежская пуща (Belovezhskaya Pushcha, the Bialowieza Forest), and declared the Soviet Union at an end, establishing in its place the Commonwealth of Independent States. On 25 December mikhail-gorbachev resigned as President of the USSR, and the red flag was lowered over the Kremlin. Seventy-four years after the revolution that created it, the Soviet Union was gone — and in its place stood fifteen independent states, including the Russian Federation under its President boris-yeltsin.
The road to Belovezhskaya Pushcha
The dissolution had been prepared by the whole course of the reform. Gorbachev’s glasnost and democratisation had released the nationality question that the old system had suppressed; the republics, beginning with the Baltic states and the Caucasus and culminating in the Declaration of State Sovereignty of Russia of June 1990, had asserted their independence of the centre; the “war of laws” between Moscow and the Union had paralysed government. Gorbachev’s effort to hold the union together in a renewed form — the referendum of March 1991 on preserving the USSR, the negotiations at Novo-Ogaryovo toward a new Union Treaty — was overtaken by the August putsch. The failure of the ГКЧП discredited the centre and the Communist Party and left the republics free to go their own way. Through the autumn of 1991 the republics declared their independence one by one, and the Union government found itself governing little more than its own offices. Pikhoya, who lived through these months as chief state archivist, records the path from the Novo-Ogaryovo process to Belovezhskaya Pushcha as a steady collapse of the possibility of holding the country together.
The Belovezhskaya accords
On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus — Yeltsin, Leonid Kravchuk and Stanislav Shushkevich — met at the Belovezhskaya Pushcha, in the hunting lodge of the Belarusian state, and signed the accords that ended the Soviet Union. Declaring that the USSR had ceased to exist as a subject of international law and a geopolitical reality, they established the Commonwealth of Independent States (the СНГ, SNG) as its successor framework. The meeting was clandestine and startlingly swift; it was undertaken, Pikhoya notes, without the participation or consent of the President of the USSR, and it confronted Gorbachev with a fait accompli. On 21 December, at Alma-Ata, the remaining republics joined the Commonwealth, and the eleven former republics, now independent states, recognised the dissolution. The attempt by Gorbachev to preserve some form of union came too late; the republics no longer trusted the centre, and the centre no longer possessed the means to compel them. Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook treats the Belovezhskaya accords as the decisive act that formalised the collapse that the nationality policy and the failure of the reform had made unavoidable.
The end of the Soviet Union
The final act was a formality. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned as President of the USSR, transferring the nuclear command and the state’s powers to the Russian President, and on the same day the red flag was lowered from the Kremlin and the flag of Russia raised in its place. The Soviet Union had existed for seventy-four years; its end was accomplished almost without ceremony, in a few weeks, by men who had been born inside it. The consequences were immense. Fifteen independent states emerged from the wreck, the largest of them the Russian Federation, whose sovereignty and statehood Yeltsin had asserted in opposition to the Union. The Cold War, which the USSR had waged and embodied, was over; the superpower that had divided the world with the United States was gone; the millions who had been Soviet citizens found themselves citizens of new states. Pikhoya, reflecting on why the union fell, points to the system’s own inner weaknesses — Soviet federalism, the common property of the whole people, the CPSU as the core of the political system, the economic crisis and the exhaustion of belief in the socialist ideal. The dissolution, in his account, was at once the collapse of a state and the end of an idea, and the new Russia of vladimir-putin was to be built on its ruins. The generation that had been taught that the system was eternal, the last-soviet-generation that Yurchak describes, lived to see the “forever” come to an end.

events/east-german-uprising-1953.title: The East German Uprising (17 June 1953)
events/east-german-uprising-1953.content:
The East German Uprising (17 June 1953)
On 17 June 1953 the German Democratic Republic, scarcely four years old, came within a moment of being overthrown by its own workers. What had begun the day before as a protest of the building workers of East Berlin against an increase in their work norms exploded within hours into a general strike and a rising that swept across the republic, from Berlin to Halle, Magdeburg, Jena and Dresden, demanding the resignation of the government and free elections. It was the first great challenge to the Socialist Unity Party and, in Hermann Weber’s judgment, the tragic culmination of the whole Stalinization of the state that had followed the founding of the GDR — an uprising of the very class in whose name the regime claimed to rule, crushed within a day by Soviet tanks. The date became in the West a symbol and a national holiday of the Federal Republic, and in the East a wound the state could never heal.
The causes
The revolt was the product of the harshness of the preceding years, brought to the point of explosion by the uncertain aftermath of Stalin’s death. Since 1949 the SED had pressed a ruthless drive for heavy industry and collectivization; the Stalinisierung of the republic, as Weber documents it, had meant forced coordination, purges and repression, and a population ground down by scarcities and austerity. When Stalin died in March 1953, the new Soviet leadership urged a “New Course” and a retreat from the harshest measures, and the party in Berlin wavered between reform and dogmatism. Yet the leadership, fearful of any concession, raised the work norms — the Normenerhöhung — demanded of the workers, telling them that the standard of living could not rise unless they produced more. To the workers of the construction sites in Berlin the increase, coming on top of years of sacrifice, was the last provocation. On 16 June they downed tools and marched; by the morning of the 17th the protest had become a general strike and the cry for the removal of the government was ringing through the streets.
The rising
On 17 June the capital was in the hands of the crowd. Demonstrators streamed through East Berlin, converging on the government quarter; they stormed the offices of the SED and tore down the party’s banners, called for strikes across the country, and raised demands that went far beyond the work norms — for the resignation of Ulbricht and his ministers, for free elections, for an end to the dictatorship. The regime, taken by surprise and abandoned for a moment by its nerve, could not control the streets on its own. The answer came from outside: the Soviet Military Administration, which still held the ultimate power in the republic, proclaimed a state of emergency, and the tanks and troops of the Red Army moved into the cities to restore order. The fighting was brief and one-sided. By nightfall the rising had been put down with Soviet help; hundreds were killed or wounded, and the arrests and sentences of the following weeks completed the work of the guns. Weber stresses that the revolt was suppressed not by the party but by the armed might of the Soviet Union — a fact that revealed the true foundations of the state.
The consequences
The uprising of 17 June 1953 was a watershed in the history of the GDR and of the Cold War. For the regime it was a shock that came close to destroying it, and it shaped everything that followed. The party beat back the inner-party opposition that the events had encouraged, and Ulbricht, saved from the consequences of his own dogmatism by the very crisis, emerged strengthened; the “New Course” was abandoned or applied only as the leadership saw fit, and the Stalinist consolidation of the state continued. Yet the price of survival was the permanent loss of any claim the party might have made to the allegiance of its own workers. In the West, the rising was seized upon as proof of the illegitimacy of the East German state and of the falsehood of its name: the Federal Republic declared 17 June a public holiday, the Tag der deutschen Einheit, the day of German unity, and made the crushed revolt a standing protest against the division of Germany. Winkler places the uprising at the centre of the confrontation of the two systems, the moment when the East German dictatorship was exposed as an imposition that could only be maintained by force. For the GDR the memory of 17 June was unmentionable and unforgettable — the day when its own people rose against it, the repressed foretaste of the autumn of 1989 in which the same people would finally bring it down.

events/eastern-enlargement-2004.title: Eastern Enlargement (2004)
events/eastern-enlargement-2004.content:
Eastern Enlargement (2004)
The enlargement of the European Union on 1 May 2004 was the largest and most consequential act of widening in the history of european-integration — the admission, at a stroke, of ten new member states that had only fifteen years before been prisoners of a divided continent. Eight of them — Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — had emerged from behind the Iron Curtain; two, Cyprus and Malta, were Mediterranean islands that had long waited at the Union’s gates. The accession of 2004 reunited Europe politically for the first time since the Second World War, and with the subsequent admission of Romania and Bulgaria in 2007 it carried the Union’s eastern frontier to the borders that were still to be tested in the century’s crises. It was the moment at which the Union, founded as the project of six Western states, became a genuinely continent-wide political order.
The promise of the Copenhagen criteria
The door to the East was opened at the European Council held in Copenhagen in June 1993, in the very year the Union was born at Maastricht. There the heads of state and government declared that the associated countries of central and eastern Europe could become members of the Union, and set out the conditions that would govern their admission — the famous Copenhagen criteria of political stability, a functioning market economy, and the capacity to take on the obligations of membership. The criteria were the Covenant by which the eastern applicants were to be judged: they had to have achieved stable institutions guaranteeing democracy and the rule of law, a working market economy capable of competing within the Union, and the administrative capacity to apply the entire corpus of Union law, the acquis communautaire. Enlargement was thus framed from the outset not as a simple expansion of the market but as an exercise in transformation — a condition-bound promise that would draw the former communist states toward the standards of the West.
The transformation of the candidates
Between 1993 and 2004 the candidates remade themselves in the image the Union demanded. The terms of the accession negotiations, formally opened in March 1998 with the first group of candidates and extended thereafter, required each state to adopt thousands of pages of European legislation and to build the institutions to enforce it. The process was a school of Westernisation, in which the prospect of membership supplied the motive and the Union’s conditional demands supplied the discipline. The eastern states adopted the acquis wholesale — the customs union and the internal market, the common agricultural policy and the structural funds, the environmental and social standards — as the price and the promise of return to a Europe they had been torn from in 1945. The negotiations were themselves a lesson in the asymmetrical interdependence that liberal-intergovernmentalism would recognise: the candidates bargained from weakness against a Union that held the ultimate prize of membership, and yet the prize was so coveted that they accepted conditions that the older member states had never had to meet.
The Big Bang of 2004
The accession treaty, signed in Athens on 16 April 2003, was ratified by the ten candidates in referendums held through 2003 — a remarkable sequence in which the peoples of the newly democratic states voted, in decisive majorities, to join the Union, most of them within weeks of one another. On 1 May 2004 the ten acceded together, in a “big bang” enlargement that the Union’s architects had judged the only workable route, since to admit the candidates one by one would have poisoned the politics of the region. The ceremony took place in Dublin and in the newly joined capitals, beneath the flags of a Union that had grown from fifteen to twenty-five members overnight. The Mediterranean pair, Cyprus and Malta, entered in the same wave — Cyprus joining, as an applicant whose island remained divided, under terms that admitted the whole island while the acquis was held in abeyance in the north. Romania and Bulgaria, judged not yet ready in 2004, followed in 2007, carrying the Union’s boundary across the Carpathians and the Danube.
A Union reuniting Europe
Eastern enlargement was the crowning act of the reunification of Europe that the end of the Cold War had set in motion. It fulfilled the promise made to the peoples of the East in the darkest days of their captivity, and it bound the memory of division — the history of the eastern states that european-integration had been built to transcend — into the Union’s own story. Yet it also raised, in acute form, the questions that were to run through the Union’s subsequent life. The newcomers entered poorer and structurally weaker economies, and their admission strained the Union’s institutions, designed for fifteen members, and its finances, asked to extend the structural funds and the agricultural subsidies eastward. Enlargement was the expansion of an order built for the West, and it posed in new terms the questions of solidarity and of democracy that euro-crisis-2010 and brexit-2016 were to make inescapable. In 2004, however, these were for most Europeans questions for the future. The moment itself was an act of reunion — the return, in freedom and in peace, of the nations of the East to the Europe from which they had been so violently severed.

events/euro-crisis-2010.title: Euro-Area Crisis (2010)
events/euro-crisis-2010.content:
Euro-Area Crisis (2010)
The euro-area crisis of the 2010s was the gravest trial that european-integration had faced since its foundation — a crisis of the single currency that brought the Union to the edge of fracture and reshaped its politics and institutions for a generation. It began, in 2010, as a crisis of one small member state, Greece, whose public finances were exposed as unsustainable when the global financial collapse of 2008 turned a chronic weakness into a catastrophe. But it did not remain Greek. Through 2010 and 2011 the contagion spread across the southern periphery — to Ireland, to Portugal, to Spain, and finally to the very centre of the monetary union, to Italy and Cyprus — as markets lost confidence in the debts of states that no longer possessed the means, the national central banks and the devaluation of a national currency, by which insolvency had once been managed. The crisis laid bare the design of the euro: a monetary union without the fiscal and political union that might have supported it, an experiment in which the irrevocable locking of currencies that the maastricht-treaty-1992 had proclaimed had been built, as its critics had warned, on sand.
The Greek explosion
The crisis broke in the winter of 2009–10, when a new Greek government announced that its predecessor had concealed the true scale of the public deficit — a deficit far beyond the convergence criteria that had admitted Greece to the single currency a decade before. The announcement shattered confidence in Greek debt, and as the cost of borrowing soared, the euro area faced a choice it had never prepared itself to make: whether to let a member state default and so rupture the single currency, or to rescue it. After weeks of hesitation the member states chose rescue. In May 2010 the euro area and the International Monetary Fund assembled the first of a series of bailouts — a loan to Greece conditional on a programme of austerity so severe that it transformed the country’s politics and its society. The rescue was conducted in the name of the stability of the euro, but it was the creditor states, above all Germany, that dictated its terms, and it was the debtor peoples of the periphery who were asked to bear the cost.
The sovereign debt crisis and the bailout funds
The Greek rescue did not contain the disease. In November 2010 Ireland was forced to accept a bailout when its banks collapsed, in 2011 Portugal followed, and through 2011 and 2012 the crisis reached Spain and Italy, where the largest economies of the southern euro area saw their borrowing costs climb toward unsustainability. To meet the storm the Union built, in haste and under duress, a new architecture. The European Financial Stability Facility and then the permanent European Stability Mechanism were created to lend to states that had lost the market; the “six-pack” and “two-pack” legislation tightened fiscal surveillance; and the Fiscal Compact bound the member states, in treaty form, to balanced budgets. The euro area thus acquired, in the space of three years, a fiscal governance that it had conspicuously lacked at its birth — but it acquired it as a discipline imposed from the centre, on terms set by the creditor states, rather than as the solidarity of a genuine political union.
The European Central Bank and the defence of the euro
At the decisive moment it was not the governments but the European Central Bank that saved the single currency. Having initially resisted the role, the ECB moved under its President, Mario Draghi, to the edge of its mandate and beyond: it lent to the banks, bought the bonds of the embattled states, and in the summer of 2012 Draghi delivered the words that came to be seen as the turning point — that within its mandate the ECB was ready to do whatever it took to preserve the euro. The promise, eventually made good by the announcement of outright monetary transactions, was a commitment to defend the currency that the states themselves had been unable or unwilling to make. Yet the Bank’s interventions could not heal the division the crisis had opened. The years of austerity — the wage cuts, the unemployment, the collapse of public services across the southern periphery — set the creditor North against the debtor South in a confrontation over the meaning of european-integration itself, and over whether the Union was a community of solidarity or a discipline of creditors.
The aftermath and the German question renewed
The euro crisis did not end the single currency; by 2015 the acute phase had passed and the euro had survived, but the crisis had transformed the Union. It had created a permanent machinery of bailout and surveillance, elevated the European Central Bank to a political actor of the first rank, and made the monetary union a zone of permanent tension between its North and its South. The editors of the Cambridge History read the crisis as one of the shocks that renewed the German question in its post-Cold War form — the question of the place of a reunited Germany, and of a German-dominated monetary order, at the heart of a Europe that could no longer be balanced against any other power. For the peoples of the periphery, the memory of the crisis was a memory of imposed austerity and diminished sovereignty; for the creditor states, a memory of averted catastrophe bought at a price. The euro had been saved, but the questions of solidarity, of legitimacy and of the distribution of the costs of interdependence that the crisis had forced into the open were to remain, unresolved, at the centre of the Union’s life.

events/euro-introduction-1999-2002.title: Euro Introduction (1999–2002)
events/euro-introduction-1999-2002.content:
Euro Introduction (1999–2002)
The single currency of the European Union was not born at once, but in three stages at the turn of the millennium. On 1 January 1999 the currencies of eleven member states were irrevocably locked together and the euro became the unit of a monetary union governed by a new European Central Bank; and on 1 January 2002, after a transitional period, euro banknotes and coins entered the hands of the citizens of Europe, replacing the national currencies that had measured the lives of generations. It was the fulfilment of an ambition that had lain at the heart of the integration project since the Werner Report of 1970, and the creation of a currency without a single nation to back it — an experiment without precedent in modern history.
The convergence and the launch
The launch of the euro was the culmination of the process set out in the Treaty of Maastricht. Eleven states — the whole of the Community except Britain, Denmark and Sweden — had by 1998 fulfilled, or appeared to fulfil, the convergence criteria: sustainable public finances, price stability, exchange-rate stability and stable long-term interest rates. The criteria were demanding, and their fulfilment had required a sustained national effort. In Italy, as the historian Gentiloni Silveri recounts, the commitment to the euro became the great uniting mission of the age — a “new external constraint,” in the phrase of the time, that could gather the country’s energies and project them beyond the confines of a seemingly ungovernable politics. Under a succession of governments from the Amato and Ciampi cabinets onward, the country pursued a policy of austerity to meet the Maastricht criteria, going so far as to levy, in the end-of-year decree of 1996, a special “Europe tax” on households to accelerate the consolidation of the public accounts. Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, the future President of the Republic, was the prophet of the enterprise, convinced that participation from the first steps of the single currency was essential for a founding nation of the Community.
On 1 January 1999 the exchange rates were irrevocably fixed and the euro came into being as the currency of the union, replacing the mark, the franc, the lira and the other national moneys at first as a book currency of the financial markets and of public accounting. The management of the new currency was entrusted to the European Central Bank, established in Frankfurt, a federal monetary institute to which the national central banks of the members were joined as components of the European System of Central Banks. The independence of the bank, its primary mandate of price stability, and its governing structure had been settled in advance of the negotiations, and its design deliberately modelled on — and even surpassing — the independence of the Bundesbank. The German emphasis on sound money, which had given Germany credibility as the anchor of the European Monetary System, was written into the constitution of the new currency itself.
The Stability and Growth Pact
To the treaty’s convergence criteria the members added a Stability and Growth Pact, invented to ensure that the discipline of convergence would be maintained once inside the union. Under its rules the Council of the EU could ultimately impose monetary fines on member states whose budgetary deficits rose above three per cent of GDP, and public debt was to be held near sixty per cent of GDP or brought down gradually towards it. The pact embodied the fear that some governments might run high deficits and free-ride on the discipline of others, pushing up long-term interest rates at the cost of all. In the event, the pact was more honoured in the breach: once inside the union, member states — notably France and Germany themselves — did not comply with the budgetary and fiscal rules, a portent of the strains the euro was later to endure.
Notes and coins, 2002
The third stage came on 1 January 2002, when the euro was physically introduced in the participating countries and the banknotes and coins of the new currency entered daily circulation, with national currencies withdrawn from use. The European Central Bank became a note-issuing institution, carrying out open-market operations, supporting the foreign-exchange market and participating in policymaking. The introduction of the single currency eliminated currency risk within the zone and gave a further push to integration and to the merging of the European banking sector; cross-border financial activities increased sharply within the eurozone. The euro, and the Central Bank that governed it, became the most important supranational institution Europe had ever created, and the euro area the most integrated part of the Union. For Italy, as Gentiloni Silveri notes, the outcome vindicated a long rincorsa, a long chase to join the first ranks — the sense, shared across party lines, that the country’s place was among the founders of the new monetary Europe. The eleven members of 1999 were joined in the years that followed by Greece and others, until the single currency covered the greater part of the Union. That the union lacked a fiscal counterpart, a single treasury to stand behind a single currency, was a question that would not long remain academic; it was to break upon the euro area in the crisis of the following decade.

events/european-monetary-system-1979.title: European Monetary System (1979)
events/european-monetary-system-1979.content:
European Monetary System (1979)
The European Monetary System was the first institution of the Community to impose upon its members a permanent obligation in the field of money. Born of a Franco-German bargain struck by two Chancellors-turned-partners in the late 1970s, it answered the collapse of the postwar monetary order with a zone of exchange-rate stability built around the strongest currency on the continent. Its creation in March 1979 marked the moment when the states of Western Europe, unable to stabilise their exchanges alone in a world of floating currencies, chose to bind themselves together around the Deutsche Mark.
The crisis of the dollar and the failure of the snake
The immediate occasion lay not in Brussels but in Washington. When the Bretton Woods system of fixed parities collapsed in the early 1970s, the currencies of the Community were set adrift, and the successive attempts to restore order had already failed once. The Community’s first answer, the “snake in the tunnel,” a narrow band within which European currencies moved together, had proved unable to hold against the tides of speculation and divergent national policies; by the middle of the decade it had shrunk to little more than a German-led core of strong-currency states. The dollar crisis of the late 1970s, with the American currency sliding against the mark and pushing the value of the Deutschen Mark ever upward, placed an unbearable strain upon the French franc, the lira and the other weaker currencies. For the German Chancellor Helmut Schmidt and the French President Valéry Giscard d’Estaing, the answer was a new and more ambitious arrangement, conceived between them and presented to the Community as a fait accompli. As the Cambridge history observes, the system was the result of the Bonn–Paris axis in the years after the abandonment of the gold standard, an attempt to shelter Europe from the disorder of an international monetary system dominated by the collapse of the American reserve currency.
The Bremen initiative and the ECU
The plan was launched at the European Council of Bremen in July 1978, on the strength of a bilateral Franco-German understanding worked out by Schmidt and Giscard before the other capitals were consulted. The two men had agreed, as the German account of the Schmidt era records, that monetary cooperation should be the instrument through which Europe was “Europeanised” by Franco-German cooperation — a way of giving the Community a monetary identity of its own. The scheme rested on three elements: an artificial unit of account, the European Currency Unit (ECU), a name coined by Giscard to echo the ancient French écu, the coin of the Valois kings; an exchange-rate mechanism; and facilities for intervention, credit and transfer. So closely was the whole design guarded that even the president of the Bundesbank, Otto Emminger, was systematically excluded from the inner circle and informed of the details only in the days before Bremen.
The negotiations that followed were an education in the underlying politics of money. At their heart lay the perennial conflict between weak- and strong-currency countries over who should bear the cost of adjustment. France, Italy and Belgium sought a “symmetrical” system, in which any currency diverging from the ECU would be obliged to adjust. Germany, supported by the Netherlands and Denmark, insisted on the continued existence of the old parity grid of the snake, in which the burden of intervention fell above all on the deficit countries. The French case was pressed with particular urgency by the head of the French negotiating team, Bernard Clappier, who recalled that “three out of four problems” in the snake had arisen because the strongest currency, the mark, had reached its upper limit. It was Giscard who ultimately conceded the point: at the Aachen summit of mid-September 1978 he accepted the German parity-grid system, with the ECU’s divergence indicator reduced, in the dry phrase of one contemporary, to a “bureaucratic nicety offering jobs for computers and statisticians.” The appearance of a French success was preserved by including both mechanisms in the agreement, though all concerned understood that the ECU could never influence de facto obligations.
The design and the strains
The German side drove a hard bargain on every technical detail. The Bundesbank insisted that the system be constructed as bands rather than fixed parities, with the obligation to intervene triggered only when currencies reached their margins — a design that left the central bank considerable discretion. There was to be no joint policymaking over the dollar, a role that fell by default to the Bundesbank. On the question of a European Monetary Fund with pooled reserves, which Schmidt himself had initially favoured, the “fundamental reservations” of the Bundesbank placed a “severe constraint on the discussions,” yielding a watered-down agreement close to the German ideal. Germany’s assent even required a private letter permitting the Bundesbank to exempt itself from intervention and lending obligations. The weaker members extracted what concessions they could: Italy and Ireland, and initially Britain, sought generous regional subsidies, and Giscard sided with Germany against them, declaring that membership “ought to be an act of political will rather than a question of cash,” even while quietly negotiating a modest bilateral arrangement with the Irish. The Italians and Irish, doubtful of their capacity to hold a narrow band, received wide six-percent margins; Britain, calculating the costs of entry, held aloof altogether.
Launch and consequence
The system was put into force by the European Council in Paris on 9–10 March 1979, and the Exchange Rate Mechanism began to operate on 13 March. With the exception of Britain, which remained within the EMS but outside the mechanism, all the members of the Community — Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands — participated. Its performance exceeded the scepticism with which it had been received. Though the first years saw large currency fluctuations and frequent realignments, the system survived the second oil-price shock of 1979 and the recession of the early 1980s, its discipline administered through the Committee of Central Bank Governors and the Council of Economic and Finance Ministers. By the mid-1980s it had matured into a relatively stable exchange-rate system in which the Deutsche Mark fulfilled the role of anchor currency, and its members had learned to live within its margins. It was, in the judgement of the Cambridge history, a success of integration — the foundation upon which the renewed ambitions of a single currency would later be built. The British remained outside until 1990 and left again in 1992, but for the continental core the EMS pointed the way forward from a common market to the prospect of an Economic and Monetary Union.
