events/evian-accords-1962.title: Evian Accords (1962)
events/evian-accords-1962.content:
The Evian Accords (1962)
By the winter of 1962 the war that had torn France and Algeria apart for seven and a half years was drawing, against the resistance of nearly everyone who had once demanded it, toward its end. The negotiations opened with the Front de libération nationale — the FLN — had survived the wreck of earlier hopes, and in March 1962, at the lakeside spa of Évian, the two delegations at last put their names to an agreement that extinguished the war the Republic had never quite declared. The peace was signed in the spa town of Évian-les-Bains on the French shore of Lake Geneva on 18 March 1962.
A settlement pressed by the state
The accords were the product of a policy that charles-de-gaulle had driven, with an iron patience, against the passions of the settlers and the fury of the army. From the self-determination offer of September 1959, through the semaine des barricades of January 1960 and the generals’ putsch of April 1961, the General had bent the course of the war toward a settlement that he alone seemed able to impose. The Évian agreements recognised the right of the Algerian people to self-determination, arranged a ceasefire, and provided for the withdrawal of the French forces and the transition of power. Algeria was to be consulted on its own future; the war, fought for so long over the word Algérie française, ended with the recognition that the future belonged to the Algerians themselves.
The referendum of 8 April 1962
The General carried the settlement to the metropole, and on 8 April 1962 the French people ratified the accords in a referendum by an overwhelming majority. The Oui across the country registered the immense relief of a nation that had long since wearied of a war it could neither win nor abandon. For charles-de-gaulle, the referendum was the culminating act of the winding-down he had pursued since 1959 — the confirmation that France had taken its decision and that the nation, whatever the passion of a minority, had chosen peace. In the autumn of the same year he would carry the reform of the institutions to the country in a second referendum, but it was in April that the Algerian question was, in law, closed.
The end of a world: the exodus
The signing of the accords did not bring immediate tranquillity. The Organisation armée secrète, the OAS, the gathering of the settlers and the army officers who refused to accept the abandonment of Algérie française, answered the peace with a last convulsion of terror — bombing and assassination in both Algeria and the metropole, an attempt by violence to overturn a settlement the government had already ratified. The fury of the spring was the death-throe of a world. For the pieds-noirs, the Europeans of Algeria, the accords were the end of everything: nearly the whole European population would leave the land of their birth in the space of a single year, in an exodus that emptied the society the settlers had built across the Mediterranean. Algeria achieved its independence on 5 July 1962, and France was left with the legacy of a million displaced French Algerians and a wound in the national conscience that would not close for decades.
The legacy of Évian
The Evian accords ended the longest and most bitter of France’s colonial wars. They destroyed the Algérie française that had been woven into the very fabric of the Republic since 1830, and in doing so they removed the question that had broken the fourth-republic. The settlement, imposed by the man who had returned to power to resolve it, was the foundation upon which the fifth-republic consolidated itself — the proof that a strong state could settle what the régime of the parties had only prolonged. Yet the peace left scars that outlived it: on the army, on the political right, on the displaced pieds-noirs and the harkis left behind, and on the memory of the war itself. The accords of March 1962 closed the conflict, but the questions of Évian echoed through French politics for the rest of the century.

events/fall-of-berlin-wall-1989.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall (9 November 1989)
events/fall-of-berlin-wall-1989.content:
Fall of the Berlin Wall (9 November 1989)
On the night of 9 November 1989 the wall that had divided Berlin for twenty-eight years, and with it the two German states and the two halves of the Cold War world, opened in a single evening. What began as a confused announcement at a press conference became, within hours, the most iconic scene of the German autumn — tens of thousands of East Berliners streaming through the checkpoints, embraced on the western side, climbing the wall itself in the city that had built it to keep its people in. The border was not thrown open by decree from above but breached from below, by a citizenry that had already, over many weeks, torn down the walls of the state’s authority in the squares of the East. It was the end of a regime, and the opening of the question of the nation.
The crisis of the GDR and the flight through Hungary
The fall of the Wall was the climax of a collapse that had been running for months. Through the summer of 1989 the crisis of the founding-gdr-1949 state had become uncontainable. In May Hungary had begun to dismantle its own Iron Curtain fence on the border with Austria, and from August East German holidaymakers, tens of thousands of them, had poured through that breach, abandoning the republic of erich-honecker for the West by way of a third country. In September and October the West German embassies in Prague and Warsaw filled with East Germans demanding passage to the Federal Republic. Those who stayed took to the streets. In Leipzig the Monday demonstrations (Montagsdemonstrationen) swelled week by week — a few thousand, then tens of thousands, then a hundred thousand and more, gathering in the city’s centre after prayer in the Nikolai church, chanting “Wir sind das Volk” (“We are the people”). The regime, which had celebrated its fortieth anniversary on 7 October in a hollow pageant, found itself without the means or the will to fire on its own citizens.
The anniversary and the fall of Honecker
The fortieth anniversary of the GDR on 7 October 1989, the state’s last Republikgeburtstag, was the moment at which the terminal crisis became unmistakable. In East Berlin the regime staged its celebration while the state around it staggered; the atmosphere, as Kowalczuk recorded, was one of a tension that reminded the Chilean emigrants present of the eve of the coup that had destroyed the Allende government in 1973. The anniversary revealed a party leadership in full retreat. Days earlier, on 18 October, the Politburo had deposed erich-honecker, the man who had built and personified the republic’s separation from the West, and replaced him with Egon Krenz. The change of the guard changed nothing essential. The citizens had stopped listening to the state, and the state had lost the power of coercion over them. Within the SED and in the streets alike the question was no longer whether the regime would fall, but how.
The announcement of 9 November
The opening came almost by accident. On the evening of 9 November the Politburo member Günter Schabowski, charged with announcing a new, more permissive travel law, faced a press conference in which he was asked when the new regulations would take effect. Uncertain and evidently improvising, he answered that they applied “immediately, without delay” (sofort, unverzüglich) — an answer more sweeping than the law as drafted actually was. The news spread through the city and the world within the hour. East Berliners, incredulous and then convinced, gathered at the border crossings and demanded passage. The border guards, without orders to resist the stream, opened the gates. By midnight the Wall was being crossed in the tens of thousands, and the city that had for nearly three decades been the symbol of division became overnight the symbol of its end.
The end of the two states
The opening of the Wall on 9 November 1989 was the decisive event of the German autumn — the moment the division of Germany, sealed by the building of the Wall in 1961, began to be undone. Its immediate consequence was the unprecedented movement of people: East Germans flowed into the West in numbers that the GDR could not contain, and the regime, discredited and helpless, was swept along toward dissolution. The Central Round Table, where the government and the opposition sat down together, took shape in December; the SED’s monopoly of power was dissolved; the road to the free elections of the spring lay open. For the two German states the night of 9 November marked the point of no return — the fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 set in motion the german-reunification-1990 that was to be accomplished within the year, and posed with new urgency the german-question that forty years of division had been unable to answer.

events/first-chechen-war-1994-96.title: First Chechen War (1994-96)
events/first-chechen-war-1994-96.content:
First Chechen War (1994-96)
The first war of the new Russia was fought against itself. In December 1994 the army of the Russian Federation, the state that boris-yeltsin had brought into being after dissolution-ussr-1991, invaded its own territory to bring the republic of Chechnya to heel. The republic, which had declared its independence from Russia in 1991 under the warlord Dzhokhar Dudayev, had been a running sore in the new state from the first — a fragment of the Soviet collapse that Moscow could neither accept nor subdue. What was meant to be a swift punitive operation to restore the constitutional order became instead a grinding two-year war of conquest and resistance, the storming of Grozny, the slaughter of civilians, and a guerrilla insurgency that the Russian army could neither crush nor leave. It ended in 1996 in the Khasavyurt accords, a humiliating ceasefire that conceded to the rebels nearly everything the war had been fought to prevent — and it left behind a ruined republic that was to be the scene of second-chechen-war-1999 under vladimir-putin only three years later.
The republic in revolt
Chechnya had been a problem long before the troops crossed the border. Pikhoya, tracing the place of the Caucasus in the collapse of the Soviet Union, treats the Chechen revolt as a prologue to tragedy already visible in 1991 — the republic that slipped from Moscow’s control in the general disintegration of the state. Dudayev, a former Soviet air-force general, took power in Grozny in the autumn of 1991 and declared the republic’s independence; Moscow, consumed by the crisis of the Union and then by the reconstruction of the Russian state, never accepted the secession but was too weak to reverse it. For three years Chechnya existed in a condition of de facto independence, beyond the reach of Russian law and the Russian state. The region had long been the scene of banditry, hostage-taking and the shadow economy of the Caucasus, and the Kremlin came to see the independent republic as a source of disorder and a challenge to the integrity of the state. By the autumn of 1994 the leadership in Moscow, Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook records, had concluded that the separatist régime could not be allowed to stand — and resolved to restore control by force.
The invasion and the storming of Grozny
In December 1994 the Russian army, joined by the opposition Chechen forces that Moscow had armed, invaded Chechnya and advanced on the capital. The war that the Kremlin had expected to end in a matter of days foundered in the streets of Grozny. In the first weeks of the new year of 1995, Russian forces assaulted the city in a series of battles of appalling ferocity; the Chechen fighters, outnumbered and outgunned, turned the streets and basements of Grozny into a trap, and the Russian armour that pushed into the city was burned in the narrow streets by anti-tank weapons and close-range fire. The storming of Grozny became the emblem of the war’s brutality — a modern European capital reduced to rubble, tens of thousands of civilians killed or made homeless, soldiers and rebels dying in the rubble of a city that had once been the industrial centre of the north Caucasus. The Russian army took the city, but the victory was hollow: the Chechen fighters withdrew into the mountains and the countryside, and the war that Moscow had hoped to finish with the fall of Grozny merely changed its form.
The guerrilla resistance
From the spring of 1995 the war became what the Russian command could not win. The Chechens abandoned pitched battle for a partisan war of ambush, raid and terror — attacks on convoys, on garrisons, on the oil infrastructure, hostage-taking that drew in foreign journalists and aid workers, and raids that struck deep into Russian-held territory. The most dramatic of these, the seizure of the city of Budyonnovsk in the summer of 1995 by the commander Shamil Basayev, brought the war to the heartland of Russia itself, as hundreds of hostages were taken in a hospital and the affair was ended only by negotiation. The Russian army, demoralised, unpaid and poorly led, found itself fighting a war it could not win against an enemy it could not find, in a country where the population had largely sided with the rebels. Pikhoya, recording the years of what he calls the усталая Россия (ustalaya Rossiya, ‘tired Russia’) of 1994-1999, depicts the war as a catastrophe that the state could neither end nor afford, an exhausting and bloody drain on the strength and the legitimacy of the Russian government.
The Khasavyurt accords and the aftermath
By 1996 the war had become politically and militarily unsustainable. Yeltsin, who had carried the war into a re-election year, was unable to deliver the victory that would have justified it. In the summer of 1996 the Chechen forces re-entered Grozny and seized the capital once more, humiliating the Russian army that had taken it eighteen months before. The war was over in all but formality. On 31 August 1996, at Khasavyurt in neighbouring Dagestan, the Russian general Aleksandr Lebed and the Chechen commander Aslan Maskhadov signed the accords that ended the war: a ceasefire, the withdrawal of Russian troops, and the deferral of the question of Chechnya’s final status to the year 2001 — in effect, a Russian retreat that conceded the rebels’ control over the republic they had defended. The first Chechen war had cost the lives of thousands of soldiers and tens of thousands of civilians, ruined the republic, and ended in a settlement that satisfied no one. Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook treats the war and its disastrous outcome as one of the gravest failures of the Russian state in the 1990s, a conflict that damaged the country’s army, its society and its standing. The interlude of uneasy Chechen independence that followed, with its lawlessness and its slide toward extremism, proved to be only a breathing-space. In the autumn of 1999, after the invasion of Dagestan by Chechen militants and the apartment bombings in Russian cities, Moscow went to war again — and the second-chechen-war-1999, waged by the new premier vladimir-putin, was to be fought as the instrument by which a man rose to the presidency of Russia.

events/founding-frg-1949.title: The Founding of the Federal Republic (1949)
events/founding-frg-1949.content:
The Founding of the Federal Republic (1949)
On 23 May 1949 a new German state came into being in the West — the Bundesrepublik Deutschland, the Federal Republic of Germany, born of the rubble of the Third Reich and of the failure of the four victorious powers to agree on the future of a common Germany. Its foundation, prepared through the years of occupation and brought to completion in the wake of the Berlin Blockade, was the decisive turning of the road to the West. The Germans of the western zones, led by Konrad Adenauer, chose freedom, federation and the West — a choice whose consequences would shape Europe for the rest of the century.
The Grundgesetz
The constitution of the new state was drafted by a Parlamentarischer Rat (Parliamentary Council), a body of delegates chosen by the parliaments of the western Länder (states), which convened at Bonn under the presidency of Konrad Adenauer. The founding fathers were careful to avoid the word “constitution,” calling their work instead the Grundgesetz (Basic Law) — a provisional instrument, they insisted, intended to last only until the reunification of Germany. Yet in substance it was a constitution of the most deliberate kind, shaped in conscious reaction to the weaknesses of Weimar. The Basic Law rested on the dignity and inviolability of the human person, guaranteed fundamental rights, and established a Rechtsstaat — a state bound by law. It was a “wehrhafte Demokratie,” a defensive democracy, armed against the enemies of freedom: the parties that sought to abolish the free order could be banned, and the Verfassungsfeinde denied the tolerance that had been fatal to the republic in 1933. A federal structure divided power between the central government in Bonn and the Länder; the Bundesrat (Federal Council) gave the states a voice; and the position of the Chancellor, the Kanzler, was strengthened against the instability that had destroyed the cabinets of the Weimar era through the konstruktives Misstrauensvotum, the constructive vote of no confidence, by which a chancellor could be removed only if a successor was already chosen. The Basic Law was promulgated on 23 May 1949, subject to the reservations of the occupation statute that still governed the new state’s foreign relations and defence.
The first Bundestag election
The constitution completed, the West Germans went to the polls. On 14 August 1949 the first Bundestag was elected — the first free and general election held in Germany since 1933. The campaign set the pattern of West German politics for a generation: the Christlich-Demokratische Union (Christian Democratic Union) under Adenauer, with its allies in Bavaria, the Christian Social Union, stood for a market economy, Western alignment and Christian social teaching; the Social Democratic Party under Kurt Schumacher, the fiery veteran of the concentration camps, stood for socialism, the unity of the nation and a state-directed economy. The CDU/CSU emerged the strongest party, with 31 percent of the vote against the SPD’s 29 percent, but without an absolute majority.
Adenauer’s first government
The election of the Chancellor fell to the new parliament. On 15 September 1949 the Bundestag elected Konrad Adenauer Federal Chancellor — by a margin of one vote, a single vote cast by Adenauer himself. He formed a coalition of the CDU/CSU with the liberal Freie Demokratische Partei (Free Democratic Party) and the small German Party, and took office with a government of veteran politicians and fresh faces. Into the economics ministry he brought Ludwig Erhard, the man who had already unleashed the recovery with the social market economy. The new republic began its life under the shadow of the occupation statute, its sovereignty limited, its frontiers open to the east, and its capital in the provisional Rhineland city of Bonn — yet Adenauer at once set it upon the course that was to define it: Westbindung, the binding of the Federal Republic to the West, through the European institutions and the Atlantic alliance, in the hope that a free and prosperous Germany in the West would one day draw the whole nation, and Europe, together.

events/founding-gdr-1949.title: The Founding of the GDR (7 October 1949)
events/founding-gdr-1949.content:
The Founding of the GDR (7 October 1949)
On 7 October 1949 the German Democratic Republic was proclaimed in the Soviet zone of occupation — a second German state called into being in direct answer to the Federal Republic that had been established in the West the previous spring. Where Bonn had chosen federation, freedom and the market, Berlin proclaimed a deutsche demokratische Republik, a “German democratic republic” of workers and peasants under the leadership of the Socialist Unity Party. Its foundation was the consummation of the division of Germany, the point at which the eastern zone, which the Soviet Union had been moulding since 1945, took on the outward forms of a sovereign state. Winkler locates the event within the confrontation of the two systems that culminated the whole first decade of the Cold War: the western half of Germany had turned decisively toward the West, and the eastern half was now locked to the East, the two states born of the same catastrophe and set upon opposite roads.
The preparation of the Soviet zone
The new state was no sudden creation. From the summer of 1945 the Soviet Military Administration had governed the zone toward a separate destiny — licensing the antifascist parties under SMAD Order No. 2, forcing the merger of Communists and Social Democrats into the SED in 1946, carrying through a land reform and the nationalization of industry, and pushing the zone toward a volksdemokratische, a “people’s democratic,” order on the Soviet model. Weber traces this prehistory in the first chapter of his documentation, from the surrender of May 1945 through the elections and the ever closer alignment of the zone with Moscow. The constitutional text itself was of a piece with the larger strategy: a constitution drafted in 1948 that, on its face, promised a parliamentary republic with fundamental rights, but whose guarantees were from the outset subordinate to the claim of the party, and which in practice served as the legal facade of a dictatorship of the SED.
The proclamation
The formal inauguration followed the establishment of the Federal Republic and the election of its first Bundestag in August. The German People’s Council, the zone’s handpicked assembly, constituted itself on 7 October 1949 as the provisional Volkskammer (People’s Chamber) and proclaimed the constitution and the new state in force. The old communist Wilhelm Pieck was chosen President of the Republic, Otto Grotewohl, the former Social Democrat, became Minister-President, and the decisive power fell to Walter Ulbricht as General Secretary of the SED — the distribution of offices that made visible the reality of the regime. The proclamation was accompanied by the customary declarations of friendship with the Soviet Union, and the occupation powers of the SMAD were formally transferred to the new government in a manner that left the substance of control in Moscow’s hands. The GDR came into the world claiming the name of democracy while its constitution’s “leading role of the party” gave the lie to that claim from the first.
A state of the SED
The founding of the GDR completed the partition and at once set the pattern of the next four decades. Weber’s account of the years that followed stresses the Stalinisierung of the new state — the forced coordination of the parties and mass organizations into a single front, the purge of the party itself, and the construction of the security apparatus that made the republic, in his phrase, an Angleichung an die Sowjetunion, an assimilation to the Soviet Union. The party state rested on the monopoly of the SED; the constitution that proclaimed democratic rights coexisted with a reality in which those rights were subordinated to the party’s claim to lead. Even the name of the state — “democratic” — was itself a weapon of the confrontation, a claim to legitimacy against the Federal Republic to which the East German population, in the great migration of the following years, gave their own answer by leaving. The GDR founded on 7 October 1949 stood for forty years, its constitutional facade and its dictatorial reality in permanent tension, until the crisis of 1989 brought it down and the fall of the Wall dissolved it into the Federal Republic.

events/fourth-republic-founding-1946.title: Founding of the Fourth Republic (October 1946)
events/fourth-republic-founding-1946.content:
Founding of the Fourth Republic (October 1946)
The invention of a republic
The Fourth Republic was not proclaimed in a single dramatic act but invented laboriously across two years of constituent assembly and referendum. After the Liberation, France set about re-founding its institutions on the ruins of the Third Republic, which had collapsed in the débâcle of 1940. The framework was set in the ordonnances of 1944 on the organisation of powers after the Liberation and by the introduction of genuine universal suffrage, including the vote of women. A first Constituent Assembly, elected in October 1945, unanimously named General de Gaulle head of the government, but the General resigned in January 1946 rather than accept the primacy of the parties he distrusted. The constitution was then drafted against his advice, through a first text rejected in the referendum of 5 May 1946, a second Constituent Assembly elected in June, and finally the constitution adopted in the referendum of 13 October 1946 — over the open opposition of de Gaulle, who had campaigned against both drafts with declarations through the summer and autumn.
A régime of the primacy of the Assembly
The institutions that emerged were the very opposite of what de Gaulle had demanded at Bayeux. The Fourth Republic was a parliamentary régime of the primacy of the Assembly: the government depended on the confidence of the chamber, the executive was weak and unstable, and the old régime des partis (rule of the parties) — the system de Gaulle condemned — reigned supreme. The constitution of October 1946 institutionalised the Assembly’s sovereignty, with no strong head of state to stand above the parties, no effective check on the ministerial game. It was a framework that carried within it the ministerial instability that was to become the régime’s signature, the constant fall of governments and the paralysis of decision that the gaullist interpretation — and, later, the Fifth Republic — was to diabolise as the régime of the parties.
The framework de Gaulle fought
The founding of the Fourth Republic was, above all, the defeat de Gaulle had predicted and the failure he would spend twelve years condemning. Against the drafts he had set the Bayeux doctrine of June 1946 — a strong executive, a head of state as arbiter — and he had denounced the successive texts in declarations of 27 August, 19 September, 9 October and 1 November 1946 and at Épinal on 29 September, urging the country to reject a constitution that enshrined the weakness he had seen deliver France to catastrophe in 1940. The adoption of the constitution in October 1946 sent him into opposition and, soon, into the traversée du désert (crossing of the desert), where he would wait, nourishing the R.P.F., until events proved him right.
A balance reconsidered
The Fourth Republic was not, in the eyes of its own later historians, simply the régime of chaos its successors claimed. Rénovators would argue that it laid the foundations of the economic modernisation and the European construction that the Fifth Republic was to reap; that it was not inéluctablement condemned — not inevitably doomed. Yet for its contemporaries it was experienced as a régime that could neither govern nor resolve the problems that pressed upon it. The ministerial instability it institutionalised, and above all its incapacity to master the problème algérien, the Algerian war that began in 1954, were to break it. When the crisis of May 1958 came, the republic founded in October 1946 proved unable to save itself, and it gave way to the régime de Gaulle had conceived at Bayeux — the Fourth Republic ending as the Fifth Republic began.

events/gdr-crisis-1980s.title: The Crisis of the GDR, 1976–1989
events/gdr-crisis-1980s.content:
The Crisis of the GDR, 1976–1989
The last decade and a half of the German Democratic Republic was a long accumulation of crisis — a period in which the contradictions of the sed-state gathered and thickened until, in the autumn of 1989, they broke the state apart. The republic that erich-honecker had promised to make stable and prosperous proved instead to be sinking under the weight of its own debts, its own emigration, and its own dissent. The historian’s chronology marks the turning point in the mid-1970s, when a regime that had once derived its confidence from the sealing of its borders began to find that the border was no longer enough.
Economic trouble and foreign debt
At the centre of the crisis was the economy. The promise of the Honecker era had been the Einheit von Wirtschafts- und Sozialpolitik (unity of economic and social policy) — that the state would keep its citizens fed, housed and employed while industry advanced. But by the mid-1970s the model was faltering. The GDR had staked its social programme on credit from the West, borrowing heavily to buy the imports and hard currency its own exports could not earn, and the loans came due at the worst possible moment, as the world economy turned and the terms of trade shifted against it. Weber’s documents from the chapters on the crisis-ridden development of 1976–80 and the problems of the early 1980s record the mounting difficulty: the state’s foreign indebtedness grew to a scale that alarmed even its own leadership, and the early 1980s brought desperate efforts to revive the economy, to overcome the instability of the system, and to reassure a creditor West. The X. Party Congress of April 1981 reaffirmed the party’s leading role and its unity of economic and social policy, but the words could not conjure the means.
The Biermann expatriation of 1976
The political crisis announced itself in November 1976, with an act that turned a singer into a symbol of the regime’s intransigence. Wolf Biermann, the dissident poet and songwriter who had lived in the GDR and been watched and restricted by the stasi for years, was stripped of his citizenship while on a concert tour of West Germany and forbidden to return. The expatriation was meant to silence a critic; instead it detonated a protest that ran through the entire cultural and intellectual life of the republic. Artists, writers and scientists who had previously accommodated themselves to the regime signed petitions and issued public letters in Biermann’s defence, and many paid for it with their positions, their passports or their expulsion. The affair marked, as Weber notes, the turn to a renewed tightening of the system and a wave of dissent that the party answered with the full weight of its security apparatus. From 1976 the breach between the state and its own intelligentsia never really closed.
The growth of emigration and dissent
The crisis fed a counter-current that ran beneath the surface of GDR life: emigration. Despite the Wall, the desire to leave — to be ausreisen — never died, and in the eighties it swelled into a demand the state could neither satisfy nor suppress. Those who applied to leave were branded as traitors, dismissed from their work, and often punished; the churches, the one public space the state could not fully control, became the refuge of peace movements and civil-rights groups that gathered under their protection and increasingly spoke a language the sed-state could not answer. Kowalczuk, describing the mood of the later eighties, recalls the hopelessness of East Germans as they entered 1989 — when even the hope of change was rare and a growing minority risked their lives to flee westward. The regime’s response, a mixture of repression and grudging concession, solved nothing; it only postponed the reckoning.
Toward 1989
The crisis reached its breaking point in the summer and autumn of 1989. As the emigration crisis turned into a mass exodus — citizens flooding through Hungary’s newly-opened border and crowding into the West German embassies in Prague and Warsaw — the GDR leadership, to the very end, refused to understand what was happening. The fortieth anniversary of the republic on 7 October 1989 was meant to be a celebration of the state’s endurance; instead, as Kowalczuk describes it, the anniversary exposed the terminal crisis of a collapsing regime, its aged leaders celebrating amid the wreckage of their own system while the stasi stood by, unable to stop what was coming. Within weeks the Wall fell on 9 November 1989, and the sed-state that had been built to endure gave way to german-reunification-1990. The crisis that had been accumulating since 1976 — economic, political, demographic — had at last become revolution, not because the state had changed but because it had refused to.

events/german-autumn-1977.title: The German Autumn (1977)
events/german-autumn-1977.content:
The German Autumn (1977)
In the autumn of 1977 the Federal Republic passed through a trial of its own strength such as no other Western state had yet endured — nearly seven weeks in which the republic lived under the threat of terrorism, and in which the government of helmut-schmidt was forced to choose between the life of a single man and the capacity of the state to defend itself. The Germans came to call it the Deutscher Herbst, the German Autumn, and for the generation that lived through it the two words marked the deepest crisis of the young republic since its founding.
The immediate occasion was the kidnapping of Hanns Martin Schleyer. On 5 September 1977 the president of the Federal Association of German Employers and of the Federation of German Industry was seized in Cologne by a commando of the Red Army Faction (Rote Armee Fraktion, the RAF) that named itself for the dead terrorist Siegfried Hausner. His chauffeur and the three accompanying police officers were murdered on the spot. The next day the kidnappers demanded the release of eleven RAF prisoners, 100,000 D-Mark for each, and an immediate end to the manhunt. The RAF was the armed wing of a revolutionary project that had turned against the republic itself — a movement whose first generation, Andreas Baader, Gudrun Ensslin, Jan-Carl Raspe and Ulrike Meinhof, had been tried and imprisoned in Stuttgart-Stammheim, and whose scattered remnants had rebuilt the organisation in the mid-1970s to carry out a campaign of murder against the representatives of the state: the Federal Prosecutor Siegfried Buback, gunned down in Karlsruhe in April 1977, and Jürgen Ponto, the head of the Dresdner Bank, shot in his own home in July.
The chancellor met the crisis with a cold calculation of priorities. He created two bodies unknown to the constitution: a small crisis staff, the Kleine Lage, which met daily with the foreign, interior and justice ministers, and a larger Großer Politischer Beratungskreis (Great Political Advisory Circle) of party and parliamentary leaders and the minister-presidents of the Länder, meeting once or twice a week. Together they embodied the Solidarität der Demokraten (solidarity of the democrats) so often invoked in those days, binding the opposition into the government’s decisions. The guiding principles were set down in a documentation the government later published: to free the hostage alive, to seize the kidnappers and bring them to justice, and not to endanger the state’s capacity to act — which meant not releasing the prisoners whose freedom was being extorted. The state’s strategy was to gain time, in the hope that Schleyer might be found by a hidden manhunt; and it was aided by a news blackout agreed between the government and almost all the media — an act of self-censorship without precedent in the republic.
The most important instrument of delay was the Kontaktsperre (contact ban). Because it was believed that the kidnapping had run according to a preconceived plan, and that the prisoners in Stammheim — above all Baader, who was assigned a certain leading role — would signal the kidnappers through coded words, the federal justice minister had the prisoners’ contacts with one another and the outside world suppressed. The legal basis was at first doubtful; a Kontaktsperre law was rushed through parliament in a criticised emergency procedure and came into force on 2 October. The measure gained the government the weeks of time it needed, even as it deepened the suspicion, in Germany and abroad, of a state that had turned upon its own.
Then, on 13 October, the crisis doubled. Four Arab hijackers seized the Lufthansa jet Landshut with eighty-six passengers and five crew aboard on a flight from Mallorca to Frankfurt, and revealed themselves as allies of the German kidnappers. The Kommando Martyr Halimeh demanded everything the Schleyer captors had demanded, plus fifteen million dollars and the release of two “Palestinian comrades” from an Istanbul prison. A fourth and paramount goal now stood before the three the chancellor had formulated after the Schleyer kidnapping: the rescue of ninety-one more lives. The Landshut flew an odyssey across the Mediterranean and the Middle East — Rome, Larnaca, Bahrain, Dubai, where the federal minister of state Hans-Jürgen Wischnewski landed to prepare a rescue — and then, its pilot murdered in Aden when the hijackers forced a landing on a sand strip, on to the Somali capital Mogadishu. The ultimatum was extended and re-extended by negotiation. After dark on 17 October a special Lufthansa aircraft landed at Mogadishu carrying the counter-terrorist unit of the border guard, the Grenzschutzgruppe 9 (GSG 9), committed for the first time since its creation. Shortly after midnight the unit stormed the Landshut. Three of the four hijackers were killed; all the passengers and the four remaining crew were rescued, and the unit suffered no losses. Seven minutes after the action began, Wischnewski telephoned the chancellor: “The work is done.” The same night the German kidnappers were urged to release Schleyer. Instead, on the following morning, came the news from the Baden-Württemberg justice ministry that Baader, Ensslin and Raspe had taken their own lives in Stammheim — Ensslin by hanging, Baader and Raspe shot with pistols they had hidden despite the strict surveillance — while Irmgard Möller, who had tried to stab herself, was not dangerously wounded. The prisoners had staged their deaths as an execution from outside; the suicides were to serve, in the words of the prisoners’ circulars, as a final signal, proving their freedom and accusing the enemy.
On 19 October, the twenty-fifth message of the kidnappers arrived. Schleyer, it announced, had been killed; his body was found in the boot of a green Audi in the Rue Charles Péguy in Mulhouse, near the French border. The murderers wrote of “our pain and our rage over the massacres of Mogadishu and Stammheim”. The state had saved the hostages of the aircraft and lost the hostage it had sought to free; the autumn ended in a bitter and unresolved balance.
The Deutscher Herbst left a lasting mark on the republic. The state had shown, at the price of Schleyer’s life and amid grave and repeated criticism, that it would not be blackmailed; it had answered terrorism with a determined demonstration of its own capacity to act, and it had accepted that this capacity could only be affirmed at a terrible human cost. The chancellor who bore that decision — Schmidt spoke before the Bundestag on 20 October of the tragedy of having to choose, and of the government’s responsibility — was hardened and confirmed by the crisis. For the years that followed, the image of the republic as a state threatened from within and holding firm, the Modell Deutschland (model Germany) of firm government, was inseparable from the memory of the autumn of 1977 and its dead.

events/german-reunification-1990.title: German Reunification (1990)
events/german-reunification-1990.content:
German Reunification (1990)
The reunification of Germany on 3 October 1990 was the resolution of the german-question that had stood open since 1945 — the recovery, in peace and freedom, of the national unity that two world wars and forty years of division had seemed to make impossible. It was accomplished not by the force that had built and then unmade the Bismarck Reich, but by the agreement of the two German states and the assent of the four wartime powers, in the single year between the fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 and the day on which the German Democratic Republic acceded to the Federal Republic. The path ran through free elections, a monetary union, and a treaty that restored to the Germans full sovereignty. In the space of twelve months what Winkler called the remnant of the Bismarck Reich after two world wars was reunited, and reunited in freedom.
The free elections of March 1990
The opening of the Wall on 9 November 1989 had settled the fate of the GDR, but not the form of unity. Through the winter the question of the nation was fought out within the republic itself. The Central Round Table, convened in December, presided over the dissolution of the SED’s monopoly of power; the state moved toward the first free elections of its history. On 18 March 1990 the Volkskammer, the GDR’s parliament, was elected in a vote whose result surprised both East and West: the conservative Alliance for Germany, led by the East German Christian Democrats, swept the polls. The election was fought in the shadow of the West German campaign — the deutsch-deutsche Wahlkampf of helmut-kohl — and its outcome cleared the way for rapid unity. The citizens of the GDR, in Kowalczuk’s account, entered 1990 with the boundless hope that had been so scarce as they had entered 1989; they had voted for a German unity that would bring the freedoms of the West.
The monetary and economic union
Unity had to be built on a common currency, and that was done in the summer of 1990. The Treaty on the Monetary, Economic and Social Union, concluded between the two German states and in force from 1 July 1990, introduced the Deutschmark into the GDR and extended to it the social market economy of the Federal Republic. It was the most dramatic and the most contested step on the road to unity — a decision, taken in the Chancellor’s office, to carry the Western currency eastward at a politically chosen rate of exchange that favoured the wage-earner and the saver of the East but burdened the economy of the reuniting country for years to come. The monetary union bound the two states together before their political union, and it set the terms on which the far larger task of economic transformation — the collapse of the GDR’s industries, the work of the Treuhand, the rise of unemployment — was to be carried through.
The accession of the GDR
The legal form of unity was determined by the choice of path under the Basic Law. The GDR acceded to the Federal Republic under Article 23, the clause that allowed further parts of Germany to join the federation — a route presented, as Kowalczuk critically observed, as without alternative (alternativlos), in preference to the drafting of a wholly new constitution under Article 146. The accession treaty (Einigungsvertrag), signed in August 1990, carried the Basic Law and the legal order of the Federal Republic into the territory of the dissolving GDR and restored Berlin to the position of capital. On the night of 2-3 October 1990 the two German states ceased to exist as two: the five new Länder — Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Brandenburg, Sachsen-Anhalt, Thüringen and Sachsen — joined the federation, and at midnight on 3 October Germany was whole again, celebrated in Berlin with the raising of the black, red and gold flag.
Unity within Europe and the West
Reunification was inseparable from the anchoring of the new Germany in the West and in Europe. The two-plus-four-1990 Treaty of September 1990, signed by the two Germanies and the four wartime powers, had restored full sovereignty while confirming the united Germany’s place in NATO and in the European Community; the recovery of unity went hand in hand with the construction of the European monetary union that helmut-kohl had long insisted must accompany it. For the Germans, the year 1990 marked the end of the sonderweg — the special path that had led through catastrophe — and their entry into what Winkler called Western normality. For the East Germans, the accession was experienced with a mixture of liberation and loss: the hope of 1990, as Kowalczuk chronicled, was to be followed by the disappointment of the transformation, as the adapted citizens of the East met the demands of the West and the republic learned the price of the unity it had so swiftly and so freely achieved.

events/grundvertrag-1972.title: The Grundvertrag (1972)
events/grundvertrag-1972.content:
The Grundvertrag (1972)
Of all the treaties of the neue Ostpolitik — the new-ostpolitik-1969-73 with Moscow and Warsaw, the Four-Power Agreement on Berlin — none cut so close to the heart of the German question as the treaty that the Federal Republic concluded with the other German state. The Vertrag über die Grundlagen der Beziehungen zwischen der Bundesrepublik Deutschland und der Deutschen Demokratischen Republik, the Treaty on the Basis of Relations between the Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic, was the supreme test of a policy built on a paradox. In it Bonn recognised the existence of the second German state in order to keep alive the unity of the nation.
The negotiations fell to the two secretaries of state, Egon Bahr for the Federal Republic and Michael Kohl for the German Democratic Republic, and they ran from June 1972 amid the deadlock of the parliamentary crisis at home. The disputed points were the oldest wounds of German–German relations: the status of Berlin, the question of citizenship, the terms on which Germans on either side of the border would meet their relatives. Only on 10 October, after the Soviet party leader Leonid Brezhnev had received Bahr in the Kremlin, did East Berlin show itself more yielding. On 6 November the talks were concluded, on 7 November the federal cabinet approved the result, and on 8 November 1972 the two secretaries of state initialled the treaty in Bonn, together with its additional protocol, protocol notes, several exchanges of letters and a written “oral agreement” on political consultations.
By the treaty both sides bound themselves to develop good-neighbourly relations on the basis of equality, to be guided by the goals and principles of the United Nations, to settle their disputes exclusively by peaceful means and to refrain from the threat or use of force. They affirmed the Unverletzlichkeit (inviolability) of the frontiers existing between them now and in the future, and pledged unrestricted respect for their territorial integrity. Neither state, the treaty ran, could represent the other internationally or act in its name; the sovereign authority of each state was confined to its own territory; each respected the independence and self-sufficiency of the other in its internal and external affairs. Provision was made for cooperation in a wide range of fields — from economics through culture and sport to environmental protection — to be settled in further agreements. At the seat of the other’s government the two states would maintain not embassies but ständige Vertretungen (permanent representations), as befitted relations that were not those of one foreign country to another.
The limits of the treaty were as carefully drawn as its substance. Bahr had not been able to secure any mention of the goal of German unity. Instead the preamble, in the spirit of an “agree to disagree”, spoke of the unterschiedlichen Auffassungen (different views) of the two sides on fundamental questions, including the national question. And although neither the treaty nor the declaration of the Four Powers said anything of a peace-treaty settlement or of “Germany as a whole”, the two states acted under the continuing roof of Allied rights and responsibilities. The Four Powers, in a joint declaration of 9 November 1972, confirmed that their rights and responsibilities were not affected by the treaty and recommended the admission of the two German states to the United Nations. Their relationship, as Brandt had put it in his government declaration of 28 October 1969, was one von besonderer Art — of a particular kind — constitutional in character but not international-legal. The Federal Republic and the German Democratic Republic were not, through the treaty, made “foreign countries” to one another.
The treaty divided the parties and the country as no other act of the Ostpolitik had done. In the election campaign of the autumn of 1972 the parliamentary ratification of the Grundvertrag became a plebiscite. The opposition’s leader, Rainer Barzel, declared that after a Union victory he would not sign the treaty unless the German Democratic Republic at once stopped shooting at refugees. To many in the republic such demands appeared unfulfillable, and to help neither the Germans in the East nor the Federal Republic. As the treaty, initialled but not yet signed, hung in the balance, the election of 19 November delivered a resounding mandate to the coalition and to the policy that had produced it.
The final signature came on 21 December 1972. The seven-year period of the new Ostpolitik had reached its completion — the treaties with the East, the Berlin settlement, and now the formal basis of the German–German relationship. Yet the Grundvertrag was a gesamtdeutsche Zäsur (all-German caesura), a dividing line as much as a settlement. The German Democratic Republic read it as the recognition of its permanent and separate existence; the Federal Republic read it as the framework that kept the nation’s unity alive. Both readings were inscribed in the same document, which was why it could never wholly satisfy either side. Its ratification was challenged before the Federal Constitutional Court, which on 31 July 1973 confirmed the treaty’s compatibility with the Basic Law and bestowed on it a Doppelcharakter (double character) — a treaty between states that yet left open the possibility of the restoration of the German unity it seemed to consecrate.
By the terms of its own logic the Grundvertrag put an end to the Alleinvertretungsanspruch (sole-representation claim): henceforward neither German state could pretend to speak for the other. It admitted the second German state into the community of nations even as it refused to abandon the national question to which it owed its existence. For a decade and more the two states — bound together by the treaty even as the German Democratic Republic pursued its policy of Abgrenzung (delimitation), the deliberate drawing of distance — would conduct their permanent negotiations under its roof, carrying the deutsch-deutschen (German–German) relationship through the estrangement of the later years. In the recognition of the two states, Brandt’s government insisted, lay the preservation of the one nation. See new-ostpolitik-1969-73, ostpolitik and willy-brandt.

events/hot-autumn-1969.title: Hot Autumn (Autunno caldo) 1969
events/hot-autumn-1969.content:
Hot Autumn (Autunno caldo) 1969
The autunno caldo — the hot autumn — was the great wave of labour conflict that swept Italy in the autumn of 1969, the most intense and politically charged workers’ struggle the Republic had yet seen, and one of the defining events in the history of the Italian working class. In the factories of the industrial North — Fiat and Pirelli and the great engineering works of Turin and Milan — tens of thousands of workers struck and occupied, not merely for wages but for a transformation of the conditions of work and of the power of the factory floor. The hot autumn was the culmination of the social pressures that the economic miracle and the centro-sinistra (centre-left) had released but not absorbed, and it opened the turbulent decade of the anni di piombo (years of lead).
The long 1968 and the crisis of reform
The hot autumn must be understood as part of the lungo Sessantotto (the long 1968), the international wave of contestation that in Italy, as Gentiloni Silveri observes, was not confined to the student movement but overflowed into the factories and the working class. The student revolt of 1968, which convulsed the Italian universities, found its echo and its larger meaning in the world of work. At the same time the limits of the centre-left were becoming evident: the reforms of the 1960s had not been able to keep pace with the speed of Italian industrialisation, and a new generation of workers, many of them migrants from the South into the factories of the North, had arrived in a working world still marked by old hierarchies, piece-work, and the arbitrary power of the bosses.
The result was a movement of the operai (workers) that went beyond the traditional concerns of the trade unions. The strikes of the autumn of 1969 were not the disciplined, wages-first struggles of the past. They were mass assemblies, factory occupations, wildcat actions and the formation of autonomous consigli di fabbrica (factory councils) — new organs of representation that bypassed the old union structures and the established left. The demand was not simply more money but salario, orario, libertà — higher pay, shorter hours, and freedom and dignity on the shop floor. The workers of 1969 sought, in a word, to challenge the very organisation of production and the subordination of labour to capital.
The unions and the Workers’ Statute
The great beneficiary of the hot autumn, and the instrument through which its gains were made permanent, was the trade-union movement. The unions, initially overtaken by the rank-and-file explosion, moved to lead it, and their new militancy was reflected in the reform of the labour movement’s internal structure and in a new unity among the three great confederations — the Communist-leaning CGIL, the Catholic CISL and the socialist-republican UIL — which in the years after 1969 came to act together and to negotiate jointly with the employers and the state.
The concrete and lasting achievement of the hot autumn was the Statuto dei lavoratori (Workers’ Statute), the law of 1970 that regulated the rights of workers in the factory. The statute guaranteed freedom of opinion and association at work, protected workers against dismissal without just cause, and established the legal framework of the factory councils and of union activity inside the enterprise. It was, as Mammarella stressed, the legal codification of the power the workers had won in the streets and factories of the autumn of 1969 — a victory that transformed the Italian workplace and gave the unions a recognised place in the running of the economy. Together with the pension and housing reforms of the same years, the statute completed the social legislation that the centre-left had promised and that the hot autumn finally delivered.
Consequences
The hot autumn had consequences far beyond the factory gates. It marked the end of the docile, apolitical Italian working class of the miracle years and the beginning of a decade in which social conflict was at the centre of national life. In the years that followed, the unions grew into a great and recognised social power, and the wage gains of the early 1970s reshaped Italian living standards. But the movement also carried the seeds of the troubles to come: the rank-and-file radicalism that the unions could not entirely contain fed, in part, the far-left extremism that contributed to the anni di piombo, and the intensity of the labour conflict frightened the middle classes and the right, sharpening the social and political polarisation of the 1970s. The hot autumn, Gentiloni Silveri concludes, marked the end of innocence for the Republic’s social order — the moment the apparently harmonious miracle gave way to a decade of conflict whose outcome was uncertain.

events/hungarian-revolution-1956.title: The Hungarian Revolution (1956)
events/hungarian-revolution-1956.content:
The Hungarian Revolution (1956)
In the autumn of 1956 the socialist world was shaken by a crisis that brought Soviet forces into battle on the soil of a fraternal country for the first time since the war. The de-Stalinisation of the XX Congress had raised a ferment among the peoples of the people’s democracies, and nowhere did the ferment run so deep as in Hungary. There, in a country whose revolution of 1848 and rising of 1956 were to be forever linked in its national memory, an explosion of popular revolt overthrew the Stalinist leadership, promised free elections and a return to the nation, and was at last crushed by the armed might of the Soviet Union in November 1956. To the official Soviet histories of the age the events were the work of kontrrevolyutsiya (counter-revolution) — a conspiracy of Hungarian reaction and international imperialism against the people’s-democratic order, whose defeat was a victory for the socialist camp and a grave warning of what the easing of control could unleash.
The crisis of the bloc
Hungary in 1956 was the most Stalinist of the satellites. Its ruler Mátyás Rákosi had governed through terror and the cult of the personality in the model of the age that the XX Congress had just condemned, and the economic hardship of the country had made the name of the party hated among wide sections of the people. The shock of de-Stalinisation shook the leadership itself. In July 1956 Rákosi was removed and replaced, after pressure from Moscow, by Ernő Gerő — a change that satisfied no one. On 23 October the students of Budapest and the writers who had breathed the spirit of the thaw took to the streets; a peaceful demonstration for reform, for the return of the imprisoned reformer Imre Nagy, for national independence, swelled into a mass rising. The statues of Stalin were toppled, the security police were attacked, and the revolution spread from the capital across the country. Soviet troops, stationed in Hungary under the Warsaw Treaty, were called in and were at first driven back by a population that had seized the arms of the army and the police.
The revolution and the invasion
On 28 October the Soviet leadership, uncertain and divided, withdrew its forces and accepted a ceasefire; on 30 October, in a declaration that acknowledged the errors of the past, Moscow seemed to concede the principle that the socialist states were equal and that no one should impose its will on a fraternal people. Imre Nagy, recalled to the premiership, announced a programme of reform, restored a coalition government, and finally, on 1 November, declared Hungary’s neutrality and its withdrawal from the Warsaw Treaty. For twelve days Hungary appeared to have slipped out of the bloc. It was an appearance that Moscow could not tolerate. Fearing the loss of the whole socialist commonwealth and the encouragement it would give to every opposition in the East, the Soviet leadership decided on intervention. On 4 November 1956, in an operation launched under the code name Whirlwind, Soviet armoured and motorised divisions struck into Budapest and across the country. The Hungarians resisted street by street, but the outcome was never in doubt. The kontrrevolyutsiya (counter-revolution) was drowned in blood; thousands died, and tens of thousands fled to the West as the tanks restored the order of the party.
The consequences
The crushing of the Hungarian revolution defined the limits of de-Stalinisation. Moscow had shown that the razryadka of the thaw stopped at the frontier of the bloc — that no country could leave the community of socialist states, and that no popular movement, however just its grievances, would be suffered to overturn a people’s democracy. The new Hungarian government of János Kádár, installed under the shadow of the Soviet tanks, set about rebuilding the country on a more cautious path than Rákosi’s — a path of reconstruction and eventual reform that came to be known, in time, as the kádárizmus, and which earned Budapest a grudging domestic peace. In the West, the events of 1956 were seized upon as proof of the nature of the Soviet system and of the hollowness of its professions of peace; the Hungarian uprising, crushed while the world’s attention was fixed on the Suez crisis unfolding at the same moment, became a central symbol of the Cold War confrontation. The Soviet histories of the Brezhnev era, for their part, drew from 1956 the lesson of the fragility of the socialist commonwealth and the resolve of the party to defend it — a lesson that was to govern the conduct of the bloc until, thirteen years later, it was applied once more in Prague.

events/italian-elections-1948.title: Italian General Election (18 April 1948)
events/italian-elections-1948.content:
Italian General Election (18 April 1948)
On Sunday, 18 April 1948, Italy went to the polls in the first general election of the Republic, and delivered the most decisive verdict in its history. The vote was cast as a confrontation of two opposed blocs: on one side the Democrazia Cristiana (Christian Democracy) of Alcide De Gasperi, the party of government, Atlanticism and the Catholic masses; on the other the Fronte Democratico Popolare (Popular Democratic Front), the alliance of the communists and the socialists, led by Palmiro Togliatti, which offered itself as the alternative order of the Italian left. The result was a landslide for the Christian Democrats, which won an absolute majority of the Chamber of Deputies. The election of 18 April fixed the orientation of the Republic for a generation: it confirmed Italy in the Western camp, condemned the communist opposition to permanent exclusion, and gave the Christian Democratic centrismo the majority on which it was to govern through the 1950s.
A Cold War battle on Italian soil
The election was fought in the shadow of the deepening Cold War. The rupture of the grand anti-fascist coalition had already occurred: in 1947 De Gasperi had expelled the communists and socialists from the government, and the Marshall Plan and the hardening of the blocs had drawn the lines of the postwar world across Italy. Italy, with the largest communist party outside the Soviet bloc, stood at the fault line of the two camps, and the election of April 1948 was experienced by contemporaries as a decision of international as much as national significance — a test of whether the country would remain in the Western system or incline toward the other side. The communists and socialists stood together in the Fronte Democratico Popolare, offering a united popular front; the Christian Democrats answered with a mobilization of the Catholic world, the Church and the laity, in defence of the republic’s Western and Catholic identity. The contest was conducted as a struggle of civilizational alternatives, the two visions of Italy’s future set against each other in the most charged political atmosphere of the Republic’s early years.
The American role
The United States took a direct and active interest in the outcome. The Truman administration, committed to containing Soviet influence, regarded the Italian election as a decisive test of the containment policy, and acted to influence it — economic aid through the Marshall Plan, the promise of American support to an Italy that remained in the Western camp, and a campaign of political pressure and encouragement in favour of the Christian Democrats and against the communist front. The American intervention, open and concealed, was one of the decisive circumstances of the election: it held before the Italian voter the material promise of reconstruction under a Western Italy, and the threat of the alternative, and it contributed substantially to the mobilization that brought the Christian Democrats their triumph. The election was thus, for its contemporaries, not only a national contest but a front line of the Cold War, in which the fate of Italy appeared to hang in the balance and in which the great Western power made its weight felt.
The Christian Democratic landslide
When the votes were counted, the Christian Democrats had won an absolute majority in the Chamber of Deputies — a result without parallel in the history of the Italian Republic, never repeated since. The Popular Democratic Front was heavily defeated. The election delivered to De Gasperi the secure majority that was to sustain the centrismo: the government could henceforth be formed around the dominant D.C., with the smaller parties of the centre as auxiliaries, and the communist opposition was confined permanently to the margins of power. The result was at once the triumph of the anti-communist republic and the foundation of its political order. From the victory of 18 April the centrismo — the D.C.-centred coalition of the centre parties, sustained by the exclusion of the communists and by the Atlantic and Catholic alignment of the country — was built and endured through the 1950s. The election of 1948, as decisive a moment as the Republic had known, set the terms of Italian politics for a generation.

events/italian-republic-referendum-1946.title: Italian Republic Referendum (2 June 1946)
events/italian-republic-referendum-1946.content:
Italian Republic Referendum (2 June 1946)
The Italian Republic was born on Sunday, 2 June 1946, in a single day of universal suffrage and constitutional choice. On that day the Italian people, voting for the first time in the history of the country, went to the polls to decide the institutional form of the state — monarchy or republic — and to elect, in the same breath, the Assemblea Costituente (Constituent Assembly) that was to write the Constitution of the new order. The referendum ended the Savoy monarchy, which had reigned over Italy for almost a century, and opened the age of the democratic republic. It was the decisive act of the reconstruction, the moment in which the country, emerging from the catastrophe of fascism and war, chose its form of government and set about the founding of its democracy.
The choice between monarchy and republic
The institutional question had divided the anti-fascist forces throughout the Resistance and the liberation. The monarchy of the house of Savoy was compromised in the eyes of much of the country by its association with the fascist regime, with the flight of the king to the south in 1943 and with the surrender and the German occupation that followed; the republic was the cause of the greater part of the anti-fascist coalition, the Comitato di Liberazione Nazionale (National Liberation Committee) and its parties. The referendum of 2 June 1946 offered the question to the people directly. The vote was by universal suffrage, and for the first time Italian women voted — the republican choice thereby drawing on the support of the newly enfranchised female electorate, which turned out in great numbers. When the votes were counted, the republic had won. The monarchy was abolished, King Umberto II went into exile, and the Repubblica Italiana (Italian Republic) was proclaimed — the result, close enough to reflect a deeply divided country, yet clear enough to decide the state.
The election of the Constituent Assembly
On the same day the country elected the Assemblea Costituente, the assembly charged with writing the new Constitution. The election gave no party an absolute majority: the Democrazia Cristiana (Christian Democracy) of Alcide De Gasperi emerged as the largest party, ahead of the socialists of the Partito Socialista Italiano and the communists of the Partito Comunista Italiano. The three great parties of the anti-fascist coalition — the Catholic, the socialist and the communist — divided the assembly among them, and it was from their collaboration that the Constitution was to be written. The assembly, in which the parties of the anti-fascist resistance sat together despite the approaching Cold War, produced in 1948 the republican Constitution, a document of compromise that enshrined the social and democratic values of the new republic. The referendum and the election were thus one founding act: the choice of the republican form, and the gathering of the constituent power that would give the republic its law.
The birth of the Republic
The Republic of 2 June 1946 was born out of the ruin of the war and the humiliations of the peace. Italy had entered the postwar years defeated, isolated and diminished, its institutions discredited by the twenty years of fascism and its place in the world uncertain. The referendum was the first free and general exercise of the popular will in the history of the peninsula, the point at which the Italian people took the reconstruction of their state into their own hands. The institutional choice of 1946, the election of the Constituent Assembly and the writing of the Constitution were to be completed, in the years that followed, by the peace treaty, the economic reconstruction and the anchoring of the republic in the Western alliance — a course set, in its first and most fundamental decision, by the vote of 2 June. From that day the republic, with all its divisions, was the settled form of the Italian state, and the monarchy a memory.

events/italian-second-republic-1994.title: The Italian Second Republic (1994)
events/italian-second-republic-1994.content:
The Italian Second Republic (1994)
The elections of 27 and 28 March 1994 returned to power, in a country that had just endured the political earthquake of Tangentopoli, a coalition of new parties built around a television magnate who had never before held office. The victory of Silvio Berlusconi’s Forza Italia and its allies, and the collapse of the historic parties of the First Republic, appeared to contemporaries the passage to a new order — a Seconda Repubblica. Whether a new republic truly began in 1994, or whether what followed was rather a mancata transizione, a transition that never arrived, became one of the central questions of Italian political history.
The crisis of the First Republic
The old order had died before the new one was born. The Republic of the parties, the Prima Repubblica that had governed Italy since 1948, was swept away in the biennium 1992-1993 by the combined shocks that Gentiloni Silveri groups under the heading of the crollo: the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, which dissolved the Cold War framework in which the whole postwar system had been inscribed; the inquests of Mani pulite, which revealed a diffuse corruption and destroyed the credibility of the governing class; and the rise of the regional leagues of the North, which threatened the very bond between centre and periphery. The Democrazia cristiana dissolved in 1993, the Partito socialista crumbled, and the great confessional and class parties of the postwar era were replaced, in the space of a few years, by a fragmented landscape of new formations.
The institutional response was a new electoral law. After the referendum of April 1993, in which an overwhelming majority voted against the proportional system and the public financing of parties, the government of Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, formed after the fall of Giuliano Amato, drew up a law — known by the ironical name of the Mattarellum, after its first signatory Sergio Mattarella — that assigned seventy-five per cent of seats by majority ballot in single-member constituencies and twenty-five per cent proportionally. The aim was a simplification of the political landscape, a bipolarisation of forces and alignments that would bring Italian politics closer to a dialectic of majority and opposition. It was a design, as Gentiloni Silveri writes, that was to have little fortune: the coalitions lacked a solid base, and the road toward a competitive and simplifying bipolarism was neither simple nor obvious.
The discesa in campo
Into this vacuum stepped Silvio Berlusconi. The owner of the Fininvest group, the largest private conglomerate in the country after that of the Agnelli family, had built his fortune on the commercial television empire that the political class had failed to regulate. The disintegration of the PSI and the personal ruin of his old protector Craxi robbed him of political protection, and the prospect of a victory of the left appeared to him a serious danger. On 26 January 1994 he announced his candidacy and the birth of a new movement, Forza Italia, built in barely a month largely on the staff and clients of his own companies — a partito aziendale, a company party — and backed by the mobilisation of his television networks. His recorded message of January, broadcast simultaneously on the two broadcasting giants, presented him in the reassuring idiom of a television advertisement: the orderly white study, the family photographs, the promise that “L’Italia è il paese che amo.” Around him he assembled two coalitions: the Polo delle Libertà with Umberto Bossi’s Lega Nord in the North, and the Polo del Buon Governo with Gianfranco Fini’s Alleanza Nazionale — the reborn post-fascist MSI — in the South.
The victory of March 1994
The elections returned a decisive victory for the Pole. Forza Italia, founded barely a month before the ballot, emerged as the first national party with twenty-one per cent of the proportional vote. Alleanza Nazionale, with thirteen and a half per cent, became the third party and triumphed in the South, where it reached twenty per cent. The Lega held its ground, and thanks to Berlusconi’s generosity in ceding it the representation of a large number of constituencies, it secured a great haul of seats. The left was routed: the Partito democratico della sinistra won 20.3 per cent, Rifondazione comunista six, the Partito Popolare eleven; the old Partito socialista collapsed to 2.2 per cent. The Pole won the absolute majority in the Chamber, and Berlusconi, as the recognised leader of the winning party, was the natural candidate for the presidency of the Council. He formed a government, sworn in on 11 May 1994.
A new republic, or a transition mancata?
The outcome confirmed that a new party system had replaced the old. Yet the great hopes of a simplification and of a clear alternation were not fulfilled. The new electoral law had been intended to reduce the parties, but in practice it fragmented the alignments still further; the country emerged from the vote divided into three electoral zones — the North where Lega and Forza Italia were overwhelming, a centre dominated by the left, and a South where Alleanza Nazionale inherited the positions of the old Democrazia cristiana. The first Berlusconi government lasted barely a summer, brought down in December 1994 by the withdrawal of the Lega. Gentiloni Silveri, surveying the decades that followed, concludes that the enthusiasm for a new beginning gave way to the uneasy scenarios of a world without rules and an internal transition without reassuring landings — a bipolarismo imperfetto, an imperfect bipolarism, that never quite became the clean two-party system the reformers had imagined. Whether the Second Republic truly began in 1994, or whether the country merely passed from one unstable equilibrium to another, remained a question at the heart of the interpretation of contemporary Italy.
