events/khrushchev-secret-speech-1956.title: The Secret Speech and De-Stalinisation (1956)
events/khrushchev-secret-speech-1956.content:
The Secret Speech and De-Stalinisation (1956)
On the night of 24–25 February 1956, in the great hall of the Kremlin, nikita-khrushchev delivered a report that was to shake the socialist world to its foundations. The twentieth congress of the Communist Party, convened in Moscow in February 1956, had already heard the First Secretary’s public account of the party’s tasks in building communism and of the international situation — a congress that in the official histories marks the restoration of Leninist norms of party life after the long shadow of the past. But it was the closed session, the zakrytyi doklad (closed report) addressed to the assembled delegates on the final day, that broke the silence of three decades. There Khrushchev denounced what he called the kult lichnosti — the cult of the personality — of the dead Stalin, and set in motion the razoblachenie, the unmasking, that the whole world came to know as de-Stalinisation. The speech was never published in the Soviet press in its own time, and it passed at first by word of mouth and by the reading of its text to party and komsomol organisations across the country; but no secret of that kind could long remain confined to the party. The thaw, ottepel, had begun.
The congress and the unmasking
The XX Congress of the CPSU opened on 14 February 1956 as the triumphant assembly of a party that had, in the years since Stalin’s death in 1953, begun to recover the collective leadership it had lost. The official histories present it as the moment when the party restored the Leninist norms of party and state life and condemned the violations of the past — a turning of the party back to the principles of the founder after the distortions of the age of the cult. Khrushchev’s report on the work of the Central Committee set out the new course: the priority of heavy industry and the struggle for peace, the victory of socialism, the general line of peaceful coexistence with the capitalist world. Then, in the closed session, he turned to what the congress could not say in public. He laid before the delegates the crimes of the Stalin era — the repressii (repressions), the great purges, the confessions exacted from innocent party men, the terror that had destroyed so many of the old Bolsheviks. The effect on the delegates, on the whole country as the report was read out in party cells, and on the communist parties of the world, was overwhelming. The monument of the infallible leader was toppled from within.
De-Stalinisation
The speech was the opening of the process the party called the restoration of Leninist norms and socialist legality — sotsialisticheskaya zakonnost. The organs of state security were brought under control and the system of terror that had made them a law unto themselves was curbed; hundreds of thousands of the victims of the purges were rehabilitated, reabilitirovany, their names restored and their reputations cleared. In the factories and fields Khrushchev pushed his programme of economic reform — the virgin lands campaign, osvoenie tseliny, the decentralisation of industry, the raising of the standard of living. In the world of ideas, the writers and artists of the shestidesyatniki, the men of the sixties, felt the wind of the thaw. Yet the process was strictly bounded and strictly controlled. Khrushchev and his colleagues were not confessing on behalf of the party or the system; they were denouncing the cult in order to restore the party to itself, and the limits of the freedom they permitted were made brutally plain before the decade was out. De-Stalinisation was not the end of the system but its correction — the party remaking itself from within.
The earthquake in the socialist world
The consequences of the secret speech reached far beyond the borders of the USSR. In the people’s democracies of Eastern Europe the denunciation of the dead dictator raised a storm. In Poland it emboldened a movement of reform that forced the return to power of Władysław Gomułka in the autumn of 1956; in Hungary it fed the ferment that exploded a few months later in the hungarian-revolution-1956. The communist parties of the West lost members who could not reconcile the faith with the revelations; the great schism between Moscow and Peking, between the future leadership’s insistence on Soviet leadership and Mao’s contempt for the Soviet line, was opened in part by the different readings of the Khrushchev revelations. The official histories of the party, looking back from the height of the Brezhnev era, preserved a careful memory of the XX Congress — the restoration of Leninist norms and the renunciation of the cult as the indispensable condition of the party’s renewal, while holding fast to the socialist system itself. The secret speech was the hinge of the Khrushchev decade: it made possible the easing of tension and the whole opening toward the world, and it made impossible any simple return to the world of Stalin. The ottepel (thaw) had come, and nothing after it would ever be quite frozen again.

events/korean-war-1950-53.title: Korean War (1950–1953)
events/korean-war-1950-53.content:
Korean War (1950–1953)
The coldest front of the early Cold War was fought in a peninsula of East Asia that few had imagined as a world battlefield. The Korean War of 1950–1953 — which the Soviet histories present as a war of imperialist aggression answered by the heroism of the Korean people and the fraternal aid of the socialist camp — was the first great armed clash of the era of the two blocs, and the only one in which the armies of the United States and the communist powers fought one another directly in the field. For three years it held the world at the edge of a third world war, and its outcome fixed the frontier of the Cold War in Asia for half a century.
The partition of Korea
The division of Korea had its origin in the defeat of Japan and the collapse of its colonial empire in 1945. The Red Army, entering Korea from the north, liberated the country from Japanese colonial rule and opened the way for its national independence and social transformation; the Soviet forces and the Korean democratic forces established a people’s power in the North, carried out a land reform, nationalised the property of the Japanese monopolists and the traitors of the Korean people, and set the country on the path of building socialism. The United States, for its part, hurried to take Japan’s place in the South, landing its troops after the surrender and refusing the restoration of Korean independence promised in the Cairo and Potsdam Declarations. The Moscow agreement of December 1945 provided for the formation of a single all-Korean democratic government, but the joint Soviet-American commission was sabotaged by the American representatives, who did not want a democratic and independent Korea. In May 1948 the American occupation authorities held elections in the South under open terror, and raised the reactionary Syngman Rhee to the head of a separatist South Korean government — a puppet regime, in the Soviet view, that was intended to turn the country into an American strategic base. In August 1948 the Korean people answered by electing a Supreme People’s Assembly and proclaiming the Korean People’s Democratic Republic (Koreyskaya Narodno-Demokraticheskaya Respublika, the KNDR), the first government of which was formed the following month. In March 1949 the USSR concluded economic and cultural agreements with the KNDR, granting it credit and technical aid.
The outbreak of war
From the moment the Syngman Rhee regime was installed it began to prepare an attack on the North. A secret American–South Korean military agreement of August 1948 created a South Korean army under American control; the United States supplied it with 75 million dollars of military aid in 1949 and 110 million for 1950, so that by the end of 1949 the South Korean army, armed with American weapons, numbered more than a hundred thousand men. Provocations along the 38th parallel — tridtsat vosmaya parallel — became daily: between January 1949 and April 1950 the South Korean forces and police carried out over twelve hundred raids on the territory of the KNDR and more than a hundred violations of its sea and air frontiers. On 25 June 1950 the South Korean troops, in the Soviet account, launched the American-planned aggression against the KNDR, opening the civil war. To repel the aggression the government of the KNDR ordered its forces to counter-attack, throw back the enemy and pursue him into the territory of South Korea.
The intervention of the United Nations and the Chinese volunteers
The American government responded by armed intervention. On the evening of 25 June the 7th Fleet was ordered into the Taiwan Strait, and on 27 June President Truman announced the despatch of ground troops to Korea and the use of the war for the occupation of Taiwan. The American diplomacy, in the Soviet reading, sought to cover its intervention with the flag of the United Nations. Taking advantage of the absence of the Soviet representative — who, in protest against the refusal to seat the People’s Republic of China, had withdrawn from the Security Council from January 1950 — the United States pushed through the Council resolutions that branded the KNDR the aggressor, authorised aid to the Syngman Rhee forces, and finally, on 7 July, renamed the interventionist troops the “United Nations forces” and placed them under General MacArthur. Fifteen states, allies or dependents of the United States, formally joined the intervention, but only Britain and Turkey sent troops in any strength, and the “UN forces” were ninety per cent American. The Soviet government, in a statement of 4 July 1950, denounced the aggression, denied the legality of the Council’s resolutions and demanded the ending of the American intervention and the withdrawal of all foreign forces. In November 1950 the Chinese government, in response to the Korean people’s struggle and to the threat to China’s own borders, permitted the volunteers of the People’s Republic of China, the kitayskiye dobroltsy, to join the liberation struggle. The Soviet Union supplied the Korean People’s Army and the Chinese volunteers with arms, ammunition, transport, fuel, food and medicines, maintained Soviet military advisers in Korea, and, at the request of the Chinese government, transferred several Soviet air divisions to the north-eastern provinces of China, whose pilots engaged and shot down American aircraft and shielded the north-east from aerial attack. By mid-December 1950 the territory of the KNDR had been liberated.
The armistice
For nearly three years the war ground on, its cost in Korean lives enormous, its front swinging across the peninsula. The American command, faced by the coalition of the Korean People’s Army and the Chinese volunteers, was never able to overrun the North; the Soviet and Chinese delegations pressed, through the United Nations and the good offices of India, for a ceasefire and the withdrawal of foreign troops. After long negotiations — begun at Kaesong and continued at Panmunjom — a truce on the repatriation of prisoners of war was signed on 8 June 1953, and on 27 July 1953 the armistice agreement was concluded, providing for the complete cessation of military operations, the mutual withdrawal of forces from the 38th parallel, and the establishment of military armistice and supervision commissions. The war ended where it had begun, on the line of the old frontier, leaving Korea divided and the world with the demonstration of what a direct clash of the two blocs could cost. For the Soviet Union the Korean War had been, as the histories insist, both a defence of the socialist camp against imperialist aggression and the proof that the camp would not be overrun — a victory that fixed the boundary of the Cold War in Asia and set the stage for the easing of tension that followed Stalin’s death and the armistice of 1953.

events/legge-truffa-1953.title: The Legge Truffa (1953)
events/legge-truffa-1953.content:
The Legge Truffa (1953)
In the spring of 1953 the government of the centrismo — the ruling coalition of the Democrazia Cristiana and the centre parties, alarmed at the erosion of its strength — pressed through a new electoral law designed to secure its majority. The law, which gave a large premium of seats to the list or coalition that obtained a majority of the votes, was denounced by its opponents as a legge truffa (the “swindle law”), a rigging of the electoral system to keep the ruling parties in power. The elections held under it on 7 June 1953 failed, however, to deliver the intended premium: the centrist coalition fell narrowly short of the majority required, and the law was soon repealed. The failure of the legge truffa marked the end of the certain majority on which the centrismo had been built since 1948, and opened the difficult second legislature of the centrist decade.
The majority premium
The law was introduced by the centrist government in the name of ensuring stable government. Under the proportional system in force since the birth of the Republic, the coalitions of the centre had seen their vote shrink steadily since the triumph of 1948, and the governing parties feared that without intervention their majority might be lost. The new law — the “electoral law of the majority” — provided that the party or coalition of allied parties which obtained at least one half of the votes plus one in the election would receive a premium of seats, giving it a comfortable majority in the Chamber of Deputies. The effect would be to guarantee the governing centre a working majority, and to deny to the opposition — in particular to the great mass of the communist and socialist left — the chance of translating a close result into power. It was this mechanical guarantee, this tilting of the system toward the parties that had written it, that earned the law the name by which it is remembered.
The swindle
The name legge truffa (swindle law) came from the opposition, which saw in the law a fraud upon the electorate — an attempt by the parties of government to rig the electoral system in their own favour. The communist, socialist and other opposition forces campaigned against the law as a corruption of the democratic principle, and the contest of 7 June 1953 was fought in part over the law itself. The centrist parties presented the law as a means to stable and efficient government; the opposition denounced it as the swindle of a government that could no longer command the confidence of the country by honest means. The very name, legge truffa, passed into the language of Italian politics as the lasting label of the affair, a byword for the manipulation of the electoral system.
The failure of the law
The outcome of 7 June 1953 confounded the calculations of the government. The centrist coalition — the D.C. and its centre allies — fell narrowly short of the required majority, by a small margin of votes, and the premium was not triggered. The law, which had been designed to guarantee the majority, failed to deliver it, and the centrismo lost the certain majority it had enjoyed since the election of 1948. The centrist coalition no longer commanded an absolute majority in the Chamber, and the government that had staked its authority on the law emerged weakened. The legge truffa, discredited by its failure and by the storm of opposition it had provoked, was shortly repealed, and Italian electoral politics returned to the pure proportional system. The episode stands as a singular and telling moment in the history of the centrist decade — the attempt of the ruling coalition to secure itself by electoral engineering, and its decisive failure.
The end of the certain majority
The failure of the legge truffa marked a turning of the tide of the centrismo. The landslide majority of 1948, on which the De Gasperi governments had governed with such security, was gone, and the centre could no longer rely on the automatic majority of its own strength. The elections of 1953 opened the “difficult second legislature,” a period of more fragile coalitions, of constant negotiation among the centre parties, and of growing difficulty for the centrist formula. The failure also struck at the prestige of Alcide De Gasperi, the architect of the centrist system, whose premiership came to an end in its aftermath. The legge truffa thus stands at the hinge of the centrist decade: the moment when the certain majority of the reconstruction years gave way, and the centrismo, deprived of its mechanical security, was forced to negotiate its survival through the remainder of the 1950s.

events/maastricht-treaty-1992.title: Maastricht Treaty (1992)
events/maastricht-treaty-1992.content:
Maastricht Treaty (1992)
The Treaty on European Union, signed at the Dutch border town of Maastricht on 7 February 1992, transformed the European Community into the European Union and committed its members to the boldest project in the history of integration — an Economic and Monetary Union with a single currency. It was at once the crowning achievement of the integration built over four decades and the moment when the European project, moving from the economics of the market into the very substance of the nation-state, first ran against the limits of popular consent.
From single market to political union
The road to Maastricht ran directly through the Single European Act. The completion of the internal market reopened the question of money, and the success of the European Monetary System, in which the Deutsche Mark had become the anchor of continental exchange, made a single currency seem both possible and, to many, necessary. The European Council of Hannover in June 1988, on the strength of a prior Franco-German understanding and in the wake of a proposal from the German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher, established a committee under the presidency of the Commission’s Jacques Delors, composed of the central bank presidents of the twelve member states, to study the design of a monetary union. The Delors Committee reported in April 1989 with a plan for a three-stage advance to a single currency, without a fixed timetable, and the European Council of Madrid adopted its recommendations the following June, setting in motion an intergovernmental conference on Economic and Monetary Union.
The revolutions of 1989 transformed the stakes. The fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 brought the German question back to the heart of European politics, and the prospect of a reunified Germany at the centre of the continent sharpened the urgency, for the French and their neighbours, of binding the new Germany into a common European architecture. Chancellor Helmut Kohl brought forward the intergovernmental conference to December 1990, and in April 1990 Kohl and the French President François Mitterrand jointly proposed a second, parallel conference on political union. The two conferences, on economic and on political union, were agreed at Dublin in June 1990 and concluded after a year of negotiation at the European Council of Maastricht on 9–10 December 1991.
The three pillars and the design of EMU
The treaty that emerged restructured the edifice of integration. The European Economic Community was rebaptised the European Community and became the first pillar of the new European Union; a second pillar established a Common Foreign and Security Policy, an intergovernmental domain reflecting the determination, in the words of the Cambridge history, to give Europe an independent voice in the superpower-dominated world; and a third pillar created cooperation in justice and home affairs. The upgrade from a Community to a Union was itself a statement of ambition, a move beyond the common market towards integration in the core functions of the state.
The most important achievement was the agreement on Economic and Monetary Union. Following the Delors report, the Community would advance in three stages to a single European currency — at that time still called the “écu” — and a European Central Bank. Membership of the final stage was made dependent on the fulfilment of convergence criteria: sustainable public finances, with limits on deficit and debt; price stability; exchange-rate stability; and stable long-term interest rates. If the date of the third stage was not set by the end of 1997, it would begin in January 1999. The treaty also advanced the institutional and political agenda: it made the European Parliament a co-legislator on an equal footing with the Commission in several fields, extended qualified majority voting, strengthened social policy, and introduced two innovations of lasting importance — the principle of subsidiarity, a particular concern of the German Länder, and, at the instigation of Spain, a European citizenship that conferred rights upon the citizens of the member states without replacing their national citizenship.
The negotiation bore the marks of the central bargain between Paris and Bonn. For France, with the Commission and such countries as Belgium, Italy and Spain, it was essential to move quickly and fix a firm timetable. For Germany, and for Denmark and the Netherlands, it was essential first to create economic convergence. The compromise set stringent convergence criteria in exchange for the irreversible character of the move to a single currency and a concrete starting date. Against a resistant Mitterrand, Kohl pressed for greater powers for the European Parliament, needing to demonstrate to his domestic audience — above all to the Bundesbank and to the constitutional court — that the surrender of the mark was accompanied by democratic safeguards. Britain, deeply sceptical, obtained an opt-out that would not oblige it to move to the third stage; Denmark received a similar exemption.
Referendums and ratification
The ratification of the treaty proved almost its undoing, and exposed the gap that had opened between the governments and the peoples of Europe. Denmark and Ireland were the only states constitutionally obliged to hold referendums. The Danes voted first, on 2 June 1992, and to nearly everyone’s surprise rejected the treaty by a narrow majority of 50.7 to 49.3 per cent. Mitterrand, hoping to stage a dramatic show of support and with domestic motives of his own, then called a French referendum — a miscalculation. On 20 September 1992 the French approved the treaty by the embarrassingly small margin of 51.05 to 48.95 per cent. The near-disasters of Copenhagen and Paris emboldened the Eurosceptics, and in Britain the crisis of September 1992, which forced sterling out of the Exchange Rate Mechanism, added to the difficulty. Denmark voted a second time on 18 May 1993, after securing opt-outs and concessions, and approved the treaty; the Treaty on European Union entered into force on 1 November 1993. Against the widespread view that Maastricht was a response to the geopolitical revolution of 1989 — the locking-in of a reunited Germany, the alleged German monetary quid pro quo for unification — Moravcsik argues that the treaty is best explained as the culmination of converging national economic interests, the same commercial and economic forces that had produced the earlier negotiations. What the referendums made unmistakable was that the era of permissive consensus, in which the peoples of Europe had allowed their governments to integrate in silence, was at an end.

events/may-1958-crisis.title: The Crisis of May 1958
events/may-1958-crisis.content:
The Crisis of May 1958
The rising of Algiers
On 13 May 1958 Algiers rose against the Fourth Republic. The settler population of European origin and the army, exasperated by a war in Algeria they could neither win nor be allowed to abandon, seized the moment in a coup d’État in the city — committees of public safety were formed, the Government-General was seized, and the cry went up for the return of the man who alone seemed able to hold Algeria to France: General de Gaulle. The insurrection spread across Algeria and threatened the metropole; there were those who spoke of paratroops landing in Paris. The Fourth Republic, riven by the ministerial instability and the problème algérien that had paralysed it, could neither master the army nor settle the war. Within days the régime de Gaulle had condemned since Bayeux was in its death agony.
The investiture of the General
From Colombey, through the traversée du désert (crossing of the desert), de Gaulle let himself be called. He issued his readiness to assume the powers of the Republic, and on 1 June 1958 he was invested by the National Assembly — the same assembly of the Fourth Republic that had so often refused him — with full powers, the mandate to govern by decree and to draft a new constitution. The transfer of power from the old régime to the new was accomplished almost without resistance: the Republic, unable to save itself, delivered itself into the hands of the man who had foretold its failure. From the Palais d’Orsay and the Hôtel Matignon, then in the speech at Algiers itself, de Gaulle presented himself to the nation as the arbiter above the parties, ready to restore the state.
The fall of the Fourth Republic
The crisis of May 1958 brought the Fourth Republic to its end. The constitution of October 1946, drafted against de Gaulle’s Bayeux doctrine, had been tested and found wanting: it could not contain the army, could not end the Algerian war, could not govern. Its fall confirmed, in the gaullist reading, everything the General had said since 1946 about the régime of the parties. The investiture of June 1958 was the rupture — the transition from the Assembly-dominated Fourth Republic to the presidential Fifth Republic that de Gaulle had conceived twelve years earlier at Bayeux. The very date, 13 May, became a founding moment of the new régime, the day the old order gave way.
The new constitution
De Gaulle’s government drafted a new constitution through the summer of 1958, and in September he carried it to the country — the great public address from the place de la République in Paris, the journey to Madagascar, Dakar and Constantine with its programme of development for Algeria. The referendum of 28 September 1958 adopted the constitution by a large majority — 79.2% of Oui — with 15.06% abstentions in the metropole. On 21 December the college of grands électeurs elected de Gaulle President of the Republic, and on 8 January 1959 he was installed at the Élysée with Michel Debré as Prime Minister. The Fifth Republic had begun — the régime of the strong executive and the head of state as arbiter, the constitution of Bayeux at last realised in the crisis of May 1958.

events/may-1968.title: May 1968
events/may-1968.content:
May 1968
In the spring of 1968 the most powerful state the French had built in the twentieth century was shaken, in a matter of weeks, by a revolt that came not from the parties or the army but from the students and the workers of a society at the apogee of its prosperity. The crisis of May–June 1968 began as a university agitation and swelled into the greatest general strike of the century, a challenge to the very foundations of the régime that charles-de-gaulle had founded ten years earlier. For a moment it seemed that the fifth-republic might be swept away; in the end it survived, but the General who had founded it never recovered his old authority.
The student revolt
The movement was born in the universities, where the massification of higher education had crowded lecture halls beyond capacity and left a generation of students confronting a society that seemed to offer them only the ranks of the bureaucracy and the factory. In March 1968 a handful of protests at Nanterre, the new faculty in the Paris suburbs, spread to the Sorbonne and then to the streets. When the police entered the Latin Quarter in May, the barricades went up and Paris was convulsed by nights of street-fighting. The slogans painted on the walls — Changer la vie, the Rimbaud line diffused by Henri Lefebvre and the situationnistes — proclaimed a contestation of everything: the university, the family, the state, the consumer society. What had begun as a student affair became a soulèvement mondial de la jeunesse, a global rising of youth of which Paris was the epicentre.
The great strike
From the students the movement leapt to the workers. On 13 May the unions called a general strike in sympathy and in their own demands, and the strike that followed was the largest in the history of France — ten million workers on strike, the factories occupied, the country brought to a standstill. The working world, whose Trente Glorieuses prosperity had not delivered the social peace the régime had promised, joined the students in a common refusal. The traditional chronology that read the crisis only as a student affair was a simplification: the generalised revolt of May touched the whole of French society. The government of Georges Pompidou sought to negotiate a settlement, and at Grenelle, in the ministry of social affairs, the accords of the night of 27 May granted the workers substantial wage increases and union rights. But the Grenelle settlement was repudiated on the shop floor, and the strike continued.
The disappearance of 29 May
At the height of the crisis the state itself seemed to waver. On 29 May 1968 the General was, famously and mysteriously, absent from Paris — he had flown to the military headquarters at Baden-Baden, to see the commander of the French forces in Germany, in an episode whose meaning has been endlessly debated. For a day it was whispered that he had abandoned the régime, and the country held its breath. He returned to reassert his authority with a broadcast to the nation, dissolved the National Assembly, and called the country to a choice between the state and the disorder of the contestation. At the press conference of 7 June he spoke of the dissolution and of the participation he offered in place of the upheaval. The crisis of authority had passed; the appeal to the country was his answer.
The June elections
The elections that followed in June 1968 were a landslide for the gaullist order. The country, frightened by the spectacle of the barricades and the general strike, rallied to the régime and returned a massive majority for the supporters of the General — the greatest victory the Fifth Republic had yet seen. The great strike ended within weeks, and May 1968 was, on the surface, an unqualified defeat of the revolt: a month of upheaval closing in a crushing electoral victory for the state it had risen against. But the traces of 1968 were longer than the moment. The régime had survived, but aged; the General’s authority, though triumphant at the polls, was never quite the same. The questions of participation and of a society in ferment would return, and within a year de Gaulle would stake his presidency on a referendum and lose.
The legacy
May 1968 was both a rupture and the beginning of something new. It opened what historians have called the années 1968, a longer period of contestation — a galaxy of social, political and cultural movements that outlived the single crisis and reshaped French society. It struck the foundations of the Fifth Republic, which recovered its institutions but not its old confidence. For the régime the lesson was ambiguous: the strong state had survived the greatest challenge of the century, but the General who embodied it chose, in 1969, to test his authority again and fell. May 1968 stands in the history of the fifth-republic as the crisis that revealed how much of the old order the post-war prosperity had left untouched — and how far a generation of youth and workers was ready to go to change it.

events/messina-conference-1955.title: Messina Conference (1955)
events/messina-conference-1955.content:
Messina Conference (1955)
In June 1955 the six foreign ministers of the European Coal and Steel Community gathered at Messina, on the straits of Sicily, to decide the future of the enterprise they had begun at Paris five years earlier. The conference is remembered as the relaunch — the moment when European integration, which had seemed to collapse with the failure of the European Defence Community the year before, was set moving again upon a new, more practical course. The meeting of 1 to 3 June 1955 produced a declaration that, in Moravcsik’s phrase, found the thread: the thread that led within two years to the treaty-of-rome-1957 and the creation of the wider European Economic Community.
After the EDC failure
The path to Messina ran through the wreckage of an earlier, more ambitious project. In 1950 the same Six had set out to build a European Defence Community, a supranational army that was to have crowned the Coal and Steel Community with a military union. But the project, championed by the supranational enthusiasts and dreaded by the nationalists, was rejected by the French National Assembly in August 1954, and with it died the hopes of those who believed that the Coal and Steel Community would lead almost automatically to ever-deeper integration. The lesson was not lost on the federalists. If the attempt to leap to political and military union had failed, the road of economic integration lay open. Within a year the governments had turned back to that road, and it was in this spirit that the foreign ministers came to Messina.
The Spaak Committee and the road to Rome
The declaration issued at Messina charged the governments to study the creation of a general common market among the Six, free of internal tariffs, and a community for atomic energy. It was a programme far more ambitious than the sectoral method of the Coal and Steel Community — nothing less than the merger of the whole economies of the Six. To give it concrete form, the conference appointed a committee of government experts under the Belgian foreign minister Paul-Henri Spaak, with jean-monnet’s former collaborators among its leading figures, to draft the detailed proposals. The Spaak Committee met through 1955 and into 1956, and its report became the working paper of the intergovernmental conference that negotiated the Treaties of Rome through 1956 and 1957. Moravcsik, weighing why the customs-union option prevailed over the alternatives — the industrial free-trade area without agriculture or supranational institutions that many in the German and British governments preferred, or continued piecemeal liberalisation through the OEEC and GATT — reads the outcome as the product of commercial interest and asymmetrical interdependence rather than of federalist enthusiasm. The Cambridge history likewise opens its treaty history “from Messina and Rome”, treating the two as the twin foundation of the Community’s first decades. In the space of two years, the relaunch begun on the straits of Sicily had carried the Six from the failure of the Defence Community to the threshold of a common market that would unite them economically as they had never been united before.

events/mitterrand-election-1981.title: The Election of François Mitterrand, 10 May 1981
events/mitterrand-election-1981.content:
The Election of François Mitterrand, 10 May 1981
On the evening of 10 May 1981 France accomplished what the founders of the Fifth Republic had imagined impossible: the peaceful passage of power to the left, the first alternance in the history of the régime. François Mitterrand, the socialist candidate of the united left, defeated the incumbent Valéry Giscard d’Estaing in the second ballot of the presidential election. The event was at once the triumph of a patient political construction — the union of the left built over a decade — and the opening of a new epoch in French political life, one in which the institutions of 1958 proved able to change their masters without changing their nature.
The union of the left
The victory was the fruit of an alliance patiently assembled through the 1960s and 1970s. The Parti socialiste born of the congress of Épinay in 1971, under Mitterrand’s leadership, had taken up the slogan Changer la vie (change life) drawn from the poetry of Rimbaud, and had set itself the task of uniting the left around a common programme. That programme, the Programme commun de gouvernement, was signed with the Communist Party on 26 June 1972 — the formal alliance between the socialists and the communists, the two great parties of the French left, for the first time since the breakdown of the tripartisme of the late 1940s. It was a fragile and contested union, strained by the rivalry of the two parties and by the cold war that divided Europe, but it held long enough to carry the left to the threshold of power.
The campaign and the two ballots
Mitterrand had already carried the united left into the presidential election of 1974, where he had lost narrowly to Giscard d’Estaing. Through the 1970s the union waxed and waned, broken at moments by the communist leadership, restored by the logic of the common adversary. The campaign of 1981 was fought against the background of the mounting crisis — the unemployment and the consciousness of a durable economic turn that the Giscard presidency could not master. Mitterrand’s programme, his 110 propositions (one hundred and ten proposals), promised nationalisations, the restoration of purchasing power, and the transformation of society. On the first ballot of 26 April he came first; on the second ballot of 10 May he defeated Giscard d’Estaing.
The état de grâce
The aftermath was a season of extraordinary political exaltation — the état de grâce (state of grace) of a left that had waited a generation for power. The new President dissolved the Assembly and obtained a socialist majority in the legislative elections of June 1981, and the government of Pierre Mauroy set about the great reform programme that the Programme commun had promised: the nationalisations of the banks and major industries, the abolition of the death penalty, the rise of the minimum wage, the grands travaux that were to remake Paris. For a brief, luminous moment the left in power seemed to command the future. The état de grâce did not last — the tournant de la rigueur of 1983 would bring it to a close — but the election of 10 May 1981 itself marked the passage of the Fifth Republic into a new age, the age of alternance in which no party could any longer claim the régime as its own.

events/moro-kidnapping-1978.title: Moro Kidnapping 1978
events/moro-kidnapping-1978.content:
Moro Kidnapping 1978
On the morning of 16 March 1978, in Via Fani in Rome, a commando of the Brigate Rosse (Red Brigades) ambushed the car of Aldo Moro, the president of the Democrazia Cristiana and the architect of the compromesso storico (historic compromise). Moro’s escort was shot dead — five bodyguards killed in the street — and the most eminent politician of the Republic was dragged away, thrown into a car and carried off. He was held prisoner for fifty-four days in what his captors called a “people’s prison,” and on 9 May 1978 his body was found in the boot of a red Renault in Via Caetani, in the centre of Rome. The kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro was the supreme act of the anni di piombo (years of lead), the deepest wound inflicted on the Republic in its history, and an event that came to be called, in Gentiloni Silveri’s words, the funerale della Repubblica (funeral of the Republic).
The blow at the historic compromise
The timing of the attack was not an accident. On that very day the Italian parliament was to vote on the formation of a new government — a Christian Democrat cabinet under Giulio Andreotti with the participation, for the first time, of the Partito Comunista Italiano. The kidnapping struck precisely at the compromesso storico: the project, championed by Moro himself and by the Communist secretary Enrico Berlinguer, of a collaboration between the two great popular parties to defend the Republic against terrorism and subversion. The Red Brigades had every reason to prevent that collaboration, which would have united the state’s strongest forces against them, and the kidnapping was understood from the first as an attack not merely on a man but on the political project that Moro embodied. The vote was postponed; the government was formed, but the historic compromise was never to recover.
The days of captivity and the hard line
During the fifty-four days that followed, the Red Brigades held Moro in a “people’s prison,” a hideout in Rome, and subjected the Republic to a prolonged ordeal. They issued photographs of their prisoner and released a series of letters written by Moro himself — to his family, to his party, to the political leaders of the country — in which he appealed for a negotiated solution, argued that his life might be saved by bargaining, and seemed, to many, to be pleading for his survival against the firmness of his own side. The letters threw the country into a crisis of conscience, for they set Moro’s own appeal for a negotiated solution against the principle, advanced by the state, that a democracy must not bargain with terrorists.
The state’s response was the linea della fermezza (hard line), the refusal to negotiate. Led by the government of Andreotti — the very man Moro was seeking to bring to the head of a wider majority — and supported by the Communist party, the Italian state held firm, declining to exchange the captured Red Brigaders for whom the kidnappers demanded Moro’s release. The hard line was a deliberate and contested choice: its defenders argued that to yield would be to open the Republic to blackmail and to condemn others to the same fate; its critics, then and since, argued that a state that refused even to attempt to save the life of its most eminent citizen had betrayed its first duty. The controversy over the decision, and over the conduct of the state during those weeks, was to divide Italians for decades.
The murder and its aftermath
On 9 May 1978, after holding his body in the boot of a car for days, the Red Brigades abandoned Moro’s corpse in Via Caetani, in Rome, at a point deliberately chosen — halfway between the headquarters of the Christian Democrats and those of the Communist Party, the two parties of the compromised historic compromise. He had been killed, shot multiple times, the day before. The Republic had failed to save him.
The murder produced an outpouring of grief and of national unity: a vast state funeral, the declaration of a day of mourning, and the momentary closing of the ranks of the parties he had tried to unite. But it also left the Republic with an open wound. The compromesso storico died with Moro, and the hope of bringing the Communists into the government — and of reforming the Republic by widening its majority — was lost. For Gentiloni Silveri the event was the funerale della Repubblica in a double sense: it was the death of a statesman, and it was the beginning of the end of the old Republic itself, the moment from which the postwar political order, and the certainties of the Cold War that sustained it, began their long decline toward the crisis of Tangentopoli. The mysteries of the case — what was negotiated, what was known, what might have been done — remained unresolved, and Moro’s name hung over Italian politics as a question no government has ever fully answered.

events/new-ostpolitik-1969-73.title: The Neue Ostpolitik (1969–1973)
events/new-ostpolitik-1969-73.content:
The Neue Ostpolitik (1969–1973)
When the social-liberal coalition came to power in October 1969, the Federal Republic stood before an accumulation of diplomatic walls far higher than the one then rising through the heart of Berlin. The West treaties that konrad-adenauer had concluded a decade and a half earlier had anchored Bonn firmly in the Atlantic and in the European Community, but they had left it almost wholly isolated before the East. From the second half of the 1950s the danger of foreign-policy isolation had returned again and again to German politics — the threat that the Soviet Union and her allies would deal over the heads of the Germans, and that the claim to represent all of Germany, the Alleinvertretungsanspruch (sole-representation claim), would leave the republic frozen out of any settlement in Europe. It was against this wall that the new Chancellor willy-brandt and his Foreign Minister Walter Scheel launched the policy that Germans came to call the neue Ostpolitik, the new Eastern policy.
The idea had been stirring for years. It had been Egon Bahr, Brandt’s closest adviser, who in a speech of July 1963 at the Evangelical Academy of Tutzing had given the strategy its watchword — Wandel durch Annäherung, change through rapprochement. Where the old policy had insisted that nothing could be done with the East until the national question was settled, Bahr and Brandt argued the reverse: only by dealing with the East as it actually existed could the Federal Republic ever hope to change it, and only by accepting the reality of division could the nation’s unity be preserved. The insight had matured in the years of the Grand Coalition, when Brandt, as Foreign Minister, had already begun to test the ground against the resistance of an older school of German diplomacy. It was the policy’s central paradox, and its wager: that by recognising the existence of the two German states, the Federal Republic would keep alive the unity of the nation.
The first and greatest obstacle was the Soviet Union. Negotiations with Moscow opened in the winter after the change of government, and they proved hard. The great difficulty of the Moscow talks was the linkage the Soviets insisted upon — the acceptance of the Oder–Neisse line as the western frontier of Poland and the renunciation of force. For months the two sides wrestled over the wording that would reconcile the German position — that only a final peace treaty could fix the frontiers — with the Soviet demand for their irrevocable recognition now. At length agreement was reached. On 12 August 1970, Brandt and Scheel signed the Moscow Treaty (Moskauer Vertrag) in the Kremlin, in which the two states renounced the use of force and the Federal Republic declared its respect for the territorial integrity of all European states within their existing frontiers, including the Oder–Neisse line and the border between the Federal Republic and the German Democratic Republic.
The second Eastern treaty concerned Poland. In the Federal Republic nothing divided opinion so deeply as the Polish frontier, which carried within it the memory of the expulsion of millions of Germans and the grief of the Vertriebene (expellees). A poll taken before the negotiations still showed a large minority of Germans refusing to accept the Oder–Neisse line as final. It was against this resistance that Brandt and Scheel signed the Warsaw Treaty (Warschauer Vertrag) in the Polish capital on 7 December 1970, in which both sides confirmed that the Oder–Neisse line formed the western state frontier of the People’s Republic of Poland, affirmed the Unverletzlichkeit (inviolability) of their existing frontiers now and in the future, and declared that they advanced no territorial claims against one another. But the Warsaw Treaty was remembered above all for a gesture that no clause could have anticipated. After laying a wreath at the memorial to the fallen and murdered Jews, the Chancellor knelt before the monument to the victims of the Warsaw Ghetto uprising of spring 1943. The image went round the world. Right of centre it was received as exaggerated, even as a form of German self-humiliation; left of centre it drew a broad wave of respect and admiration for a chancellor who took upon himself a guilt that was not his own. Brandt himself later wrote that he had planned nothing, but had felt that the Besonderheit (particularity) of the remembrance had to be given expression — “at the abyss of German history and under the burden of the millions of murdered, I did what human beings do when speech fails.”
The third treaty concerned Berlin and fell within the competence of the Four Powers. The ambassadors of the three Western powers and of the Soviet Union opened their negotiations on 26 March 1970 in the building of the former Allied Control Council, and for a long time questions of status blocked every advance. Only in the spring of 1971 did the four ambassadors agree on an “agree to disagree”, and on 3 June 1972 the Four-Power Agreement on Berlin was signed. Its terms eased access to West Berlin, secured the ties of the city to the Federal Republic, and removed the standing threat that had hung over the divided metropolis since the building of the Wall. Of the three Eastern treaties, the Moscow and the Warsaw treaties depended for their coming into force on a satisfactory Berlin regulation; with the Berlin Agreement that condition was at last met.
The completion of the design came with the treaty to the East with which the Federal Republic had the most conflicted relationship of all — the treaty with the other German state. Negotiations between the state secretaries Egon Bahr and Michael Kohl had run since June 1972, and only after the Soviet party leader Leonid Brezhnev received Bahr in the Kremlin on 10 October did the German Democratic Republic show itself more yielding on the disputed points. On 6 November the negotiations were concluded; on 8 November the two secretaries of state initialled the document in Bonn. On 21 December 1972 the Grundvertrag, the Basic Treaty between the Federal Republic and the German Democratic Republic, was signed — the grundvertrag-1972 that at once embodied and defied the German question.
The Eastern treaties did not pass without a desperate parliamentary struggle. In the course of 1972 a succession of deputies — the FDP members Erich Mende, Heinz Starke, Siegfried Zoglmann, the Social Democrat Herbert Hupka and others — crossed to the opposition, until the coalition’s majority was gone and two votes decided the fate of the treaties and of the government. On 27 April 1972 Rainer Barzel moved the first constructive vote of no confidence (konstruktives Misstrauensvotum) in the history of the republic. Most observers, including Vice-Chancellor Scheel, expected the government to fall. Barzel received 247 votes — two short of the number needed. Two or three deputies of the CDU/CSU withheld their votes, and for years the shadows of the East German secret service hung over the mystery of how the government had been saved. Brandt survived, and staked his authority on the treaties. The Bundestag election of 19 November 1972, advanced to resolve the deadlock, became a plebiscite on the Ostpolitik — and delivered the greatest triumph of Brandt’s life. The SPD emerged as the largest party in the Bundestag for the first time since 1949, and Brandt was re-elected Chancellor on 14 December.
For the whole of Europe the neue Ostpolitik changed the climate. By conducting a policy of active détente itself, the Federal Republic became, in a real sense, more “Western” than before the change of government of 1969 — it differed less from its Western allies because it no longer stood alone and isolated before the East. The treaties made the republic a normal Western state to the extent that was possible, overcoming what the political scientist Richard Löwenthal was to call the Sonderkonflikt (special conflict) of the Federal Republic with the Soviet Union and the Soviet bloc. Brandt’s own biography — the lifelong opponent of Hitler, the Mayor of Berlin, the man with a profile at once national and Western — lent the policy a credibility no one else could have given it. In the recognition of the two German states the government claimed to serve the unity of the nation; and the claims of the 1973 government declaration placed the preservation of peace even above the question of the nation. It was the deepest transformation of the Federal Republic’s place in the world since konrad-adenauer’s Western integration, and its architect was the most significant chancellor since Adenauer himself. See ostpolitik and grundvertrag-1972.

events/perestroika-1985-91.title: Perestroika (1985-1991)
events/perestroika-1985-91.content:
Perestroika (1985-1991)
Perestroika — перестройка (perestroika, ‘restructuring’) — was the name given to the attempt, launched by mikhail-gorbachev after he became General Secretary of the CPSU in March 1985, to renew and reform the Soviet system from within. It was, in its own early terms, a programme to accelerate the country’s development and to overcome the decades of застой (zastoy, stagnation) that had settled over the state under the aged Brezhnev leadership. Its declared purpose was to strengthen socialism, to make the planned economy work, to restore the confidence of the people in a party that had grown complacent. It ended, within six years, in the dissolution of the Soviet Union itself — a gap between intention and outcome so vast that the very word perestroika has come to stand for the unforeseen consequences of reform, and for the paradox that a system perceived by its citizens as eternal proved, in the judgement of those who lived through it, to be capable of collapsing almost overnight.
From uskorenie to perestroika
The reform began as acceleration, not transformation. Gorbachev’s first watchword was ускорение (uskorenie, ‘acceleration’) — the quickening of economic and social development through harder work and more honest management within the existing structure. He carried this message to Leningrad in May 1985 and to the XXVII Party Congress in 1986, launched the dramatic campaign against drunkenness, and swept out the old guard of the Politburo for a younger team. But the economy of the late Soviet Union could not be made to accelerate; the remedies administered within the old frames had no purchase on a system whose resources were exhausted and whose structure resisted improvement. Pikhoya’s account of these years — “acceleration, where to?” he titles his first sketch — shows the leadership groping from the failure of the first campaign toward a deeper reform. Within a year or two the word on the party’s lips had changed: not uskorenie but perestroika, a restructuring of the system itself, and with it гласность (glasnost, ‘openness’), the demand for truth and public discussion. The reform, in Pikhoya’s phrase, passed the point of no return.
The reforms and their contradictions
The substance of perestroika unfolded in the economy, in the political system, and in the culture of the country at once. In the economy, Gorbachev sought to give enterprises more independence, to introduce elements of self-accounting and cooperatives, and to loosen the grip of the central plan — a course that produced scarcity, queues and inflation rather than abundance, and that the authorities themselves never resolved into a coherent programme. The abortive “500 Days” programme for a market transition, embraced and then dropped, became a symbol of the improvisation. In the political system the reform was more radical still: the creation of the Congress of People’s Deputies in 1989, the first contested elections since the revolution, the debate and confrontation carried by television into every home, the abolition of the party’s constitutional monopoly of power in 1990 and the creation of the presidency of the USSR. Glasnost dissolved the taboos of the whole Soviet era — the history of the system was reopened, its crimes confessed, its heroes questioned — and released energies the party could not control. Yurchak, the anthropologist of the last Soviet generation, reads these years as the destruction from within of the party’s authoritative discourse: the very forms of Soviet speech and belief, faithfully reproduced for two generations, had emptied of meaning, so that when the reform let them be tested they collapsed, and with them the legitimacy of the CPSU. The reform of the system, Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook concludes, became the reform of the political system and then the abandonment of the old one altogether.
The unintended consequences
What perestroika intended to save, it instead destroyed. The economic failure produced shortages and disillusion; glasnost opened a space in which the suppressed nationality question — Nagorny Karabakh, the Baltic states, the republics’ cry of “вплоть до выхода” (vplot do vykhoda, ‘up to secession’) — burst into open politics; the democratisation that Gorbachev had sought to manage became a democratisation no one could manage; and the rise of the Russian factor under boris-yeltsin, the sovereignty of the RSFSR, the referendum of March 1991 and the failure of the Novo-Ogaryovo negotiations to hold the union together, all swept the reformer along toward an end he had never imagined. The August putsch of 1991 and the Belovezhskaya accords of December brought the sequence to its close: the union that perestroika had meant to renew was dissolved, and with it the whole Soviet system. Yurchak’s title captures the paradox of the age: это было навсегда, пока не кончилось — “everything was forever, until it was no more.” The system that had seemed eternal to those who lived inside it, that had reproduced itself for two generations, proved to be held together by its own fixed forms of speech and belief — and once perestroika began to dismantle those forms from within, the eternity proved to have been an illusion. The story of perestroika is thus the story of dissolution-ussr-1991 and of mikhail-gorbachev himself, and the shadow of its failure fell across the Russia of vladimir-putin and the whole last-soviet-generation that watched its certainties end.

events/postwar-reconstruction-1945-53.title: Postwar Reconstruction of the USSR (1945–1953)
events/postwar-reconstruction-1945-53.content:
Postwar Reconstruction of the USSR (1945–1953)
The Soviet Union emerged from the Great Patriotic War a victor and a ruin. Some twenty-six or twenty-seven million of its people had perished; more than seventeen hundred towns and seventy thousand villages lay in rubble; the industry of the western regions, of Ukraine and Belorussia, had been carried off or destroyed; and tens of millions of survivors had been left homeless, living in cellars and dugouts. The task that faced the country in 1945 was to rebuild from these ashes while the new confrontation with the West, the kholodnaya voina (the cold war), demanded at the same moment the forging of heavy industry and armaments. The years 1945 to 1953 were the years of the fourth five-year plan and of the passage from the mobilisation of war to the austerity of peace — an epoch of furious labour and, in its opening, of renewed hunger.
The return to peaceful construction
The transition from war to peace began at once. The army was demobilised; more than five million Soviet citizens were repatriated from the labour of the German occupation; the state and party organs were rebuilt on a peacetime footing. In the summer of 1945 holidays were restored, obligatory overtime abolished and the eight-hour working day returned. In 1946 the Sovnarkom (the Council of People’s Commissars) was renamed the Council of Ministers and the narkomaty (commissariats) became ministries, as the whole apparatus of war industry turned to civilian production: the ministries of munitions and tank production were recast as ministries of instrument-building and of transport and agricultural machinery. From 1946 the GAZ-51 truck and the celebrated GAZ M-20 “Pobeda” (Victory) motor-car went into series production. The restoration of cities began almost as soon as they were freed — fifteen towns, among them Smolensk, Rostov-on-Don, Sevastopol, Voronezh and Novgorod, were designated for priority rebuilding, and a special administration was created for the raising of the “Volga bastion” of Stalingrad, where students and demobilised soldiers worked beside one another.
The fourth five-year plan
In March 1946 the fourth five-year plan, the chetviortaya pyatiletka, was adopted for 1946–1950, fixing the aim of raising industrial output to 138 percent of the prewar level. Stalin defined its tasks in the formula the textbooks would repeat: to restore the ruined regions, to restore the prewar level of industry and agriculture, and then to surpass it. The plan was served by an extraordinary labour enthusiasm — the movement of the “speedy workers,” the skorostniki, who fulfilled several daily norms at once — and financed by the regular issue of state loan bonds and, on the initiative of the head of Gosplan Nikolai Voznesensky, the re-introduction of piece-rate wages. Millions of peasants moved to the towns and the industrial sites; hundreds of thousands of prisoners of war — Germans, Hungarians, Romanians, Japanese — laboured on the rebuilding of what their armies had destroyed, and equipment stripped from the German factories of the Soviet zone of occupation came in as reparations. The speed of recovery outstripped the plan: already in 1947 the main kinds of production regained the level of 1940, and by 1950 the volume of industrial production had exceeded the prewar level by seventy per cent. More than six thousand large enterprises were restored or built anew, the Volga–Don canal was completed, and new oil and gas fields were opened in the Urals.
The famine of 1946–1947
The opening years of reconstruction were darkened by catastrophe. The drought and harvest failure of 1946 brought famine to the western regions of the country, to the Volga and the Central Black Earth zone — golod (hunger) on a scale that the authorities neither admitted nor wholly concealed. The countryside was the hardest hit; in the villages the position was desperate, while the great cities were better supplied. Until 1947 the basic foodstuffs were distributed by ration cards, po kartochkam, and the standard of living of ordinary people, millions of widows working the factories and the fields in men’s places, remained very low. Demobilised soldiers went on wearing their military greatcoats and tunics for want of civilian clothing. Yet the memory of the war years made the austerity seem, to most, an improvement; the worst, it was felt, lay behind, and the country looked forward with a genuine, if strained, optimism. The rationing system was finally abolished in 1947, accompanied by a currency reform, and the following years brought a gradual rise in real incomes, pensions and the state’s social payments.
The results of the era
By the death of Stalin in March 1953 the reconstruction was substantially complete. The heavy industry had been rebuilt and surpassed; the prewar level of the economy had been exceeded; and the way had been laid for the industrial expansion of the 1950s. The price had been paid in the continued priority of heavy industry over consumption, in the subordination of agriculture to the demands of the state, and in the austerity of a people asked, once again, to endure for the sake of the future. The reconstruction of 1945–1953 was the great unrecorded effort that turned the ruined homeland of 1945 into the industrial power that would confront the West across the whole of the Cold War — the foundation upon which the Soviet Union of the 1950s and beyond was built.

events/prague-spring-1968.title: The Prague Spring and the Invasion of Czechoslovakia (1968)
events/prague-spring-1968.content:
The Prague Spring and the Invasion of Czechoslovakia (1968)
In the spring of 1968 the most liberal of the people’s democracies set out to give socialism “a human face”, and by the end of the summer the tanks of the Warsaw Treaty had entered Prague to put an end to the experiment. The Czechoslovak reform movement of Alexander Dubček — the Pražská jaro, the Prague Spring — was the boldest attempt within the socialist commonwealth to reconcile the party and the people, to build a socialism of democracy and freedom, and it was brought down by the armed intervention of the Soviet Union and its allies in August 1968. The event divided the communist world, hardened the Cold War front in Europe, and gave the age its most fateful doctrine: the right of the socialist community to defend its achievements — the principle the West was to call the Brezhnev Doctrine.
Socialism with a human face
Czechoslovakia had entered the 1960s in a deep crisis. The economy had stagnated under the old Stalinist leadership of Antonín Novotný, the country’s Stalinist past had never been confronted as it had in the USSR after the XX Congress, and the discontent of the writers and intellectuals had grown into a demand for reform. In January 1968 the party, alarmed and self-critical, elected Alexander Dubček First Secretary in place of Novotný. What followed was the most open and daring reform programme the bloc had ever seen. The party adopted a Action Programme that promised the democratisation of the party and the state, freedom of speech and of the press, the rights of the nationalities, and the revival of a distinctive Czechoslovak socialism — the celebrated project of socialism s lidskou tváří, socialism with a human face. The censorship fell, the assemblies and clubs of the “Spring” sprang up everywhere, and the people of Prague, in the streets and squares, enjoyed a freedom unknown in the East since the war. For the leaders in Moscow and in the other socialist capitals, watching from the fraternal countries, the experiment was a mortal danger: a socialism that admitted criticism and pluralism, if it succeeded, would threaten the order of every party in the bloc.
The intervention
The reform could not be contained within Czechoslovakia. The Soviet leadership and its allies, above all the German Democratic Republic and Poland, watched the Prague Spring with mounting alarm, denouncing it as a threat to the socialist commonwealth and the product of counter-revolutionary forces. Dubček was summoned again and again to conferences with the fraternal leaders, and assured the worried parties of the loyalty of Czechoslovakia to the Warsaw Treaty; but no assurance could satisfy Moscow, which came to the conclusion that the reformist leadership, whatever its professions, was leading the country out of the socialist camp. On the night of 20–21 August 1968, while Czechoslovakia lay undefended, the armies of the Soviet Union, Poland, the GDR, Hungary and Bulgaria — the forces of the Warsaw Treaty — invaded the country in overwhelming strength. The Czechoslovak army, ordered by its own government not to resist, did not fight; the people of Prague, incredulous and unarmed, met the tanks of the invaders with banners, with jeers and with passive resistance. Dubček and the other leaders were seized and carried to Moscow, and the country was brought under the control of a restored leadership. The Prague Spring was over; the invasion of 21 August 1968 is remembered in Czechoslovakia, and remembered around the world, as the day the tanks crushed the hopes of a people.
The doctrine
The intervention of 1968 was unprecedented and never openly avowed in the language of empire. In its wake the Soviet leadership formulated the doctrine of the limited sovereignty of the socialist states: that the interests of the socialist commonwealth as a whole, and the cause of socialism and peace, took precedence over the internal affairs of any single socialist country, and that no fraternal party might be suffered to carry its country out of the community. The Western world gave this principle its name — the Brezhnev Doctrine — and read in it the declaration that the borders of the bloc were closed, that the gains of socialism were irreversible, and that the Soviet Union would intervene wherever the order of the bloc was threatened. The immediate effect was the restoration of orthodoxy in Prague: the reforms were reversed, the experiment of “socialism with a human face” was buried, and Czechoslovakia settled, under Gustav Husák, into the grey normalization of the 1970s. The wider effect was to confirm the permanence of the division of Europe. The détente that followed 1968 unfolded across an Iron Curtain that had been shown, in the most unmistakable way, to be policed by force; and the memory of August 1968, repressed in Czechoslovakia, was to survive to reappear in the revolutions of 1989, when the peoples of the bloc finally did what the tanks of 1968 had been sent to prevent. Even the German Democratic Republic, whose own party had been among the loudest in demanding the intervention, was to discover that the doctrine that held the bloc together could be turned against any of its members in turn.

events/psoe-victory-1982.title: The PSOE Victory of October 1982
events/psoe-victory-1982.content:
The PSOE Victory of October 1982
On 28 October 1982 the Spanish left, led by felipe-gonzalez, won the general election by a landslide, and the country passed for the first time into the hands of the party that had been its principal opposition to the dictatorship. The result was a plebiscite for the democracy. It was the political end of the Transition, the moment when the party that had held the protagonist role in the democratic settlement — the centrist Union of the Democratic Centre of adolfo-suarez — not only lost power but disappeared, replaced, and the transfer of power to the former opposition sealed the consolidation of the regime.
The end of the Transition
Tusell was precise about the date. Institutionally the Transition had ended with the constitution-1978 in December 1978; politically, it ended with October 1982, for three reasons. First, the political group that had been the protagonist of the whole process not only lost power but was swept from the political stage altogether. Second, the military conspiracy had been defeated at 23-f-coup-1981 and dissatisfaction with democracy had fallen. Third, the results themselves became a plebiscite consolidating the regime: an overwhelming majority of Spaniards had voted for the two great parties of the settled democratic order, and the age of transition gave way to the age of consolidated, ordinary government.
The agony of the centrists
The victory was made possible by the self-destruction of the centre. The Union of the Democratic Centre, which had played a transcendental role in the Transition, decomposed through 1981 and 1982, its decline parallel to the fall of Calvo-Sotelo’s government and unintelligible without it. After Suárez’s resignation from the party presidency, the sterile congress at Palma de Mallorca in January 1981 had failed to heal it; the 23-F had only postponed its internal war; the divorce law and the “plataforma moderada” of some forty centrist deputies split its ranks; and in the Galician elections of October 1981 the right-wing Alianza Popular of manuel-fraga overtook it for the first time. The agony of the centrists opened the opportunity for the PSOE, the second electoral force, as the logical government alternative. It was a party that had prepared itself to govern through the reformation of its two 1979 congresses — from radical opposition positions to the reformism that could connect with majority Spanish society — and it swept into the vacuum.
The landslide
The scale of the victory was overwhelming. González carried the PSOE to power with a comfortable parliamentary majority, and the right, for all its hopes, could not match it. The arrival of the Socialists met genuine yearnings for governmental stability after the spectacle of the collapsing centre, and answered a very negative judgment of the UCD. At thirty-one the new government — González, forty years old, at its head — took office as the representative of a new political generation, the generation that had been the anti-Franco opposition and now became the state. Involucionist dangers disappeared in the Socialist stage; a peculiar political system settled, with clearly positive and more ambivalent aspects; and democratic legitimacy, already consolidated by 23-F, was confirmed by the peaceful transfer of power.
The first Socialist government
The victory opened the long socialist era of 1982 to 1996. González’s first government set the programme that was to mark the age: the modernisation of the Spanish economy, the development of the state of the autonomies under Title VIII, and the completion of European integration. Democratisation had always been equated with Europeanisation, with homologation with the Western world, and the great external project of the socialist governments was Spain’s entry into the European Economic Community, accomplished in 1986 — the end of the isolation that the Transition had only begun to break. The election of October 1982, in which the party of the anti-Franco opposition took power by an overwhelming vote and received it peacefully, was the last great act of the Transition and the first great act of the democracy that had been its object.

events/putin-accession-2000.title: Putin's Accession to Power (1999–2000)
events/putin-accession-2000.content:
Putin’s Accession to Power (1999–2000)
The transfer of power from boris-yeltsin to vladimir-putin was the first peaceful and constitutional succession in the history of the Russian state, and it was arranged with care by a president who had long known that he must find an heir. Yeltsin, ageing and ailing, had spent the years after the russian-default-1998 searching for a successor who would guarantee that the changes of the nineties would not be undone — and who would, not incidentally, guarantee the safety of Yeltsin himself and his family. The operation came to be called, in the political shorthand of the period, the “heir operation” (operatsiya «naslednik», операция «наследник»). It brought to the threshold of supreme power a man almost unknown to the country, a career officer of the security service who had entered the Moscow government only in the late nineties.
The appointment of the heir
The decisive appointment came in the crisis of the Caucasus. On 9 August 1999, as the second Chechen war was breaking out and the failure of the Khasavyurt accords of 1996 had become evident, Yeltsin proposed to the State Duma that Vladimir Putin — until then the director of the Federal Security Service — be confirmed as Chairman of the Government. The historian Pikhoya notes that Yeltsin had earlier set up one premier, Sergei Stepashin, to replace a popular one, Yevgeny Primakov, and that the possibility of Stepashin in turn giving way to Putin was already in the air. The new Caucasian crisis, the spread of Wahhabism into Dagestan and the sharp worsening of the situation on the North Caucasus, accelerated the succession. Putin took the war upon himself, and through the whole second half of 1999 his popularity rose without interruption.
The Duma election of December 1999
The succession was consolidated in the elections to the State Duma held on 19 December 1999 — the third elections under the Constitution of 1993. The main contender for a majority, and the principal rival for the presidency, was Yevgeny Primakov in alliance with the mayor of Moscow, Yuri Luzhkov, their bloc “Fatherland–All Russia” (Отечество — Вся Россия) openly proposing to revise the political inheritance of Yeltsin. Against them stood the bloc “Unity” (Единство), created with the direct participation of the presidential administration, whose informal leader was the premier, Putin. The contest was not merely one of programmes but a struggle of two political generations — the old leaders grown weary and hated against the young man who promised order. The voters chose the new. The Communists won 24.29 percent and Unity 23.32 percent; Fatherland–All Russia took 13.33 percent. The outcome was even more favourable to Unity than the figures suggested, for it soon became the “party of power”, merging with its recent rival Fatherland–All Russia to command an absolute majority in the chamber. For the first time since 1993, the State Duma was loyal to the government.
The resignation of 31 December 1999
With the parliament secured, Yeltsin executed the last and boldest step of his presidency. On 31 December 1999 he came to the Kremlin in the morning, summoned the Chairman of the Government, and at noon appeared before the television cameras that had been prepared for the recording of his traditional New Year address. He told the country that he was leaving — “I am leaving. I have done all I could. A new generation is coming to replace me, a generation of those who can do more and better.” He asked forgiveness of the citizens of Russia for the hopes that had not been fulfilled, and he signed the decree resigning the presidency and naming the Chairman of the Government, Vladimir Putin, acting President. The transfer had been carefully thought through and, in the judgement of Pikhoya, brilliantly executed. The preemstvennost’ vlasti, the continuity of power, was secured.
The presidential election of March 2000
As acting President, Putin went to the country. On 26 March 2000 he was elected President of the Russian Federation already in the first round of voting — the peaceful, constitutional transfer of power that Yeltsin had set out to achieve. On taking the oath Putin declared: “We have proved that Russia is becoming a modern democratic state. The peaceful succession of power is the most important element of the political stability about which we dreamed, towards which we strove, which we achieved.” The country received him with relief. Sociologists of the Russian Academy of State Service found that in November 1999, before the election, 54.3 percent of those asked trusted the still-future president; by May 2000, 64.1 percent expressed a favourable opinion of him. He was trusted, the sociologists concluded, as a man capable of stopping the destructive processes of the disintegration of the state — trusted, in effect, before he had acted, in a mass repudiation of the Yeltsin years and a yearning for a leader who stood for the state itself. The accession was complete. A new man held the Kremlin, and the building of the vertical-of-power — the restoration of the state’s control over its own country — was about to begin.
