events/russian-constitutional-crisis-199.title: Russian Constitutional Crisis (1993)
events/russian-constitutional-crisis-199.content:
Russian Constitutional Crisis (1993)
The new Russia began its independent life in a state of civil war fought without armies. In the two years after dissolution-ussr-1991 the authority of the state was divided between two powers that each claimed to embody it — the elected President boris-yeltsin and the Съезд народных депутатов (S”yezd narodnykh deputatov, the Congress of People’s Deputies) with its standing organ, the Supreme Soviet, the institutions of the old Soviet power that the Russian parliament had inherited. For the whole of 1992 and 1993 the country was governed in a condition of dual power, a двоевластие (dvoyevlastiye) recalling the standoff between the Provisional Government and the Soviets in 1917. The conflict between the President and the Soviet power, as Pikhoya frames it, was a question of which of the two would defeat the other — президент и советская власть: кто кого? — and it was resolved only in October 1993, when the army turned its guns on the parliament building in Moscow, and then in December, when a new constitution created a strong presidency and buried the Soviet form of power for good.
The two powers and the road to conflict
The constitutional order of the Russian Federation rested on a constitution inherited from the Soviet era and a Congress of People’s Deputies that had been elected in 1990, at the height of the struggle against the Union centre. After 1991 the two heads of this awkward body — the President, armed with the legitimacy of the first popular election in Russian history, and the Congress, which claimed to be the supreme and sovereign organ of power — turned against one another. The economic shock that accompanied the freeing of prices and the first years of privatisation, the шоковая терапия (shokovaya terapiya, ‘shock therapy’) of the market reforms, gave the parliamentary majority its cause: the Congress refused to endorse the course of the government and the President and sought instead to take control of the economy and the state itself. Pikhoya, who as chief state archivist had presided over the making of the very documents of the new state, traces the conflict from the two powers’ paths into collision — the CPSU case, the growing rift over the course of reform, and the enduring question of how to adopt the Constitution, for each power wished to write a fundamental law that would preserve itself.
The VII Congress and the skirmishes of 1992-1993
The conflict came into the open at the VII Congress of People’s Deputies in December 1992. The President demanded extraordinary powers to carry through his reforms; the Congress refused and moved to strip him of authority, forcing the replacement of the reformist government of Yegor Gaidar by a premier more acceptable to the deputies, Viktor Chernomyrdin. It was the first skirmish, the first open test of strength, and neither side accepted the verdict. Through 1993 the confrontation hardened. The Congress and the Supreme Soviet, under its chairman Ruslan Khasbulatov and the Vice-President Aleksandr Rutskoy, sought to rein in the President, to control the budget, the security organs and the conduct of policy; the President, for his part, resolved to break the Soviet power that he judged an obstacle to reform. Twice the deputies moved toward the removal of the President, the abortive impeachment of the spring of 1993, and the confrontation played out against the failure to agree on a new constitution. The old law, Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook observes, gave the Congress the right to decide the fate of the constitution and of the President himself — a power the deputies were increasingly willing to use.
Decree 1400 and the last Congress
On the evening of 21 September 1993 the President broke the deadlock by an act of sovereign will. By Decree No. 1400 he dissolved the Congress of People’s Deputies and the Supreme Soviet, announced elections to a new parliament, the Federal Assembly, and suspended the operation of the old constitutional order. The constitutional court pronounced the decree unlawful, and the deputies refused to submit. The Congress gathered in the White House, the seat of the Russian parliament on the banks of the Moscow river, and there, in defiance of the President’s decree, it proclaimed its authority to continue and declared the President deposed, naming the Vice-President Rutskoy in his place. For the first days of October the two governments confronted one another in the heart of Moscow, the President’s forces besieging the White House where the deputies, barricaded and increasingly desperate, were joined by armed volunteers — the третья сила (tret’ya sila, ‘third force’) of the radical opposition that Pikhoya describes. On 3 October the crowd that had rallied to the parliament broke out, marching on the Ostankino television tower and clashing with troops in the streets. The attempt to take the capital by force gave the President the pretext and the resolve to end the matter. On the morning of 4 October 1993 the army, at the President’s order, stormed the White House, shelling the parliament building with tanks until its defenders surrendered. The building that had been the cradle of Russian resistance in the august-putsch-1991 was now blackened and bloodied by the fire of the Russian state itself. Scores were killed in the storming; Pikhoya records the bloodshed of those days without embellishment — the кровь (krov’, ‘blood’) that sealed the victory of one power over the other.
The new Constitution and the reordering of the state
The October crisis was followed by a reordering of the institutions of power on the President’s terms. In December 1993 elections were held for the new Federal Assembly — the two chambers of the Совет Федерации (Sovet Federatsii, Federation Council) and the Государственная дума (Gosudarstvennaya duma, State Duma) — and simultaneously a referendum was held on a new constitution drafted under the President’s aegis. The Constitution of the Russian Federation, adopted by popular vote on 12 December 1993, created a powerful executive presidency, the strongest institution in the new state, and swept away the Soviet system of soviets with its sovereign congresses. The victory of the President was complete: the Soviet power, the form that had given the country its name for seventy-five years, was abolished, and in its place stood a constitution and a parliament of the President’s making. Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook treats the adoption of the constitution as the definitive settlement of the constitutional crisis, the moment when the political development of the Russian Federation at last found its institutional form. The вертикаль власти (vertikal’ vlasti, ‘vertical of power’) that vladimir-putin was to build in the next decade, and that came to define the Russia of the twenty-first century, had its foundation in the strong presidency created in the blood of October 1993 — a state that had chosen order and executive authority over the unstable sovereignty of the soviets.

events/russian-default-1998.title: Russian Financial Crisis (1998)
events/russian-default-1998.content:
Russian Financial Crisis (1998)
In August 1998 the Russian state, which had survived the political storms of russian-constitutional-crisis-1993 and the slaughter of the first-chechen-war-1994-96, collapsed financially. On 17 August 1998 the government of boris-yeltsin announced that it could no longer service its debts — that Russia was in default — and simultaneously devalued the rouble and imposed a moratorium on the repayment of foreign obligations. The state that had once ruled a sixth of the earth, which had inherited the superpower’s seat at the table of the nuclear powers, had become a bankrupt. The default of 1998 was the climax of the economic collapse that had run through the whole of the 1990s, the moment when the market experiment that had followed the end of the Soviet Union delivered its most shattering verdict. It wiped out the savings of millions of Russians, brought down banks and businesses, and humiliated the state in the eyes of the world — and out of its wreckage, and of the exhaustion it caused, the way was opened to a new order under vladimir-putin.
The road to the abyss
The financial crisis of 1998 was the product of a decade of economic ruin and of a doomed attempt to arrest it. The Russia of the 1990s had been remade by the market reforms of the years after 1991 — the freeing of prices, the privatisation of the state’s vast industrial property, the creation of a class of oligarchs who had acquired the country’s natural wealth in exchange for their support of the President. But the new market economy rested on fragile foundations: a state that could not collect taxes, a population stripped of its savings by inflation, an economy that had fallen far below the output of the Soviet era, and a government that lived by borrowing. Through the mid-1990s the state financed itself through the issue of short-term treasury bonds, the ГКО (GKO), paying enormous rates of interest to attract the money it needed. The system worked so long as confidence held and capital flowed in; but the obligations mounted, the budget deficit yawned, and the whole edifice came to depend on a constant influx of new borrowing. Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook describes the Russia of these years as an economy caught on the swings of the international market — the качели (kacheli, ‘swings’) of 1998 — exposed to the flight of foreign capital and the collapse of the currencies of East Asia that shook the emerging markets through 1997 and 1998.
The default of August 1998
The crisis broke in the summer of 1998, as falling oil prices, the Asian financial contagion and the flight of investors from Russian assets pushed the state toward the brink. The government and the Central Bank fought a desperate rearguard action through the spring, borrowing ever more expensively and burning their reserves to defend the rouble within its currency corridor. Pikhoya, who recorded the economy of the усталая Россия (ustalaya Rossiya, ‘tired Russia’) of the late 1990s, describes the steady slide of those months as the state’s instruments of resistance ran out one by one. On 17 August 1998 the struggle was abandoned. The government announced a moratorium on the repayment of foreign debts and on the payment of the treasury bonds that had financed the state, effectively declaring Russia unable to meet its obligations — the first major sovereign default of the modern era — and simultaneously devalued the rouble, letting the currency float and fall. The immediate consequence was catastrophic. Banks that had held the government’s paper and the people’s deposits collapsed; the rouble lost much of its value within weeks; inflation surged; and the savings and wages of ordinary Russians were devoured by the fall. The state, the government and the currency had failed at once, in a single blow to the entire population.
The aftermath and the exhaustion
The default of 1998 left Russia poorer, angrier and more disillusioned than it had been even in the difficult years before. The political consequences were immediate: the government fell, and the man who had once been the emblem of the market reform, the liberal Yegor Gaidar, was gone, while the new premier Yevgeny Primakov presided over a government that shifted away from the radical reformism of the early 1990s. The financial collapse discredited the institutions of the new Russia — the state, the banks, the market itself — in the eyes of a population that had already been stripped of its certainties by the fall of the Soviet Union. Pikhoya, reflecting on the decade, depicts the Russia of 1994-1999 as a society exhausted by failure: privatisation that had enriched a few and impoverished the many, elections that had brought no deliverance, war and financial collapse and the daily struggle of survival. Medinsky and Torkunov’s textbook treats the economic crisis of 1998 as the low point of the post-Soviet economy, the moment that marked the exhaustion of the first, ruined decade of Russian capitalism. And yet, remarkably, the default proved to be the beginning of a recovery rather than the final catastrophe. The cheap rouble made Russian goods competitive again; the oil price rose; and the economy, freed of its crushing debt burden, began in the late 1990s to grow once more. The ruined state of 1998 was, in time, rebuilt into the more prosperous Russia of the new century — but the political settlement that followed belonged not to the exhausted Yeltsin but to his chosen heir. In the last hours of 1999 Yeltsin resigned, and the presidency passed to vladimir-putin, who was to turn the stability and rising prices of the new decade into the foundations of the vertical-of-power that came to define his Russia.

events/second-chechen-war-1999.title: Second Chechen War (1999–2000)
events/second-chechen-war-1999.content:
Second Chechen War (1999–2000)
The war that had been thought settled in 1996 did not stay settled. The first-chechen-war-1994-96 had ended in the summer of that year with the Khasavyurt accords, signed between the President’s representative Alexander Lebed and the Chechen commander Aslan Maskhadov, under which the Russian troops withdrew from Chechnya and the status of the republic was left unresolved. It was an attempt, as one historian of the period put it, to end the war on the southern edge of Russia that had cost three or four times the losses of the Afghan war — and it failed. The power in Grozny slipped into the hands of the field commanders; lawlessness, hostage-taking, criminal racketeering and terrorism became the daily order of the republic, and Maskhadov’s authority was too weak to command it. The failure of the Khasavyurt arrangement became obvious when, in the autumn of 1999, the war returned.
The invasion of Dagestan
The second war began not in Chechnya but in Dagestan. In August 1999 a force of Chechen fighters under Shamil Basayev crossed into the neighbouring republic of Dagestan, declaring as its aim the creation of an “Islamic republic” on the territory of the Caucasus and its separation from Russia. The movement was fed by the spread of Wahhabism, the militant Islamist current, along the Chechen border, which had alarmed the Moscow authorities through the summer. The people of Dagestan, however, saw the incursion not as liberation but as aggression. In repelling it, federal forces were joined by local militiamen (ополченцы); the attackers were beaten back, and the stand of Dagestan marked, in the telling of the official Russian school history, a turning point in the affairs of the Caucasus. The incursion was followed by a new series of terrorist acts, including bombings in Moscow itself.
A presidential war
It was in this crisis that the campaign returned to Chechnya. The federal authorities now had, in the person of a new and untested premier, a leader willing to take the war wholly upon himself. When vladimir-putin was confirmed as Chairman of the Government on 9 August 1999, the direction of the Caucasus fell into his hands. Under his guidance the Chechen fighters who had invaded Dagestan were driven back, and the federal forces reopened their operations against the separatists on the territory of Chechnya. In October 1999 the Russian troops entered the republic again — and this time the young premier took the full responsibility for the operation upon himself. It was, in a real sense, a presidential war from its first weeks: a war waged for the authority of the state, and inseparable from the man who conducted it. The contrast with the first war was deliberate. Where the campaign of 1994–1995 had been begun by a distracted and ailing leadership and prosecuted with catastrophic improvidence — the disastrous storming of Grozny that winter — the new campaign was presented as a disciplined, deliberate restoration of constitutional order, and its waging served to build the popularity of the premier who promised to carry it through to the end.
The fall of Grozny
Through the autumn of 1999 the federal forces advanced, and the fighters suffered heavy losses. In the beginning of 2000 Grozny, the capital that had already been devastated in the first war, fell to the federal troops after weeks of fighting. Part of the separatist forces managed to slip away into the mountains, but in the broader situation a change had come. By the spring the main populated centres of the republic were under federal control, and on 20 April 2000 the authorities declared the counter-terrorist operation (контртеррористическая операция) on the North Caucasus complete. The official history of the period stresses that much of the Chechen population had wearied of the lawlessness, the terrorism and the ruin the republic had endured, and that the federal centre and the authoritative leaders of Chechnya came onto a path of reconciliation and of the republic’s development within Russia. The war that had been waged to restore the unity of the state was followed by the rebuilding of the Chechen administration — first under direct presidential rule, then under the former mufti Akhmad Kadyrov, who was made head of the republic in 2000 and elected its president in October 2003.
The war and the making of a leader
The second Chechen war was not only a military campaign; it was the crucible in which a new political order was forged. It gave vladimir-putin his public identity — the resolute defender of the state who spoke plainly of the enemy and promised no half-measures. The campaign accelerated his rise: it was fought through the very weeks in which the succession from boris-yeltsin was being arranged, and it delivered him to the presidential election of March 2000 with a reputation already made. It also imposed its own course on the relationship of power and the great fortunes: the media magnate Vladimir Gusinsky, whose television channel NTV criticised the conduct of the war, was among the first targets of the new president’s discipline. The war did not wholly end with the declaration of April 2000. Terrorism against civilians continued — the taking of hostages in the theatre on Dubrovka in Moscow in 2002, the seizure of the school in Beslan in 2004, the assassination of Akhmad Kadyrov by a bomb on 9 May 2004. The main forces of the fighters were broken only toward the end of 2005, and most of their leaders killed. But the decisive phase — the war of 1999–2000 that returned the republic to the state — was over. What began as the repulse of an invasion of Dagestan had become the reconquest of Chechnya and the first great act of the restored Russian state under its new leader.

events/single-european-act-1986.title: Single European Act (1986)
events/single-european-act-1986.content:
Single European Act (1986)
The Single European Act was the treaty that relaunched European integration after the stagnation of the 1970s and gave the Community its greatest single enterprise of the twentieth century — the completion of a single internal market. Signed in Luxembourg in February 1986, it was the first substantial amendment of the Treaty of Rome and the clearest statement yet that the Community, long becalmed in a sea of unanimity and intergovernmental veto, was to become a genuinely common market of goods, services, capital and persons by the end of 1992.
The crisis of “Europessimism”
The act was the answer to a decade of disappointment. The customs union had been completed in 1968, but the Community that emerged from the crisis-ridden 1970s had lost its momentum. The Luxembourg Compromise, enshrined after the “empty chair” crisis, had given each member an informal power of veto; enlargement had brought in Britain, Ireland, Denmark and Greece, each with its own reservations; and the oil shocks and monetary disorder of the decade had turned governments inward. This was the era of “Europessimism,” a term of the time for a Community that seemed incapable of moving forward. The revival came from a conjunction of forces: the success of the European Monetary System, which had taught the members that cooperation worked; a new Commission, appointed in 1985 under the presidency of Jacques Delors, which set out to make the Community dynamic again; and a growing conviction among European business leaders that the fragmentation of the European market into a dozen national compartments was an intolerable handicap against American and Japanese competitors.
The White Paper and the 1992 programme
The instrument of revival was a White Paper drafted under the direction of Lord Arthur Cockfield, the Commission’s vice-president, and adopted by the member states at the Milan summit of June 1985. It assembled some 287 proposals for the removal of the barriers — physical, technical and fiscal — that divided the national markets, and set a deadline for their implementation: 31 December 1992. This was the “Europe 1992” programme, as it was universally known, the promise of a genuine single market of nearly three hundred and twenty million people. The Commission marketed the idea with skill, publishing in 1988 the “Cecchini Report,” a study that sought to quantify the enormous “costs of non-Europe” — the price the Community paid for maintaining an incomplete market. Moravcsik, in his study of the negotiation, is careful to give the credit to the national governments rather than to the Commission’s entrepreneurship; he argues that the relaunch was driven above all by the converging commercial and economic interests of France, Germany and Britain in the internal market, and that the celebrated activism of Delors and Cockfield did not by itself create the impulse. Yet the new Commission, and Delors in particular, gave the programme its face and its sense of purpose.
Qualified majority voting
The political question at the heart of the treaty was how decisions would be taken. A programme of three hundred measures could never be completed if a single member could veto each one, and so the Single European Act reformed the legislative process, introducing a cooperation procedure and extending qualified majority voting in the Council to the areas covered by the internal market programme. This was the decisive reform. Henceforward a qualified majority — not unanimity — would decide the great work of market construction, and the internal market programme of 1992 became the chief beneficiary of the new voting. The change was not made without resistance. At Milan, the British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, the Danish Poul Schlüter and the Greek Andreas Papandreou all resisted the reform of the EEC Treaty, preferring informal agreements that would leave national vetoes intact. It was the Italian Prime Minister Bettino Craxi who forced the issue, invoking Article 236 of the Treaty of Rome and calling for a vote in the European Council — a split decision, seven to three, in favour of an intergovernmental conference. Political union was not adopted, but was affirmed as a declared goal. The European Council, meanwhile, was for the first time given formal recognition and agreed to meet at least twice a year.
Signature and consequence
The amending treaty was signed in Luxembourg on 17 February 1986 by nine of the twelve members, with Denmark, Greece and Italy following on 28 February after a Danish referendum, and entered into force on 1 July 1987 after Ireland ratified it, the last of the twelve to do so. Its consequences ran far beyond the removal of tariffs. The Single European Act gave the Community a new legal and constitutional footing, deepened its competence, and — in the judgement of the Cambridge history — laid the constitutional groundwork for the ambitious plan it embodied. Just as decisively, the decision to complete the internal market relaunched the debate about Economic and Monetary Union, for a single market without a single currency seemed to many incomplete. At the European Council of Madrid in June 1989 the twelve leaders agreed to convene an intergovernmental conference on how to realise such a union gradually — the road that would lead, within five years, to the Treaty of Maastricht.

events/soviet-invasion-afghanistan-1979.title: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan (1979)
events/soviet-invasion-afghanistan-1979.content:
The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan (1979)
On 25 December 1979 a Limited Contingent of Soviet troops — the Ограниченный контингент советских войск — crossed the frontier of the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan at the request of the Afghan government. So began the longest and costliest war in the history of the Soviet Union after 1945, a nine-year intervention at the far edge of the socialist commonwealth that was to drain the country’s resources, break the morale of its leadership, and bring the era of détente to a definitive close. The intervention was conceived, in the official account, as a defensive act of the socialist state — the support of a friendly government against a rebellion of Islamist forces armed from across the border — yet its consequences reached far beyond the Hindu Kush, into the very fabric of the Soviet system and of the Cold War itself.
The road to Kabul
The origins of the intervention lay in the revolutions and counter-revolutions that convulsed Afghanistan in the late 1970s. In 1978 a revolution had brought to power a new government that proclaimed a course of strengthening relations with its great neighbour, the USSR. Moscow, ever watchful of its southern border, looked with favour on the transformation. The United States, seeking to prevent the growth of Soviet influence, began to support the opposition forces that gathered against the Kabul regime. As the rebellion spread, and a further change of power in Afghanistan threatened to bring enormous problems directly to the Soviet frontier, the leadership in Moscow resolved that it could not stand aside. At the request of the Afghan government the decision was taken to send in the troops — a decision in which the whole weight of the Soviet state, from the party to the organs of state security, was engaged.
The war
The Limited Contingent’s aim was to support the Afghan army in its struggle against the Islamist forces whose bases, with the aid of the United States and NATO, had been set up on the territory of neighbouring Pakistan. What was meant to be a swift reinforcement became a grinding, decade-long war. The Soviet soldiers and officers fought against the моджахеды (mujahideen) across the mountains and valleys of Afghanistan, guarding convoys, defending garrisons, and contending with an elusive enemy supplied from across the Pakistani border. Over the whole period of the presence of Soviet troops in Afghanistan, from 1979 to 1989, some 14,000 Soviet soldiers and officers perished — in military operations, in clashes while guarding convoys of humanitarian cargo, and at the hands of saboteurs and terrorists. The war exacted a heavy price in materiel and in men, and it became a running sore in Soviet society, spoken of quietly in the kitchens of the последнее советское поколение (the last Soviet generation) that was being asked to sacrifice its sons in a distant and unresolved conflict.
The end of détente
The intervention destroyed the architecture of relaxation that the Soviet Union had built through the 1970s. The great campaign in the West in defence of human rights in the USSR had already strained the relationship; after the entry of Soviet troops into Afghanistan the period of разрядка (relaxation of international tension) finally receded into the past. The West used the Soviet presence in Afghanistan for propaganda attacks on the USSR, and the second Cold War of the early 1980s descended upon the world. The boycott of the Moscow Olympics, the intensification of the arms race under the new American administration, the sanctions against Soviet industry, and the mounting Soviet economic burden of the war all combined to harden the confrontation anew. In Afghanistan itself the Soviet state, which had long supported the national-liberation movements of the developing world — Vietnam, the Arab states, Angola, Mozambique, Ethiopia, Nicaragua — found itself committed to a war that consumed the resources of a system already entering the stagnation of the late Brezhnev years.
The long retreat
The war outlived several leaders of the Soviet state. It continued through the Andropov interlude, through the brief tenure of Chernenko, and into the era of perestroika; only in 1989, under Gorbachev, were the last Soviet troops withdrawn from Afghanistan. The intervention had become, in the judgement of the era that followed, one of the great miscalculations of Soviet foreign policy — a war undertaken to defend a friendly state and the security of the southern border, which instead bled the country dry and hastened the very crisis of the system it was meant to protect. The veterans who returned, the афганцы (Afghantsy), carried with them a memory that sat uneasily with the official certainties of their elders. Afghanistan was the point at which the confident, expansionist Soviet power of the postwar decades met its limit — and the shadow it cast fell across the whole remaining history of the state.

events/suez-crisis-1956.title: The Suez Crisis (1956)
events/suez-crisis-1956.content:
The Suez Crisis (1956)
In the autumn of 1956, while the world’s attention was torn between Budapest and the banks of the Nile, the old colonial powers of Western Europe made their last great attempt to reverse the current of history and found themselves humbled in the space of a week. The nationalisation of the Suez Canal by the Egyptian leader Gamal Abdel Nasser in July 1956 had brought the great waterway of empire under the control of the Arab nation that had built its fortunes through it; and against that assertion of sovereignty Britain, France and Israel launched a concerted aggression — an attack that the official Soviet history of foreign policy presents as the last gasp of the imperialist age, defeated by the unity of the Arab peoples, the pressure of world opinion and the firm stand of the Soviet Union. The Suez crisis of 1956 was the moment when the old masters of the Middle East finally lost their grip, and the moment when the Cold War reached out to embrace the Arab world.
The nationalisation and the conspiracy
Nasser’s decision of 26 July 1956 to take the Suez Canal Company into Egyptian ownership, in response to the withdrawal of Western finance for his great project of the Aswan High Dam, was a direct blow at the two empires that had ruled the region for a century. Britain, which held the canal as the artery of its power in the East, and France, which saw in Nasser the instigator of the revolt that was bleeding it in Algeria, resolved to strike back. In the eyes of the Soviet account they wove a conspiracy — secret collusion with Israel, whose army was to strike across Sinai toward the canal, and a plan for British and French forces to “separate the belligerents” and occupy the waterway under the cover of restoring peace. On 29 October 1956 Israeli forces invaded Sinai; on the following days British and French aircraft bombed Egyptian airfields, and on 5 November Anglo-French paratroops and marines landed at Port Said to seize the northern end of the canal. The aggression was carried out in open defiance of the United Nations and in the name of a right of intervention that the age of empire could no longer claim.
The humiliation of the old powers
The invaders had reckoned without the breadth of the opposition they had roused. The United Nations General Assembly, moved by the American government, called for a ceasefire and the withdrawal of the aggressors; the United States, which had not been consulted and which saw its own interests in the Arab world threatened by the return of its European allies, refused to shore up the British pound and let the British and French discover the price of defying Washington. The Soviet Union, for its part, took up the cause of Egypt with the utmost firmness. Premier Bulganin’s government warned that it could not remain indifferent to the aggression and that the use of force against Egypt must be answered — threatening, in the words of the Soviet leaders, measures that would not be limited to the Middle East. The diplomatic and financial pressure, the threat from Moscow, and the refusal of the United States to support its allies combined to bring the adventure to an end. The ceasefire came on 6–7 November; by the end of December the British and French forces had been withdrawn, and in March 1957 the last Israeli troops left Sinai. The canal, nationalised, remained in Egyptian hands. Britain and France had suffered a defeat that announced the end of their pretensions to empire; the British Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigned, his reputation destroyed, and the two powers were left to draw the lesson that the age of Suez was over.
The shadow over the Cold War
The Suez crisis redrew the map of the Middle East and of the world. It revealed that the old European empires could no longer act without the assent of the two superpowers, and it opened the region to the rivalry of the blocs: the United States, its own reputation rising in the Arab world, proclaimed in the Eisenhower Doctrine its readiness to defend the region against communism, while the Soviet Union, by its bold stand for Egypt and the Arabs, established itself as the champion of the peoples struggling against colonialism and against the newly-created state of Israel. In the official Soviet narrative the crisis was a victory for the forces of peace and national liberation — proof that aggression could be checked when the peoples were united and the socialist power stood firm. For the Cold War itself the coincidence of the Suez and Hungarian crises in the same weeks of 1956 was a defining conjunction: the intervention in Hungary had shown the West the limits of the thaw inside the bloc, and the settlement of Suez had shown the old world that its day was done. The Middle East, drawn into the great confrontation, was to be a theatre of Soviet-American rivalry and of recurrent war for decades to come — and the name of Nasser, the canal and the humbled empires of Suez were to remain the emblem of the awakening of the Arab peoples.

events/tangentopoli-1992.title: Tangentopoli (1992)
events/tangentopoli-1992.content:
Tangentopoli (1992)
The year 1992, which Queen Elizabeth II had called the annus horribilis for the scandals that struck her own family, proved no less horrible for the politics of Italy. It was the year in which a vast and long-tolerated system of corruption was exposed, in which the currency crisis shook the economy, and in which the murders of the anti-mafia judges Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino brought the country to the edge of despair. Above all, it was the year in which the Mani pulite, the Clean Hands, investigations of the Milan magistrates detonated a political earthquake that swept away the entire governing class of the postwar Republic and opened the passage to what would be called the Second Republic.
The trigger: Mario Chiesa
The phenomenon of corruption in the life of the parties was well known to those who followed politics, even from outside, but the great mass of the people ignored its dimensions. It fell to an apparently trivial episode to reveal them to an indignant and stunned country — an episode destined to become the greatest scandal in the history of the Republic. On 17 February 1992, Mario Chiesa, an influential Milanese socialist and president of the Pio Albergo Trivulzio old people’s home, was surprised while receiving a mazzetta of seven million lire paid him by a supplier of the institution. The investigations, conducted with scrupulous patience by a young magistrate, Antonio Di Pietro, and his collaborators of the Milan prosecutor’s office, laid bare an extraordinarily dense network of corruption and complicity — the system that would come to be called Bribesville.
The inquests spread
In the spring and summer the investigations passed from Milan to other cities of north and south, revealing the national dimensions of the phenomenon. All the parties were involved in some measure — save the MSI, the Greens and a few formations without positions of local power — but the Democrazia cristiana and the Partito socialista of Bettino Craxi carried the greatest responsibilities and suffered the heaviest denunciations. The corruption was a tangentocrazia, a rule of the bribe, fed by the great public works of the previous twenty years — metro, airport, motorways, public buildings — and by the connivance of politicians with the great contractors who paid in exchange for contracts. Gentiloni Silveri describes the explosion of a mechanism that brought to light a diffuse system of corruption, a network of behaviour and constraints marked by a hidden, tolerated and consolidated illegality, striking at symbols and customs in a crescendo of accusations that shook the entire system of the country.
The election of April 1992 and the fall
The elections of 5 April 1992, held before the scandal had shown its real dimensions, were nonetheless influenced by the wear of the political system and the climate of acrimony among the leaders of the majority parties. Their results registered the defeat of the governing parties and a diffuse protest against parties, institutions and politics. The DC lost almost five points, falling below thirty per cent; the PDS, the successor of the Partito comunista, collapsed to 16.1 per cent plus the 5.6 per cent of Rifondazione comunista; the PSI suffered its first setback after years of constant growth; and the great victor was the Lega Lombarda of Umberto Bossi, which swept to 8.7 per cent and fifty-five seats in the Chamber. The party of protest against the partitocrazia had become a national force.
In the months that followed the avalanche of Tangentopoli reached its point of no return. The pool of Mani pulite distributed judicial notices almost daily, and by the end of the year more than fifteen per cent of parliamentarians stood under investigation. The mafia, for its part, struck at the very institutions: on 23 May 1992 Giovanni Falcone was murdered with his wife and escort on the motorway at Capaci, near Palermo, and in July Paolo Borsellino fell in the Via d’Amelio — assassinations that stunned the country and, as Gentiloni Silveri writes, fused with the financial, political and institutional crises into a single gathering storm. Six ministers resigned after receiving notice of investigation, and the great names of the governing parties were drawn into the inquests. In February 1993 Craxi abandoned the secretariat of the PSI after seventeen years of unchallenged power; by the summer the Democrazia cristiana, with its secretary Mino Martinazzoli, announced its dissolution. The political earthquake had done its work: the Republic of the parties, the Prima Repubblica, lay in ruins.
A frattura storica
Gentiloni Silveri, following the testimony of Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, who was called to form a government of technicians after the resignation of Giuliano Amato, describes the biennium 1992-1993 as a frattura storica, a historical rupture — a turning that carried the itinerary of the Republic to the edge of the abyss, in a condition of dangerous and destabilising uncertainty. Financial, political and institutional crises superimposed themselves on one another; the season of Tangentopoli put in question the very relationship between the elected and the electors and the credibility of an entire political-institutional architecture. The end of the Cold War, the collapse of the Berlin Wall in 1989, was the international plane of the crollo: the postwar Italian system had inscribed itself in the world of the Cold War, and when that world ended, the equilibrium of the Republic lost its reason for being. From the ruins rose the demand for a new politics, the new electoral law of the majority, and the new formations — most spectacularly the movement of Silvio Berlusconi — that would contest the elections of 1994 and open the Second Republic.

events/transicion-democratica-1975-78.title: The Democratic Transition, 1975–1978
events/transicion-democratica-1975-78.content:
The Democratic Transition, 1975–1978
On 20 November 1975 Francisco Franco died, and Spain was left with a dictatorship and no dictator. For three years the country walked the narrow path between its authoritarian past and a democratic future, in a process Spaniards came to call la Transición — the Transition — and which historians would later hold up as the paradigmatic case of a negotiated break, a ruptura pactada (negotiated break), between an old order and a new one. Its outcome was not written in advance. No near model, local or temporal, suggested that such a process could succeed without external aggression; the Spanish case, Tusell observed, had to be created from circumstance and from the choices of individuals. That it ended in the democracy of 1978, and consolidated in the decade that followed, made Spain one of the two great events of its twentieth century, beside the Civil War that had opened it.
The beginning of the third wave
The Spanish Transition belonged to a wider movement. Samuel Huntington named it the “third wave” of democratisation, and it began in the Mediterranean in 1974, toppling the non-totalitarian right-wing dictatorships of Greece, Portugal and Spain before crossing the Atlantic and, unpredictably, reaching the communist world. Transitions, in this view, occur when the cost of repression or of violent insurrection is perceived as excessive by all parties, and a democratic consensus appears when institutions come to seem what unites rather than what divides. Every transition is a multi-sided chess game whose final result is not written; individuals and circumstance matter. Spain’s way was peculiar and exemplary at once — a path without the uncertainty of a Gorbachev, without the “authoritarian enclaves” of a Pinochet, in which a political class converted sincerely to democratic principles rather than merely adapting to them. A decisive transformation already accomplished under the dictatorship, with no parallel among Spain’s neighbours, made the outcome possible.
The monarchy and the reform
The distinctive Spanish instrument was the monarchy. The gravest danger in any transition is the break of legitimacy between the vanished dictatorship and the democracy not yet consolidated, and the Crown supplied the means to avoid that break. From the first moment juan-carlos-i chose to be a great king rather than a small Caudillo. The new king first had to establish his supreme responsibility, obtaining the resignation of the president of the government, Arias Navarro, whose reformismo was impossible from the start and whose government served only as a cushion, a colchón, between two periods. With Torcuato Fernández Miranda at the head of the Cortes and the Council of the Kingdom, the substitution was engineered, and in July 1976 the king appointed adolfo-suarez, a young reformist minister of the régime, to carry the change forward.
The Law for Political Reform
Suárez’s instrument was the Law for Political Reform, drafted through the summer of 1976 by Fernández Miranda’s team and presented to the senior military commanders on 8 September. Its formula was the reform de la ley a la ley (from the law to the law): by its own legal provisions the régime would provide for free elections to a constituent Cortes, voting itself out of existence in conformity with its own forms. In the referendum of December 1976 the Spanish people approved the law by an overwhelming margin, and the path to free elections was open. Between that referendum and the elections of June 1977 the process passed through weeks in which terrorism and military pressure could have aborted it; it survived through the Spanish will for democratic coexistence, the attitude of the party leaders, and the government’s patient timing, which deliberately put off a harsh economic programme that might have derailed the political calendar.
Legalisation of the parties
The great test of the reform was the question of the communists. The murder of the labour lawyers of Atocha on 24 January 1977, in which seven men died, produced a wave of solidarity and demonstrated the PCE’s capacity to control its masses; and on 9 April 1977, months after the authorities had begun to tolerate it in practice, the party was legalised. Santiago Carrillo had already returned from exile in February 1976 to open contacts with the opposition. The legalisation of the party that had fought the dictatorship, carried by a government of the régime, was the act that proved the rupture was real. Meanwhile the party system reconfigured itself: a new politics emerged mainly from the opposition forces to the previous régime, and the unitary opposition organisms lost the initiative once Suárez reached the presidency. Spaniards spoke of the devolución de España — the return of Spain — the recovery of a country long held apart from its European peers.
The constituent elections
In the general election of 15 June 1977, the first free elections in forty-one years, Suárez’s Union of the Democratic Centre emerged as the largest party, ahead of the socialist left and the reconstituted right. The new Cortes, elected as a constituent assembly, set about the long work of drafting a constitution. The consensus that would produce the constitution-1978 was the culminating act of the Transition: a settlement arrived at by the principal parliamentary forces, by which a parliamentary monarchy, the state of the autonomies, and the catalogue of democratic rights were fixed as the common ground of all Spaniards. The Transition did not end with the constitution — the nationalisms and terrorism of the Basque and Catalan tracks remained the great unsettled question, and the army would test the settlement at 23-f-coup-1981 — but with December 1978 the institutional work was done. Politically, the Transition would run on until October 1982 and the psoe-victory-1982, when the party that had held the protagonist role not only lost power but disappeared, and the transfer of power to the former opposition sealed the democracy as a plebiscite. It was, in the balance, a settlement whose positive aspects predominated clearly — not only because it ended well, but because the starting point had justified little optimism.

events/treaty-of-rome-1957.title: Treaties of Rome (1957)
events/treaty-of-rome-1957.content:
Treaties of Rome (1957)
On 25 March 1957, in the Palazzo dei Conservatori on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, the six member states of the European Coal and Steel Community — France, Germany, Italy and the three Benelux countries — signed the two treaties that were to become the true foundation of the Common Market. The Treaties of Rome established the European Economic Community, built around a customs union and a common market, and the European Atomic Energy Community, Euratom. Together with the Coal and Steel Community they formed the institutional core of what would grow, over four decades, into the European Union. Where messina-conference-1955 had relaunched the enterprise after the failure of the European Defence Community, the Treaties of Rome gave that relaunch its permanent legal and constitutional form — the milestones, in the Cambridge history’s phrase, from which the whole treaty history of integration unfolds.
The two Communities
The first and decisive treaty created the European Economic Community. Its heart was the customs union: the abolition of internal tariffs among the Six, to be completed in stages over a transition period, together with a common external tariff and a common commercial policy toward the rest of the world. But the treaty went beyond the simple removal of barriers. It provided for the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital; it established a set of common institutions — a Commission, a Council of Ministers, a European Assembly and a Court of Justice — modelled on those of the Coal and Steel Community but governing a far wider field; and it laid the framework of common policies, above all the Common Agricultural Policy, designed to shield and support the farmers of the Six, and a competition policy to police the market. The second treaty created Euratom, a Community for the peaceful development of atomic energy, the product of the atomic hopes and anxieties of the mid-1950s. Both treaties came into force on 1 January 1958.
The common market, the customs union and the CAP
The Treaty of Rome was in the first instance an economic instrument, and it is as such that Moravcsik analyses it. Against the emphasis of the supranational literature on geopolitical fear and federalist vision, he argues that the customs-union option won because it answered the commercial interests of the dominant states — above all the French desire for the Common Agricultural Policy (the “grain”) and the political ambitions of the Fourth and Fifth Republics (the “grandeur”), and the German acceptance of a common market that opened export markets in exchange for a protected agriculture. The treaty set the Six upon a path of deepening economic interdependence, completing the customs union ahead of schedule in the 1960s and giving the CAP a central place in the Community’s budget. It was this treaty, and not the Coal and Steel Community, that provided the durable frame of European integration; the Cambridge history treats the Treaties of Rome and the Single European Act as the twin legal-constitutional landmarks of the Community’s first three decades, and it was within this frame that the later architecture of the single-european-act-1986 and the maastricht-treaty-1992 would be built. On the steps of the Capitoline, the Six had chosen not a federation proclaimed at a stroke, but a common market patiently constructed — and it was that choice that proved decisive.

events/treuhand-privatization-1990-94.title: The Treuhand Privatisation of the East German Economy, 1990–94
events/treuhand-privatization-1990-94.content:
The Treuhand Privatisation of the East German Economy, 1990–94
Between the fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 and the first years of the Federal Republic’s new eastern Länder, the economy of the GDR was dismantled and re-made in a span of barely four years. At the centre of that process stood the treuhandanstalt, the trustee agency that took the Volkseigene Betriebe — the people’s enterprises of the planned economy — and privatised, liquidated or gesundgeschrumpft (“shrunk to health”) some eight thousand of them. What the East had built up over four decades of state ownership was handed over, sold off, or shut down, and the human cost of that transfer defined the decade for millions who had expected something else entirely from unity.
The scale of the collapse is the first fact that imposes itself. The GDR had kept its people at work by the very structure of a planned economy that guaranteed each person a place. In 1989 there were 9.7 million employed; by the end of 1993 there were only 6.2 million. A third of the eastern workforce lost its job, and with it entered a condition the East had never known — Arbeitslosigkeit, unemployment, no longer the remote Western problem it had been taught to pity but the immediate texture of daily life. The Treuhand was the instrument of this catastrophe as much as its witness: it closed the plants that could not be sold, and it sold those that could be sold on terms that left the new owners free to cut away the surplus of workers the old economy had carried. The Reichsbahn strike of the railwaymen was one of the first open signals that the old order of guaranteed employment had given way to a new order of defended jobs.
For many the process was experienced as deindustrialisation — the emptying of a landscape of work that the GDR had organised around heavy industry and full employment. The people’s enterprises had been the great employers and the bearers of the collective life of their towns; when they closed, the town’s purpose closed with them. The economists and the officials who ran the Treuhand spoke of Privatisierung and of the market’s judgement, and they were not wrong that much of the GDR economy could not survive exposure to it. But the manner of the change was one-sided, and it was felt as an Übernahme, a takeover, in which western capital and western managers moved in to pick over what was left. The new unemployment was concentrated, permanent for many, and it marked out a class of Verlierer, the losers of the transformation, who had invested their working lives in a system that was now being dismantled around them.
The collapse was never purely economic. Kowalczuk insists that the transformation was lived and fought out by East Germans also as a cultural struggle — the economic collapse as Kulturkampf, an assault on ways of life, on self-respect, on the meaning of a working life. The farmer whose collectivised LPG was dissolved, the engineer whose knowledge was no longer wanted, the worker whose plant closed: each lost not only a job but a standing in the world. The burden of Altschulden, the inherited debts of the old economy, dragged down firms that might otherwise have survived, and the Eigentumsfrage, the property question with its principle of Rückgabe vor Entschädigung (restitution before compensation), kept investment and lives in suspense for years. Through it all the East watched the West assume the posture of the creditor and the judge.
By 1994 the great work of privatisation was largely done; the Treuhand had passed out of the central role that had made it the most powerful shaper of the early 1990s. What it left behind was an eastern economy rebuilt but scarred, with a permanently higher rate of unemployment, a drained and depleted industrial base, and a population that had learned to count itself among the Verlierer even where individual fortunes had risen. The winners and losers of the transformation were not the simple opposites of cliché — some profited handsomely from the sale and the reconstruction — but the collective sense of loss, of having been acted upon rather than acted with, proved durable. The privatisation of 1990–94 fixed the economic shape of eastern Germany for a generation, and it fixed too the memory of how the East had been absorbed — as the object of a takeover rather than the subject of a negotiation. On the wider transformation of which this was the economic heart see east-german-transformation; on the agency itself see treuhandanstalt.

events/two-plus-four-1990.title: Two-Plus-Four Negotiations and Treaty (1990)
events/two-plus-four-1990.content:
Two-Plus-Four Negotiations and Treaty (1990)
The external face of German unity was the work of the Two-Plus-Four negotiations, the diplomatic settlement through which the two German states and the four powers that had occupied and divided Germany in 1945 agreed on the conditions of its reunification. “Two-Plus-Four” (Zwei-plus-Vier) named the composition of the conference — the two Germanies, which had come together in the course of 1990, and the four victorious powers of the Second World War: the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and France, which had together held the rights and responsibilities over Germany and Berlin as a whole since the defeat of 1945. The negotiations of 1990 had to reconcile the German will to unity with the treaty rights of the four powers, and they issued in the Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany, signed in Moscow on 12 September 1990, which restored to the reunified Germany its full and unrestricted sovereignty. It was the formal end of the war settlement, the point at which the four powers surrendered the powers they had held over Germany for forty-five years.
The rights of the four powers and the problem of the East
The obstacle to unity was not in Bonn or Berlin but in the structure of the peace settlement itself. Since 1945 the four wartime powers had exercised rights and responsibilities over Germany as a whole and over Berlin; the two German states had come into being within the frame of that occupation in 1949, the founding-gdr-1949 of the East answering the foundation of the Federal Republic in the West. The division of Germany was therefore not merely a German condition but a condition of the victors of 1945 and of the Cold War that followed. Any restoration of unity had to unwind the rights of the four powers — above all those of the Soviet Union, which held the eastern third of Germany and had every reason to fear a new German state. The negotiations of 1990 were accordingly conducted by helmut-kohl and his Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher in concert with the allied governments, and they turned on the one question the East cared most about: whether the united Germany would be a Germany of the West, bound into NATO and the European Community.
The terms of the settlement
The Treaty on the Final Settlement settled the external conditions of unity in the form the Federal Republic had sought. The united Germany would comprise the territory of the two German states; it would be a member of NATO, and the western parts of Berlin and Germany would continue to host allied forces while the territory of the former GDR would be free of foreign troops and of nuclear weapons for a transition period. Germany declared that no weapons of mass destruction would ever be made or possessed on its territory, and it confirmed the border with Poland along the Oder-Neisse line as its permanent western neighbour’s eastern frontier — a renunciation of the revisionism that had haunted German politics since 1945. In exchange for these assurances the four powers declared their rights and responsibilities in respect of Berlin and of Germany as a whole to be at an end. The treaty thus achieved what the events of 1945 had left undone: it ended the state of occupation and confirmed the sovereignty of the German state.
The restoration of full sovereignty
The Treaty of 12 September 1990, signed in Moscow and ratified through the following year, took effect in March 1991. With it Germany recovered the full sovereignty of a normal state — the power to conduct its affairs as a member of the community of nations without the tutelage of the occupying powers. The recovery of sovereignty and the recovery of unity were the two faces of a single act: the german-reunification-1990 on 3 October 1990 rested on the external settlement that the Two-Plus-Four process had secured, and the treaty in turn presupposed the unity that the accession of the GDR was to accomplish. For Winkler the achievement belonged to the larger story of the end of the sonderweg: the German question was resolved in freedom, with the assent of all the powers, and Germany entered its unity anchored in the West, in the Atlantic alliance and in the European project. The Two-Plus-Four Treaty was the instrument by which the Germans at last came out from under the shadow of 1945, whole, free and at peace with their neighbours.

index.title: Rest of Europe 1946–Present
index.content:
Rest of Europe 1946–Present
A narrative-research knowledge base on continental European history from the end of the Second World War and the postwar settlement through the Cold War division of the continent, decolonisation, the collapse of the communist states, and the reordering of Europe to the present day. The United Kingdom is treated separately in its own wiki. Pages are grounded in the deposited source corpus — French (de Gaulle’s Discours et messages, Zancarini-Fournel, Bantigny), Spanish (Tusell), German (Winkler, Jäger & Link, Weber’s GDR documents, Kowalczuk), European-integration (Moravcsik, the Cambridge History of the EU), Italian (Mammarella, Gentiloni Silveri, Perrone on Mattei), and Soviet/Russian (the История СССР, История КПСС, Gromyko-Ponomarev, Pikhoya, Yurchak, Medinsky-Torkunov).
Narrative arc
The postwar settlement and the Cold War division of Europe opened with reconstruction and the hardening of two blocs — the iron curtain and the cold-war confrontation of world-socialist-system and the West. France rebuilt under the weak fourth-republic while de Gaulle waited through his traversée du désert, then returned in may-1958-crisis to found the fifth-republic, settle the algerian-war-1954-62, and pursue a policy of national independence. Germany was divided into two states, the Federal Republic under Adenauer’s Westintegration and the GDR under the SED, whose Stalinization climaxed in east-german-uprising-1953 and the building-berlin-wall-1961. Italy became a republic and, under centrismo and the DC, anchored itself in the Atlantic alliance. Spain stayed frozen in francoism until the dictator’s death.
The two Germanies and the era of détente saw the FRG’s sozialmarktwirtschaft and wirtschaftswunder, Brandt’s new-ostpolitik-1969-73, and the Schmidt years (the german-autumn-1977) even as the GDR drifted toward crisis. European integration advanced from the treaty-of-rome-1957 through the european-monetary-system-1979, the single-european-act-1986, and the maastricht-treaty-1992 toward the euro. France passed from the trente glorieuses through may-1968 to the Mitterrand presidency and cohabitation. Italy moved from centro-sinistra through the anni di piombo — the moro-kidnapping-1978 — to the Tangentopoli collapse. Spain made the Transition to democracy.
The end of the USSR and the reordering of Europe followed from the stagnation of the Brezhnev era and the perestroika-1985-91 of Gorbachev — the chernobyl-1986, the august-putsch-1991, and the dissolution-ussr-1991. The fall-of-berlin-wall-1989 and german-reunification-1990 ended the division of Germany; the eastern eastern-enlargement-2004 and the euro-crisis-2010 reshaped the Union. The Russian Federation under Yeltsin moved through the russian-constitutional-crisis-1993 and russian-default-1998 to the consolidation of the vertical-of-power under vladimir-putin.
How to read

Start with the major events (postwar reconstruction, 1956, 1961, 1968, 1975–78, 1989–91, 1992).
Read entities as continuous political biographies tied to those crises.
Use concepts for structures that span decades (cold-war, fifth-republic, ostpolitik, european-integration, centrismo, developed-socialism).
Every page ends with a Sources section pointing at the underlying books.
Native-language glosses follow the house conventions.
