sources-map.title: Sources Map
sources-map.content:
Sources Map
This page maps the wiki’s source pages by what they cover. It will grow as sources are ingested.
France / Fifth Republic

Charles de Gaulle — Discours et Messages, Tome 2 : Dans l’attente (1946-1958) (1970) — the second volume of the collected edition of de Gaulle’s speeches, messages and press conferences, covering his withdrawal from power after January 1946, the campaign against the draft constitution of the Fourth Republic and the Bayeux declaration of June 1946, the foundation and campaigns of the R.P.F. (1947–1955), and the long “traversée du désert” to the eve of the return of May 1958; the General’s own voice on France under the Fourth Republic.
Charles de Gaulle — Discours et Messages, Tome 3 : Avec le renouveau (1958-1962) (1970) — the third volume of the collected edition of de Gaulle’s speeches, messages and press conferences, covering the return to power of May 1958, the drafting and adoption of the Constitution of the Fifth Republic (autumn 1958), his election and installation as President, the Algerian war and the first phase of decolonisation of the French Community, and the foreign and defence policy of 1959–1962; the President’s own voice on the founding of the Fifth Republic.
Charles de Gaulle — Discours et Messages, Tome 4 : Pour l’effort (1962-1965) (1970) — the fourth volume of the collected edition, covering the consolidation of the Fifth Republic and the October 1962 referendum on the election of the President by universal suffrage, the settlement of the Algerian question, the German tour and the Franco-German treaty of January 1963, the policy of national independence, the Latin-American tour of 1965 and the presidential re-election of December 1965; the President’s own voice on the middle years of the Fifth Republic.
Charles de Gaulle — Discours et Messages, Tome 5 : Vers le terme (1966-1969) (1970) — the fifth and final volume of the collected edition, covering the departure from the integrated command of NATO and the policy of national independence, the Moscow visit of 1966, the “live Quebec” affair of July 1967, the Polish, Romanian and Turkish visits, the crisis of May 1968 and the dissolution of the Assembly, and the retirement of General de Gaulle after the referendum of April 1969; the President’s own voice on the closing years of the Fifth Republic and the end of his presidency.

France / 1945 to the present — synthesis

Michelle Zancarini-Fournel — La France du temps présent (1945-2005) (2010) — the modern scholarly synthesis of the French “temps présent” in the Cornette Histoire de France, covering reconstruction (1944–1951), the Fourth Republic and the “transition modernisatrice”, the Algerian war, the founding of the Fifth Republic (1958–1968), May 1968 and its traces, and the crises, political responses and recompositions of 1975–2005; continuous social, cultural, economic and political history, complementary to (and in dialogue with) the de Gaulle Discours et Messages.
Ludivine Bantigny — La France à l’heure du monde. De 1981 à nos jours (2013) — volume 10 of the Histoire de la France contemporaine series, a synthesis of France from the 1981 Mitterrand election to the near-present written from a “planetary” angle: the Mitterrand years, the cohabitations and the Sarkozy presidency; globalisation, “néolibéralisme”, the ambiguities of Europe and France in the world; work, gender, the crisis of the “creuset” and the territories; and the cultural imagination of the “ère planétaire”.

Spain / Dictatorship and Transition

Javier Tusell — Historia de España en el siglo XX, III. La dictadura de Franco (2000) — the third volume of Tusell’s four-volume history, the continuous political, social and cultural history of the Franco dictatorship from 1 April 1939 to the dictator’s death in November 1975: the fascist temptation and wartime alignment (1939–1951), the years of consensus and economic opening (1951–1965), and the developmentalism, apertura and tardofranquismo of 1966–1975.
Javier Tusell — Historia de España en el siglo XX, IV. La transición democrática y el gobierno socialista (2000) — the fourth and final volume, covering the democratic Transition from Franco’s death (1975) — the third wave of democratisation, Juan Carlos, Arias, Suárez, the political reform law, the Constitution of 1978, the nationalisms, the 1979 elections, the fall of Suárez and 23-F, Calvo-Sotelo and the crisis of the centre, the PSOE victory of October 1982 — and the Socialist governments of Felipe González to the loss of the majority in 1989–1993.

Germany / Federal Republic (West Germany)

Hermann Weber (Hrsg.) — DDR, Dokumente zur Geschichte der Deutschen Demokratischen Republik 1945–1985 (1986) — a comprehensive source collection of 234 documents covering the whole history of the German Democratic Republic (dtv, München, Originalausgabe 1986; ISBN 3-423-02953-6; 476 pp.), edited by Hermann Weber, the leading Western scholar of GDR history (University of Mannheim). Eight chronological chapters each with an Einleitung and numbered documents: 1. Die Vorgeschichte der DDR 1945–1949 (Dok. 1–77 — the Soviet occupation zone, the SMAD, the SED fusion, land reform, the drift toward a separate state); 2. Stalinisierung der DDR 1949–1953 (Dok. 78–111 — the founding of the GDR, the Gleichschaltung and repression culminating in the uprising of 17 June 1953); 3. Der Ausbau des neuen Systems 1953–1961 (Dok. 112–146 — the post-Stalin “thaw”, Ulbricht against the inner-party opposition, the building of the Wall on 13 August 1961); 4. Die Festigung der DDR 1961–1965 (Dok. 147–161 — consolidation, the NÖS economic reforms); 5. Ulbrichts Modellversuche 1966–1970 (Dok. 162–180 — Ulbricht’s experiments and the Prague Spring crisis of 1968); 6. Anpassung an die UdSSR 1971–1975 (Dok. 181–205 — the change of leadership to Honecker and the closer alignment with the USSR that made the Ostpolitik détente with the Federal Republic possible); 7. Krisenhafte Entwicklung 1976–1980 (Dok. 206–216 — economic difficulty, dissent and emigration, the expatriation of Wolf Biermann 1976); 8. Probleme der DDR 1981–1985 (Dok. 217–234 — the X. Party Congress of April 1981, Honecker’s “Einheit von Wirtschafts- und Sozialpolitik”, the personality cult). Appendix: Zeittafel, Verzeichnis der Dokumente mit Quellennachweisen, Personenregister. The East-German counterpart to the West-German volumes in this section; built entirely from the local PDF (no further internet fetch).
II: Republik im Wandel 1974–1982, Die Ära Schmidt (1986) — the contemporary-history volume (Band 5/II) of the standard five-volume Geschichte der Bundesrepublik Deutschland (ed. Bracher, Eschenburg, Fest, Jäckel; Deutsche Verlags-Anstalt, Stuttgart / F. A. Brockhaus, Mannheim; set ISBN 978-3-421-06731-9), covering the era of Federal Chancellor Helmut Schmidt (1974–1982): Wolfgang Jäger’s Die Innenpolitik der sozial-liberalen Koalition 1974–1982 (pp. 9–274 — the first and second Schmidt/Genscher cabinets, economic crisis-management, the 1976 and 1980 Bundestag elections, the party system, terrorism at its height and the German Autumn, the nuclear-energy protest and the Greens, the trade unions and churches, the break of the SPD–FDP coalition and the change of government to Kohl in October 1982, and the domestic-political balance-sheet of the Schmidt era); Werner Link’s Außen- und Deutschlandpolitik in der Ära Schmidt 1974–1982 (pp. 275–432 — stabilisation and crisis-management, the European Monetary System and the European direct elections of 1979, the Ostpolitik in the phase of détente and relations with the Soviet Union, co-ordination difficulties with the USA, the “Europeanisation” through German–French co-operation, the German–German relations and the Uckermark summit of December 1981, and the worldwide dimension of UN policy and the Third World); and Joachim C. Fest’s closing essay Die deutsche Frage: Das offene Dilemma (pp. 433–446) plus Nachwort and Anhang (Zeittafel, Wahlen und Regierungen, Auswahlbibliographie, Anmerkungen, registers).
Heinrich August Winkler — Der lange Weg nach Westen, Band 2: Deutsche Geschichte vom «Dritten Reich» bis zur Wiedervereinigung (2000) — the second volume of Heinrich August Winkler’s acclaimed two-part German history (Verlag C.H. Beck, München, first ed. 2000; ISBN 3-406-49524-9 Band II). A “Problemgeschichte” centred on the relation of democracy and nation, and on the German “Sonderwege” and their ending: Einleitung (the author’s method and values); 1. Die deutsche Katastrophe: 1933–1945 (the Nazi seizure of power, the Gleichschaltung, the SS, war and the Holocaust); 2. Demokratie und Diktatur: 1945–1961 (the post-1945 German self-interrogation, occupation and division, the founding of the FRG and GDR, Adenauer’s Westintegration, the Wirtschaftswunder and rearmament, the Berlin Wall); 3. Zwei Staaten, eine Nation: 1961–1973 (the FRG under Erhard and the Grand Coalition, 1968, and Brandt’s neue Ostpolitik — the Moscow, Warsaw and Grundlagenvertrag treaties); 4. Annaherung und Entfremdung: 1973–1989 (the Schmidt era, economic crisis, terrorism and the German Autumn, the GDR’s Abgrenzung, the “Wende” of 1982, the German debates of the 1980s); 5. Einheit in Freiheit: 1989/90 (the collapse of the GDR, the fall of the Wall, the Two-plus-Four process, reunification); and the closing essay Abschied von den Sonderwegen: Rückblick und Ausblick plus Anhang (Abkürzungsverzeichnis, Anmerkungen, Personenregister).
Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk — Die Übernahme: Wie Ostdeutschland Teil der Bundesrepublik wurde (2019) — an avowed essay (a Versuch) by the East German historian Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk (Verlag C.H. Beck, München, first published August 2019, for the thirtieth anniversary of the fall of the Wall; ISBN 978-3-406-74020-6 Print, 978-3-406-74021-3 E-Book; 8,033 lines of extracted text), explaining “how our present has become historical”: the personal opening (Zwischen Aufbruch und Abbruch, framed by his father’s and his wife’s father’s biographies) and essay proper (Der Essay), then twenty-two topical chapters — Der letzte Republikgeburtstag (7 October 1989); Unmittelbare Folgen des Mauerfalls; Vom Runden Tisch zu freien Wahlen; Neue Erfahrung: Arbeitslosigkeit; Der Beitritt: alternativlos?; Was wäre wenn …?; In was für einer Verfassung?; Wer sind Ostdeutsche?; Ostdeutsche als «Andere»; Die Forderung: «Anpassung»; Die Angepassten; Die Hauptstadtdebatte; Stagnation; Die Treuhand; Die Eigentumsfrage; Die Landwirtschaft; Der ökonomische Kollaps als Kulturkampf; Das Unverständnis für Ostdeutschland; Das Beschäftigungsproblem; Die kulturelle Ausgrenzung; Mobilität als Problem; Rentenprobleme; Gewinnerinnen oder Verliererinnen?; Neue Benachteiligungen; Der Elitenaustausch an den Universitäten; Ost-Eliten im vereinigten Deutschland; Irgendwie alle! (the Academy of Arts fusion and Heiner Müller’s “Eroberung, Unterwerfung, nicht Vereinigung”); Gesellschaftspolitische Dimensionen der Aufarbeitung; Demokratie ohne Demokraten (87.5% of the GDR population without personal experience of a functioning democracy); Antisemitismus; Illiberale Einstellungen; Nationalismus; Rassismus; Medien in Ostdeutschland; Wahlen im Osten; and the closing Zwischen 1989: Hoffnungslosigkeit und 1990: Hoffnungen — plus Danksagung, Anmerkungen, Literaturhinweise, Personenregister. A critical East German view of the “Übernahme” (takeover) of the GDR by the Federal Republic and of the eastern German present — the natural post-reunification sequel to the Winkler and Weber volumes.

European Union / European Integration

Andrew Moravcsik — The Choice for Europe: Social Purpose and State Power from Messina to Maastricht (1998) — the foundational statement of the “liberal intergovernmentalist” theory of European integration (Cornell University Press, Ithaca, 1998; Routledge, London & New York, 1999; ISBN 0-8014-3509-9 Cornell, 1-85728-191-8 cased / 1-85728-192-6 paper Routledge; 22,790 lines of extracted text). Moravcsik argues that European integration is best explained as a series of rational choices by national leaders, responding to the economic interests of powerful domestic constituents (above all commercial interests), the relative power of states, and the role of international institutions in making commitments credible. He tests this account across the five most salient negotiations in EC history: the Treaty of Rome (1955–58), the consolidation of the customs union and the CAP (1958–69), the European Monetary System (1969–83), the Single European Act (1984–88), and the Maastricht Treaty on EMU (1988–91) — concluding that commercial and economic motivations dominated national preference formation, that bargaining outcomes reflected asymmetrical interdependence, and that institutional delegation (the pooling and delegation of sovereignty) served the purpose of credible commitment, while geopolitical threats, federalist ideas, technocratic imperatives and supranational entrepreneurship played a decidedly secondary role. Chapters: Introduction (The Choice for Europe); 1. Theorizing European Integration; 2. Finding the Thread: The Treaties of Rome, 1955–1958; 3. Grain and Grandeur: Consolidating the Common Market, 1958–1969; 4. Divergence and Convergence: Toward Monetary Integration, 1969–1983; 5. Relaunching Integration: The Single European Act, 1984–1988; 6. Economic and Monetary Union: Negotiating the Maastricht Treaty, 1988–1991; 7. European Integration in Retrospect. The cent… [truncated]
Mathieu Segers & Steven Van Hecke (eds.) — The Cambridge History of the European Union, Volume II: European Integration Inside-Out (2024) — the second volume of the two-volume Cambridge History of the European Union (Cambridge University Press, first published 2024; two-volume set ISBN 978-1-009-28437-0; Vol. II hardback ISBN 978-1-108-47893-9; DOI 10.1017/9781108781480; 33,406 lines of extracted text), examining the EU from an “inside-out” perspective — the internal developments that shaped the integration process. Organised thematically rather than as a strict timeline. Editorial “Reflections on the History and Historiography of European Integration” (Segers & Van Hecke) + three parts with 24 chapters by 25 contributors: Part I Milestones: Treaties and Treaty Changes (1. Early Forms of European Unity, Bossuat; 2. From Messina and Rome to the Single European Act, Gehler; 3. The Making of the European Union, Vanhoonacker; 4. From Maastricht and Copenhagen to Amsterdam and Nice, Dinan; 5. The Constitution Project, Lisbon and Beyond, Monar; 6. Moving beyond British Exceptionalism, Ludlow); Part II Instruments of Integration (7. In the Name of Social Stability: The European Payments Union, Steehouder; 8. Competition versus Planning, Warlouzet; 9. Commercial Banks, the Eurodollar Market and the Beginnings of Monetary Integration, Altamura; 10. From the Werner Report to the Start of EMU, Zimmermann; 11. The Euro Area Crisis, Verdun; 12. The Institutional and Legal Culture of European Integration, Bajon; 13. The Formation of the Migration Regime of the EU, Comte; 14. The Constitutional Dimension, Jakab & Kirchmair; 15. EU Enlargement: Origins and Practice, Maresceau); Part III Narratives and Outcomes (16. A Global Perspective on European Cooperation and Integration since 1918, Richard; 17. War, Peace and Memory: Franco-German Reconciliation, Germond; 18. The ‘Saints’ of European Integration, Gehler; 19. The EU and the Narrative of Prosperity, Hiepel; 20. Changing Europe’s Economic History, Berend; 21. The EU and the Narrative of Solidarity, Ross; 22. European Solidarity: The Difficult Art of Managing Interdependence, Crespy & Verschueren; 23. Ideologies of EU Democracy since 1950, Sternberg; 24. Democratic Challenges since Maastricht, Wolfs). The editors stress that every chapter builds on original multinational and/or transnational archival research, stretching beyond “silo studies” toward a richer, more comprehensive, interdisciplinary picture.

Italy / Republic

Giuseppe Mammarella — L’Italia contemporanea (1943-1998) (2000) — a classic single-volume scholarly history of Italy in the “Le vie della civiltà” series, from the fall of fascism and the war (1943–1948), through the centrismo (1948–1958), the centro-sinistra (1958–1974), the end of centro-sinistra and the 1980s, to “verso la seconda Repubblica” (1989–1998): the elections of 1948, the “legge truffa” of 1953, the “apertura a sinistra”, the strategy of tension and the “hot autumn”, the “compromesso storico”, the 1976 elections, the return to the Cold War, the fateful 1989, the annus horribilis of 1992, Tangentopoli, and the governments of the left.
Umberto Gentiloni Silveri — Storia dell’Italia contemporanea (1943-2019) — a modern scholarly synthesis of contemporary Italian history from the summer of 1943 as a “theatre of war” to 2019: the fall of fascism, democracy, the referendum and the Constitution, the reasons of the “miracle”, the anni Settanta and the “funerale della Repubblica” (the Moro kidnapping), the beginning of the end, the fall of the Wall and Tangentopoli, the “transizione mancata” and the imperfect bipolarism, the eurozone, and Italy between rinascita and declino to the present.
Nico Perrone — Enrico Mattei (2012) — compact Il Mulino biography of Enrico Mattei (1906–1962): Agip after the Liberation, the founding of Eni/Snam (1953), Italian energy autonomy and oil diplomacy (Mediterranean, Africa, Soviet crude), Italo–American friction over hydrocarbons, and Mattei’s death in the Bascapè air disaster (27 October 1962); essential for the economic miracle and state enterprise under centrismo.

USSR / Communist Party of the Soviet Union

История СССР с древнейших времен до наших дней, Том 11: Советский Союз на пути к развитому социализму (1945–1961) (1980) — Volume 11 of the twelve-volume academic История СССР (Наука, Москва, 1980), edited by И. Б. Берхин, covering the Soviet Union from the end of the Second World War through the fourth five-year plan and postwar reconstruction (1945–1950) and the transformation of the 1950s, to the XXI and XXII Congresses and the 1961 Programme for building communism (1945–1961).
История КПСС (History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union), 6th supplemented edition (1982) — the official party-history textbook by an authorial collective led by академик Б. Н. Пономарев (Политиздат, Москва, 1982; 784 pp.), a single-volume narrative from the origins of Russian Marxism (1883, Plekhanov’s Liberation of Labour group) through the XXVI Party Congress (23 February – 3 March 1981). Chapters in this wiki’s span (XVI–XX, 1945–1981): postwar reconstruction and the formation of the world socialist system (XVI), developed socialism and the Congresses from XIX to XXII (XVII), the leading role of the party and the socialist community 1962–1970 (XVIII), developed socialist society and the Programme of Peace 1971–1980 (XIX), and the XXVI Congress (XX).
Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin: A Short Biography (2nd ed., 1948) — the official short biography of Stalin (Институт Маркса — Энгельса — Ленина при ЦК ВКП(б), OGIZ — State Publishing House of Political Literature, Moscow, 1948), from his birth in Gori (1879) through the Great Patriotic War and postwar reconstruction; its final chapter (XI) carries the narrative into 1946, the post-war reconstruction and the elections to the Supreme Soviet of February 1946.
История внешней политики СССР 1917–1980, Том второй (1945–1980 гг.) (1981) — Volume Two of the two-volume official history of Soviet foreign policy, edited by А. А. Громыко and Б. Н. Пономарев (Наука, Москва, 4th rev. ed., 1981; Institute of History of the USSR), covering Soviet foreign policy from the end of the Second World War and the postwar settlement (Ch. XIV) through the German question and the division of Germany, the Korean and Indochinese wars, disarmament and the nuclear test ban, the Hungarian events and the Suez crisis, decolonisation and aid to the peoples of Asia and Africa, relations with the capitalist states and the policy of détente, and the Peace Programmes of the XXIV and XXV Party Congresses to the close of the 1970s (Ch. XXXII, 1976–1980).

USSR / Post-Soviet Russia

Пихоя Р. Г. — Москва. Кремль. Власть. Две истории одной страны. Россия на изломе тысячелетий (1985–2005) (2007) — Rudolf Pikhoya’s political history of Soviet and Russian power, 1985–2005, in two parts: «Закат империи» (The Decline of the Empire), covering Gorbachev’s accession, «ускорение» and perestroika, the Chernobyl disaster, glasnost and managed democratisation, the rise of the nationality question and Nagorny Karabakh, the elections of the USSR people’s deputies, the Russian factor and the Declaration of State Sovereignty, the “war of laws”, the referendum and Novo-Ogaryovo, the August putsch and the collapse of the CPSU, and the analysis of why the Soviet Union fell apart (1985–1991); and «Россия в поисках себя» (Russia in Search of Itself), covering the market reforms, the political-constitutional crisis of 1992–1993 and the new Constitution, the “tired” Russia of 1994–1999, the default of 1998, and the building of the vertical of power under Putin to 2005.
Юрчак А. — Это было навсегда, пока не кончилось. Последнее советское поколение (2014) — Alexei Yurchak’s anthropological study of the last Soviet generation (НЛО, Москва, 2014; Princeton University Press original 2005), an analysis of the system of late socialism (mid-1950s to mid-1980s, including the gap years 1980–1985) through the performative shift of the Soviet authoritative discourse and the practice of «вненаходимость» (vnenakhodimost, being simultaneously inside and outside the discursive field of the system): the hegemony of form, ideology turned inside out, the “imagined West”, Western rock and «Разноцветный коммунизм», and the irony of vnenakhodimost (necro-aesthetics, stiob, the anecdote); its Заключение carries the argument through perestroika to the collapse of the Soviet system (1985–1991).
Мединский В. Р., Торкунов А. В. — История России. 1945 год — начало XXI века. 11 класс (2024) — the official Russian school textbook (Просвещение, Москва, 3-е изд., обновл., 2024), a survey of the history of the USSR and the Russian Federation from 1945 to the early 2020s: postwar reconstruction and the early Cold War (1945–1953), the Khrushchev thaw (1953–1964), the Brezhnev period of “developed socialism” (1964–1985), perestroika and the collapse of the USSR (1985–1991), and the Russian Federation from 1992 through the 1990s, the Putin era, and the events of the early 2020s including the special military operation (СВО).

sources/bantigny-la-france-a-l-heure-du-.title: Ludivine Bantigny — La France à l'heure du monde. De 1981 à nos jours (2013)
sources/bantigny-la-france-a-l-heure-du-.content:
Ludivine Bantigny — La France à l’heure du monde. De 1981 à nos jours
Full bibliographic citation — Ludivine Bantigny, La France à l’heure du monde. De 1981 à nos jours, volume 10 of the Histoire de la France contemporaine collection (direction scientifique: Johann Chapoutot). Éditions du Seuil, Paris; copyright © Éditions du Seuil, novembre 2013 (digital ePUB produced by Nord Compo). ISBN 978-2-02-114369-0. French text, 18,413 lines of extracted plain text.





























AuthorLudivine Bantigny — French historian, maîtresse de conférences at the Université de Rouen-Normandie, specialist in contemporary political, social and cultural history; author of Le plus bel âge? Jeunes et jeunesse en France (Fayard, 2007) and co-director (with Ivan Jablonka) of Jeunesse oblige (PUF, 2009); associated with the équipe of the Centre d’histoire de Sciences PoEditionÉditions du Seuil, novembre 2013; volume 10 of Histoire de la France contemporaine (collection directed by Johann Chapoutot); ISBN 978-2-02-114369-0; digital ePUB by Nord CompoStructureIntroduction (L’histoire d’un temps vivant) + four parts in fifteen chapters + conclusion (Faire histoire encore) + annexes (chronologie indicative, bibliographie sélective, index, remerciements); 18,413 lines of extracted plain textPeriod1981 (the election of François Mitterrand, the alternance) to the near-present of the book’s writing (c. 2013) — the Mitterrand years, the cohabitations, the Sarkozy presidency, and the France of the “ère planétaire”: globalisation, Europe, the crisis of the “creuset,” the recompositions of work, gender and territory, and the cultural imagination of the eraNoteA synthetic history of contemporary France written from a deliberately “planetary” angle: the book insists that post-1981 France can only be understood through the lens of mondialisation and the French relationship to a changing world. Its framing — the “ère planétaire,” the fragility of politics, the “néolibéralisme,” the crise du creuset, gender and daily life, and the cultural imagination — makes it the French counterpart, in the wiki, to the Zancarini-Fournel La France du temps présent (1945–2005), extending the French narrative from 1981 onward
The text is 18,413 lines, extracted from the EPUB container (clean text layer; no OCR required). French text clean; no U+FFFD replacement characters.
Content Summary
Introduction — L’histoire d’un temps vivant. The volume opens against the 1867 dictum of the historian Jules Thiénot that history begins only when an epoch is dead; Bantigny reverses it to write the history of a living time. The book covers the period from 1981 (Mitterrand’s election) to “nos jours” and poses the question of what “fait époque” — of the tension between the old and the new, tradition and transformation. Its organising horizon is the “ère planétaire”: globalisation, the fading of frontiers, the dominance of technologies and networks. Three framing essays structure the introduction: Les frontières de l’ère planétaire (the nation questioned by a world that has become the best criterion for understanding the new era; France at once “pétrie de sa tradition” and “en retard sur l’horaire planétaire”); La modernité: avancées, détours et arrière-cours (modernity with its advances, detours and dark corners); and La fin des fins? (the end of ends — the exhaustion of teleological readings of history).
PREMIÈRE PARTIE — Politiques de crise et crises du politique
Chapitre I — Des roses et des épines
The first chapter opens the political narrative at the election of 10 May 1981 and the “état de grâce.” Sections: Les nouveaux maîtres du temps (the new masters of time — the Mitterrand presidency and its break with the previous period); Quels fers de lance pour la croissance? (the economic programme of the 1981–1983 moment, the nationalisations, the “relance” and its reversal); L’éducation à la « modernité » (education in the service of modernity).
Chapitre II — Les partages du pouvoir
The divisions and shared spaces of political power. Sections: La droite revient (the return of the right); Vague à l’âme pour gauche au pouvoir (the malaise of the left in power); D’une cohabitation à l’autre: alternances sans alternatives (from one cohabitation to the next — alternations without alternatives, the 1986, 1993 and 1997 cohabitations).
Chapitre III — Bouillons de ruptures
Breaks and ruptures in the political field. Sections: La norme des réformes (the norm of reform); Tensions et contestations (tensions and contestations — the 1995 “grève par procuration,” the sans-papiers movement, the dissolution of 1997); Le « sarkozysme » ou la droite « décomplexée » (Sarkozy’s presidency and the “uninhibited” right, 2007–2012).
Chapitre IV — Ambiguïtés sur l’échiquier
The ambiguities of the political chessboard. Sections: Passes d’armes à gauche (the internal duels of the left); Les droites et leur extrême (the rights and their extreme — the Front national, its rise and its electoral anchors); Politiques du triangle (the triangular political geometry of the three-way contest).
Chapitre V — La politique est leur affaire
Politics as the business of ordinary people. Sections: États de disgrâce (the discredit of the parties and the political class, abstention); Le vent se lève: nouvelles formes de politisation (new forms of political engagement — associations, mobilisations, alter-globalism); Les intellectuels et l’histoire au présent (intellectuals and history in the present).
DEUXIÈME PARTIE — La France du nouveau monde
Chapitre VI — Domination et contestations du « néolibéralisme »
The French encounter with neoliberalism. Sections: La loi des marchés (the law of the markets); L’impuissance de la puissance? (the powerlessness of power — the constraints of globalisation on the French state); Critiques de crise (critiques of the crisis — alter-globalism, ATTAC, the 2008 financial crisis).
Chapitre VII — Les équivoques de l’Europe
France and European construction, in all its ambiguities. Sections: Les faiseurs d’Europe (the makers of Europe); Morne plaine: enthousiasmes et désillusions (the changing French enthusiasm for and disenchantment with Europe, the Maastricht referendum of 1992, the 2005 referendum on the Constitutional Treaty); Turbulences et impuissances (the turbulence of the eurozone crisis).
Chapitre VIII — Au risque du monde
France in the world. Sections: Défaire Yalta? (the end of the Cold War order); Un nouvel ordre du monde (the new world order after 1989); Dans l’Occident désorienté (France in the disoriented West — the Gulf war, the wars of the post-9/11 era, France’s interventions and its place in the Atlantic alliance).
TROISIÈME PARTIE — Vivre ensemble?
Chapitre IX — Genres de vie
Ways of life and the intimate. Sections: La vie, l’amour, la mort (life, love, death — the demographic and family transformations); Hommes, femmes: nouveaux modes d’emploi (the recomposition of gender relations); Les usages de l’âge (the uses of age — youth, ageing, the generations).
Chapitre X — Travail: les mots et les maux
Work in the contemporary period. Sections: Le capitalisme des fragilités (the capitalism of fragilities — unemployment, precarity, the “nouveau monde économique”); Le sexe du travail (the gendered division of labour, the feminisation and segregation of work); De haute lutte: les intensités de la conflictualité (the intensities of social conflict — strikes and mobilisations).
Chapitre XI — La crise du creuset
The crisis of the French “creuset” (melting pot). Sections: L’ère du soupçon: haro sur l’immigration (the era of suspicion and the campaign against immigration); L’inégalité des chances (the inequality of opportunity, the banlieues, the “ghetto” and its representation); Nouveaux suspects d’altérité (new suspects of otherness — Islam and the laïcité debates, the foulard affairs, the “identité nationale” question).
Chapitre XII — Au miroir des territoires
France through the mirror of its territories. Sections: Espèces d’espaces: les bouleversements des rapports villes/campagnes (the upheaval of urban–rural relations); Lieux et non-lieux communs (places and non-places); Habiter: si loin, si près (housing, mobility, peri-urban France).
QUATRIÈME PARTIE — Imaginaires de l’ère planétaire
Chapitre XIII — Écrire le temps
The writing of time. Sections: L’écho du monde et les fils du quotidien (the echo of the world in everyday life); Temps incertains (uncertain times); Coups de théâtre: la scène et ses passages de témoins (the theatre of politics and its changes of guard).
Chapitre XIV — Regards-caméra
The gaze of the camera. Sections: Grand spectacle (the great spectacle); Le monde à bras-le-corps (the world grasped head-on); Cinémonde (French cinema and the world).
Chapitre XV — Mises en culture
The putting-into-culture of the era. Sections: Faire écrans (making screens — television and the audiovisual); Airs du temps (the airs of the time — music, the “variétés,” the “chanson”); Sport national (football and national sport — the 1998 World Cup, “Black-Blanc-Beur,” Zidane).
CONCLUSION — Faire histoire encore
Le changement: maintenant ou jamais? The choice of change. Faire société (making society). L’histoire faite monde (history become world). Le sacre du présent? (the consecration of the present). Sens de l’histoire (the sense of history). Un avenir pour le futur (a future for the future). The conclusion reflects on the meaning of writing contemporary history in the planetary era — the historian’s task, the question of the present, and the open future.
Annexes

Chronologie indicative — a chronological frame of the period 1981 to the 2010s.
Bibliographie sélective — a selective bibliography organised thematically: ouvrages généraux; évolutions de la vie politique; cultures politiques; politisations et formes de l’engagement; mondialisation et globalisation; évolutions économiques et pratiques du néolibéralisme; construction européenne et rapports à l’Europe; politique étrangère; groupes sociaux et enjeux de société; travail, relations et conflictualités de travail; âges et générations; sexe et genre; immigration et crise du « creuset français »; modes de vie et pratiques du quotidien; territoires et paysages; pratiques culturelles; temps, usages du passé et imaginaires du futur.
Index — subject index.
Remerciements — acknowledgements, including to colleagues who read chapters (Antoine de Baecque, Christine Bard, Raphaëlle Branche, Quentin Deluermoz, Ivan Jablonka, Marc Lazar, Enzo Traverso, Michelle Zancarini-Fournel, among others).

Key Data Points

















































AttributeDetailAuthorLudivine BantignyTitleLa France à l’heure du monde. De 1981 à nos joursSeriesHistoire de la France contemporaine, volume 10; collection directed by Johann ChapoutotPublishedÉditions du Seuil, novembre 2013 (© Seuil 2013; digital ePUB by Nord Compo)SourceEPUB container; clean French text layer; ISBN 978-2-02-114369-0Raw filewiki/raw/bantigny-la-france-a-l-heure-du-monde-1981-nos-jours-2013.txtLines18,413StructureIntroduction + four parts in fifteen chapters + conclusion + annexes (chronologie, bibliographie, index)Coverage1981 to the near-present (c. 2013) — Mitterrand years, cohabitations, Sarkozy presidency; globalisation, Europe, the crisis of the creuset, work and gender, territories, and the cultural imaginationSignificanceThe continuation of the wiki’s French narrative from 1981 onward — the third French volume, extending the de Gaulle Discours et Messages (T2–T5) and the Zancarini-Fournel La France du temps présent (1945–2005) into the Mitterrand and post-Mitterrand era
Relationship to the Wiki
Bantigny completes the French strand of the wiki. Where de Gaulle’s Discours et Messages (T2–T5) supply the first-person voice of the founder of the Fifth Republic (1946–1969), and Zancarini-Fournel’s La France du temps présent (1945–2005) gives the critical scholarly synthesis of reconstruction, the Algerian war, the Fifth Republic, May 1968 and the post-1973 crises, Bantigny carries the story forward from the 1981 alternance to the early twenty-first century. Her deliberately “planetary” framing — the era of globalisation, the “néolibéralisme,” the crisis of the creuset, gender and everyday life, and the cultural imagination — complements the Zancarini-Fournel volume as the French pillar of the wiki’s postwar continental coverage, read alongside the two Tusell volumes for Spain and the Italy volumes of Gentiloni Silveri and Mammarella.

sources/cambridge-history-european-union.title: The Cambridge History of the European Union, Volume II: European Integration Inside-Out
sources/cambridge-history-european-union.content:
The Cambridge History of the European Union, Volume II: European Integration Inside-Out
Full bibliographic citation — Mathieu Segers & Steven Van Hecke (eds.), The Cambridge History of the European Union, Volume II: European Integration Inside-Out, Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, first published 2024; two-volume set ISBN 978-1-009-28437-0 Hardback, Volume I ISBN 978-1-108-49040-5 Hardback, Volume II ISBN 978-1-108-47893-9 Hardback; DOI 10.1017/9781108781480; © Cambridge University Press & Assessment 2024. English text; extracted plain text of 33,406 lines.





























EditorsMathieu Segers — Professor of Contemporary European History, Maastricht University; member of The Netherlands Scientific Council for Government Policy (WRR) and the SSH Board of the Dutch Research Council (NWO). Steven Van Hecke — Professor in Comparative and EU Politics, Public Governance Institute, University of LeuvenSeriesThe Cambridge History of the European Union — two volumes edited by Segers and Van Hecke: Vol. I European Integration Outside-In, Vol. II European Integration Inside-Out. The volumes adopt a diachronic, multidisciplinary and multi-institutional approach, presenting some fifty essays from experts across the fieldStructureEditorial “Reflections on the History and Historiography of European Integration” + three parts (Part I Milestones: Treaties and Treaty Changes; Part II Instruments of Integration; Part III Narratives and Outcomes) containing 24 chapters by 25 contributors + Index; extracted plain text of 33,406 linesPeriodThe full history of European integration from the first steps and early forms of European unity to the present day (from the Pan-Europa movement and the 1918 settlement, through the Treaty of Rome, the Single European Act, Maastricht, Amsterdam, Nice, Lisbon and Brexit, to the euro-area, migration, Covid-19 and Russia–Ukraine crises)NoteThe second volume of the Cambridge History of the European Union, examining the EU from an “inside-out” perspective — the internal developments that shaped the integration process. Unlike a strict chronological narrative, the volume is organised thematically: Part I traces the principles defining integration through the treaties and their changes over time (with Brexit a core milestone); Part II considers the instruments within the architecture of integration, with special focus on policies, money/the euro and enlargement; Part III concentrates on the narratives surrounding integration — the concepts, goals and ideas (the “longue durée”, peace, European culture, religion and its absence, prosperity, solidarity and democracy) that did and did not speak to the hearts and minds of Europeans. The editors stress that every chapter builds on original multinational and/or transnational archival research, stretching beyond “silo studies” toward a richer, more comprehensive, interdisciplinary picture
Content Summary
Reflections on the History and Historiography of European Integration (Mathieu Segers & Steven Van Hecke). The editorial introduction. The editors survey the shifting scholarly effort to explain “why and how” of European integration — the “big questions” of ideas, interests and institutions — and argue that new disciplinary perspectives (beyond the usual suspects of history, political science, law and economics) are needed to rejuvenate the research in light of the transformations since “Maastricht”. They stress the continuing topicality of the classic questions: the position of reunited Germany in post-Cold War Europe (“the German Question”, renewed since the euro, migration and Covid-19 crises and the Russian war in Ukraine); the British relationship with the continent culminating in Brexit; and the geopolitical role of the EU vis-à-vis revisionist powers like Russia and China. The CHEU is presented as a diachronic, multidisciplinary and multi-actor reconceptualisation of integration history, its chapters based on original multinational and transnational archival research, and it revisits the big questions — why did Europeans integrate, and how does the resulting system work, with what outcomes.
Part I — Milestones: Treaties and Treaty Changes
Chapter 1: Early Forms of European Unity (Gérard Bossuat, Professor Emeritus, University of Cergy-Pontoise; Jean Monnet ad Personam Chair, History of European Unity). The pre-1945 and wartime origins of the idea and practice of European unity — the long genealogy of schemes for a united Europe before the Communities.
Chapter 2: From Messina and Rome to the Single European Act (Michael Gehler, Professor of History, University of Hildesheim). The treaty history from the Messina conference (1955) and the Treaties of Rome (1957) establishing the EEC and Euratom, through the consolidation of the 1960s and the crisis decades, to the Single European Act (1986) — the legal-constitutional milestones of the Community’s first three decades.
Chapter 3: The Making of the European Union (Sophie Vanhoonacker, Professor of European Governance, Maastricht University). The negotiation of the Treaty of Maastricht on European Union (1991) — the founding act of the EU, with the three pillars, EMU, and the new competences. (Contains Tables 3.1 and 3.2, key dates for the SEA and the Maastricht Treaty.)
Chapter 4: From Maastricht and Copenhagen to Amsterdam and Nice (Desmond Dinan, Professor of Public Policy, George Mason University). The treaty revisions of the 1990s — the accession process launched at Copenhagen (1993), the Amsterdam Treaty (1997) and the Nice Treaty (2000).
Chapter 5: The Constitution Project, Lisbon and Beyond (Jörg Monar, Professor, Vrije Universiteit Brussel / College of Europe). The failure of the Constitutional Treaty (2004–05 referenda) and the Lisbon Treaty (2007, in force 2009), and the further evolution of the Union’s constitutional order thereafter.
Chapter 6: Moving beyond British Exceptionalism (N. Piers Ludlow, Professor of International History, London School of Economics). Britain’s troubled relationship with European integration — from the EFTA years and the failed membership applications to membership and the eventual vote for Brexit — read against the grain of “British exceptionalism”.
Part II — Instruments of Integration
Money and Society. Chapter 7: In the Name of Social Stability: The European Payments Union (Jorrit Steehouder, historian). The European Payments Union (EPU, 1950–58), the postwar intra-European clearing and payments mechanism that laid the monetary foundations for European economic cooperation. Chapter 8: Competition versus Planning: A Battle That Shaped European Integration (Laurent Warlouzet, Professor of History, Sorbonne University). The contest between competition-policy liberalism and economic planning in shaping the European economic order. Chapter 9: Commercial Banks, the Eurodollar Market and the Beginnings of Monetary Integration (Carlo Edoardo Altamura, Swiss National Science Foundation Ambizione Fellow, Graduate Institute, Geneva). The role of private commercial banks and the Eurodollar market in the early monetary integration of the 1960s. Chapter 10: From the Werner Report to the Start of EMU (Hubert Zimmermann, Professor of International Relations, Philipps University Marburg). The monetary odyssey from the Werner Report (1970), through the “snake” and the EMS, to the start of Economic and Monetary Union. (Contains Figures 10.1–10.3: inflation rates 1969–80, EMS realignment rounds 1979–95, convergence of European interest rates prior to EMU.) Chapter 11: The Euro Area Crisis: From Pre-history to Aftermath (Amy Verdun, Professor of Political Science, University of Victoria). The euro-area crisis of the 2010s and its aftermath.
Challenges of Expansion: Protection and Security. Chapter 12: The Institutional and Legal Culture of European Integration (Philip Bajon, Max Planck Institute for Legal History and Legal Theory, Frankfurt). The distinctive institutional and legal culture of the EU. Chapter 13: The Formation of the Migration Regime of the EU (Emmanuel Comte, Senior Research Fellow, ELIAMEP; Vienna School of International Studies). The construction of the EU’s migration and asylum regime. Chapter 14: The Constitutional Dimension: Centralisation, Democratisation and the Rule of Law (András Jakab, University of Salzburg, and Lando Kirchmair, Bundeswehr University Munich). The constitutional development of the Union — centralisation, democratisation and the rule of law. Chapter 15: EU Enlargement: Origins and Practice (Marc Maresceau, Professor Emeritus, Ghent University). The enlargement of the Union from the Six to the Twenty-eight — its origins and practice.
Part III — Narratives and Outcomes
War and Peace. Chapter 16: A Global Perspective on European Cooperation and Integration since 1918 (Anne-Isabelle Richard, University of Leiden). European cooperation and integration in global perspective since the First World War. (Contains Figure 16.1: Coudenhove-Kalergi’s Paneuropa world map, 1923.) Chapter 17: War, Peace and Memory: Franco-German Reconciliation (Carine Germond, Nanyang Technological University). The narrative of war, peace and memory in the Franco-German reconciliation — the decline of the “hereditary enemies” narrative and the rise of the “couple franco-allemand” / “deutsch-französische Versöhnung” / “Franco-German engine” narratives. (Contains Figures 17.1–17.8: the quantitative history of these narratives in French-, German- and English-language literatures, and the Merkozy and Merkron media narratives 2008–22 and 2015–21.) Chapter 18: The ‘Saints’ of European Integration: From Visionaries to Architects (Michael Gehler). The founding figures of integration — from the “visionaries” (Monnet, Schuman, Adenauer, de Gasperi) to the “architects” of later decades.
Prosperity and Solidarity. Chapter 19: The EU and the Narrative of Prosperity (Claudia Hiepel, University of Duisburg-Essen). The EU’s self-narrative of prosperity and its limits. Chapter 20: Changing Europe’s Economic History (Ivan T. Berend, Distinguished Research Professor, UCLA). Europe’s economic history and its transformation — the divergence of central/eastern from northwestern Europe and the postwar convergence. (Contains Tables 20.1–20.5: per capita GDP 1870–1938 and postwar, Central Europe as a percentage of northwestern Europe, regional growth 1913–2013, and world HDI in 2016.) Chapter 21: The EU and the Narrative of Solidarity (Malcolm Ross, University of Sussex). The EU’s narrative of solidarity and its contested reality. Chapter 22: European Solidarity: The Difficult Art of Managing Interdependence (Amandine Crespy, Professor, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, and Nicolas Verschueren). The practical management of interdependence as the “difficult art” of European solidarity.
Democracy and Legitimacy. Chapter 23: Ideologies of EU Democracy since 1950 (Claudia Sternberg, University College London). The ideologies of EU democracy from the 1950s. Chapter 24: Democratic Challenges since Maastricht (Wouter Wolfs, University of Leuven). The democratic challenges of the Union since Maastricht — the persistent question of the EU’s democratic legitimacy.
Index (person and subject, p. 701 onwards).
Key Data Points

sources/de-gaulle-discours-et-messages-t.title: Charles de Gaulle — Discours et Messages, Tome 2 : Dans l'attente (1946-1958)
sources/de-gaulle-discours-et-messages-t.content:
Discours et Messages, Tome 2 : Dans l’attente (1946-1958)
Charles de Gaulle — Discours et messages, Tome II : Dans l’attente (Février 1946–Avril 1958). Librairie Plon, Paris, 1970; the present digital edition Plon / Édi8, 2014. The second of the five-tome collected edition of the speeches, messages and press conferences of General de Gaulle from 18 June 1940 to 28 April 1969, edited with the assistance of François Goguel; this volume covers the years of his withdrawal from power and of the R.P.F. (Rassemblement du peuple français).





























AuthorCharles de Gaulle (1890–1970) — French soldier and statesman, head of the Free French, head of the Provisional Government 1944–46, founder and first President of the Fifth Republic (1959–1969)EditionLibrairie Plon, 1970; digital edition Plon, a department of Édi8, 2014; EAN numérique 9782259228510; text established with the collaboration of M. François GoguelStructureNote de l’éditeur + note de l’éditeur pour le tome II + aide-mémoire historique + speeches, messages and press conferences arranged chronologically by year (1946–1957), then the Notes at the end; 144 files in the EPUB, ~1,610,000 characters of extracted textPeriodFebruary 1946 to April 1958 — de Gaulle’s resignation from the head of the Provisional Government (January 1946), the passage of the Fourth Republic’s constitution, his retirement to Colombey-les-Deux-Églises, the foundation and campaigns of the R.P.F. (1947–1955), and his long wait (“traversée du désert”) until the eve of his return to power in 1958NoteA contemporary collection of de Gaulle’s own written and spoken texts, not a narrative history. The five-tome edition gathers only the speeches delivered in circumstances determined in advance whose exact text could be preserved — those written by his hand, or noted by official stenography. The numerous improvised allocations whose text could not be reconstituted are excluded. François Goguel’s aide-mémoire and notes are set in the text. For this wiki it supplies, from the voice of the General himself, the French case for the years 1946–1958, the period of the Fourth Republic in which this folder’s later tomes find their sequel
Contents. A chronological record of de Gaulle’s principal statements during his years out of power. The volume opens with the Note de l’éditeur explaining the series, the note for Tome II defining its scope as February 1946 to April 1958, and a short aide-mémoire historique. The speeches of 1946 record his departure and the campaign against the draft constitution of the Fourth Republic: the discourse on the tomb of Clemenceau, the Bayeux declaration (16 June 1946) setting out his constitutional ideas, the declarations against the two draft constitutions, and the Épinal speech. The year 1947 opens the R.P.F. with the Bruneval speech and the great provincial tours — Strasbourg, Bordeaux, Lille, Rennes, Lyon, Vincennes, Alger — and the first press conferences at the Maison de la Résistance. The years 1948–1953 record the annual Vœux, the provincial meetings and press conferences of the R.P.F., the communications on the defence of France and the German question, the discourses at Marseille (April 1948), Nevers, Verdun, Compiègne, Saint-Étienne, and the November 1949 press conference. The years 1951–1954 cover the electoral campaigns, the communications of the R.P.F. on the régime and on European defence, the discourses at Bagatelle, Lille and Paris, the Bamako discourse (1953), and the growing isolation. The years 1955–1957 — the “traversée du désert” — contain few texts: the great press conference of 30 June 1955 at the hôtel Continental, the Cerdon allocution (24 June 1956) at the monument to the maquis of the Ain, the Saint-Cyr-Coëtquidan allocution (August 1956), and the final communiqué of 12 September 1957. The volume ends with the Notes (307 numbered notes) prepared by François Goguel.
Character of the source. A first-person record of the General’s own words during his withdrawal from office — a corpus of state pronouncements, political declarations, press conferences, broadcast allocations and R.P.F. campaign texts. Their character is that of public statements of a statesman out of power who nonetheless continues to pronounce on the régime, on the constitution, on European defence and on France’s place in the world, sustained by the apparatus of the R.P.F. Goguel’s aide-mémoire, printed in bistre in the edition, situate each text in its circumstances.
Quality. Good. Born-digital EPUB of the Plon/Édi8 edition, extracted via OPF spine order with page markers (===== FILE n: ...). French text clean and complete; the aide-mémoire historique and the 307 numbered notes are present. The dates span from 12 May 1946 to 12 September 1957 in the speeches, the volume’s nominal range being February 1946 to April 1958; a small number of typographical irregularities (accent and apostrophe artefacts, e.g. “Strasrourg”) noted from the source typesetting; no OCR errors, the text being digital in origin.
Raw text: wiki/raw/discours-t2.txt.

1946
The departure from power and the campaign against the draft constitution of the Fourth Republic.

Discours prononcé sur la tombe de Georges Clemenceau (12 May 1946) — at the first anniversary of the Victory, the homage to Clemenceau.
Discours prononcé à Bayeux (16 June 1946) — the great statement of his constitutional ideas, the “Bayeux speech”.
The discourses of the summer tour: à Robert-Espagne and à Bar-le-Duc (28 July), the discours prononcé à Épinal (29 September).
The Déclarations of 27 August, 19 September, 9 October and 1 November 1946 against the two successive draft constitutions.
The closing Déclaration of 28 December 1946.

1947
The foundation of the R.P.F. and the great provincial campaigns.

Discours prononcé à Bruneval (30 March 1947) — the inaugural speech of the R.P.F. on the country’s need for rallying.
The discourses of Strasbourg (6 and 7 April), Bordeaux (15 May), Lille (29 June), Rennes (27 July), Alençon (10 August), Bayonne (7 September), Lyon (20 September), Vincennes (5 October) and Alger (12 October).
The allocution devant la presse anglo-américaine de Paris (9 July) and the allocution à Saint-Marcel (27 July).
The Conférences de presse tenues à la maison de la Résistance (24 April and 12 November).
The Message of 15 October and the Déclarations of 18 August, 24 August and 27 October 1947.

1948
The R.P.F. at its height; the press conferences and the discourses of the “rassemblement”.

The discours prononcé à Saint-Étienne (4 January 1948).
The discourses at Compiègne (7 March) and the three discourses at Marseille (16, 17, 18 April).
The discourses at Saint-Cloud (1 May), Nevers (13 June), Verdun (20 June), Nice (12 September) and Paris (14 December).
The Conférences de presse tenues à la maison de la Résistance (1 October and 17 November).
The Lettre aux délégués (19 October) and the Déclaration of 9 June.

1949
The consolidation of the R.P.F. and the press conferences at the Palais d’Orsay.

The Vœux of 1 January and the discours prononcé à Lille (12 February).
The Appel of 23 February and the Communiqué of 28 February on the defence of France.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais d’Orsay (29 March) — the R.P.F. and the national interest.
The discourses at Bagatelle (1 May), Vincennes (22 May), the discours d’inauguration de l’avenue et de la porte du Général Leclerc (18 June), and at Bordeaux (25 September).
The allocutions at Versailles (2 October) and Le Mans (23 October); the Conférence de presse au Palais d’Orsay (14 November).
The Communiqué of 7 August on the Council of Direction.

1950
The press conferences of the year and the first statements on Korea.

The Vœux of 1 January and the discours prononcé à Paris (11 February).
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais d’Orsay (16 March) and the Message aux étudiants (18 March).
The discourses at Bagatelle (1 May), Paris (25 June and 21 October) and Lille (11 December).
The Communiqué of 12 April on the Carrefour article, and the Interview donnée à M. Bradford (10 July) on the Korean war.
The Déclaration of 17 August and the press statement of 4 December on the United Nations and Korea.

1951
The electoral year of 17 June 1951 and the R.P.F.’s campaign.

The Vœux of 1 January and the discourses at Nîmes (7 January) and Bourges (25 February).
The discourses at Reims (15 April), Toulouse (6 May), the Texte d’affiche of 15 April and the Communiqués and Textes d’affiche of the campaign.
The Discours prononcé à la pelouse de Bagatelle (1 May).
The Lettre aux grands électeurs de l’Union Française (1 June) and the allocution à la radiodiffusion française (8 June).
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais d’Orsay (22 June) after the elections; the closing discourse of the fourth Assises du R.P.F. (25 November).
The allocutions at Nieppe (2 September), Saint-Mandé (4 November), the inaugurations of the monuments to the Bretons and to the Surcouf and the sailors of the France Libre (15 July, 23 September), and the Conférence de presse au Palais d’Orsay (21 December).

1952
The R.P.F. and the European and defence questions.

The Vœux of 1 January to the companions of the R.P.F.; the discours prononcé à Paris (23 February).
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais d’Orsay (10 March).
The discours prononcé à la pelouse de Bagatelle (1 May); the Déclaration of 6 June.
The allocutions at Bayeux (14 June) and the Message aux Aviateurs de la France Libre (18 June) for the anniversary of the 1940 appeal.
The allocutions at Saint-Maur (6 July) and Neuilly-sur-Seine (12 October); the discours prononcé à Paris (11 November).
The Communiqués of 25 June, 24 July and 23 December; the Déclaration of 8 October.

1953
The R.P.F. at the turn; the Bamako discourse.

The Déclaration of 16 February and the Conférence de presse tenue à l’hôtel Continental (25 February).
The discours prononcé à Bamako (8 March) — de Gaulle’s address in French Sudan.
The discours prononcé à Saint-Lô (7 June) and the Message of 6 June.
The Communiqués of 6 June and 27 June on the governmental crises.
The Conférence de presse tenue à l’hôtel Continental (12 November).

1954
The isolation deepens; the last discourses of the “traversée du désert”.

The Vœux of 1 January (two texts) to the companions of the R.P.F.
The Conférence de presse tenue à l’hôtel Continental (7 April).
The Déclarations of 22 June and 26 August and the discours prononcé à Paris (4 December).

1955–1957
The years of silence and the eve of return.

The Conférence de presse tenue à l’hôtel Continental (30 June 1955) — de Gaulle’s principal statement of this period, on the régime and on the Fourth Republic.
The allocution à Cerdon (24 June 1956) at the monument to the maquis of the Ain.
The allocution à Saint-Cyr-Coëtquidan (2 August 1956) — the address to the officer cadets.
The Communiqué of 12 September 1957 on the law-framework for Algeria — the last text, ending the volume on the eve of the return of May 1958.


Notes
The volume closes with the aide-mémoire historique and 307 numbered notes (prepared by François Goguel) which identify persons, places and events referred to in the texts — for example the referendum of 5 May 1946 on the first draft constitution, the second Constituent Assembly of June 1946, the French occupation of the Sarre, the growing tension between Russia and the western powers in 1946, the Épinal speech, the R.P.F. and its electoral campaigns, the question of the German federal constitution, and the Algerian situation of 1957.

sources/de-gaulle-discours-et-messages-t.title: Charles de Gaulle — Discours et Messages, Tome 3 : Avec le renouveau (1958-1962)
sources/de-gaulle-discours-et-messages-t.content:
Discours et Messages, Tome 3 : Avec le renouveau (1958-1962)
Charles de Gaulle — Discours et messages, Tome III : Avec le renouveau (Mai 1958–Juillet 1962). Librairie Plon, Paris, 1970; the present digital edition Plon / Édi8, 2014. The third of the five-tome collected edition of the speeches, messages and press conferences of General de Gaulle from 18 June 1940 to 28 April 1969, edited with the assistance of François Goguel; this volume covers the return of de Gaulle to power and the establishment of the Fifth Republic.





























AuthorCharles de Gaulle (1890–1970) — French soldier and statesman, head of the Free French, head of the Provisional Government 1944–46, founder and first President of the Fifth Republic (1959–1969)EditionLibrairie Plon, 1970; digital edition Plon, a department of Édi8, 2014; EAN numérique 9782259228497; text established with the collaboration of M. François GoguelStructureNote de l’éditeur + note de l’éditeur pour le tome III + speeches, messages and press conferences arranged chronologically by year (1958–1962); 18 files in the EPUB, ~5340 lines / ~937,000 characters of extracted textPeriodMay 1958 to July 1962 — the return of General de Gaulle to power (May 1958), the drafting and referendum on the Constitution of the Fifth Republic (autumn 1958), his presidency (elected December 1958, installed January 1959), the Algerian war and its winding-down, the decolonisation of the French Community in Africa, and the first phase of his foreign and defence policyNoteA contemporary collection of de Gaulle’s own written and spoken texts, not a narrative history. The five-tome edition gathers only the speeches delivered in circumstances determined in advance whose exact text could be preserved — those written by his hand for the broadcast and televised allocations, or noted by official stenography for his public speeches and addresses before the Assemblies. The numerous improvised allocations whose text could not be reconstituted are excluded. François Goguel’s aide-mémoire and notes are set in the text. For this wiki it supplies, from the voice of the President of the Fifth Republic himself, the French case for the years 1958–1962
Contents. A chronological record of de Gaulle’s principal statements as he returned to power and founded the Fifth Republic. The volume opens with the Note de l’éditeur explaining the series, and the note for Tome III defining its scope as May 1958 to July 1962. The speeches of 1958 run from the return to power (the June allocation from the Palais d’Orsay and the address at Algiers), through the establishment of the new institutions — the speeches of the referendum campaign of autumn 1958, the adoption of the Constitution, the new President’s messages and the opening of the Community — to the first Conference de presse of the new regime. The year 1959 records the installation of the presidency, the presidential tour of Algeria, the inauguration of the Community’s institutions, de Gaulle’s state visit to Italy and his North African policy, the addresses of the Algerian self-determination offer, and his journey to the German Federal Republic. The year 1960 covers the Algerian policy of self-determination, the January week of the barricades, the Community’s transition to independence, de Gaulle’s reception of the heads of the new African states, his American tour (the address before Congress at Washington), and the continuing constitutional consolidation. The years 1961–1962 carry the Algerian crisis and its resolution — the April 1961 generals’ putsch and its address, the referendum on self-determination, the Évian negotiations — together with the development of the institutions, the visit of M. Khrushchev, and the closing speeches of 1962 up to the summer. The volume ends with the aide-mémoire chronologique and the Notes (235 numbered notes) prepared by François Goguel.
Character of the source. A first-person record of the founder of the Fifth Republic’s own words, kept as exact texts for the determined occasions and official addresses. It is not an analytic or reflective work but a corpus of state pronouncements — broadcast and televised allocations written by de Gaulle himself, and speeches and press conferences taken down by official stenography. Their character is that of acts of government and public declarations of policy, on Algeria, on the Community and decolonisation, on the constitution of the Fifth Republic, and on France’s place in the world. Goguel’s aide-mémoire, printed in bistre in the edition, situate each text in its circumstances.
Quality. Good. Born-digital EPUB of the Plon/Édi8 edition, extracted via OPF spine order with page markers (===== FILE n: ...). French text clean and complete; the aide-mémoire chronologique and the 235 numbered notes are present at the end of the volume. A small number of typographical irregularities (a few accent and apostrophe artefacts, e.g. “PRONCONCÉE”) noted from the source typesetting; no OCR errors, the text being digital in origin.

1958
The return to power and the foundation of the Fifth Republic.

Conférence de presse tenue au Palais d’Orsay (June 1958) — the first great press conference of the return, in which de Gaulle presents himself as ready to assume the powers of the Republic and sets out his conception of the task.
Allocution prononcée à Alger — the speech at Algiers to the population and the army in the wake of the events of May 1958.
The radio and televised allocations from the Hôtel Matignon of June and July, and the allocation at the Préfecture de Police.
Discours devant l’Assemblée représentative de Madagascar, the discours prononcé à Tananarive and the discours prononcé à Dakar — the tour of the overseas territories at the moment of the referendum.
Discours prononcé place de la République à Paris — the great public address of the referendum campaign of September 1958.
Discours prononcé à Constantine (October 1958) — the Constantine programme of economic and social development for Algeria.
The referendum of 28 September 1958 and the adoption of the Constitution.
The speeches of November–December: the return to Paris, the message to the Parliament, the allocation to the Cité universitaire de Toulouse, and the first Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée.

1959
The installation of the presidency and the first full year of the Fifth Republic.

The New Year allocations; the allocation à l’École Polytechnique; the allocation à l’Hôtel de Ville de Paris and the allocation à la Sorbonne.
The state visit to Italy: the allocations at the Hôtel de Ville de Milan, at San Martino, at Solferino and the discours prononcé à Rome, au Capitole.
The Algerian policy: the tour of Tananarive and La Réunion, the discours d’ouverture de la session du Sénat de la Communauté, and the broadcast allocation of 16 September 1959 offering Algerian self-determination.
The reception of President Eisenhower at Le Bourget and the addresses of Paris.
The allocation à la Cour de Cassation and the allocation à l’École Militaire.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée (October 1959).
The African Community and the tour of Saint-Louis du Sénégal and the Assemblée fédérale du Mali; the message aux Armées and the message à la Métropole, à l’Algérie, à la Communauté.

1960
Self-determination for Algeria, the week of the barricades, and the Community’s passage to independence.

The January broadcast allocation at the time of the week of the barricades in Algiers; the allocation à l’École de l’Air de Salon-de-Provence.
The reception of M. Khrushchev: the allocation at Orly on his arrival.
The visit to Great Britain — the allocation au Guildhall de Londres and the discours prononcé à Westminster Hall.
The message to the Governor of Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon; the discours prononcé à Ottawa.
The American tour of 1960: the Conférence de presse au National Press Club de Washington, the discours devant les deux Chambres réunies en Congrès at Washington, and the allocations at New York, San Francisco and La Nouvelle-Orléans.
The African independence movement and the Community states.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée and the year’s closing allocations.

1961
The Algerian crisis: the generals’ putsch of April and the referendum on self-determination.

The January messages; the allocation à l’École Nationale d’Administration.
The allocation of 23 April 1961 in the face of the generals’ putsch; the measures of authority.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 11 April 1961 on Algeria and the nation.
The negotiations toward self-determination and the referendum of January 1961 on Algeria.
The agricultural and social allocations; the addresses to the armed forces.
The foreign policy of the year — the German question, the Atlantic alliance and the conception of a European Europe.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 15 May 1962 (see under 1962 below for the sequence).

1962
The close of the Algerian war and the consolidation of the Fifth Republic’s institutions.

The ordre aux armées of 1 January 1962 and the New Year allocations.
The end of the Algerian war and the referendum of 8 April 1962 approving the Évian accords.
The visit to the provinces; the allocation at the Palais de l’Élysée on the reform of the institutions.
The referendum of 28 October 1962 on the election of the President of the Republic by universal suffrage.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of May 1962 and the great press conferences of the year.
The closing allocations of June and July 1962 (to 8 July) which end the volume.


Aide-mémoire chronologique et Notes
The volume closes with the aide-mémoire chronologique, situating each speech and message in the circumstances of the period, and with 235 numbered notes (prepared by François Goguel) which identify persons, places and events referred to in the texts — for example the press conference of 30 June 1955, the Anglo-American good offices after the bombardment of Sakkiet (February 1958), the decision of 6 May 1953 on the R.P.F., the referendum of 28 September 1958 (15.06% abstentions in the metropole, 79.2% Oui), the status of Algeria and its two electoral colleges under the Fourth Republic, the instructions to General Salan of 14 October, and the figures of the June–July 1958 loan (34 tonnes of gold in four days, 324 billion francs in the 17 June–17 July subscription).

sources/de-gaulle-discours-et-messages-t.title: Charles de Gaulle — Discours et Messages, Tome 4 : Pour l'effort (1962-1965)
sources/de-gaulle-discours-et-messages-t.content:
Discours et Messages, Tome 4 : Pour l’effort (1962-1965)
Charles de Gaulle — Discours et messages, Tome IV : Pour l’effort (Août 1962–Décembre 1965). Librairie Plon, Paris, 1970; the present digital edition Plon / Édi8, 2014. The fourth of the five-tome collected edition of the speeches, messages and press conferences of General de Gaulle from 18 June 1940 to 28 April 1969, edited with the assistance of François Goguel; this volume covers the reform of the institutions of the Fifth Republic, the Algerian settlement consolidated, the re-election campaign of 1965 and the great state visits of the years of the “effort.”





























AuthorCharles de Gaulle (1890–1970) — French soldier and statesman, founder and first President of the Fifth Republic (1959–1969)EditionLibrairie Plon, 1970; digital edition Plon / Édi8, 2014; text established with the collaboration of M. François GoguelStructureNote de l’éditeur + speeches, messages and press conferences arranged chronologically by year (1962–1965); 16 files in the EPUB, ~5326 lines / ~961,000 characters of extracted textPeriodAugust 1962 to December 1965 — the years of the “effort”: the consolidation of the Fifth Republic, the referendum of October 1962 on the election of the President by universal suffrage, the settlement of the Algerian question, the policy of national independence in defence and foreign affairs, the great state visits of the period, and the presidential election campaign and victory of December 1965NoteA contemporary collection of de Gaulle’s own texts, not a narrative history — the exact texts of his determined speeches, his hand-written broadcast and televised allocations, and his official addresses and press conferences. For this wiki it supplies, from the President’s own voice, the French case for the years 1962–1965
Contents. A chronological record of de Gaulle’s statements from August 1962 to December 1965. The volume opens with the closing texts of 1962 — the German tour of September 1962 (the allocations at Bonn, Cologne, Düsseldorf, the Thyssen works, the German war college, Munich, and the great allocation à la jeunesse prononcée à Ludwigsburg), the October referendum on the election of the President by universal suffrage and its accompanying messages and allocations, the November legislative elections, and the year’s closing addresses including the obsequies of President René Coty. The year 1963 carries the international turn — the Conférence de presse of 14 January 1963 on the veto of British entry into the Common Market and the German-French treaty, the addresses to the new institutions, the reception of the King of Norway and of President Kekkonen of Finland, the discours devant la Chambre des députés grecque, the visits to the Académie des Inscriptions, the reception of King Hassan II of Morocco, and the Conférence de presse of July 1963. The year 1964 covers the economic and social policy of the “effort,” the discours prononcé à Lyon, the visit to the Cour de Cassation, the reception of the Grand-Duchess of Luxembourg, the discours devant le Parlement iranien, and the autumn tours including the discours à l’inauguration de la Maison de la Radio. The year 1965 brings the great Latin-American tour of September–October 1965 (the speeches and allocations at Mexico, at the Mexican Congress, at the University of Mexico, at Basse-Terre, Fort-de-France, Caracas, Bogotá, Quito, Lima, Santiago, Buenos Aires, Assomption, Montevideo and Brasilia), the reception of the King of Jordan, the discours prononcé à Strasbourg, and the presidential election campaign culminating in the second-round victory of December 1965, with the year’s closing Vœux aux Armées. The volume ends with the Notes (338 numbered notes) prepared by François Goguel.
Character of the source. A first-person record of the President of the Fifth Republic’s own words, kept as exact texts for the determined occasions. Its character is that of acts of government and declarations of policy — on the reform of the institutions (the October 1962 referendum), on national independence and the conception of a “European Europe,” on the German-French rapprochement, on the independent deterrent and defence policy, on economic and social development, and on France’s relations with the wider world including the tour of Latin America. Goguel’s aide-mémoire and notes situate each text in its circumstances.
Quality. Good. Born-digital EPUB of the Plon/Édi8 edition, extracted via OPF spine order with page markers. French text clean and complete; the 338 numbered notes are present at the end. A few typographical artefacts from the source typesetting (e.g. “maiSON de la Radio,” “RUENOS-AIRES,” “L’ELYSÉE” for “l’Élysée”) noted; no OCR errors, the text being digital in origin.
