1962
The reform of the institutions and the close of the year of the “effort.”

The German tour of September 1962: the allocations at Bonn, at Cologne, at Düsseldorf, at the Thyssen works, before the officers of the German war college, at Munich, and the allocation à la jeunesse prononcée à Ludwigsburg — the reconciliation of French and German youth.
The radio and televised allocation of the autumn on the reform of the institutions.
The message au Parlement and the referendum of 28 October 1962 on the election of the President of the Republic by universal suffrage.
The reception of King Olaf V of Norway; the allocation de bienvenue à M. Kekkonen, President of Finland.
The allocations of the November legislative elections.
The allocation at the obsequies of President René Coty; the message à l’Assemblée nationale; the message to the President of the UNESCO conference; the Vœux aux Armées and the allocation lors de la présentation des vœux des Corps constitués.

1963
The international turn and the policy of national independence.

The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 14 January 1963 — on the veto of Great Britain’s entry into the Common Market and on the Franco-German treaty.
The allocation à l’École Nationale d’Administration and the allocation à l’École Militaire.
The reception of President López Mateos of Mexico; the reception of King Gustave VI Adolphe of Sweden.
The discours prononcé devant la Chambre des députés grecque; the allocation à l’occasion du centenaire de la Croix-Rouge internationale.
The allocation à l’Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres; the reception of King Hassan II of Morocco.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 29 July 1963; the discours prononcé à Lyon.
The allocation à la Cour de Cassation; the reception of the Grand-Duchess of Luxembourg.
The discours prononcé devant le Parlement iranien; the allocation lors de l’inauguration de la Maison de la Radio; the message aux Armées.

1964
The “effort” in economic and social policy, and the great autumn tours.

The allocation lors de la présentation des vœux des Corps constitués and the Vœux aux Armées.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 31 January 1964.
The reception of President Segni of Italy; the reception of President Grunitzky of Togoland.
The visit to Mexico: the allocation du balcon du Palais national de Mexico, the discours devant les Chambres réunies en Congrès, the discours à l’Université de Mexico; the allocations at Basse-Terre and Fort-de-France.
The allocation prononcée à Trèves; the reception of the Chinese ambassador at the Palais de l’Élysée.
The reception of Prince Norodom Sihanouk, head of state of Cambodia; the allocation à l’inauguration de l’École des Hautes Études Commerciales à Jouy-en-Josas.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 23 July 1964; the allocations at Toulon and Paris; the discours prononcé à Reims.

1965
The Latin-American tour and the presidential re-election.

The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 4 February 1965.
The allocation à l’École Navale and the allocation à l’École Spéciale Militaire de Saint-Cyr-Coëtquidan.
The reception of King Frédéric IX of Denmark; of President Hélou of Lebanon; of King Mohammad Zaher Shah of Afghanistan; of President Frei of Chile.
The allocation à l’occasion de l’inauguration du tunnel sous le Mont-Blanc.
The Latin-American tour of September–October 1965: the speeches and allocations at Mexico, Caracas (the discours au Parlement de Caracas), Bogotá (the discours au Parlement de Bogota), Quito, Lima (the discours devant le Parlement), Cochabamba, Santiago (the discours au Congrès), Buenos Aires (the discours au Congrès), Assomption, Montevideo (the discours au Congrès) and Brasilia (the discours au Congrès).
The reception of King Hussein of Jordan; the discours prononcé à Strasbourg.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 28 October 1965 — the close of the election campaign.
The presidential election of December 1965 and the re-election of General de Gaulle; the allocation lors de l’inauguration de la IXe Exposition nationale du travail; the Vœux aux Armées and the closing allocations of 31 December 1965.


Notes
The volume closes with 338 numbered notes (prepared by François Goguel) identifying persons, places, dates and events referred to in the texts — the obsequies of President René Coty, the figures of the October 1962 referendum, the circumstances of the Franco-German treaty, the events of the Algerian settlement, and the details of the state visits of the period.

sources/de-gaulle-discours-et-messages-t.title: Charles de Gaulle — Discours et Messages, Tome 5 : Vers le terme (1966-1969)
sources/de-gaulle-discours-et-messages-t.content:
Discours et Messages, Tome 5 : Vers le terme (1966-1969)
Charles de Gaulle — Discours et messages, Tome V : Vers le terme (Janvier 1966–Avril 1969). Librairie Plon, Paris, 1970; the present digital edition Plon / Édi8, 2014. The fifth and last of the five-tome collected edition of the speeches, messages and press conferences of General de Gaulle from 18 June 1940 to 28 April 1969, edited with the assistance of François Goguel; this volume covers the last years of his presidency, ending with the referendum of April 1969 and his retirement.





























AuthorCharles de Gaulle (1890–1970) — French soldier and statesman, founder and first President of the Fifth Republic (1959–1969)EditionLibrairie Plon, 1970; digital edition Plon / Édi8, 2014; text established with the collaboration of M. François GoguelStructureNote de l’éditeur + speeches, messages and press conferences arranged chronologically by year (1966–1969); 16 files in the EPUB, ~5326 lines / ~950,000 characters of extracted textPeriodJanuary 1966 to April 1969 — the years “towards the term”: the second presidential mandate, the policy of national independence (the departure from the integrated command of NATO, the Moscow visit of 1966), the “live Quebec” affair of 1967, the Polish, Romanian and Turkish visits, the crisis of May 1968, and the retirement of General de Gaulle after the referendum of April 1969NoteA contemporary collection of de Gaulle’s own texts, not a narrative history — the exact texts of his determined speeches, his hand-written broadcast and televised allocations, and his official addresses and press conferences. It is the closing volume of the series and ends the record of his public life on 28 April 1969. For this wiki it supplies, from the President’s own voice, the French case for the years 1966–1969
Contents. A chronological record of de Gaulle’s statements from January 1966 to April 1969. The volume opens with the texts of 1966 — the year of the Conférence de presse of 21 February 1966 on the reform of the alliance and the departure from the integrated command of NATO, the addresses to the Foire Internationale de Lille, to the Congrès international de la responsabilité médicale at Versailles, to Douaumont for the fiftieth anniversary of Verdun, and to the Institut de France for the tricentenary of the Académie des Sciences, and then the great state visit to the Soviet Union of June–July 1966 (the allocations at Moscow, the Mossoviet, the University of Moscow, Academgorod, Leningrad, Kiev, Volgograd, the military exercise, and the broadcast to the Soviet radio and television), the reception of the King of Laos, the tour of Djibouti, and the Pacific tour of September 1966 (Phnom-Penh, Nouméa, Papeete, the Polynesian Territorial Assembly, Pirae and Taravao in Tahiti). The year 1967 carries the Vœux aux Armées, the visit to the Vatican, to the French ecclesiastical colony of Rome and to Venice, the reception of the President of Turkey, the North American visit of July 1967 (Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, the Anse au Foulon, and the balcony of the Hôtel de Ville of Montreal with the celebrated closing to the “live Quebec” — Vive le Québec libre!), the Polish visit of September 1967 (Cracow, the Diète polonaise, and the broadcast at Wilanów), the reception of Ayub Khan, and the visit to the Cour de Cassation. The year 1968 carries the Romanian visit of May 1968 (the discourse before the Grande Assemblée nationale, the University of Bucharest, the Romanian radio and television), the crisis of May 1968 and the broadcast allocations at its height, the Conférence de presse of June 1968, the dissolution of the National Assembly, the closing of the events, the Turkish visit of October 1968 (the allocation at the Lycée Galatasaray of Istanbul, the Turkish radio and television), and the allocation at the Invalides. The year 1969 brings the final texts — the Vœux aux Armées, the Conférence de presse of January 1969, the allocations at Quimper and at the reception of President Bokassa of the Central African Republic, the reception of President Richard Nixon, the allocation radiodiffusée et télévisée on the referendum of 27 April 1969 on the reform of the Senate and the regionalisation, and the final text of 28 April 1969 announcing his retirement. The volume ends with the Notes (383 numbered notes) prepared by François Goguel.
Character of the source. A first-person record of the President of the Fifth Republic’s own words, kept as exact texts for the determined occasions. Its character is that of acts of government and declarations of policy — on national independence and the reform of the Atlantic alliance (the departure from the integrated command in 1966), on the rapprochement with the Soviet Union and with the states of eastern Europe, on the relationship with the French of Quebec, on the crisis of May 1968, and on the closing reform projects of the presidency. Goguel’s aide-mémoire and notes situate each text in its circumstances.
Quality. Good. Born-digital EPUB of the Plon/Édi8 edition, extracted via OPF spine order with page markers. French text clean and complete; the 383 numbered notes are present at the end. A few typographical artefacts from the source typesetting noted (e.g. “PRONCONCÉE” for “prononcée,” “FLOSSE” for “Floess” in the Pirae text); no OCR errors, the text being digital in origin.
Raw text: wiki/raw/discours-t5.txt.

1966
National independence, the departure from the integrated command, and the great eastern and Pacific tours.

The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 21 February 1966 — on the reform of the Atlantic alliance and the withdrawal of France from the integrated command of NATO.
The allocation lors de l’inauguration de la Foire internationale de Lille; the allocation à Versailles au Congrès international de la responsabilité médicale.
The allocation à Douaumont pour le cinquantième anniversaire de la bataille de Verdun.
The allocation à l’Institut de France à l’occasion du tricentenaire de l’Académie des Sciences.
The state visit to the Soviet Union of June–July 1966: the allocations at the Mossoviet, at the University of Moscow, at Academgorod (Novosibirsk), at Leningrad, at Kiev, at Volgograd, at the military exercise in the suburbs of Moscow, the allocation at Moscow, and the broadcast to the Soviet radio and television.
The reception of King Savang Vatthana of Laos; the allocation à Djibouti devant l’Assemblée territoriale de la Côte française des Somalis.
The Pacific tour of September 1966: the allocation at Phnom-Penh to the popular meeting, at Nouméa, at Papeete (place Joffre), before the Assemblée territoriale de la Polynésie française, at Pirae (Tahiti) in reply to the speech of the mayor Gaston Flosse, and at Taravao (Tahiti) in reply to the discourse of the doyen of the district chiefs.
The allocation à la Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations; the reception of King Mahendra of Nepal.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 28 October 1966; the allocation à l’occasion du XXe anniversaire de l’U.N.E.S.C.O.; the allocation lors de l’inauguration de l’usine marémotrice de la Rance; the reception of M. Kossyguine, President of the Council of Ministers of the U.S.S.R.

1967
The Vatican, the “live Quebec” affair, and the Polish visit.

The Vœux aux Armées and the allocation lors de la présentation des vœux des Corps constitués.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 16 May 1967.
The visit to the Vatican: the allocation au Vatican and the allocation devant la colonie ecclésiastique française de Rome; the allocation à Venise.
The reception of President Sunay of Turkey.
The North American visit of July 1967: the allocations at Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon and at the Anse au Foulon; the allocation au balcon de l’Hôtel de Ville de Montréal — the address to the crowd on the balcony, closing with “Vive le Québec libre!” — and the allocation à l’Université de Montréal.
The Polish visit of September 1967: the allocation à l’Université de Cracovie, the discours devant la Diète polonaise, and the allocation radiodiffusée et télévisée à Varsovie au palais de Wilanów.
The reception of Marshal Ayub Khan, President of Pakistan; the allocation à la Cour de Cassation; the reception of M. Soglo, President of Dahomey.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 27 November 1967; the Vœux aux Armées and the closing allocations of the year.

1968
The Romanian visit, the crisis of May 1968, and the dissolution of the Assembly.

The reception of General Abdul Rahman Mohammad Aref, President of Iraq; the allocation à la mémoire des officiers et marins du sous-marin « Minerve »; the allocation à l’ouverture de la 50e Foire internationale de Lyon.
The Romanian visit of May 1968: the discours à la Grande Assemblée nationale de la République socialiste de Roumanie, the discours à l’Université de Bucarest, and the allocation à la radiodiffusion et à la télévision roumaines.
The crisis of May 1968: the broadcast allocations at the height of the events of May–June 1968.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 7 June 1968 — on the dissolution of the National Assembly and the “participation.”
The allocation à la Butte Chaumont.
The Turkish visit of October 1968: the allocation à Istanbul au Lycée Galatasaray, the allocation à la radiodiffusion et à la télévision turques.
The allocation aux Invalides; the Vœux aux Armées and the closing allocations of the year.

1969
The final texts and the retirement of General de Gaulle.

The allocation à Quimper.
The reception of President Bokassa of the Central African Republic; the reception of President Richard Nixon of the United States.
The Conférence de presse tenue au Palais de l’Élysée of 16 January 1969.
The allocation radiodiffusée et télévisée on the reform of the Senate and the regionalisation.
The referendum of 27 April 1969 and its rejection.
The final allocation radiodiffusée et télévisée of 28 April 1969 announcing the retirement of General de Gaulle — the last text of the series.


Notes
The volume closes with 383 numbered notes (prepared by François Goguel) identifying persons, places, dates and events referred to in the texts — the details of the reform of the alliance in 1966, the circumstances of the Moscow visit, the reception at Montreal of July 1967, the events of May 1968, and the closing referendum of April 1969.

sources/gentiloni-silveri-storia-italia-.title: Umberto Gentiloni Silveri — Storia dell'Italia contemporanea (1943-2019)
sources/gentiloni-silveri-storia-italia-.content:
Umberto Gentiloni Silveri — Storia dell’Italia contemporanea (1943-2019)
Full bibliographic citation — Umberto Gentiloni Silveri, Storia dell’Italia contemporanea (1943-2019), Società editrice il Mulino, Bologna. ISBN 978-88-15-28089-3. Italian text, 408 pages in the PDF; extracted plain text of 17,718 lines.





























AuthorUmberto Gentiloni Silveri — Italian historian, professor of contemporary history at the Sapienza University of Rome; specialist in twentieth-century Italian and European political history, postwar Italy, the Cold War and the Atlantic allianceEditionSocietà editrice il Mulino, Bologna; ISBN 978-88-15-28089-3; PDF creation stamp January 2020 (digital scan of the printed volume)StructurePremessa + eight chronological/thematic chapters + Conclusioni + Indice dei nomi; extracted plain text of 17,718 linesPeriod1943–2019 — from the fall of fascism and the summer of 1943 as a “theatre of war” through the birth of the Republic and the Constitution, the “miracle” years and the distensione, the anni Settanta and the years of the Republic’s crisis (the Moro kidnapping and the «funerale della Repubblica»), the fall of the Berlin Wall and Tangentopoli, the “mancata transizione” to a bipolar order, the eurozone, and the Italy of the 150th anniversary and the early twenty-first centuryNoteA modern scholarly synthesis of contemporary Italian history from 1943 to the present, one of the volume V “contemporary Italy” contributions to the “Le vie della civiltà” series. Written by a professional academic historian with no political function; reads as continuous political, social, economic and institutional history of the Italian Republic and its pre-history in the war
Content Summary
Premessa. On the meaning of studying the past in an age of constant connection and of an invasive flow of continuous information. The preface argues that the past appears as a distant world full of silent and lost traces, yet warns that this alterity risks slipping toward an irrelevant distance, as though one could make a tabula rasa of what preceded us and fix an “year zero.” The history of contemporary Italy becomes, in this light, a set of errors, missed occasions, unresolved mysteries, betrayed or modified revolutions, and unattainable horizons. Against this, the most documented reflections on our times highlight the complexity of the present and the need for languages and methods able to construct paths and strategies of knowledge. The past can help understand the current world if frequented with rigour and respect, investigated starting from the questions and anxieties of today. Historical knowledge proceeds by problems and unanswered questions requiring deepening, not by a mere succession of events to be put in sequence.
I. Dopoguerra
1. Estate 1943: un teatro di guerra — The summer of 1943 as a “theatre of war”: Italy as a battlefield, the fall of fascism (25 July 1943), the armistice of 8 September 1943, the German occupation and the Resistance.
2. Democrazia, referendum, Costituzione — From the war to democracy: the parties of the CLN, the referendum of 2 June 1946 and the choice between monarchy and republic, the Constituent Assembly and the writing of the 1948 Constitution.
3. Nazionale e Internazionale — The national and the international dimensions of the Italian reconstruction: the peace treaty, the Atlantic orientation, and the place of Italy between the two blocs.
4. «Un partito di Centro che cammina verso sinistra» — The construction of the centrist political order: the Christian Democracy and its orientation in the first years of the Republic.
II. Le ragioni di un miracolo
1. Dentro l’età dell’oro — Inside the “golden age”: Italian economic growth and the transformation of society in the boom years.
2. La stanza dei bottoni — “The room of the buttons”: the centres of power and economic decision-making in the miracle years.
3. Magliette a strisce — “Striped shirts”: the world of football and popular culture as a mirror of Italian society in the growth years.
4. Distensione, Concilio, dialogo — Détente, the Second Vatican Council and dialogue: the international and religious context of the Italian 1960s.
III. Anni Settanta
1. Il lungo Sessantotto — The “long 1968”: the student and worker movements and the contestation of the late 1960s.
2. La fine dell’innocenza — “The end of innocence”: the beginning of the years of political violence and terrorism.
3. In mezzo al guado — “In the middle of the ford”: the political crisis and instability of the mid-1970s.
4. Compromesso storico e solidarietà nazionale — The “historic compromise” and “national solidarity”: the strategy of the PCI and the politics of the late 1970s.
IV. Il funerale della Repubblica
1. Generazione contro — “Generation against”: the emergence of the generation of protest and its challenge to the established order.
2. Il giorno più lungo — “The longest day”: the kidnapping of Aldo Moro by the Red Brigades (16 March 1978) and the crisis that followed.
3. L’ombra di Moro — “The shadow of Moro”: the aftermath of Moro’s murder (9 May 1978) and its long political shadow.
4. Riflusso — “Riflusso” (the retreat/reflux): the return to private life and the political and cultural reaction of the early 1980s.
V. L’inizio della fine
1. Dal confronto al conflitto — From confrontation to conflict: the re-emergence of the East–West confrontation in the early 1980s (the “second Cold War”).
2. Una lenta agonia — “A slow agony”: the gradual crisis and decline of the postwar political system in the 1980s.
3. Una strana modernità — “A strange modernity”: the Italian society and economy of the 1980s and their paradoxes.
4. Duelli senza vincitore — “Duels without a winner”: the political stalemate and the confrontation between the major parties.
VI. Il crollo
1. Indimenticabile Ottantanove — “Unforgettable 1989”: the fall of the Berlin Wall and the end of the Cold War’s European order.
2. Tangentopoli — The corruption investigation (“Tangentopoli,” “Bribesville,” 1992) and the collapse of the traditional party system.
3. Mafia e politica — Mafia and politics: the connections between organised crime and political power exposed in the early 1990s.
4. Media e potere — Media and power: the role of television and Silvio Berlusconi’s entry into politics.
VII. Transizione mancata
1. Un bipolarismo imperfetto — “An imperfect bipolarism”: the attempt to build a bipolar party system after 1994.
2. Politica e antipolitica — Politics and anti-politics: the distrust of the parties and the rise of protest movements.
3. Vizi antichi e nuove virtù — “Ancient vices and new virtues”: the continuities and novelties of Italian political life in the 1990s.
4. Eurozona — The Eurozone: Italy’s entry into the euro and the constraints of European monetary union.
VIII. Tra rinascita e declino
1. Una normalità difficile — “A difficult normality”: the alternation of centre-left and centre-right governments in the early 2000s.
2. Crepuscolo — “Twilight”: the Italy of the late 2000s and the world financial crisis (2007–2008).
3. I primi centocinquant’anni — “The first one hundred and fifty years”: the anniversary of Italian unification (2011) and reflections on the national history.
4. Europa e Mediterraneo — Europe and the Mediterranean: Italy’s place in the European Union and the Mediterranean world of the 2010s.
Conclusioni
The concluding chapter on the state of contemporary Italy and the uses of its history, drawing together the threads of the volume and its argument about the Italian present.
Key Data Points

















































AttributeDetailAuthorUmberto Gentiloni Silveri — professor of contemporary history, Sapienza University of RomeTitleStoria dell’Italia contemporanea (1943-2019)SeriesOne of the “contemporary Italy” volumes of the “Le vie della civiltà” series (il Mulino)PublishedSocietà editrice il Mulino, Bologna, 2019; ISBN 978-88-15-28089-3SourcePDF scan (creation stamp January 2020), 408 pagesRaw filewiki/raw/gentiloni-silveri-storia-italia-contemporanea-1943-2019.txtLines17,718StructurePremessa + chapters I–VIII + Conclusioni + Indice dei nomiCoverage1943–2019 — fall of fascism, war and Resistance, Republic and Constitution, the miracle years, the anni Settanta, the crisis of the Republic (Moro), the end of the Cold War and Tangentopoli, the “mancata transizione,” the eurozone, and Italy to 2019SignificanceThe modern scholarly synthesis of contemporary Italian history in the wiki, complementing the older Mammarella L’Italia contemporanea (1943-1998) with an account that extends to the present
Relationship to the Wiki
Gentiloni Silveri gives this wiki its modern scholarly history of Italy from 1943 to 2019, carried to the present. It reads alongside the older Mammarella L’Italia contemporanea (1943-1998) — the two Italian syntheses now held in the wiki, the newer extending the older’s coverage by two decades. It stands beside the French (Zancarini-Fournel) and Spanish (Tusell) syntheses as the Italian pillar of the wiki’s postwar continental coverage.

sources/geschichte-bundesrepublik-deutsc.title: Wolfgang Jäger & Werner Link — Geschichte der Bundesrepublik Deutschland, Band 5/II: Republik im Wandel 1974–1982, Die Ära Schmidt
sources/geschichte-bundesrepublik-deutsc.content:
Wolfgang Jäger & Werner Link — Geschichte der Bundesrepublik Deutschland, Band 5/II: Republik im Wandel 1974–1982, Die Ära Schmidt
Full bibliographic citation — Wolfgang Jäger and Werner Link, Geschichte der Bundesrepublik Deutschland, Band 5/II: Republik im Wandel 1974–1982. Die Ära Schmidt, with a closing essay by Joachim C. Fest, ed. Karl Dietrich Bracher, Theodor Eschenburg, Joachim C. Fest and Eberhard Jäckel, Deutsche Verlags-Anstalt, Stuttgart / F. A. Brockhaus, Mannheim. Set ISBN 978-3-421-06731-9. German text; scanned volume of 592 page-files; extracted plain text of 52,690 lines (printed pagination pp. 9–567 plus unpaginated plates).

































AuthorsWolfgang Jäger (the domestic-political part: Die Innenpolitik der sozial-liberalen Koalition 1974–1982); Werner Link (the foreign- and Germany-political part: Außen- und Deutschlandpolitik in der Ära Schmidt 1974–1982); with a concluding essay Die deutsche Frage: Das offene Dilemma by Joachim C. FestEditorsKarl Dietrich Bracher, Theodor Eschenburg, Joachim C. Fest, Eberhard Jäckel (general editors of the five-volume Geschichte der Bundesrepublik Deutschland)EditionDeutsche Verlags-Anstalt, Stuttgart / F. A. Brockhaus, Mannheim; set ISBN 978-3-421-06731-9; the second half-volume of Band 5 (Band 5/I Im Zeichen des Aufbruchs covers 1969–1974; this Band 5/II covers 1974–1982)StructureWolfgang Jäger, Die Innenpolitik der sozial-liberalen Koalition 1974–1982 (pp. 9–274) + Werner Link, Außen- und Deutschlandpolitik in der Ära Schmidt 1974–1982 (pp. 275–432) + Joachim C. Fest, Die deutsche Frage: Das offene Dilemma (pp. 433–446) + Nachwort (pp. 447–450) + Anhang: Zeittafel, Wahlen und Regierungen in Bund und Ländern, Auswahlbibliographie, Archivalien, Abkürzungsverzeichnis, Anmerkungen, Namenregister, Sachregister, Quellennachweis der AbbildungenPeriod1974–1982 — the era of the Federal Chancellor Helmut Schmidt: from the formation of the first Schmidt/Genscher cabinet after Willy Brandt’s resignation (May 1974), through the two Bundestag elections of 1976 and 1980 and the economic and terrorism crises, to the break of the SPD–FDP coalition and the change of government to Helmut Kohl in October 1982NoteThe contemporary-history volume of the standard multi-volume scholarly Geschichte der Bundesrepublik Deutschland series (general editors Bracher, Eschenburg, Fest, Jäckel). Written by professional academic historians shortly after the events; combines an analytical political history of the Schmidt years in domestic, foreign and German (East–West) policy with a critical opening essay by Joachim C. Fest on the German question
Content Summary
Die Innenpolitik der sozial-liberalen Koalition 1974–1982 (Wolfgang Jäger, pp. 9–274) — the domestic-political history of the SPD–FDP coalition under Helmut Schmidt. Jäger opens with the formation of the first Schmidt/Genscher cabinet (May 1974) in the shadow of Brandt’s resignation, and the slogan of «Kontinuität und Konzentration» (continuity and concentration); the economic crisis-management of the oil-price shock and the world recession; the turn of the FDP away from reform politics; the two governing parties and the shift of the SPD–FDP coalition; the strains in the governmental system (polarisation and consensus-building), the opposition’s offensive of the «Neue Soziale Frage» and Helmut Kohl’s first candidacy; the Bundestag election of 1976; the question of governability and the Federal states and Federal Constitutional Court as “co-governors”; the second Schmidt/Genscher cabinet of 1976–1980 and its challenges — the false start, Wildbad Kreuth and the unity of the Union, terrorism at its height (the German Autumn of 1977), and the citizens’ protest against nuclear energy; the party system’s signs of change — Schmidt as “Superstar” and the SPD before the ecological challenge, the FDP’s liberal independence, the Union’s programme work and its internal quarrels up to the “enthronement” of Franz Josef Strauß as candidate; the office of Federal President from the liberal Walter Scheel to his Christian-democratic successor Karl Carstens; citizens’ initiatives, the protest movement and the Greens; the Bundestag election of 1980, the “duel of the giants” between Schmidt and Strauß; the social forces and politics — trade unions and churches; and finally the sickness and end of the last Schmidt/Genscher cabinet of 1980–1982: the irritated coalition negotiations and a united opposition, the break and the “master strategy of the Chancellor”, and the change from a social-democratic minority cabinet to the Christian-liberal coalition of Helmut Kohl (October 1982). Jäger closes with the domestic-political balance-sheet of the Schmidt era.
Außen- und Deutschlandpolitik in der Ära Schmidt 1974–1982 (Werner Link, pp. 275–432) — the foreign- and Germany-policy of the Schmidt years. Link opens with stabilisation and crisis-management — continuity and concentration, and the European and world-economic crisis-management (the new Atlantic Charter controversy settled by the Ottawa Declaration); the European direct elections of 1979 and the European Monetary System; the Ostpolitik in the phase of détente — relations with the Soviet Union, multilateral détente policy in Europe, and bilateral policy toward Eastern Europe in a multilateral context; the co-ordination difficulties with the United States; the détente-policy crisis-management; the “Europeanisation” through German–French co-operation; the development of the German–German relations — German policy through permanent German–German negotiations, agreements despite the policy of delimitation (Abgrenzung), the policy of damage-limitation in the German–German relations, and the “summit” in the Uckermark (the meeting between Schmidt and Honecker near the Werbellinsee in December 1981); the worldwide dimension — the United Nations and the Third World: the elimination of residual colonialism in Africa, German development aid, the disputes over a New International Economic Order, German UN policy as worldwide peace policy, and cultural foreign policy and international cultural relations; and a résumé of the foreign- and Germany-policy of the Schmidt era.
Die deutsche Frage: Das offene Dilemma (Joachim C. Fest, pp. 433–446) — Fest’s closing essay. From the observation that the Reich which collapsed in 1945 received no epitaph and that the German nation-state was for a long time a burden of which many felt Europe and Germany were overdemanded, he traces the renewed awareness of the German question since the late 1960s: the recovery of a national consciousness and the search for a German position between East and West, the old dreams of a middle position, mediation and neutrality, and the distrust of the neighbours before a Germany that had not resolved the dilemma of its historical position.
Nachwort (pp. 447–450) — the editorial afterword, explaining that despite the nearness of the events the authors strove for objective presentation and analysis; that the two parts on domestic and foreign policy in the Schmidt era are to be read together with Karl Dietrich Bracher’s essay «Politik und Zeitgeist – Tendenzen der siebziger Jahre» and his introduction «Vom Machtwechsel zur Wende», published in Band 5/I.
Anhang — Zeittafel (chronological table, pp. 451–462); Wahlen und Regierungen in Bund und Ländern (elections and governments in the Federation and the Länder, pp. 463–474); Auswahlbibliographie (selected bibliography, pp. 475–484); Archivalien (archival sources, p. 485); Abkürzungsverzeichnis (list of abbreviations, p. 486); Anmerkungen (notes, pp. 487–538); Namenregister (index of names, pp. 539–556); Sachregister (subject index, pp. 557–566); Quellennachweis der Abbildungen (sources of the illustrations, p. 567).
Detailed Structure (from the Inhalt)

Die Regierungsparteien: Von der sozial-liberalen zur SPD/FDP-Koalition (p. 21) — Der Bruch: Die Meisterstrategie des Kanzlers; Vom sozialdemokratischen Minderheitskabinett zur christlich-liberalen Koalition

Closing essay on the German question in the postwar era.
Nachwort (p. 447) und Anhang
Nachwort (p. 447); Anhang: Zeittafel (p. 451), Wahlen und Regierungen in Bund und Ländern (p. 463), Auswahlbibliographie (p. 475), Archivalien (p. 485), Abkürzungsverzeichnis (p. 486), Anmerkungen (p. 487), Namenregister (p. 539), Sachregister (p. 557), Quellennachweis der Abbildungen (p. 567).

Javier Tusell — Historia de España en el siglo XX, III. La dictadura de Franco
Full bibliographic citation — Javier Tusell Gómez (1945–2005). Historia de España en el siglo XX, volume III, La dictadura de Franco. — First published 2000 (publication date in this edition 6 March 2000). This text from the ePubLibre digital edition (ePUB r1.3, JeSsE, 6 February 2014; UUID 03d3ce49-7a2a-4822-ad87-f6f39849e113; hash cbda17f72963c6e02278ac5597cfe884). The four-volume series covers the Spanish twentieth century; volume III is the continuous political, social and cultural history of Franco’s dictatorship from the last war bulletin of 1 April 1939 to the dictator’s death in November 1975. Volume IV (La transición democrática y el gobierno socialista) continues the series into the democratic transition and the Socialist governments.





























AuthorJavier Tusell Gómez (1945–2005) — Spanish historian, catedrático of Contemporary History at the UNED; specialist in Spanish twentieth-century political history (elections and parties, Alfonso XIII, Primo de Rivera, Franco and his regime, the opposition, Carrero Blanco, Arias Navarro, Juan Carlos)EditionFirst published 2000; this text the ePubLibre ePUB r1.3 (JeSsE, 6 February 2014); digital UUID 03d3ce49-7a2a-4822-ad87-f6f39849e113; hash cbda17f72963c6e02278ac5597cfe884StructureOpening block (dictator / regime / society) + three long period-parts — La tentación fascista y la supervivencia (1939–1951); Los años del consenso (1951–1965); Desarrollo económico, apertura y tardofranquismo (1966–1975) — with titled sections + selective bibliography + author note; ~19,406 lines of extracted plain textPeriod1 April 1939 (last war bulletin) to November 1975 (Franco’s death) — wartime foreign policy and failed fascistisation; postwar isolation and autarky; Concordat and US pacts; developmentalism and apertura; succession, Carrero, Arias Navarro; opposition unity; late decolonisation of Guinea and the SaharaNoteModern Spanish scholarly synthesis of the Franco dictatorship, not a memoir or party history. The same volume is also held in the Rest of Europe 1919–45 wiki (the argument opens in 1939); it is retained here because the bulk of the narrative after 1945–51 and the whole of the 1951–75 arc fall inside this folder’s span, and because volume IV of the series continues directly from Franco’s death into the Transition
Javier Tusell wrote the volume as a full-scale scholarly synthesis of the Franco regime — the dictator, the regime as a dictatorship, the repression and exile of 1939, the fascist temptation and wartime foreign policy of 1939–45, the postwar isolation and autarky of the 1940s, the years of consensus and economic opening (1951–65), and the tardofranquismo of 1966–75. The author’s generation, as the closing biography notes, was obsessed with why democracy failed under the Second Republic and what the Franco dictatorship and the later restoration under Juan Carlos meant for Spanish democracy.
The text is 19,406 lines, extracted from the EPUB container (clean text layer; no OCR required). Alpha-character ratio high; no Fraktur or garbled OCR layer.
Content Summary
Front matter. Title page: Historia de España en el siglo XX / III. La dictadura de Franco; ePUB r1.3 (JeSsE 06.02.14); original title note; Javier Tusell, 2000; digital-editor credits. Publisher’s blurb: “Una obra fundamental para entender la España de hoy.” Series note: four volumes covering a contested century whose knowledge is indispensable for any diagnosis of the present; volume III analyses the stages of Franco’s dictatorship from postwar repression to economic development and the final opening of the regime.
Opening block — El dictador, el régimen y la sociedad
Opens on the night of 1 April 1939: at a quarter past eleven the habitual announcer Fernando Fernández de Córdoba reads the last official war bulletin (no. 982) on the radios of the victorious Spain — “cautivo y desarmado” the Red Army, Franco’s troops have reached their last military objectives — and the less-remembered vivas that accompanied it to the exterior allies of the three preceding years, Portugal, Italy and Germany. The Victory parade of 19 May 1939 (120,000 soldiers; the grand cross of San Fernando imposed by Jordana) and the religious ceremony of 20 May in Santa Bárbara (Franco under palio; sword deposited before the Cristo de Lepanto; Cardinal Gomá) frame the volume’s three subjects: the person of the dictator, the regime as a dictatorship, and the society that lived under it. The ceremonial — military, political and religious mixed as in a medieval warrior society — is presented as evidence of the rupture at the end of the Civil War.
Franco: biografía y praxis política de un dictador
Against the tendency to reduce the regime to a psychological portrait of its founder, Tusell sets Franco’s biography and political practice — the traits that the regime itself made the centre of rumour and expectation, and that the historian must neither inflate into pure personalism nor dissolve into impersonal structure. Born 1892 at El Ferrol in a naval family of six generations; entry in 1907 to the Toledo Academy (youngest cadet of his promotion) after the fleet’s destruction closed the naval path taken by his brother Nicolás; African career, Civil War rise, and the long praxis of rule to 1975.
El franquismo como dictadura
Defines the Spanish regime of 1939–1975 as a dictatorship without making it a Spanish peculiarity: Franco’s conceptions and behaviour expressed a wider European type rather than a unique national path. What was peculiar was that, in Franco’s lifetime, the regime passed from resemblance to one type of dictatorship to another without substantial change of person at the head — a reason to name it by who personified it. Typology against fascist, authoritarian and personal-dictatorship models.
Vencedores y vencidos: Los desastres de la guerra y la represión
From Cambó’s wartime reflection (from emigration, despite conservative leanings and aid to the Franco side) that the “Año triunfal” forgot the torrents of blood, the destruction of wealth and the sediment of rancour, through the disasters of the war and the repression that fell on the defeated after 1 April 1939. Critiques the symbolic “one million dead” figure as exaggerated; engages Salas’s magnitudes (brutal ferocity on both sides, but not exceptional in the contemporary world at roughly over 1 per cent direct war dead).
El exilio y el comienzo de la posguerra en el interior
The exile of 1939 as a rupture in Spanish history — larger, longer and more severed from interior reality than earlier Spanish emigrations. Waves: ~200,000 into France after the fall of the North (35,000 remaining there); ~350,000 crossing after the fall of Catalonia (180,000 combatants); a third wave later. Penury of the French camps; negotiations in which France pressed Franco to take refugees back. Interior postwar for those who remained under the weight of the victors’ order.
La tentación fascista y la supervivencia (1939–1951)
Periodising frame for the first long phase: economic policy makes 1959 a key date, but the decades themselves differ sharply; 1939–51 is the phase of fascist temptation, wartime alignment, cosmetic adaptation after 1945, isolation, and the “noche oscura” of autarky. Predominance of politics over economy; lamentable economic management by those in power, beyond the circumstances of Spain and the world.
El «Nuevo Estado» y la «fascistización» fallida
From the end of the Civil War to the summer of 1940 — when world war seemed decided and Fascist Italy entered — Spain’s internal and institutional drift toward homologation with the Axis (more than in foreign policy alone) and the limits of that “fascistisation.” The months that seemed to decant Spain toward Axis-type institutions.
La tentación intervencionista y la lucha interna (1940–1942)
Against the late-franquista propaganda claim that Germany pressed and Franco resisted, Tusell holds that from the German victory over France there was an absolute identification of Spanish leaders with the Axis cause, prolonged with nuances into 1944; Falangist press treated the defeat of France as the great occasion awaited for decades for a repartition of Europe and French colonial possessions. Internal struggle (Serrano Suñer and others) and the interventionist temptation of 1940–42; Spanish pretensions never had a chance of success because Hitler’s Germany was far from the vision Spanish leaders projected onto it.
Un titubeante camino hacia la neutralidad (1942–1945)
Serrano Suñer’s displacement and Jordana at Foreign Affairs; the hesitant path toward genuine neutrality as the world war turned. Anglo-American landings in North Africa accompanied by assurances that the operation was not directed against Franco, even as Allied distrust remained. Facilities previously enjoyed by Germans and Italians were cut back; Jordana’s December 1942 journey to Portugal. Neutrality favoured by events as much as by any single decision of Franco.
El cambio cosmético: La política del régimen entre 1945 y 1951
At the close of the world war the regime faced simultaneous dangers: uncertainty of internal course, an opposition aiming at rupture or peaceful transition, and external isolation born of its wartime stance. Franco early discovered the need to show an appearance of institutional change through “constitutional” dispositions that barely modified the real power he retained (Ley de Cortes of 1942 read more as wartime than as postwar camouflage). Lequerica’s advice in 1945 that Arrese (and with him the Falange) “debía apartarse de la luz”; from 1944, signs of a will to offer an apparently democratising image.
La oposición de los supervivientes: La izquierda desde 1939 a 1951
The left opposition of the survivors — opened with the figure of Manuel Cortés, the socialist mayor of Mijas who reappeared in April 1969 after thirty years hidden in his house (from age thirty-four to sixty-four) under the amnesty that removed Civil-War responsibilities — from 1939 through guerrilla and exile politics to 1951. The precarious situation of the defeated in 1939, prolonged against expectation after 1945.
El gran momento de la alternativa monárquica
Prieto’s readiness, despite a trajectory close to republicanism, to deal with the monarchists as the path to substituting Franco; Western democratic powers’ preference for a monarchical path of reconciliation. After the Lausanne manifesto of 1945, emissaries between Don Juan and Franco; limited possibilities of agreement — Franco demanding that the Monarchy incarnate “las esencias antiliberales de nuestra Cruzada.”
Franco, aislado
Post-1945 isolation did not begin only with the Allied victory but became severe then; Tusell assigns primary responsibility to Franco’s maintenance of the political system, not only to wartime Axis collaboration. Spain not invited to the San Francisco conference that founded the UN; Mexican delegate’s proposal that future membership exclude the Spanish case. Survival despite the isolation.
La «noche oscura»: Autarquía y racionamiento en la década de los cuarenta
The coherence of early postwar interior and exterior policy; when the European environment changed, the political system did not, adapting only cosmetically. Spain’s postwar condition penurious though destruction was not comparable to Europe after 1945. Autarky and state interventionism before and after 1945, with a social-revolutionary tone often in contradiction with ministers’ dispositions; rationing and the economic “dark night” of the 1940s. Continuity such that 1945 was not a true caesura in economic history.
Cultura y sociedad en la primera posguerra
From the “Edad de Plata” of Spanish letters at the Civil War’s outbreak — fin-de-siècle generation still mature, heirs and new generations productive — to culture and society under the first postwar: rupture, exile of talent (Alberti’s verses on the Atlantic crossing), and the official cultural order.
Los años del consenso: el apogeo del régimen (1951–1965)
The central years as plenitude and apogee: a dictatorship stable enough that passive social acceptance could be called consensus — explained by repression and the dismantling of opposition. By 1951 the worst immediate postwar pressure had been passed.
El final definitivo del aislamiento internacional: El concordato y los pactos con Estados Unidos
Cold War conjuncture of first-order importance for the dictatorship’s survival: with the Korean conflict in 1950 Spain began rapid international rehabilitation culminating in 1953 (Concordat and US pacts). UN path: November 1950 revocation of the 1946 recommendations; entry into FAO (1950), UPU, WHO, ICAO (1951), UNESCO (1952); UN membership mid-December 1955 with a package of nations after Soviet support for the proposition. Concordat with the Holy See (August 1953) — initiative from the Spanish state (Ruiz Giménez as ambassador from 1948) despite advantages to the Church — and US pacts one month later as pure recognition of admission to the international community.
España ante Europa. La descolonización: Marruecos
European democratic memory of the Civil War versus American strategic distance; De Gaulle and Adenauer as examples of conservative European leaders still holding the Spanish dictatorship at institutional distance. Spain before Europe; the decolonisation of Morocco. Regime’s periodic fear of isolation even after rehabilitation.
La política del régimen y la oposición hasta 1956
The 1951 ministerial change among the most complete in the regime’s history — counterweight of tendencies under Franco’s arbitration, yet representing in part the return of the Falange (Girón, Fernández Cuesta, Muñoz Grandes; official reappearance of the Secretariat). Interior politics without major convulsions through the mid-1950s; limited opposition capacity.
Una nueva oposición política
After 1956, a new interior opposition not derived from prewar or exile groups but from among the victors or those hitherto absent from national political life — the germ of what late franquismo called the “oposición moderada.” Opposition and official politics ran contrary paths; only episodically did the first affect the second (most decisively at Munich 1962). Links to cultural evolution.
Por o contra la Falange: La vida política del régimen entre 1956 y 1965
From 1956 the first serious attempt at institutionalisation (Franco allergic to “constitutionalisation,” accepting only the term institutionalisation); blue revival versus technocratic course. Falangists’ sense that Franco was not one of theirs; hatred of radicals toward Carrero; Franco’s instrumental and yet indispensable use of the Falange. Process culminating more clearly after the 1965 cabinet.
El alivio de la autarquía y el cambio en la política económica
Early-1950s growth of national income; end of the ration book in 1951; Spain catching the European postwar “miracles” after exceptional backwardness (low energy consumption per inhabitant). Acceptance of Franco’s Spain as an irremediable evil by the democratic powers, especially the United States, with immediate economic effect in scarce foreign exchange. Road toward the relief of autarky and the 1959 Stabilisation Plan.
De la oposición política a la oposición social
After 1962 (Munich; ministerial change) a new stage in which social protest outweighs strictly political opposition; the “oposición social” consolidated in the second half of the 1960s. Mid-decade, not yet fully irreversible; this section is the prior stage that helps explain it.
La cultura durante el franquismo intermedio
Intermediate-franquismo culture: opening abroad, will to modernise, identification of much of the cultural world with opposition, yet contact with official circles that later fed subversive attitudes. Continuity in culture more marked than the political rupture with the past. The intellectual sector that advanced Spain, for the first time since the Civil War, in a modernising sense; a political class and an intellectual world still present in later Spanish public life.
La cultura popular y el ocio
Cinema, popular arts and leisure as defining marks of the epoch; the porous border between high culture and mass entertainment. 1951 creation of the Ministry of Information and Tourism with a directorate-general for Cinema; new generation of filmmakers and a critical consciousness parallel to literature’s evolution.
Desarrollo económico, apertura y tardofranquismo (1966–1975)
The last decade dominated more than any earlier phase by Franco’s person in decline; zones of indifference left to ministers shrink as succession and crisis concentrate on the aging dictator. Economic growth continuing to modify the closed and authoritarian Spanish society; a political system that seemed to answer to another world wrestling with modernisation’s contradictions, while the European context appeared to impose a course that was not fully followed after initial liberalising measures. Capacity of reaction of those at the head reduced to a minimum compared with the past.
La modernización de la sociedad española
Economic growth paired with deep social transformation of political repercussion. Census 1960–1970: population from 30 to more than 33 million; demographic modernisation (mortality change in the 1950s already Europeanising); internal migrations of the 1960s — roughly four million Spaniards changing residence, drawn to economic resources and fleeing rural stagnation.
El cambio en el catolicismo español
Reception of Vatican II; the Church as both mirror and motor of mental and political change, given its enormous social power. Deep into the 1950s, hierarchy and Catholics still shared identity of Spain, regime and Catholicism (e.g. Aurelio del Pino, bishop of Lérida, on Franco). Nacional-catolicismo as mentality more than precise theology — close bond to the State, “insatiability” that would claim the whole of life — already becoming extravagant as internal Catholic evolution advanced.
La apertura (1965–1969)
“Apertura” as loosening of controls without substantial transformation of the regime; optimism from growth and weak opposition; Press Law and younger politicians of imprecise affiliation, better managers with more bureaucratic formation. Apertura not the same as institutionalisation, but related: Carrero not aligned with the first, yet from 1958 defending the second as prolongation of the regime (“Si el Rey recoge los poderes que tiene V. E. … lo cambiará todo”).
La decisión sucesoria. Matesa y la división interna del régimen
Juan Carlos named successor — López Rodó’s slow process with Carrero (“Operación Salmón”); the last institutionalising decision taken with sufficient unity of the ruling class. 1963 installation of Juan Carlos at Zarzuela; Franco’s alternative thoughts (renewable regency; Alfonso de Borbón); demand for “identificación absoluta.” Fraga’s November 1965 foreign-press remarks; Matesa scandal and internal division.
La protesta laboral. El terrorismo
Rising opposition in the final phase: labour protest and terrorism; the regime coexisted with both; historical weight lies as much in that coexistence as in the pressure itself. First half of the 1950s as minimum of opposition activity; final phase the opposite. New climate influencing the opposition toward the path of unity; coincidence of journalists’ and lawyers’ movements with social protest.
El tardofranquismo: Carrero Blanco, presidente
Franco past seventy-five; failure of the old arbitral role among the victorious families; foreign visitors’ portraits of an old man who scarcely spoke. Tardofranquismo defined not only by physical decline but by lack of clear course, public-order problems, fragmentation of the political class, proliferation of antagonistic leaderships, and paralysis before the most urgent problems. October 1969 government with Carrero as vice-president, labelled monocolor by adversaries (López Rodó contesting the label in his memoirs).
El tardofranquismo: el Gobierno Arias Navarro
Almost the only continuity between Carrero’s government and Arias Navarro’s was Franco’s irremediable physical decline — senile, inarticulate, short steps, tearful, “escuchaba, pero no oía” (Fraga). Appointment of Arias as testimony to the definitive rise of the family circle in regime politics (Nieto Antúnez, Arias; Carrero never had much standing there). Fernández Miranda marginalised despite acting to check Iniesta’s excessive Guardia Civil instructions. Juan Carlos not consulted in the cabinet’s gestation — raising the question how far the change put the succession itself in doubt.
Actividad de la oposición: el camino hacia la unidad
Social protest rising slowly to 1967, sharply from 1973, peaking in the months after Franco’s death; not by itself able to overthrow the regime, but the backdrop of late politics. Terrorism incapable of substituting the regime, yet constant proof of repressive impotence and a mobiliser of part of Basque society; by this stage ETA’s brutality had alienated the relative benevolence with which part of the opposition had viewed it into the early 1970s. Path toward opposition unity.
España y el mundo occidental
External context of the final phase; the Saharan/Moroccan crisis in the regime’s last weeks. Castiella at Foreign Affairs 1957–1969, the longest-serving foreign minister of the franquismo — nationalist, youthful Falange attraction, promoted by the Catholic family of the regime (Vatican embassy then the Ministry); programme combining prior lines (Arab world) with new ones. Spain’s peculiar place in Western Europe and Western defence.
La descolonización tardía: Guinea y el Sahara
Carrero against decolonisation, Castiella promoting it (partly with Gibraltar in view); Sahara and Guinea declared provinces 1958–59, then the retreat — Guinea first, Sahara in the terminal crisis. Difference from Salazar’s Portugal: colonies meant more to Portugal, and Salazar exercised more direct foreign-policy responsibility than Franco at this stage.
¿Una cultura comprometida?
Late-franquismo culture: less simple increase of cultural belligerence than development of culture and society beside the political system, with periodic conflict. Thought and social sciences on premises wholly alien to the official political world; literature shedding exaggerated social-political pretension for experimentalism not directly tied to political or ethical demonstration. Theatre and cinema, more exposed to censorship, retained significant cases of belligerence. 1969 as a cultural as well as political marker. Homologation and recovery as keywords; disappearance of the interminable debate on national peculiarity.
España a la muerte de Franco
Last year of Franco’s life — pathos and esperpento; July 1974 thrombophlebitis from hard gift shoes; re-learning to speak and walk by narrating the Moroccan campaigns; obstinacy in remaining in power until death in November 1975. Daily routine of receiving dozens of people while barely articulating a word; sedentary distractions (television); impressibility of age, Parkinson’s, and the impact of Saharan/Moroccan news on a man whose life had centred on the Moroccan wars. Sociologically the regime represented less and less of society and was increasingly available for other options. Younger regime politicians seeking an exit (Tácito; the independent parliamentary group of summer 1975 with future UCD figures and names such as Primo de Rivera). Society not strongly politicised against the regime in Martín Villa’s sense of “motivaciones apremiantes,” yet desiring a democratic order in principle: surveys show democratic preference rising (1966: 35 per cent for decisions by persons elected by the people vs a leading man; 1974: 60 per cent); conformity values (peace, order, tradition) from 71 per cent (1966) to 55 per cent (1975); disconformity values (justice, liberty, democracy) from 20 to 33 per cent; belief that parties would be “beneficial” from 12 per cent (1971) to 56 per cent (spring 1975). At Franco’s death, ~72 per cent wanted the King to grant freedom of expression and ~70 per cent universal suffrage. The non-traumatic transition’s starting point lay in this panorama and in the political capacity of those who led it.
Bibliografía
Selective bibliography with asterisks for especially original recent monographs. Opens with Stanley Payne, El régimen de Franco, 1936–1975 (Alianza, 1987) as the best overall study, and the contrasting Biescas–Tuñón de Lara antifranquista synthesis (España bajo la dictadura franquista, Labor, 1980) versus Ricardo de la Cierva’s Historia del franquismo (Planeta, 1975 and 1978), closer to the regime. Continues through specialised works on politics, economy, Church, opposition, culture and foreign relations (Fontana ed. España bajo el franquismo, Crítica, 1986; congresses and journal special numbers from the early 1990s onward). The digital edition closes with a short author biography of Tusell (Barcelona 26 August 1945 – 8 February 2005): formation in philosophy, history and political science; teaching from 1966; production on elections and parties, Alfonso XIII, caciquismo, Primo de Rivera’s coup, Christian democracy, Franco and the regime, Spain and the Second World War, Franco and the Count of Barcelona, Catholics under franquismo, the democratic opposition, Carrero, Arias Navarro, and Juan Carlos — all ordered to the obsession of his generation with democracy in Spain.

Relationship to the Wiki
Tusell III gives this wiki its continuous scholarly history of Franco’s Spain across the whole span from the Civil War’s end to the dictator’s death. The early chapters (1939–45 fascistisation, interventionist temptation, hesitant neutrality) overlap the Rest of Europe 1919–45 wiki, where the same volume is also held; the middle and late chapters (isolation and autarky, Concordat and US pacts, developmentalism, apertura, succession, Carrero, Arias Navarro, opposition unity, late decolonisation, Spain at Franco’s death) fall squarely inside this folder’s 1946–present span. Beside the de Gaulle Discours et Messages tomes (T2–T5), which supply the French case in the General’s own voice from the Fourth Republic through the close of the Fifth Republic presidency, Tusell supplies the Spanish case as modern secondary synthesis. Volume IV of the same series (La transición democrática y el gobierno socialista) continues from this endpoint into the Transition and the Socialist governments and is processed as a sibling source in this wiki.

Content Summary
Front matter. Series blurb for the four-volume Historia de España en el siglo XX — a contested century whose knowledge is indispensable for any diagnosis of the present; Spain protagonist of two fundamental events (Civil War and Transition); Spanish culture from the early twentieth century at heights permitting comparison with the Siglo de Oro. Volume IV covers “un periodo fundamental para la España actual: la transición democrática y el primer gobierno socialista.” Title page: Javier Tusell / Historia de España en el siglo XX / IV. La transición democrática y el gobierno socialista; ePUB r1.3 (JeSsE 06.02.14); original title note; Javier Tusell, 2000; digital-editor credits.
La transición a la democracia (1975–1982)
Opens by placing Spain’s twentieth-century world role as relatively reduced, with two exceptions: the Civil War of 1936–1939 (battlefield of Europe’s antagonisms more than Spanish protagonism) and the Transition to democracy. Historians, like Vargas Llosa’s intellectuals, are often “amantes de las catástrofes,” so the Civil War has drawn more ink than a process that ended well; objective importance of 1975–1982 is not thereby reduced. No near models, local or temporal, suggested that such a process could succeed without external aggression.
El comienzo de la «tercera ola»: Las transiciones hacia la democracia en el Mediterráneo
The Spanish case framed in Huntington’s “third wave” of democratizations. The wave began in the Mediterranean in 1974 and removed the non-totalitarian right-wing dictatorships of Greece, Portugal and Spain; it then crossed the Atlantic and, unpredictably, reached the communist regimes and the Soviet Union itself. Transitions explained in terms of profitability for all political actors when the cost of repression or violent insurrection is perceived as excessive; democratic consensus appears when institutions become “what unites us all” (Thiers). Every transition is a multi-sided chess game whose final result is not written; individuals and circumstance matter.
La peculiaridad de la vía española a la democracia
A quarter-century on, the Spanish case can be treated as the paradigmatic, exemplary or canonical transition. Complete, without Gorbachev-style path uncertainty and without Pinochet-style “authoritarian enclaves”; the political class converted sincerely to democratic principles rather than fictitiously adapting. Decisive prior transformation under the dictatorship (without parallel in Greece, Portugal, Turkey, or even fascist Italy) made the outcome possible. Result of given circumstances and of individual and collective protagonists.
La nueva monarquía: El rey Juan Carlos I
The monarchical institution as a distinctive Spanish trait of the Transition. Its function was not decorative: the great danger in any transition is the break of legitimacy between the vanished dictatorship and the not-yet-consolidated democracy; the Monarchy supplied an instrument to avoid that break, without parallel in other third-wave cases. From the first moment Juan Carlos chose to be a great king rather than a small Caudillo.
Arias Navarro o el reformismo imposible
The King’s early need to establish supreme responsibility and obtain the resignation of the president of the government; appointment of Torcuato Fernández Miranda as President of the Cortes and of the Council of the Kingdom. Arias Navarro’s reformism impossible from the start; Fraga’s and Areilza’s roles; the government as “colchón” (Ossorio) between two periods.
La crisis del semestre Arias
Essential difficulties from the incoherence of the government and the limitations of its president, compounded by public-order conflicts, economic crisis and the wave of strikes of early 1976 (especially Madrid). Political demands alone could not mobilise mass protest, yet a sense of release among organised workers extended the conflictivity. Arias’s reformism proved impossible from its origins; yet the Arias period mattered as a cushion between two phases. Substitution engineered through Fernández Miranda’s control of the Council of the Kingdom; tern of Silva Muñoz, Suárez and López de Letona; Fraga and Areilza surprised and indignant.
Adolfo Suárez: el cambio empieza a hacerse realidad
Choice of Suárez among the three young reformist ministers explained by biographical traits optimal for getting franquista political class approval of a substantial Law for Political Reform through the National Council and the Cortes. Judgment on Suárez has shifted sharply within a quarter-century; there are two Suárezes separated by the cardinal date of 1979. Mere origin, charm and skill are insufficient to explain the historical protagonist.
La ley para la reforma política
Fernández Miranda’s path “de la ley a la ley.” Summer 1976 drafting of the Law for Political Reform (Fernández Miranda and Lavilla’s team, especially Herrero); several redactions. 8 September presentation to senior military commanders, to whom Suárez gave the impression that the PCE would not be admitted to legality; neither the King nor he then thought that politically possible, and the party’s statutes seemed to bar it juridically. Referendum approval of the Law.
La transición entre el terrorismo y el golpe militar
From the referendum on the Law for Political Reform to the June 1977 elections: weeks in which terrorism and military pressure could have aborted the process. Spanish will for democratic coexistence, the attitude of party leaders and of the Government prevented involution. Suárez’s best moment in measuring time for two stages of reform — first the Law through the regime’s Cortes, then free elections for a constituent work. Economic crisis constant backdrop; deliberate delay of a harsh economic programme that might have derailed the political calendar (Ossorio’s memoirs).
La legalización del PCE
Atocha massacre of labour lawyers (24 January 1977) — seven dead — produced solidarity and demonstrated the PCE’s capacity to control its masses. Legalisation on 9 April 1977; real tolerance already from December 1976. Carrillo’s return from exile (February 1976), hidden, opening contacts with the opposition.
El nacimiento de un sistema de partidos
Public attention shifted from transition difficulties to the imminent electoral campaign. New party system configured mainly from opposition forces to the previous regime rather than from the dictatorship’s associationism; unitary opposition organisms lost the initiative once Suárez reached the presidency. Spectacle of numerous groups in the months before the elections.
La devolución de España
Julián Marías’s phrase on the “return” of Spain in the Transition; intellectual and journalistic framing of the recovery of a country long held apart from its European peers.
Un largo camino hacia la Constitución
Constituent work after the 1977 elections; consensus politics; long drafting path toward the constitutional text.
La Constitución de 1978: elaboración y contenido
Constitution of eleven titles and 169 articles (plus additional and transitional dispositions). Elaboration by consensus among the principal parliamentary forces; content settling the form of the State, rights, the Crown, Cortes, government, judiciary, territorial organisation (Title VIII), constitutional reform.
La gran cuestión pendiente: nacionalismos y terrorismo
Nationalisms and terrorism as the great unresolved question beside the constitutional settlement; Basque and Catalan tracks; ETA pressure on the new democracy.
Las elecciones de 1979
Second general elections under the new system; consolidation and early strains of the Suárez majority.
Triunfo y caída de Adolfo Suárez
First error of Suárez already in the investiture debate; decline accelerated from 1980. From summer 1980 polls placed Felipe González and the PSOE ahead. Personal and party exhaustion after the constituent years.
Los enemigos de la transición: el papel del Ejército
Military as principal structural enemy of the Transition; successive conspiracies and pressures; the regime’s armed forces as inheritance that the new monarchy and civilian government had to manage without rupture.
El golpe de Estado del 23-F
23 February 1981 coup attempt; Tejero in the Congress; King’s televised intervention; defeat of the conspiracy and its effect on democratic legitimacy (dissatisfaction with the democratic regime falling from about 9 per cent before February 1981 to about 5 per cent by the 1982 elections).
El gobierno Calvo-Sotelo
Calvo-Sotelo after Suárez: collaboration without personal similarity; origin in business and “juanista” monarchist milieu, close to the Catholic family of the regime and to Europeanist sectors; prior procurador in Franco’s Cortes by the sindical third. Inheritance of Suárez including party presidency questions.
La crisis del centrismo
Decline of Calvo-Sotelo’s government parallel to the decomposition of UCD — each unintelligible without the other. A party that had played a transcendental role in the Transition practically ended its life in the 1982 parliamentary election — exceptional in comparative transition history. UCD not simply a vehicle whose only reason for being was the Transition (contrast Adenauer’s CDU); Spanish consensus hard to achieve, so the governing party filtered conflicts internally and avoided confrontation during the constitutional period. After Suárez’s resignation from party presidency, sterile Palma de Mallorca congress (January 1981); 23-F postponed divergences; divorce law and the “plataforma moderada” of some forty centrist deputies (Alzaga, Herrero); Galician elections of October 1981 as first significant region where AP overtook UCD.
El camino del PSOE hacia el Gobierno
Agony of UCD opened the opportunity for the PSOE as second electoral force and logical government alternative. Decisive transformation in the two 1979 congresses — from theoretically radical positions to reformism connecting better with majority Spanish society; Spanish factors in the internal fights beyond the European socialist pattern. Felipe González’s proposal to drop Marxism as exclusive ideological principle; XVIII congress chaos (“gran novatada”); González’s resignation after re-election; only Bustelo willing to succeed him among the radicals; extraordinary congress of September 1979 restored González with a reduced, controllable delegate body.
Octubre del 82: el final de la transición
October 1982 general elections as the political end of the Transition. Institutionally the Transition had ended with the Constitution (December 1978); politically it ends in October 1982 for three main reasons: the political group that had held the protagonist role not only lost power but disappeared, replaced; the military conspiracy had been defeated in 1981 and dissatisfaction with democracy fell; the results themselves became a plebiscite consolidating the regime.
El fin del aislamiento: Política exterior durante la transición
Interior politics predominated, so external transition was slower — not definitive until 1986 — yet democratisation equated to Europeanisation and homologation with the Western world. External factors influenced but did not decide (contrast Portugal). Socialist models Sweden or Austria rather than clear Western-bloc alignment; disappointment at the slowness of EEC entry.
Evolución económica durante la transición política
Politics has dominated the preceding pages; economy now treated at medium term. Calvo-Sotelo’s memoir claim that he governed at the worst moment of the economic crisis. Spanish economy still appeared buoyant in 1973 (8 per cent growth; unemployment barely over 1 per cent; inflation 11 per cent) but structural problems underlay the surface; small public sector yet state omnipresence. Oil shocks overlapped with the political transition; Moncloa Pacts as political pact with economic content.
El cambio social: la transición sindical
Social evolution requires a longer span than seven years, yet demography was already European (intercensal growth 1.1 per cent); first step toward a stationary society; abrupt fertility decline in a still relatively young population. Union transition and the reorganisation of labour representation.
La cultura durante la transición: El tiempo de las recuperaciones
No exact coincidence between political Transition and cultural transition. Late dictatorship already showed cultural belligerence against the political system (e.g. El espíritu de la colmena, La prima Angélica; novels published abroad). Political freedom did not produce an immediate flowering of values the previous situation had marginalised; Spanish culture continued to be led mainly by those who had begun to play their roles earlier. Cultural transition later in time; recovery as keyword.
Un balance de la transición
Positive aspects predominate clearly — not only because the Transition ended well, but because the starting point did not justify full optimism despite economic development. Among third-wave countries, only the Mediterranean starters consolidated democracy rapidly; Spain’s difficulties were comparatively greater than Greece’s or Portugal’s, yet traumas of all kinds were lesser. Spain never passed through the danger of becoming a left-wing dictatorial regime of the Portuguese revolutionary type.
El gobierno socialista (1982–1996)
Shift of the historian’s focus from “tiempo presente” (lived as memory and experience) to “Historia inmediata” — possible but provisional, reconstructing roots of the present in the past without knowing yet how deep they run.
Felipe González, como protagonista histórico
Figure and political personality of Felipe González give unity and coherence to the period; the label “felipismo” has acquired a plainly negative connotation and is set aside. Object of successive enthusiasms and hatreds, often from the same persons. Leader of the party at thirty-two, president of the government at forty — representative of a new political generation, the very counterfigure of Franco (Haro’s “primera cara del antifranquismo”; Vázquez Montalbán’s “antifranquismo inocente”). JOC and HOAC militancy; Jiménez Fernández as critical teacher. Leadership over the party, conquered in 1974 and revalidated in 1979, not seriously contested until the 1996 electoral defeat. Overload of radical ideology from opposition years superimposed by pragmatism that chose moderate reformism in fundamental decisions. First Spanish democratic leader adapted to ordinary democratic work in times of normality; far below Azaña’s intellectual capacity, knew better than Azaña how to set calendar, priorities and content of a reforming action once in power.
Los gobiernos socialistas y la opinión durante la década de los ochenta
Comfortable parliamentary majority; governing team essentially durable through the 1980s. Ministers in three groups; economic portfolios always in hands of specialists long linked to the Administration (e.g. Ministry of Commerce) — greatest continuity with the past, explaining that the essential line of economic policy did not change.
La oposición política y social
Essential factor of political stability: impotence of the opposition, especially the right-wing alternative. AP, animated by having substituted and then liquidated UCD, believed a bipartisan system was configured in which it would be the natural turn; limitations of the right’s electoral offer confirmed in elections and in memoirs of its own leaders.
Un modo de consolidación democrática
Arrival of the Socialists met genuine yearnings for governmental stability and a very negative judgment of UCD. Involucionist dangers disappeared during the Socialist stage; a peculiar political system settled with clearly positive and more ambivalent aspects. No truly significant extreme-right group, unlike other countries of the geographic area; democratic legitimacy already consolidated.
Terrorismo y antiterrorismo: los GAL y sus consecuencias
Antiterrorist policy of the Socialist governments often judged one of their greatest failures, but that judgment born mainly from the medium-term damage of the GAL (Grupos Antiterroristas de Liberación). GAL do not summarise the whole of government action in this field; negative judgment rests on broader grounds. Starting point October 1982 and the positive balance left by Rosón at the Interior Ministry.
La construcción del estado de las autonomías
During the Socialist tenure, development of Title VIII of the Constitution, whose concrete content had still to be specified; repeated earlier attempts to order the autonomic process had failed. Only five Statutes of Autonomy approved by 1981. August 1983 Constitutional Court struck down decisive parts of the LOAPA, discarding any “reconducción” of the autonomic process toward lower competence levels; the Court attributed to itself the power that politicians had been denied, but by that procedure at least a framework was reached.
La política y la realidad económica en la etapa socialista
Economic situation at the Socialists’ arrival as lamentable as earlier pages indicated; second oil shock overlapped the first without political conditions for a coherent durable response. Investment retreating; unemployment already high. Campaign promises of a different economic policy not carried out and apparently never on the real horizon of government purposes — technicians who executed economic policy had been formed in continuity with prior administration.
Hacia la pérdida de la mayoría absoluta (1989–1993)
First half of the 1980s: PSOE voting intention 30–40 per cent; satisfaction with González extremely high (46 to over 60 per cent); right averaging no more than 15 per cent of voting intention before proper campaign periods. 1986–1992 still high PSOE intention (24–33 per cent); decisive opinion change from 1991, when PSOE began definitively to lose the hegemony it had enjoyed. By 1991, 56 per cent of those surveyed thought they paid too much tax relative to services received (91 per cent among senior executives); identification with centre-left declining.
España al final de la época socialista: la sociedad
Important social changes whose origin lay in the earliest moments of the Transition; against the critique of the Transition as a purely political phenomenon. Mid-1990s Spain eighth in the world by GDP and ninth by human development index; population approaching forty million, possibly a ceiling. Demographers already forecasting eventual negative growth between 2010 and 2025.
Nuevas perspectivas culturales
Culture under the Socialist decade and a half: diffusion of education and knowledge; quasi-federal territorial organisation of the State. Gravest problem of Spanish culture at the moment of writing: making real plurality compatible with no less evident unity, or at least very close relation among its components. Development of the State of the Autonomies followed by cultural and linguistic pluralisation.
Bibliografía
Selective bibliography with asterisks for especially original recent monographs. Opens with Samuel P. Huntington, The Third Wave (1991); comparative work on Spain and Portugal (Linz and others); continues through specialised works on the Transition, Suárez, the Constitution, 23-F, UCD, the PSOE, González, autonomies, terrorism/GAL, economy and culture. Closes with the short author biography of Tusell (Barcelona 26 August 1945 – 8 February 2005).
Key Data Points

Relationship to the Wiki
Tusell IV gives this wiki its continuous scholarly history of Spain from Franco’s death to the end of the long Socialist tenure. It continues directly from volume III (La dictadura de Franco), also held here, whose closing chapter on Spain at Franco’s death is the immediate prelude. Beside the de Gaulle Discours et Messages tomes (T2–T5), which supply the French case in the General’s own voice from the Fourth Republic through April 1969, Tusell IV supplies the Spanish case for the generation after the dictatorship — institutions, parties, coup and consolidation, autonomies, terrorism, economy and culture — as modern secondary synthesis.
