sources/la-france-du-temps-present-1945-.title: Michelle Zancarini-Fournel — La France du temps présent (1945-2005) (2010)
sources/la-france-du-temps-present-1945-.content:
Michelle Zancarini-Fournel — La France du temps présent (1945-2005)
Full bibliographic citation — Michelle Zancarini-Fournel (with the collaboration of Christian Delacroix), La France du temps présent (1945-2005), volume 172 in the Histoire de France series directed by Joël Cornette. Éditions Belin, Paris; copyright © Éditions Belin, 2010 (digital ePUB metadata stamp 2015; filename “2015”; description copyright note Éditions Belin, 2013). Digital UUID 9399dd83-1b72-4f73-af24-7f624fbb7f46 (second identifier a8bd74cd-8976-4764-82ce-e3e7c995e5e9); file hash 9032da0348422fcde789951ab940b5c7. French text, ~263,000 words.





























AuthorMichelle Zancarini-Fournel — French historian, emerita professor at the Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1, specialist in twentieth-century social history and the history of women; long associated with the Institut d’histoire du temps présent. This volume written with the collaboration of Christian Delacroix, in the Histoire de France collection directed by Joël CornetteEditionÉditions Belin, 2010; digital ePUB with metadata stamp 2015; UUID 9399dd83-1b72-4f73-af24-7f624fbb7f46; file hash 9032da0348422fcde789951ab940b5c7; published with the concours of the Centre National du LivreStructurePréface + eight chronological/thematic chapters + “L’atelier de l’historien” (chapter IX on sources and method) + annexes (repères chronologiques, notices biographiques, bibliographie, and indices of iconography, sources, maps, tables and graphics); ~30,000 lines of extracted plain textPeriod1944–1945 (end of the Second World War, Liberation, first constituent assembly) to 2005 (on the eve of Sarkozy’s quinquennat, 2007, and the world financial crisis) — the Fourth Republic, the Algerian war, the Fifth Republic, May 1968, the post-1973 crises, the Mitterrand years, and the reordering of France to the early twenty-first centuryNoteA modern scholarly synthesis of the French “temps présent” (contemporary history written with the direct testimony of living actors) — the fourth volume of the “contemporary” period in the Cornette Histoire de France. Its title deliberately extends Fourastié’s Trente Glorieuses frame while challenging it; the work reads as continuous social, cultural, economic and political history, complementary to (and in dialogue with) the de Gaulle Discours et Messages also held in this wiki
The text is 30,000 lines, extracted from the EPUB container (clean text layer; no OCR required). French text clean; no U+FFFD replacement characters.
Content Summary
Préface — La France du temps présent. The volume puts a final point (or a suspension point) to the new Cornette Histoire de France for twenty-first-century readers. It covers a sequence beginning in 1944–1945 and ending about 2005, shortly before the quinquennat of Nicolas Sarkozy (2007) and the world financial crisis that followed. It is the fourth volume of the period called “contemporaine” in the French tradition — a periodisation that begins, in this collection, with the Revolution. The expression “temps présent,” used for about thirty years, designates a period immediately accessible to the historian through the direct testimony of the actors, their living memory and their physical presence; this temporality has changed nature in recent decades because average life expectancy has lengthened, creating proximity with events. The preface also (signed Zancarini-Fournel and Delacroix) explains the book’s structure and its insistence on the longue durée of the postwar years, the critique of the “Trente Glorieuses” myth, and the choice of a chronology beginning in 1944 rather than in the mid-1950s. Henry Rousso contributes a framing text on the volume’s place in the series.
Chapitre I — Lendemains de guerre et reconstruction (1945-1951)
The opening chapter takes up the narrative at the end of 1945, after the election of the first constituent assembly and the unanimous election of General de Gaulle as head of the government. Two events frame the approach: the capitulation of the German army and the establishment of genuine universal suffrage (linked to the 1944 ordonnance on the organisation of powers after the Liberation); events must be read in the “épaisseur de l’histoire.” 8 May 1945, though a moment of joy, is set below the euphoria of the Liberation the year before — the moment clouded by the émeutes of the Constantinois in colonial Algeria and their bloody repression, by the news and vision of the first returning deportees from the Nazi camps, and by the wait for the return of prisoners.
I. Lendemains de guerre : vers une stabilisation politique
Postwar political stabilisation: the electoral communist force in 1946, the invention of the Fourth Republic (1944–1946), the Bayeux discourse (16 June 1946), the tripartisme (January 1946–May 1947), the consultations nationales of 1945–1951, the triumph of parties or of parliamentarians, and the succession of GPRF and Fourth Republic governments.
II. Lendemains de guerre : les réformes de structure
Structural reforms. The French economy in ruins (agricultural and industrial production collapsed); beyond the innovations inherited from the 1930s — the idea of planning — a will to reform structures and capacities. Between the state and the market: nationalisations and the Plan (the Plan’s imperative, the nationalised enterprises); the working of the Marshall Plan; cultural democratisation; the Blum–Byrnes accords.
III. Les ruptures de 1947
The ruptures of 1947: the difficult spring, the departure of the communist ministers (the decree “dismissing” them), the “choc hexagonal” of the Cold War, the postwar European landscape, the great November–December 1947 demonstrations, the colonial question and the war in Indochina.
Chapitre II — La transition « modernisatrice » (années 1950-début des années 1960)
I. « L’état de croissance » (Robert Castel)
On the “Trente Glorieuses”: Jean Fourastié’s expression (1979) for the exceptional growth and “révolution invisible” of 1946–1975. These “glorious” years were generally not lived as such by contemporaries. Growth and inflation as the French equation; demographic “revolution” and immigration; the dynamics of modernisation; a “génération modernisatrice”; grands aménagements du territoire.
II. Une nouvelle société ?
Mass consumption: household equipment in 1966, the consumériste contagion, advertising, credit and distribution; a society at the apogee of its industrial phase (Grenadou, paysan français); a working world increasingly fragmented; salarisation, tertiarisation and feminisation (women in the factories).
III. Le social sans « relais politique » ?
Social demands without a political relay: the introuvable “paix contractuelle”; union membership figures 1945–1995; Nantes 1955 (“cette violence ne nous effraie pas”); the revolt of the independents — poujadisme.
Chapitre III — Les mutations du quotidien et du culturel (années 1950-début des années 1960)
I. Le nouvel empire du privé et du quotidien
The new empire of the private and the everyday. The keenest perception of the new place of objects and household equipment in daily life often came from artists and writers on a negative, mocking register — Boris Vian’s Complainte du progrès (1956), Georges Perec’s Les Choses (1965), the film Mon oncle of Jacques Tati. A “civilisation du loisir”? — the tourist.
II. Familles, sexualités et engagements idéologiques
Families (“Familles, je vous aime…”), marriages, divorces and births outside marriage; the campaign against the 1920 law on abortion; sexualities and representations of the feminine — invisible mutations?; the fraying of ideological and religious affiliations (the end of the prêtres-ouvriers); communist density by department in 1952.
III. L’affirmation de l’impératif culturel
The affirmation of the cultural imperative: education and democratisation in progress (university student numbers 1950–1970), médiatisation, américanisation and mass culture (the success of the “presse populaire,” the radio years); modernités artistiques and intellectual recompositions; the intellectual conjuncture between marxisms and the scientist push; the position of history in 1950.
Chapitre IV — De la IVe à la Ve République
The chapter confronts the gaulliste interpretation of the Fourth Republic as a “régime des partis” and the denunciation of the “système.” Serge Berstein recalls that the Fifth Republic “s’est valorisé en diabolisant son prédécesseur.” Historians today recognise that the Fourth Republic laid the foundations of evolutions the Fifth was to reap; the balance is often presented by opposing the successes of economic modernisation and European construction to the political wanderings (ministerial instability) and the incapacity to resolve the “problème algérien.” Against teleological readings, “la IVe République n’était pas inéluctablement condamnée” (René Rémond). The chapter is structured in three parts:
I. De Pinay à Mendès : la modernisation politique introuvable
The end of the Troisième Force and the return of the right to power; the elections of 17 June 1951; the Council of Europe (1949); the Appel de Stockholm; the great ideological-political quarrel of the Fourth Republic — the CED; threats on the Empire; the end of Indochina; the Empire as the blind spot of the national conscience; cartiérisme.
II. Mendès France, la modernité ambiguë
Pierre Mendès France — radical deputy since 1932, minister of de Gaulle at the Liberation, known for technical competence on economic and financial questions, a “Cassandre” for his language of truth (on Indochina). The strategy for the Geneva conference, the meeting with Zhou Enlai. The “style” Mendès France; the mendésiste diaspora.
III. La fin de la IVe République
The end of the Fourth Republic: the moment of Guy Mollet; the legislative elections of 2 January 1956; the deepening Algerian crisis under the Faure and Mollet governments; the investiture crisis of 1958 and the return of de Gaulle.
Chapitre V — Les années algériennes
After the Toussaint 1954 attacks, the government’s priority — shared by all parties and the opinion — was the re-establishment of order. Mendès France told the Assembly the first duty of the government was “d’affecter tous les moyens nécessaires au rétablissement ou au maintien de l’ordre public.” The “maintien de l’ordre” had become, without saying it, a war. Nearly a million French of European origin lived in Algeria in 1954 (over 80% born in Algeria), cohabiting with nearly nine million “Algériens musulmans” excluded from political rights. The chapter treats the war as the object of symbolic struggles — the terms “pieds-noirs,” “Français musulmans d’Algérie,” “guerre d’Algérie” each carrying contested ideological weight. In Algérie the responsibility of the transition and the maintenance of order is examined closely.
Chapitre VI — Mutations du politique (1958-1968)
13 May 1958 opens a period often reduced to the institutional change inaugurating the Fifth Republic. After the referendum adopting the new Constitution (October 1958), for the November legislative elections de Gaulle chose the uninominal majority two-ballot scrutiny (that of the Third Republic), which had the advantage of weakening the role of parties. The gaullist movements federated in the UNR; the abstention rate reached 23%; the UNR won 17.6% and 198 seats, the Indépendants 20% and 133 seats; de Gaulle was elected President on 21 December 1958 by the college of 80,000 grands électeurs (77% of the suffrages), installed at the Élysée on 8 January 1959 with Michel Debré as Prime Minister.
I. 1958, une rupture politique affirmée
The new institutions; the choice of the majority scrutiny; the weakening of party roles under the new regime.
Chapitre VII — Le moment 1968 et ses traces
Whether 1968 constituted a rupture. The chapter notes the successive questions — did the generalised revolt of youth in May 1968 and the greatest general strike of the twentieth century end a month later in an unqualified electoral victory for de Gaulle? The expression of Arthur Rimbaud, Changer la vie, diffused by Henri Lefebvre then by the situationnistes, was taken up by the socialist party (born of the Épinay congress, 1971) as the title of its 1972 programme. The concept of the “années 1968” integrates the crisis of May–June 1968 into a longer period; the traditional chronology (student crisis until 13 May) is criticised as effacing the wider movement. 1968 is treated as the epicentre of a broad contestation — a galaxy of very diverse social, political and cultural movements — set against the “soulèvement mondial de la jeunesse.”
Chapitre VIII — Crises, réponses politiques et recompositions (1975-2005)
The chapter opens on the crisis: “Les Trente Glorieuses brillent comme la lumière du paradis perdu.” Fourastié’s 1979 book is emblematic of the period of crisis beginning in 1973; the political directors’ consciousness of the durable character of unemployment was tardy (the first measures only in 1977), the crisis first read as conjunctural then as structural. Immigration is constructed as a national problem not from the Front national’s first electoral successes (1983) but ten years earlier, feeding on the occulted traces of the Algerian war and on the crisis. Sub-sections include:

I. Perceptions de la crise, reconfiguration de l’emploi et chômage — the visibility of the crisis after October 1973; unemployment mounting from 1975; the TGV; the crisis as “horizon d’attente” (Barre’s December 1978 announcement; the Lorrain steelworkers’ March 1979 demonstrations); redécouvertes de l’entreprise and the political alternance of 1981.
Union, désunion de la gauche et alternative politique — the Programme commun (26 June 1972); the 110 propositions of Mitterrand’s 1981 candidacy; the investiture of 21 May 1981; the Mauroy government’s first measures; the Grand Louvre and Mitterrand’s grands travaux.
Nouvelle condition salariale et recomposition politique — growth of tertiary employment; unequal unemployment; Chirac elected May 1995 and Juppé; the December 1995 “grève par procuration” and the “Tous ensemble” demonstration; the sans-papiers movement (18 March 1996); the dissolution of April 1997; the “désalignement” of electoral sociology and the decline of the working-class vote (1978–2002).
II. Nouveaux modèles familiaux — the “crise de la famille”; women on stage (deep evolution of women’s condition); the famille recomposée; sexualities, a revolution?; feminism of the 1970s; new norms of célibat and marriage; access to parenthood.
III. Massification et blocages de l’École — the democratisation of education (Des héritiers?, Bourdieu and Passeron); the “révolution silencieuse” of the baccalauréat; pupils “issus de l’immigration”; the 24 June 1984 demonstration for the private school (over a million participants); the Devaquet law and the 1986 student protests; the growth of the bacheliers proportion and of higher-education students.
IV. Villes et banlieues en crise : ethnicisation, genre et identités — the abbé Pierre’s appeal (February 1954); the time of the grands ensembles (14 million dwellings in 1954 for 43 million people); the bidonvilles of the Paris region; the 1973 Guichard circulaire halting the grands-ensembles programme; ségrégations in the banlieue; urban rebellions (Minguettes at Vénissieux; from 1969 the first urban violence); the Marche pour l’égalité (Marseille 15 October 1983–Paris); the “tournant de 1989” — la fin de l’histoire?; the fall of the Wall and German reunification (1990); European stakes since 1989 (Maastricht referendum 1992); Aimé Césaire on identity and the universal; gender and religion in “l’ethnie” (the foulard affair, autumn 1989); the Gulf war (Mitterrand’s allocution of 16 January 1991); the Ni putes ni soumises movement (Fadela Amara, 2003); the Clichy-sous-Bois émeutes (27 October 2005); the Marche des Indigènes de la République (8 May 2005); identity nationale and the extreme right.
Conclusion : la France qui bouge — mobility and migrations; the Airbus A380 (2005); France as world tourism capital; the TGV and the viaduc de l’Anguienne, the pont de Normandie; Paris and the coastal/rural resorts (La Grande Motte); mobilités et réseaux (the motorway échangeurs, the Minitel).

Chapitre IX — L’atelier de l’historien
A methodological chapter on the sources of the history of the “temps présent.” The chronological arc (1945 to today) places the book in what is conventionally called contemporary history; the Second World War long served as the “matrice du temps présent,” a concept now questioned. Against received ideas, the potential sources are innumerable — written, printed, sound and iconographic. The chapter examines the limits of written sources (which can seem “rigidifiées,” not transmitting what Philippe Braud calls “dynamiques émotionnelles”), the diversity of archives (state, private, associations, parties, unions), oral and audiovisual sources, and the craft of the historian: cross-referencing sources of different natures, situating knowledge (Michel de Certeau — “les archives ne font que révéler un manque”).
Annexes

Repères chronologiques — a chronological frame (in italics the chronology of exterior events) opening in 1944–1945: the ordonnance of 21 April 1944 establishing universal suffrage (vote and eligibility of metropolitan women); 1 September “Bataille de la production”; 9 September new Provisional Government under de Gaulle; the 30 September ordonnance on the press; 15 October foundation of the CGC; 25–26 November constitutive congress of the MRP; 27 November return of Maurice Thorez; publication of Le Monde; 16 January 1945 creation of the Régie Renault (RNUR); 22 February creation of the comités d’entreprise; and so on through to 2005.
Notices biographiques — biographical notices of the principal actors.
Bibliographie — a full bibliography, including the general works on the period (e.g. Les Idées en France (1945-1988). Une chronologie, Gallimard; “L’Aventure des idées. Chronologie 1989-1999”, Le Débat, n° 111, Septembre-octobre 2000; Guillaume Sylvie, La France contemporaine. Chronologie commentée (1946-1990), 2 tomes, Perrin, 1990; Gerbet Pierre (dir.), Dictionnaire historique de l’Europe unie, 2009; INSEE statistical works; Maitron/Pennetier, Dictionnaire biographique du mouvement ouvrier français), plus the thematic bibliography by chapter.
Références iconographiques, sources des textes, cartes, tableaux, graphiques, crédits photographiques — the documentary apparatus of the volume.

Key Data Points

















































AttributeDetailAuthorMichelle Zancarini-Fournel, with the collaboration of Christian Delacroix; collection directed by Joël CornetteTitleLa France du temps présent (1945-2005)SeriesHistoire de France, directed by Joël Cornette; volume 172; fourth volume of the “contemporaine” periodPublishedÉditions Belin, 2010 (© Belin 2010; digital ePUB metadata stamp 2015; filename “2015”; description copyright 2013)SourceEPUB container; clean French text layer; UUID 9399dd83-1b72-4f73-af24-7f624fbb7f46; hash 9032da0348422fcde789951ab940b5c7Raw filewiki/raw/la-france-du-temps-present-1945-2005-zancarini-fournel-2010.txtLines30,000StructurePréface + chapters I–IX (chronological/thematic + “L’atelier de l’historien”) + annexes (chronology, notices, bibliography, indices)Coverage1944–1945 to 2005 — reconstruction, Fourth Republic, Algerian war, Fifth Republic, May 1968, post-1973 crises, Mitterrand years, France of the early twenty-first centurySignificanceThe modern scholarly synthesis of the French “temps présent” — the continuous social, cultural, economic and political history that complements, in the wiki’s sources, the de Gaulle Discours et Messages (the General’s own voice, T2–T5) and the two Tusell volumes (the parallel Spanish case)
Relationship to the Wiki
Zancarini-Fournel gives this wiki its continuous scholarly history of France from 1945 to 2005. It reads alongside — and repeatedly in dialogue with — the de Gaulle Discours et Messages tomes (T2–T5), which supply the French case in the General’s own voice from the Fourth Republic through April 1969. Where de Gaulle provides the first-person statements of the founder of the Fifth Republic, Zancarini-Fournel provides the critical synthesis that situates, contextualises and questions that record (the Fourth Republic’s rehabilitation against the gaulliste “régime des partis” reading; the Trente Glorieuses myth; the années algériennes; May 1968 and its traces; the post-1973 crises and recompositions). It stands beside the two Tusell volumes for Spain as the French pillar of the wiki’s postwar continental coverage.

sources/mammarella-litalia-contemporanea.title: Giuseppe Mammarella — L'Italia contemporanea (1943-1998) (2000)
sources/mammarella-litalia-contemporanea.content:
Giuseppe Mammarella — L’Italia contemporanea (1943-1998)
Full bibliographic citation — Giuseppe Mammarella, L’Italia contemporanea (1943-1998), volume V of the “Le vie della civiltà” series. Società editrice il Mulino, Bologna. ISBN 88-15-07902-5. Italian text, 648 pages in the PDF; extracted plain text of 26,036 lines.





























AuthorGiuseppe Mammarella — Italian historian of contemporary politics, professor of the history of international relations and contemporary history; author of the series volume V on contemporary ItalyEditionSocietà editrice il Mulino, Bologna; ISBN 88-15-07902-5. Copyright © 1974 for the original volume L’Italia dalla caduta del fascismo a oggi; successive editions 1985, 1990, 1993 under the title L’Italia contemporanea; new edition 1998 with the title L’Italia contemporanea (1943-1998); revised new edition 2000. Digital scan (Internet Archive provenance, 2023)StructurePremessa + five parts, each subdivided into chapters + Bibliografia + Indice dei nomi; extracted plain text of 26,036 linesPeriod1943–1998 — from the fall of fascism and the end of the war through the birth of the Republic, the “centrismo” years (1948–1958), the centro-sinistra (1958–1974), the end of centro-sinistra to the 1980s, and “verso la seconda Repubblica” to the governments of the left and the eve of the millenniumNoteA classic single-volume scholarly history of contemporary Italy from the fall of fascism to 1998, originally published in 1974 and repeatedly revised, in the “Le vie della civiltà” series. Written by an academic historian; reads as continuous political, economic and social history of the Italian Republic across five decades
Content Summary
Premessa. On the half-century since the end of the war; by 1996 the Republic had completed its first fifty years. This is a period which, more than a phase of national history, covers an entire epoch rich in events and profound transformations. The country that entered it was isolated and humiliated by military defeat and political failure, with a society suspended between a condition of secular backwardness and a process of modernisation.
Parte prima: Dalla fine della guerra al «centrismo» (1943-1948)
I. La caduta del fascismo — The fall of fascism: the 25 July 1943 crisis, the end of the regime and the first steps toward a new order.
II. La ripresa dell’attività politica: 1943-1945 — The resumption of political activity: the reconstruction of the parties and the Resistance years, 1943–1945.
III. Gli anni cruciali: 1945-1948 — The crucial years: the first postwar governments, the constituent phase and the Cold War’s impact on Italy.
IV. Elezioni e referendum — Elections and referendum: the amministrative elections, the institutional referendum of 2 June 1946 and the Constituent Assembly.
V. La ricostruzione economica — Economic reconstruction: the recovery of the Italian economy after the war.
VI. Il governo dal 2 giugno 1946 al 18 aprile 1948 — The governments from June 1946 to the elections of 18 April 1948: the tripartite coalition and the crisis of 1947.
VII. Il trattato di pace — The peace treaty: Italy’s position in the postwar settlement.
VIII. Le elezioni politiche del 1948 — The political elections of 18 April 1948: the Christian Democratic victory over the Popular Front.
Parte seconda: Gli anni del «centrismo» (1948-1958)
I. Il quadripartito «centrista» — The centrist four-party coalition: DC, PLI, PRI and PSDI in government.
II. Il programma economico e riformista del quadripartito — The economic and reformist programme of the centrist coalition: the agrarian reform and the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno.
III. Nuovi orientamenti politici — New political orientations in the centrist decade.
IV. Le elezioni politiche del 1953 — The elections of 7 June 1953 and the failure of the “legge truffa” (the electoral law of the majority).
V. La società italiana nel dopoguerra — Italian society in the postwar: emigration, the south, the economic transformation.
VI. La difficile seconda legislatura: 1953-1958 — The difficult second legislature, 1953–1958.
VII. Ritorno al quadripartito — The return to the centrist four-party coalition.
VIII. I limiti del «centrismo» — The limits of centrism: its incapacity to respond to the pressures for change.
IX. L’apertura a sinistra: premesse storiche e politiche — The “apertura a sinistra” (opening to the left): the historical and political premises of the alliance with the PSI.
X. Le elezioni politiche del 1958 — The political elections of 25 May 1958.
Parte terza: Il centro-sinistra (1958-1974)
I. La terza legislatura: 1958-1963 — The third legislature: the first experiments of the centre-left.
II. Da Milazzo a Tambroni — From Milazzo to Tambroni: the political crisis of 1960 and the end of the Tambroni government.
III. Il primo governo di apertura a sinistra e le elezioni del 1963 — The first government of the opening to the left and the elections of 28–29 April 1963.
IV. La quarta legislatura: 1963-1968 — The fourth legislature: the Moro governments and the centre-left in power.
V. Il centro-sinistra alla prova — The centre-left put to the test: its reforms and its limits.
VI. La strategia della tensione — The “strategy of tension”: the bombings and the subversive designs of the late 1960s.
VII. L’«autunno caldo» e la contestazione — The “hot autumn” of 1969 and the contestation: the wave of workers’ and student struggles.
VIII. Dal governo Colombo alle elezioni presidenziali — From the Colombo government to the presidential elections.
IX. La fine anticipata della quinta legislatura — The premature end of the fifth legislature (1972).
X. Problemi economici interni e internazionali — Internal and international economic problems of the early 1970s.
Parte quarta: Dalla fine del centro-sinistra agli anni ‘80
I. L’agonia del centro-sinistra — The agony of the centre-left: the crisis of the 1970s and the end of the formula.
II. Alla ricerca di una nuova maggioranza — In search of a new majority: the political re-alignment of the mid-1970s.
III. Le elezioni della svolta: 20 giugno 1976 — The “turning-point” elections of 20 June 1976: the advance of the PCI.
IV. La società italiana alla fine degli anni ‘70 — Italian society at the end of the 1970s.
V. La nuova fase internazionale: tra crisi economiche e politiche si profila un ritorno alla guerra fredda — The new international phase: between economic and political crises a return to the Cold War takes shape.
VI. L’ora dei laici — “The hour of the secular parties”: the early 1980s and the pentapartito.
VII. Gli anni ‘80: stabilizzazione o transizione? — The 1980s: stabilisation or transition?
Parte quinta: Verso la seconda Repubblica
I. Il fatidico 1989: la fine del comunismo nell’est europeo — The fateful 1989: the end of communism in Eastern Europe and its consequences for Italy.
II. 1992. Annus horribilis — 1992, the annus horribilis: the assassination of Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino, the currency crisis and the collapse of the party system.
III. Esplode Tangentopoli — Tangentopoli explodes: the “Mani pulite” investigations and the end of the traditional parties.
IV. Verso un governo delle sinistre — Toward a government of the left: the centre-left coalitions of the 1990s and the “Ulivo.”
Bibliografia
A full bibliography on the history of contemporary Italy.
Indice dei nomi
An index of names.
Key Data Points

Original © 1974 L’Italia dalla caduta del fascismo a oggi; editions 1985/1990/1993 as L’Italia contemporanea; new ed. 1998; revised new ed. 2000SourcePDF scan (Internet Archive provenance, 2023), 648 pagesRaw filewiki/raw/mammarella-litalia-contemporanea-1943-1998.txtLines26,036StructurePremessa + Parte prima–quinta (each subdivided into chapters) + Bibliografia + Indice dei nomiCoverage1943–1998 — fall of fascism, war and Resistance, Republic and Constitution, the centrismo (1948–1958), the centro-sinistra (1958–1974), the end of centro-sinistra and the 1980s, and “verso la seconda Repubblica” (1989–1998)SignificanceA classic scholarly single-volume history of contemporary Italy held alongside the newer Gentiloni Silveri Storia dell’Italia contemporanea (1943-2019), which extends the account to the present

Mammarella gives this wiki its classic scholarly history of Italy from the fall of fascism to 1998. It reads alongside the newer Gentiloni Silveri Storia dell’Italia contemporanea (1943-2019) — the two Italian syntheses now held in the wiki, the older covering 1943–1998 and the newer carrying the account through the eurozone years to 2019. It stands beside the French (Zancarini-Fournel) and Spanish (Tusell) syntheses as part of the wiki’s postwar continental coverage.

sources/medinsky-torkunov-istoriya-rossi.title: История России. 1945 год — начало XXI века. 11 класс (2024)
sources/medinsky-torkunov-istoriya-rossi.content:
История России. 1945 год — начало XXI века. 11 класс
Владимир Ростиславович Мединский, Анатолий Васильевич Торкунов — История. История России. 1945 год — начало XXI века (History of Russia. 1945 to the Beginning of the 21st Century), учебник для 11 класса, базовый уровень, 3-е издание, обновлённое (3rd, updated edition). Издательство «Просвещение», Москва, 2024, 447 pp., ISBN 978-5-09-112830-7. An official Russian school textbook on the history of the USSR and the Russian Federation from 1945 to the early 2020s, developed in accordance with the Federal State Educational Standard of secondary general education.





























AuthorsВладимир Ростиславович Мединский (Vladimir Medinsky), historian, former Minister of Culture of the Russian Federation, and Анатолий Васильевич Торкунов (Anatoly Torkunov), political scientist, Rector of MGIMO; scientific reviewer — академик РАН Сергей Павлович Карпов (president of the Faculty of History of Moscow State University); reviewer — Г. А. Назаров, teacher of historyPublication3-е издание, обновлённое; «Просвещение», Москва, 2024; 447 pp.; ISBN 978-5-09-112830-7; signed to print 22 December 2023; the textbook is admitted for use in accredited educational programmes under the order of the Ministry of Education of the Russian FederationStructureВведение (Introduction) + Глава I «СССР в 1945—1991 гг.» (The USSR in 1945–1991, §§ 1–23) + Глава II «Российская Федерация в 1992 — начале 2020-х гг.» (The Russian Federation in 1992 to the Early 2020s, §§ 24–37) + Заключение (Conclusion) + Словарь понятий и терминов (Glossary) + хронология «Основные события истории России 1946—2022 гг.»; 448-page scan; 20,077 lines of extracted textPeriod1945 to the early 2020s (to 2022–2023): the postwar reconstruction and the Cold War; the Khrushchev thaw and its reforms; the period of stagnation under Brezhnev (1964–1985); perestroika and the collapse of the USSR (1985–1991); and the Russian Federation from 1992 through the 1990s, the Putin era, and the events of the early 2020sNoteThe stated result of the course is the formation of patriotism and Russian civic identity; the textbook covers the integration of Russian and foreign history and devotes substantial place to the history of spiritual life, culture and everyday life
Contents. An official Russian school textbook surveying the history of the Soviet Union and the Russian Federation from 1945 to the early 2020s. Глава I (The USSR in 1945–1991) covers: the restoration and development of the economy and social sphere after the war; the political system in the postwar years; ideology, science, culture and sport; the place and role of the USSR in the postwar world and foreign policy 1945–1953; the new leadership and the change of political course; economic and social development in 1953–1964 (the Khrushchev thaw); the development of science and technology; the cultural space and everyday life in 1953–1964; foreign policy 1953–1964; political, socio-economic, scientific and cultural development in the period 1964–1985 (the Brezhnev years); nationality policy and national movements; foreign policy 1964–1985; the USSR and the world in the early 1980s and the preconditions of reform; socio-economic development 1985–1991; changes in the spiritual sphere during perestroika; the reform of the political system of the USSR and its results; the “new political thinking” and changes in foreign policy; and nationality policy, the rise of national movements and the collapse of the USSR. Глава II (The Russian Federation in 1992 to the Early 2020s) covers: the Russian economy under the market; the political development of the Russian Federation in the 1990s; inter-ethnic relations and nationality policy; everyday life in the 1990s; Russia and the world and the foreign policy of the Russian Federation in the 1990s; political challenges and new priorities of internal policy at the beginning of the 21st century; Russia in 2008–2011; socio-economic development at the beginning of the 21st century and the priority national projects; culture, science, sport and public life in the 1990s to the early 2020s; foreign policy at the beginning of the 21st century; Russia in 2012 to the early 2020s; and Russia today — the special military operation (СВО, SMO).
Глава I — СССР в 1945—1991 гг. (The USSR in 1945–1991)
§§ 1–4 — Postwar reconstruction: the restoration and development of the economy and social sphere; the political system in the postwar years; ideology, science, culture and sport; and the place and role of the USSR in the postwar world and foreign policy 1945–1953 (the early Cold War).
§§ 5–10 — The Khrushchev period (1953–1964): the new leadership and the change of political course; economic and social development; the development of science and technology; the cultural space; changes in everyday life; and foreign policy — the thaw and the beginning of de-Stalinisation.
§§ 11–17 — The Brezhnev period (1964–1985): political development; socio-economic development; the development of science, education and health care; ideology and culture; everyday life; nationality policy and national movements; and foreign policy — the period of “developed socialism” and détente.
§§ 18–23 — Perestroika and the collapse of the USSR (1985–1991): the USSR and the world in the early 1980s and the preconditions of reform; socio-economic development in 1985–1991; changes in the spiritual sphere during perestroika; the reform of the political system and its results; the “new political thinking” and changes in foreign policy; and nationality policy, the rise of national movements and the collapse of the USSR.
Глава II — Российская Федерация в 1992 — начале 2020-х гг. (The Russian Federation in 1992 to the Early 2020s)
§§ 24–28 — The 1990s: the Russian economy under the market; the political development of the Russian Federation in the 1990s; inter-ethnic relations and nationality policy; everyday life in the 1990s; and Russia and the world and the foreign policy of the Russian Federation in the 1990s.
§§ 29–35 — The early 21st century: political challenges and new priorities of internal policy; Russia in 2008–2011; socio-economic development and the priority national projects; culture, science, sport and public life in the 1990s to the early 2020s; and foreign policy at the beginning of the 21st century and Russia in the modern world.
§§ 36–37 — Russia in 2012 to the early 2020s: political and socio-economic development; and Russia today — the special military operation (СВО) and the position of Russia in the contemporary world.
Заключение (Conclusion)
Draws together the course’s account of Russia from 1945 to the early 2020s, framed by the textbook’s stated educational aim of forming patriotism and Russian civic identity.

sources/moravcsik-choice-for-europe-soci.title: Andrew Moravcsik — The Choice for Europe: Social Purpose and State Power from Messina to Maastricht
sources/moravcsik-choice-for-europe-soci.content:
Andrew Moravcsik — The Choice for Europe: Social Purpose and State Power from Messina to Maastricht
Full bibliographic citation — Andrew Moravcsik, The Choice for Europe: Social Purpose and State Power from Messina to Maastricht, Cornell University Press, Ithaca, 1998 (copyright 1998); published in the UK by Routledge, London & New York, 1999 (ISBN 1-85728-191-8 cased, 1-85728-192-6 paper; US ISBN 0-8014-3509-9). English text; extracted plain text of 22,790 lines.





























AuthorAndrew Moravcsik — American political scientist (b. 1957); professor at Princeton University (later Harvard); a leading theorist of international relations and European integration; the principal exponent of liberal intergovernmentalismEditionCornell University Press, Ithaca, 1998; UK edition Routledge, 1999; ISBN 0-8014-3509-9 (Cornell) / 1-85728-191-8 cased, 1-85728-192-6 paper (Routledge)StructureIntroduction + seven chapters + Index; extracted plain text of 22,790 linesPeriodFrom the Messina conference (1955) to the Maastricht Treaty (1991) — the founding and consolidation of the European Community and the European Union, with comparative focus on five great negotiations: the Treaty of Rome (1955–58), the consolidation of the customs union and the CAP (1958–69), the European Monetary System (1969–83), the Single European Act (1984–88), and the Maastricht Treaty on EMU (1988–91)NoteThe foundational statement of the “liberal intergovernmentalist” theory of European integration, and the most influential recent work on the subject. Moravcsik argues that the history of European integration is best explained not as a neofunctionalist, federalist or geopolitical process but as a series of rational choices by national leaders responding to three pressures: the economic interests of powerful domestic constituents (above all commercial interests), the relative power of states in the international system, and the role of international institutions in making interstate commitments credible. The book tests this account against the five most salient negotiations in EC history, arguing that economic and commercial motivations dominated national preference formation, that bargaining outcomes reflected asymmetrical interdependence, and that institutional delegation served the purpose of credible commitment — while geopolitical threats, federalist ideas, technocratic imperatives and supranational entrepreneurship played only a secondary role. A landmark in both the empirical and the theoretical study of the EU, it remains the central target of debate for supranationalist, historical-institutionalist and constructivist critics
Content Summary
Introduction: The Choice for Europe. Moravcsik opens by criticising the state of the literature on European integration, which he charges with multiplying intuitive claims about the causes of integration (supranational influence, domestic politics, public opinion, path dependence) without generating reliable empirical conclusions about their relative importance. He announces the book’s central argument: European integration is best explained as a series of rational choices made by national leaders, responding to the economic interests of powerful domestic constituents, the relative power of each state, and the role of international institutions in bolstering the credibility of interstate commitments. The account is tested across the five most salient negotiations in EC history: the Treaty of Rome (1957), the consolidation of the customs union and the Common Agricultural Policy in the 1960s, the European Monetary System (1978–79), the Single European Act (1985–86), and the Maastricht Treaty on European Union (1991). Moravcsik situates the study against the “grand theories” of neofunctionalism and federalism, and against the intergovernmentalist tradition of Stanley Hoffmann and Robert Keohane.
Chapter 1: Theorizing European Integration. The theoretical foundation. Moravcsik sets out his tripartite rationalist framework: national preferences (formed domestically, dominated by economic and especially commercial interests), interstate bargaining (outcomes shaped by the relative power that stems from asymmetrical policy interdependence), and the choice of international institutions (the pooling or delegation of sovereignty to make credible commitments against defection). He presents this “liberal intergovernmentalism” against its principal competitors — neofunctionalism (Haas), federalism, supranational governance, and historical institutionalism — and develops general theories of economic preference formation over trade and monetary issues. The chapter opens with a quotation from Jean Monnet (“To succeed, always choose the path of least resistance”).
Chapter 2: Finding the Thread: The Treaties of Rome, 1955–1958. The negotiation of the Treaty of Rome. Moravcsik recounts how the failure of the European Defence Community in 1954 crushed hopes that the European Coal and Steel Community would lead automatically to deeper integration, yet within a year negotiations began that culminated in the Treaty of Rome (1957) establishing the European Economic Community (a customs union among the Six) and Euratom. He evaluates why the customs-union option was chosen over the alternatives (an industrial free-trade area without agriculture or supranational institutions, preferred by many in the German and British governments; or continued piecemeal liberalisation through the OEEC and GATT). Against the prevailing emphasis on geopolitics, supranational entrepreneurship and ideology, he argues the evidence shows the primacy of commercial interest, the distribution of relative power, and the desire for credible commitments. The chapter opens with a quotation from Robert Schuman (“Our European states are a historical reality…”).
Chapter 3: Grain and Grandeur: Consolidating the Common Market, 1958–1969. The consolidation of the EEC in its first decade, centred on the Common Agricultural Policy and the customs union. Moravcsik analyses how the French and German governments bargained over the CAP (the “grain” of the title) and the political ambitions of de Gaulle (the “grandeur”), the vetoes and the “empty chair” crisis of 1965–66 and the Luxembourg Compromise, and how national economic and commercial interests drove the consolidation. The chapter sustains the liberal-intergovernmentalist argument through the crisis decade.
Chapter 4: Divergence and Convergence: Toward Monetary Integration, 1969–1983. The winding road toward monetary integration, from the Werner Plan and the failure of the “snake” in the early 1970s to the establishment of the European Monetary System (EMS) in 1978–79. Moravcsik analyses the divergent national preferences over monetary policy and how convergence was finally achieved, locating the sources of the EMS agreement in domestic economic interests and asymmetrical interdependence rather than in technocratic or supranational pressures.
Chapter 5: Relaunching Integration: The Single European Act, 1984–1988. The negotiation of the Single European Act (1985–86), the programme to complete the internal market by 1992 with qualified-majority voting. Moravcsik examines why integration was relaunched in the mid-1980s after the difficulties of the previous decade, and again locates the driving force in national commercial and economic interests (the preferences of France, Germany and Britain over the internal market) rather than in Commission entrepreneurship or geopolitical change, against the influential “1992” accounts of the period.
Chapter 6: Economic and Monetary Union: Negotiating the Maastricht Treaty, 1988–1991. The negotiation of the Maastricht Treaty on European Union (agreed December 1991, ratified 1992–93). Moravcsik examines the transition to EMU (the “irrevocably locked currencies,” the independent European Central Bank, the convergence criteria), the parallel but modest “political union” (the second pillar on foreign policy, the third pillar on police and immigration, codecision for the European Parliament, the social policy opt-out for Britain), and the contentious ratification (referenda in France and Denmark, conditions imposed by the German constitutional court). Against the widespread view that Maastricht was a response to the geopolitical revolution of 1989 (the locking-in of a unified Germany, the French fear of a united Germany, the alleged German monetary quid pro quo for unification), Moravcsik argues that the treaty is best explained as the product of converging national economic interests — the culmination of the same commercial and economic forces that produced the earlier negotiations.
Chapter 7: European Integration in Retrospect. The concluding chapter. Moravcsik returns to Jacques Delors’s post-Maastricht statement that there will never be a “United States of Europe” and that he seeks “a federation among strong nation-states” — a sentiment, Moravcsik notes, that brings the most distinguished EC visionary of the 1980s full circle to the view of Robert Schuman, whose statement opened the book. He summarizes the empirical findings on national preferences (the preeminence of economic and commercial motivations), interstate bargaining (asymmetrical interdependence), and institutional choice (credible commitment), notes the mostly negative implications for “historical institutionalist” explanations, and draws implications for the comparative study of regional integration and for general theories of international conflict and cooperation. He adds a caveat that the documentary record for Maastricht and the SEA is thinner than for the earlier cases.
Anhang. Index (person and subject, pp. 503–527).

sources/perrone-enrico-mattei.title: Nico Perrone — Enrico Mattei (2012)
sources/perrone-enrico-mattei.content:
Nico Perrone — Enrico Mattei
Full bibliographic citation — Nico Perrone, Enrico Mattei, Storica paperbacks 98, 2ª ed. Società editrice il Mulino, Bologna, 2012. Print ISBN 978-88-15-23994-5; e-book ISBN 978-88-15-31231-0. Italian text. Extracted from the Anna’s Archive Mulino EPUB (hash 0cea1e3520bf686903438619d88c6b6b) via OPF spine order into plain text of 1,423 lines (~329 KB).





























AuthorNico Perrone — Italian historian; taught history at the University of Bari. Other works include La loggia della Philantropia (Sellerio, 2003), L’inventore del trasformismo (Rubbettino, 2009), L’agente segreto di Cavour (Palomar, 2011)EditionIl Mulino Storica paperbacks, 2nd edition, 2012 (print and Mulino e-book)StructureFive numbered chapters + Postfazione + Bibliografia e fonti + Indice dei nomiPeriodPrimarily 1945–1962 — Mattei at Agip after the Liberation, the founding and expansion of Eni/Snam, Italian energy autonomy and oil diplomacy, through Mattei’s death in the Bascapè air disaster (27 October 1962); the afterword also glances at later judicial findings and the Eni mythNoteA compact scholarly-popular biography of Enrico Mattei (1906–1962), the postwar builder of Italy’s state oil complex. Useful for Italian centrismo and the economic miracle, public enterprise, Mediterranean and Third World oil diplomacy, and Italo–American friction over energy
Content Summary
Back-cover framing (Carlo Donati): Mattei as patriot or adventurer — qualities that sometimes combine. Placed at the head of Agip after the Liberation, he set out to give Italy an energy base for development and independence; within about fifteen years he built Eni and Snam, secured direct access to energy sources, and made Italy a supplier of petroleum equipment and know-how. His boldness toward foreign competitors and Italian politics may have been fatal: the aircraft from Catania to Milan exploded in flight on 27 October 1962, a death that remains one of the mysteries of Republican history.
Capitolo primo — Le credenziali (“The credentials”)
Opens with foreign and domestic judgments on Mattei after his death (Standard Oil’s William R. Stott; Argentine and Egyptian officials; L’Express, The Guardian, The Times, Time, Sulzberger in the New York Times, and others): Mattei as Italian patriot, driver of the miracolo italiano, and challenger of the Anglo-American oil majors. Reconstructs his credentials — Resistance and Christian Democratic milieu, appointment to Agip, and the doctrine of impresa pubblica (public enterprise) as a spur to development where private capital would not go and as a corrective to concentrated private power (echoing left-Catholic / Azione cattolica currents inside the DC).
Capitolo secondo — La nazionalizzazione (“Nationalisation”)
Mattei’s drive to raise Italy to the rank of oil power: no political independence without economic independence (1958 discourse). Links the postwar oil quest to earlier Italian frustrations (fascist-era Agip abroad; wartime shortage). Narrative of building the state hydrocarbon system — research, pipelines, refineries, downstream industry — including Genoa pipeline projects, African refineries (Morocco, Ghana, Tunisia, Congo, Tanganyika), and Eni’s industrial push in the Mezzogiorno (Pisticci, Nuovo Pignone plants, methane networks, Lanerossi).
Capitolo terzo — Le regole dell’Eni (“The rules of Eni”)
Early postwar Italo–American friction over oil, defence, and Italian autonomy under De Gasperi — oil as a test of whether Italy could escape “substantially limited sovereignty.” Mattei’s theory of state control of petroleum as the motor of development; the political and legal rules under which Eni operated; US/UK pressure and CIA concern that challenges to Western companies could open doors to Soviet leverage (and the irony that Mattei’s Eni also dealt with Soviet oil).
Capitolo quarto — Un ruolo internazionale per l’Italia (“An international role for Italy”)
Late-1950s opening: Soviet efforts to sell oil westward; the US National Petroleum Council’s alarm (1962) that communist trade was political; American discouragement of allies importing Soviet crude. Mattei’s parallel diplomacy — Mediterranean and African oil deals (e.g. Morocco during the Gronchi–Fanfani state visit, 1958) — as a path for Italian economic and political autonomy within the Atlantic alliance, not merely a free-lance “foreign policy” of Eni alone.
Capitolo quinto — Il petroliere italiano (“The Italian oilman”)
Strategic vision after Eni’s founding law: closing the technological gap under a de facto US equipment embargo; need for Italian public-controlled engineering for onshore and offshore work. Public-enterprise speech at Urbino (laurea ad honorem, 4 February 1962). Closing portrait of Mattei binding his name to the myth of a reconstructed Italy among the world’s oil powers — a status that outlived him, deepened by the mystery of his death.
Postfazione
Two firm points: (1) Italy’s rise as a world oil power through Eni (law of 1953, De Gasperi government) makes Mattei a founding figure of the postwar Republic; (2) judicial investigation at Pavia concluded death by a limited onboard explosive charge at Bascapè (not engines/tanks). A third point: Mattei restored a proud national “character” to Italy’s image. The book is not an inquiry into the assassination theories; the author notes the coincidence with the opening of the Cuban missile crisis days earlier. Closing notes on later press, Montanelli, Braudel, and Eni at privatisation.
Bibliografia e fonti / Indice dei nomi
Chapter-keyed bibliography and sources, then name index.
Raw Text
