sources/pihoya-moskva-kreml-vlast-rossiy.title: Москва. Кремль. Власть. Две истории одной страны. Россия на изломе тысячелетий (1985–2005) (2007)
sources/pihoya-moskva-kreml-vlast-rossiy.content:
Москва. Кремль. Власть. Две истории одной страны. Россия на изломе тысячелетий (1985–2005)
Рудольф Германович Пихоя (Rudolf Germanovich Pikhoya) — Москва. Кремль. Власть. Две истории одной страны. Россия на изломе тысячелетий. 1985–2005 (Moscow. The Kremlin. Power. Two Histories of One Country. Russia at the Turn of the Millennium. 1985–2005). Издательства «Русь-Олимп»: «Астрель»: «АСТ», Москва, 2007, 554 pp. — series «Новейшая история. Особый взгляд» (Recent History. A Distinctive View). A political history of Soviet and Russian power from the accession of Mikhail Gorbachev to the consolidation of Vladimir Putin’s vertical of power — the crisis and collapse of the Soviet superpower and the formation of the new Russia.





























AuthorРудольф Германович Пихоя (Rudolf Germanovich Pikhoya), Doctor of Historical Sciences; in 1990–1995 head of the State Archival Service of Russia and Chief State Archivist; from 1997 chair of the department of the history of Russian statehood at the Russian Academy of State Service under the President of the Russian Federation. The author’s preface presents him as both a professional historian and a witness to and participant in the events.PublicationFirst edition, 2007 (signed to press 25 September 2006); format 84×108; print run 4,000; «Русь-Олимп», «Астрель» and «АСТ», Москва; series «Новейшая история. Особый взгляд» (founded 2006); ISBN 5-17-041086-7 (АСТ), 5-271-15660-5 (Астрель), 5-9648-0110-2 (Русь-Олимп)StructureПредисловие (Preface) + История первая «Закат империи» (First History, “The Decline of the Empire”, 7 очерков / sketches) + История вторая «Россия в поисках себя» (Second History, “Russia in Search of Itself”, 4 очерка) + Заключение (Conclusion); 554 pp.; 546-page scan; 27,458 lines of extracted OCR textPeriod1985–2005: from Gorbachev’s accession and the policy of «ускорение» (acceleration), through perestroika and the collapse of the USSR (1985–1991), to the constitutional crisis of 1993, the Yeltsin years and the first decade of Putin’s presidency (1992–2005)NoteThe title “Two Histories of One Country” refers to the two states treated — the Soviet Union at its decline and the Russian Federation — which the author treats as distinct states not to be conflated through legal continuity; the book is explicitly a political history, prepared on the basis of archival materials, the documents of the Politburo and Secretariat of the Central Committee of the CPSU, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Supreme Soviet of the Russian Federation and other documentary sources, the great majority of which, the author states, were introduced into scholarly circulation for the first time
Contents. A political history of power in the Soviet Union and Russia from 1985 to 2005, written by a historian who was head of the State Archival Service of Russia in 1990–1995. The First History, «Закат империи» (The Decline of the Empire), covers the Gorbachev years: the launch of «ускорение» and perestroika, the campaign against drunkenness, the Chernobyl disaster, the XXVII Party Congress, the turn toward democratisation and glasnost, the rise of the nationality question (Nagorny Karabakh and the “…up to secession” formula), the elections of the USSR people’s deputies and the First Congress of People’s Deputies (Очерк 1, 1985–1987; Очерк 2, 1987–1989), the emergence of the Russian factor — the founding of the Communist Party of the RSFSR, the Russian Congress and the Declaration of State Sovereignty of Russia (Очерк 3), the “war of laws” between Russia and the Union, the fate of the “500 Days” programme and the confrontation of the two Supreme Soviets (Очерк 4), Gorbachev’s attempts to preserve the USSR — the referendum of March 1991, Novo-Ogaryovo, the election of the Russian President (Очерк 5), the August putsch and the self-liquidation of the Union organs of power, the collapse of the CPSU and the path to the Belovezhskaya Pushcha agreement (Очерк 6), and the analysis of why the Soviet Union fell apart — Soviet federalism, the common property of the whole people, the CPSU as the core of the political system, the crisis of faith in “developed socialism”, the economic crisis and “new thinking” in foreign policy (Очерк 7). The Second History, «Россия в поисках себя» (Russia in Search of Itself), covers post-Soviet Russia: the road to a market economy, the freeing of prices and privatisation (Очерк 1), the political-constitutional crisis of 1992–1993 between President and the Soviet power, from the VII Congress to the dissolution of the Congress of People’s Deputies by Decree 1400 and the armed clashes of October 1993, followed by the elections to the Federal Assembly and the new Constitution of Russia (Очерк 2), the “tired” Russia of 1994–1999 — privatisation, the elections of 1995–1996, the financial crisis and default of 1998, and the “heir” operation (Очерк 3), and the building of the “vertical of power” under Putin, the “equidistance of oligarchs” and the relationship of society and power to 2005 (Очерк 4), followed by a Заключение (Conclusion).
Очерк 1 — Ускорение… куда? (1985–1987)
“Acceleration… Where to?” (1985–1987): Gorbachev’s rise to power, the economy and how the country and people lived, the trip to Leningrad, «ускорение» as the first stage of perestroika (1985–1986), the struggle with drunkenness and the budget, the continuation of repressions, the breaking of traditions, Gorbachev’s team and the new alignment of forces in the Kremlin, Shevardnadze — from General of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to Minister of Foreign Affairs of the USSR, Yeltsin as First Secretary of the Moscow city committee (МГК) of the CPSU, the XXVII Party Congress, the Chernobyl tragedy, the Politburo’s debate over “where are we going?”, “the point of no return, or the beginning of the end”.
Очерк 2 — От управляемой демократизации до неуправляемой демократии (1987–1989)
From managed democratisation to unmanageable democracy (1987–1989): the first signal, the country of the unpredictable past or what kind of socialism we had, the manifesto of Nina Andreyeva, the airport of destination — Red Square, incomes and expenditures, where the demonstrations should be, Yeltsin’s letter to Gorbachev, the scandal at the plenum, the nationality question, Nagorny Karabakh and the “…up to secession” formula, on the eve of the XIX All-Union Party Conference, how to reorganise Soviet power, the crisis of the system of administration, the acceleration of political reforms, the elections of the USSR people’s deputies, the First Congress of People’s Deputies of the USSR, and the worsening of the economic crisis in the country.
Очерк 3 — Российский фактор
The Russian factor: the Russian elections, the alignment of political forces in the first half of 1990, the Politburo’s summing up of the elections, how the post of President of the USSR was introduced, the founding of the Communist Party of the RSFSR, the preparation of the Russian Congress of People’s Deputies, political struggle at the First Congress of People’s Deputies of the RSFSR and the election of the Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the RSFSR, the search for paths to agreement, and the Declaration of State Sovereignty of Russia.
Очерк 4 — Чей суверенитет сувереннее. Война законов
Whose sovereignty is more sovereign. The war of laws: the formation of a government answerable to the Congress and the Supreme Soviet of the RSFSR, the fate of the “500 Days” programme and the economic policy of the legislative power of the RSFSR in 1990 and early 1991, the “500 Days” programme from hope to disappointment, the autumn manoeuvres or paratroopers on potatoes, the conflict of the Supreme Soviets of Russia and the USSR, and the paths of creating economic sovereignty.
Очерк 5 — Горбачев: поиски путей сохранения СССР
Gorbachev: the search for ways to preserve the USSR: the new changes in Gorbachev’s team and the course toward strengthening the positions of the President of the USSR, the signs of an approaching default and the problems of the “firms of friends”, party privatisation, troops in the streets and Vilnius, the preparation of the referendum on preserving the USSR, the revolt of the deputies, how the new Constitution of Russia was not adopted, Novo-Ogaryovo, and the election of the President of Russia.
Очерк 6 — Путч. Самоликвидация органов власти СССР
The putsch. The self-liquidation of the organs of power of the USSR: the worsening of the crisis in the Union leadership and the struggle around the draft Union Treaty, the rehearsal, the last plenum, the August putsch and its preparation, the place of action — Foros, the place of action — the Kremlin, in and around the White House, Grachev and Lebed and the art of self-defence, law against the putsch, barricades, 20 August, the Central Committee of the CPSU and the putsch, the preparation of the storm of the White House and its failure, the tragedy in the tunnel of Kalinin Prospekt, the collapse, Foros again, power after the putsch, the collapse of the CPSU, the mortal wound of the USSR, Chechnya as a prologue to tragedy, the beginning of the reconstruction of the Russian statehood, and from the Novo-Ogaryovo process to Belovezhskaya Pushcha.
Очерк 7 — Почему распался Советский Союз?
Why did the Soviet Union fall apart?: what Soviet power was, Soviet federalism and the new historical community of the Soviet people, property of the whole people, the CPSU as the core of the political system, the mounting crisis or the attempts to reform the unreformable, “developed socialism” and the crisis of faith, the economic crisis, “new thinking” as the impossibility of conducting the former foreign policy, political “self-destruction” or the reform of the political system, “all power to the Soviets” and not the CPSU, and Belovezhskaya Pushcha as the beginning or the end of the disintegration of the Soviet Union.
Очерк 1 (История вторая) — На путях рыночной экономики
On the paths of the market economy: the freeing of prices, “on freedom of trade”, and reforms and the factories.
Очерк 2 — Президент и Советская власть: кто кого? Политико-конституционный кризис 1992–1993 гг.
The President and Soviet power: who defeats whom? The political-constitutional crisis of 1992–1993: the “CPSU case”, the President and the Supreme Soviet on the path of conflict, the VII Congress and the first skirmish, the second act and the abortive impeachment, how to adopt the Constitution, the third act, the leak, Decree 1400, the last Congress of Soviets, the dangerous lull, weapons in the White House and the “third force”, blood, “reforms from above”, the elections to the Federal Assembly, and the new Constitution of Russia.
Очерк 3 — Усталая Россия (1994–1999)
Tired Russia (1994–1999): politics for politicians, economics and life, privatisation, the elections and new people in power, 1998 on the swings of the economy, the default, and the “heir” operation.
Очерк 4 — Газуем по вертикали
Full throttle up the vertical: the building of the vertical (of power), the “equidistant oligarchs”, full throttle, and society and power.
Заключение (Conclusion)
A general conclusion on the two decades of the crisis and collapse of the Soviet system and the formation of the new Russian state, drawing together the arguments of the two Histories on power, society and the paths of Russia from 1985 to 2005.

sources/stalin-kratkaya-biografiya-1948.title: Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin: A Short Biography (2nd ed., 1948)
sources/stalin-kratkaya-biografiya-1948.content:
Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin: A Short Biography
Институт Маркса — Энгельса — Ленина при ЦК ВКП(б) — Иосиф Виссарионович Сталин. Краткая биография (Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin. A Short Biography). Second edition, corrected and enlarged, OGIZ — State Publishing House of Political Literature, Moscow, 1948. The official short biography of Stalin issued during his lifetime.





























AuthorThe Institute of Marx–Engels–Lenin under the Central Committee of the CPSU(b); the named contributors to this electronic edition are G. F. Aleksandrov, M. R. Galaktionov, P. N. Pospelov, M. B. Mitin, V. S. Kruzhkov and V. D. MochalovEditionSecond, corrected and enlarged, 1948 (OGIZ / State Publishing House of Political Literature, Moscow); FB2 electronic edition (librusec-id 668549) prepared 2019 from an OCR scan; print run 3,000,000, signed to press 24 December 1947StructureTitle page + 11 numbered chapters (I–XI) + closing encomium; no separate table of contents; 636 lines / ~232,000 characters of extracted textPeriod1879–1946: from Stalin’s birth in Gori to the post-war reconstruction and the elections to the Supreme Soviet of February 1946NoteThe FB2 gives Stalin’s birth date as 21 December 1879 (the official dating used in this period, before the later change to 1878); quotations from Lenin cited by volume and page; the text is the canonical hagiographic portrait of the Stalin era
Contents. The official short biography of Stalin published in his lifetime and closed to the cult of the leader. It narrates his birth in Gori, his schooling at the Gori religious school and the Tiflis theological seminary, his early conversion to Marxism in the Georgian social-democratic milieu and the “Mesame-dasi” group, and his work as a revolutionary organiser in the Caucasus. It treats his successive arrests and exiles and his role in the underground of the Transcaucasus, his participation in the party congresses, his work on “Pravda” and in the Duma faction, and his exile to Turukhansk. It covers the February and October revolutions, the Brest peace, his work during the civil war and foreign intervention, and the transition to the New Economic Policy and the formation of the USSR. It then treats the struggle for socialist industrialisation, the collectivisation of agriculture, the adoption of the 1936 Constitution, and the political trials of the 1930s, closing with the Great Patriotic War of 1941–1945 and the post-war reconstruction. Throughout, the biography presents Stalin as the disciple and successor of Lenin and the architect of Soviet power, and it closes with the standard encomium of the Stalin era: “Stalin is Lenin today.”
Character of the source. The official biographical portrait of Stalin issued under the Institute of Marx–Engels–Lenin during the high tide of the cult of the personality (1948). Written from a strict Bolshevik standpoint, it presents Stalin’s life as inseparable from the history of the party and the building of socialism, and it narrates the political struggles of the 1920s and 1930s in the standard terms of the Stalin era — the defeat of the Trotskyists, the “rightists” and the Bukharinists, and the liquidation of the “enemies of the people.” Its date of 1948 places it before any qualification of the cult, and it therefore reflects the Stalinist periodisation of Soviet history at its fullest. It is a companion volume in this folder to the Short Course of the History of the VKP(b) (1945) and Shestakov’s Short Course of the History of the USSR (1937), with whose periodisation it is fully consistent.
Quality. Good. Extracted from an FB2 e-book via structured parsing of the FictionBook XML; continuous prose throughout. Cyrillic text clean; the 11 numbered chapter headings verified; numbered source references (footnotes) preserved inline as bracketed numbers, though the footnote text itself is not carried in the FB2 body.
Raw text: wiki/raw/stalin-kratkaya-biografiya-1948.txt.

Глава I (Chapter I)
Stalin’s birth in Gori (21 December 1879), his family and Georgian peasant origins; schooling at the Gori religious school and the Tiflis theological seminary; the spread of Marxism in the Transcaucasus and Stalin’s conversion at fifteen; his work in the “Mesame-dasi” group and the revolutionary underground; his exclusion from the seminary (1899) and his arrest and first exile. Period: 1879–1904.
Глава II (Chapter II)
Stalin’s years of prison and exile amid the rising revolutionary movement; the Second Congress of the RSDRP and the Bolshevik–Menshevik split; Stalin’s escape from exile (January 1904) and his revolutionary work in the Caucasus, in the 1905 revolution, and at the Stockholm (Fourth) and London (Fifth) Congresses. Period: 1904–1907.
Глава III (Chapter III)
The defeat of the first Russian revolution and the years of reaction; the building of the Bolshevik party of a new type in the underground; Stalin’s work of organisation and consolidation through the decade between the two revolutions. Period: 1908–1912.
Глава IV (Chapter IV)
The Prague party conference (1912), its prediction of a new revolutionary upsurge and the measures to meet it; Stalin’s work on “Pravda” and with the Bolshevik Duma faction; his arrest and exile to the Turukhansk region; the February revolution of 1917 and Stalin’s return. Period: 1912 – March 1917.
Глава V (Chapter V)
The return of Lenin to Russia (April 1917); the Bolshevik course toward the armed uprising; the October socialist revolution and the consolidation of Soviet power; the Brest peace and the defence of the Bolshevik strategy and tactics against Trotsky. Period: April 1917 – 1918.
Глава VI (Chapter VI)
The foreign military intervention and civil war; Stalin’s role as an organiser of defence and of the Red Army on the key fronts; the rout of the intervention and of the White armies. Period: 1918–1920.
Глава VII (Chapter VII)
The transition to peaceful construction after the civil war; the restoration of the national economy and the New Economic Policy; the formation of the USSR; Lenin’s illness and death and Stalin’s succession as leader of the party; the struggle against the oppositions; a portrait of Stalin as the model leader of party and people. Period: 1921–1925.
Глава VIII (Chapter VIII)
The struggle for socialist industrialisation in historically the shortest possible time; the first five-year plan; the offensive against the capitalist elements; the national and colonial question and the “great friendship” of the peoples of the USSR. Period: 1926–1929.
Глава IX (Chapter IX)
Stalin’s address to the conference of agrarian-Marxists (December 1929); the fight for the collectivisation of agriculture and the liquidation of the kulaks as a class; the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Congresses; the murder of S. M. Kirov and the measures to strengthen Bolshevik vigilance. Period: 1929–1934.
Глава X (Chapter X)
The continuing growth of industry and agriculture under the general line of the party; the fulfilment of the second five-year plan and the Stakhanovite movement; the adoption of the new (1936) Constitution; the political trials and the liquidation of the “enemies of the people”; the approach of war and the interruption of peaceful construction in June 1941. Period: 1935 – June 1941.
Глава XI (Chapter XI)
The Great Patriotic War: the German attack of 22 June 1941; Stalin as Supreme Commander; the great defensive and offensive battles, the rout of fascist Germany and the raising of the banner of victory over Berlin; the war against Japan; the dissolution of the Comintern (May 1943); the post-war reconstruction and the elections to the Supreme Soviet of February 1946; the closing encomium of Stalin as the leader, teacher and Generalissimo. Period: 1941–1946.

sources/weber-ddr-dokumente-zur-geschich.title: Hermann Weber (Hrsg.) — DDR, Dokumente zur Geschichte der Deutschen Demokratischen Republik 1945–1985
sources/weber-ddr-dokumente-zur-geschich.content:
Hermann Weber (Hrsg.) — DDR, Dokumente zur Geschichte der Deutschen Demokratischen Republik 1945–1985
Full bibliographic citation — DDR. Dokumente zur Geschichte der Deutschen Demokratischen Republik 1945–1985, herausgegeben von Hermann Weber, Deutscher Taschenbuch Verlag (dtv), München. ISBN 3-423-02953-6. Originalausgabe April 1986. German text; extracted plain text of 20,277 lines from a 476-page Internet Archive scan.





























EditorHermann Weber (b. 1928) — German historian and political scientist; from the 1960s head of the research unit “Geschichte und Politik der DDR” at the University of Mannheim; leading Western scholar of the history of the GDR and of socialism and the labour movement; author of the standard work Geschichte der DDR (dtv, 1984), to which this documentation volume is the companionEditionDeutscher Taschenbuch Verlag, München, Originalausgabe April 1986; ISBN 3-423-02953-6; printed by C. H. Beck’sche Buchdruckerei, Nördlingen; dtv “dokumente” series; 476-page Internet Archive scan (2022 Scribe OCR)StructureEinleitung + eight chronological chapters (each with a chapter introduction/Einleitung and numbered documents) + appendix (Zeittafel, Verzeichnis der Dokumente mit Quellennachweisen, Personenregister); extracted plain text of 20,277 linesPeriod1945–1985 — the entire history of the German Democratic Republic, from the Soviet occupation zone (SBZ) and the founding of the GDR through its consolidation, crises, and adaptation to the Soviet Union up to 1985NoteA comprehensive source collection of 234 documents tracing the history of “the other German state.” Besides party and state decisions on domestic, foreign, church, and cultural policy and directives on everyday life under “real existing socialism,” it contains larger extracts from the GDR constitutions. The editor also assembled orders, proclamations, appeals, newspaper and journal articles, speeches, letters, and extracts from memoirs covering each stage: the “Stalinization” of the GDR culminating in the uprising of 17 June 1953; the supposed “thaw” after Stalin’s death and Ulbricht’s struggle against inner-party opposition groups; the building of the Wall on 13 August 1961; the crisis of the “Prague Spring” 1968; and the change of leadership in the 1970s that brought a closer alignment of the GDR with the USSR — paradoxically to make détente with the Federal Republic possible at all. An extensive year-by-year Zeittafel adds the character of an indispensable compendium
Content Summary
Einleitung. Weber explains the scope and method of the collection. A comprehensive documentation of the whole history of the GDR existed only in the form of Ernst Deuerlein’s earlier dtv volume (1966, expanded 1971); this new edition links to that work while covering the further fifteen years since and curtails most documents. Beyond Deuerlein, Weber attempts not only fundamental (generally accessible) texts but also little-known and hard-to-reach characteristic materials, including previously unpublished documents from the Bundesarchiv Koblenz and the archive of social democracy of the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung. Where printed sources were used, the earliest available version was preferred, because the GDR in the fifties and sixties often handled its source editions arbitrarily — documents were cut without indication, often omitting the most important parts and falsifying them for political reasons (e.g. Ulbricht’s article of March 1946, Doc. 24, mutilated in the 1953 Ulbricht selection because his 1946 thesis of a “special German path” no longer fit the line). 234 documents were included to give an approximate overview of the whole breadth of GDR history 1945–1985: the political system and in particular the party system, the state, economy, ideology, culture, foreign and Germany policy, and problems of women and youth. The dates Mannheim, November 1985.
1. Kapitel: Die Vorgeschichte der DDR 1945-1949
The prehistory of the GDR, from the end of the war to the founding of the two German states. Covers the unconditional surrender of May 1945 and the division of Germany into occupation zones; the Soviet Military Administration in Germany (SMAD) and its orders, including the licensing of antifascist-democratic parties and trade unions (SMAD Order No. 2) and the KPD appeal after its re-admission; the unification of KPD and SPD into the SED (1946) and the drive toward a “volksdemokratische” system; the land reform, the elections, and the development of the Soviet zone toward a separate state as the Cold War intensified. Documents 1–77.
2. Kapitel: Stalinisierung der DDR 1949-1953
The Stalinization of the GDR, from its founding (7 October 1949) to the uprising of 17 June 1953. Covers the consolidation of the SED dictatorship on the Soviet model — the Gleichschaltung of parties and mass organizations, the purge of the party, the strengthening of the state security apparatus, and the repression that made the Stalinization an “Angleichung an die Sowjetunion” (assimilation to the Soviet Union). Weber identifies the tragic culmination of this development in the events of 17 June 1953, when the workers’ uprising against the party leadership was put down with Soviet help. Documents 78–111.
3. Kapitel: Der Ausbau des neuen Systems 1953-1961
The construction and consolidation of the new system from the aftermath of 17 June 1953 to the building of the Wall. Covers the supposed “thaw” after Stalin’s death and Ulbricht’s enforcement against various inner-party opposition groups; the “Neuer Kurs” and the retreat from some harsh measures; the rapid reconstruction and the industrial and agricultural policy; the tensions that culminated in the mass flight from the GDR and the closing of the border on 13 August 1961. Documents 112–146.
4. Kapitel: Die Festigung der DDR 1961-1965
The consolidation of the GDR after the building of the Wall. With the border closed, the regime achieved a certain stability; the chapter covers the economic reforms of the NÖS (Neues Ökonomisches System), the position of the state in the socialist camp, and the continued internal discipline. Documents 147–161.
5. Kapitel: Ulbrichts Modellversuche 1966-1970
Ulbricht’s model experiments. Covers the further economic and political experiments of the late sixties — the attempt to build a distinctive “socialist system” of the GDR under Ulbricht’s leadership, including the economic reforms and the ideological contest with Prague. The chapter includes the crisis of the “Prague Spring” 1968 and the GDR’s role in the confrontation with the reform movement in Czechoslovakia. Documents 162–180.
6. Kapitel: Anpassung an die UdSSR 1971-1975
The adaptation of the GDR to the Soviet Union following the change of leadership. Covers the replacement of Walter Ulbricht by Erich Honecker (1971), the consequent closer alignment of the GDR with the USSR, and — paradoxically, as Weber stresses — the very adjustment that made the policy of détente with the Federal Republic possible at all: the intra-German treaties, the Grundlagenvertrag (1972), and the GDR’s recognition within the framework of the new Ostpolitik. Documents 181–205.
7. Kapitel: Krisenhafte Entwicklung 1976-1980
The crisis-ridden development of the later seventies. Covers the economic difficulties, the renewed tightening of the system, the question of dissent and emigration (including the expatriation of Wolf Biermann in 1976 and the subsequent wave of protest), and the GDR’s position in the renewed East–West confrontation. Documents 206–216.
8. Kapitel: Probleme der DDR 1981-1985
The problems of the GDR in the early eighties. Covers the great efforts of the early 1980s to revive the economy, overcome the instability of the system, gain foreign-policy successes, and consolidate relations with the Federal Republic — efforts centered on the X. Party Congress of April 1981, which confirmed the party’s “leading role” and its “Einheit von Wirtschafts- und Sozialpolitik” at home and its peace policy and absolute commitment to the Soviet Union abroad. The chapter records Erich Honecker’s reports and Willi Stoph’s new Five-Year Plan, and notes Honecker’s now conspicuous personality cult. Documents 217–234.
Anhang
Zeittafel (pp. 405/446 ff.) — an extensive year-by-year chronology of GDR history 1945–1985, from the surrender of 1945 through the founding of the GDR, 17 June 1953, the building of the Wall, the Grundlagenvertrag, and up to the mid-1980s. Verzeichnis der Dokumente mit Quellennachweisen (p. 407 ff.) — the documentary appendix listing all 234 documents with their sources. Personenregister (p. 459 ff.) — index of persons.
Key Data Points

sources/winkler-der-lange-weg-nach-weste.title: Heinrich August Winkler — Der lange Weg nach Westen, Zweiter Band: Deutsche Geschichte vom «Dritten Reich» bis zur Wiedervereinigung
sources/winkler-der-lange-weg-nach-weste.content:
Heinrich August Winkler — Der lange Weg nach Westen, Zweiter Band: Deutsche Geschichte vom «Dritten Reich» bis zur Wiedervereinigung
Full bibliographic citation — Heinrich August Winkler, Der lange Weg nach Westen. Zweiter Band. Deutsche Geschichte vom «Dritten Reich» bis zur Wiedervereinigung, Verlag C.H. Beck, München. ISBN 3-406-49524-9 (Band II) / 3-406-49527-3 (2 Bände in Kassette). First edition 2000 (subsequent editions 2001, 2001, 2002, 2002, 2005). German text; extracted plain text of 34,423 lines.





























AuthorHeinrich August Winkler — German historian, professor of modern history (long at the Humboldt University of Berlin); leading interpreter of German political history and of the “German question” in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; author of the two-volume Der lange Weg nach Westen (2000)EditionVerlag C.H. Beck, München, first edition 2000 (sixth printing 2005 in this scan); ISBN 3-406-49524-9 (Band II); library scan from the Aston University copyStructureEinleitung + five chronological chapters + closing essay “Abschied von den Sonderwegen: Rückblick und Ausblick” + Anhang (Abkürzungsverzeichnis, Anmerkungen, Personenregister); extracted plain text of 34,423 linesPeriod1933–1990 (and after) — from the Nazi seizure of power (“die deutsche Katastrophe”) through the division of Germany and the two German states, détente and the two Germanies, to the fall of the Wall and reunificationNoteThe second volume of Winkler’s acclaimed two-part German history of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The author calls it not a “Totalgeschichte” but a “Problemgeschichte”: its central theme is the relationship between democracy and nation in Germany, and the question of the German “Sonderwege” (special paths) and their ending in 1990. Explicitly a “Diskursgeschichte” as much as a history of events — it traces how Germans thought and argued about themselves. Volume II opens with Hitler’s seizure of power (Volume I ended with the fall of Weimar) and closes with reunification and its consequences
Content Summary
Einleitung. Winkler situates the second volume: the first traced Germany from the end of the Old Reich to the fall of the Weimar Republic; the second begins with the transfer of power to Hitler and ends with reunification and its effects. He insists this is a “Problemgeschichte” focused on the relation of democracy and nation, not a “Totalgeschichte.” The years 1933–1945 shaped the following decades so deeply that the history of divided Germany is largely a history of coming to terms with the “deutsche Katastrophe.” The book deals primarily with politics and political culture, and is as much a history of discourse as of events. From the 1970s the intellectual left held the hegemony of debate in the old Federal Republic, so Winkler’s criticism in the late period is directed mainly at the Left (and is partly self-criticism, as the author participated in some of these discourses). His standards are those of Western democracy and the value-laden concept of freedom of the Basic Law; he rejects the relativism of the Weimar constitution and “postmodern, seemingly liberal arbitrariness.” He judges the GDR not “system-immanently,” yet insists historians must not treat those who lived in the GDR as though they thought and acted under the same freedom as Germans in the Federal Republic. The premise and conclusion: Germans must critically appropriate their whole history; having no “Western normality” before 1990 gives them no claim to permanent anomaly; without clarifying their national identity the Germans cannot contribute to the project of Europe.
1. Die deutsche Katastrophe: 1933-1945
The opening chapter on the Nazi dictatorship. It treats the transfer of power to Hitler on 30 January 1933 as the beginning of a regime intended to be at least as “totalitarian” as Mussolini’s; the shared traits of Italian fascism and German National Socialism (radical nationalism, anti-Marxism and anti-liberalism, militarisation of the domestic struggle, the cult of youth, masculinity and violence, the central role of the charismatic Führer); and the crucial difference — German National Socialism’s murderous antisemitism at the centre of Hitler’s “Weltanschauung,” a political religion claiming the whole man. The chapter covers the seizure of power and the Reichstag Fire, the Enabling Act of 23 March 1933, the Gleichschaltung of parties and institutions, the SS, the radicalisation that led to war and the Holocaust, and the war years that for many Germans were long “Hitler’s war, but also their war,” ending in the catastrophe of 1945. It is the historical foundation — the “deutsche Katastrophe” — against which everything that follows in the two Germanies is measured.
2. Demokratie und Diktatur: 1945-1961
From the end of the war to the building of the Berlin Wall. Covers the German self-interrogation of 1945 (Friedrich Meinecke and Thomas Mann’s Deutschland und die Deutschen as contrasting responses to the catastrophe); the four-power occupation and the division into zones; the different development of the western zones and the Soviet zone; the emergence of the parties and the founding of the Federal Republic of Germany (1949) and the German Democratic Republic; Konrad Adenauer’s policy of Western integration, the Wirtschaftswunder and the social market economy, and the question of rearmament and the West treaties (EVG/Westverträge); the Grand Coalition and the “Grundgesetz” as a consciously Western, value-bound constitution; and the confrontation of the two systems culminating in the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961.
3. Zwei Staaten, eine Nation: 1961-1973
The period of two German states within one nation. Covers the Federal Republic under Ludwig Erhard and the Grand Coalition, the debate over the “German question,” the emergence of the student movement of 1968 and its challenge to the old Federal Republic, and the rise of Willy Brandt as chancellor candidate and then Chancellor. The chapter centres on the “neue Ostpolitik” of the social-liberal coalition from 1969 — the treaties with the East (Moscow, Warsaw, the Four-Power Agreement on Berlin, the Grundlagenvertrag with the GDR of 1972) — and Brandt’s programme of “Wandel durch Annäherung” (change through rapprochement), which sought to preserve the unity of the nation by recognising the existence of the two states. The 1973 government declaration, as recorded here, placed the preservation of peace above the question of the nation.
4. Annaherung und Entfremdung: 1973-1989
The years of détente and its limits. Covers the Federal Republic under Helmut Schmidt and the challenge of economic crisis and terrorism (the RAF, the German Autumn of 1977); the growing estrangement between the two German states and between the Federal Republic and the East; the GDR’s policy of Abgrenzung (delimitation) and its attempt to consolidate its separate identity; the Schmidt era and the “Wende” of 1982 to the Kohl government; the tensions of the “second Cold War” of the early 1980s; and the German intellectual debates of the decade, in which the Left increasingly dominated the discourse, including the debate on the German nation and the “deutsche Frage.” The period is one of “Annaherung und Entfremdung” — rapprochement and estrangement running in parallel.
5. Einheit in Freiheit: 1989/90
The fall of the Wall and reunification. Covers the collapse of the GDR in 1989 (the mass emigration via Hungary and the Prague embassy, the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig, the opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989), the crisis of the SED regime, the emergence of the “Runde Tisch,” the victory of the CDU in the GDR election of March 1990, the negotiations of the “Two-plus-Four” process, the economic and monetary union of July 1990, and German reunification on 3 October 1990. The chapter records how Helmut Kohl, rather than Oskar Lafontaine, became the political figure of the day of German unity, and traces the process by which “what was left of the Bismarck Reich after two world wars” was reunified — and reunified “in freedom,” as the title puts it, through free elections and agreement rather than by force.
Abschied von den Sonderwegen: Rückblick und Ausblick
The closing essay (printed pages 640–660). A retrospective and prospect that draws together the book’s argument about the German “special paths” (Sonderwege). Winkler argues that the special German path ended in 1990: with reunification and Germany’s firm anchoring in the West and in the European project, the Germans finally achieved the “Western normality” they had lacked before 1990, and the German question was resolved in freedom. The essay both reviews the two centuries covered by the two volumes and looks forward to the tasks of the reunified Germany in Europe.
Anhang
Abkürzungsverzeichnis (abbreviations, p. 661); Anmerkungen (notes, pp. 665–725); Personenregister (index of persons, pp. 726 ff.).
Key Data Points

sources/yurchak-eto-bylo-navsegda-poka-n.title: Это было навсегда, пока не кончилось. Последнее советское поколение (2014)
sources/yurchak-eto-bylo-navsegda-poka-n.content:
Это было навсегда, пока не кончилось. Последнее советское поколение
Алексей Юрчак (Alexei Yurchak) — Это было навсегда, пока не кончилось. Последнее советское поколение (Everything Was Forever, Until It Was No More: The Last Soviet Generation). Издательство «Новое литературное обозрение» (НЛО), Москва, 2014, ISBN 978-5-444-80190-1, series «Библиотека журнала „Неприкосновенный запас”». An anthropological study of the last Soviet generation, published in Russian in 2014 (original English-language edition, Princeton University Press, 2005; Russian ed. translated and expanded).





























AuthorАлексей Юрчак (Alexei Yurchak), Professor of Anthropology at the University of California, Berkeley; the book is his study of the culture and everyday life of the late Soviet period.PublicationРусское издание, «Новое литературное обозрение», Москва, 2014; серия «Библиотека журнала „Неприкосновенный запас”»; ISBN 978-5-444-80190-1; предисловие Александра Беляева «Взгляд антрополога на книгу Алексея Юрчака»StructureПредисловие (Preface by А. Беляев) + Введение + Главы 1–7 + Заключение; the chapter headings carry both the analytic theme and epigraph-sources (e.g. «Разноцветный коммунизм. King Crimson, Deep Purple, Pink Floyd»); 40,543 lines of extracted textPeriodThe book’s analytical core is the «поздний социализм» (late socialism) of the mid-1950s to mid-1980s — the formative decades of the last Soviet generation, including the gap years 1980–1985 — and its Заключение carries the argument through perestroika (1985–1991) to the collapse of the Soviet system. It is thus a study of the late socialist period (1950s–1980s) that frames the collapse of the system at the close of the 1980s and in 1990–1991, rather than a chronological narrative running to 1991NoteThe central question of the book is the paradox that Soviet citizens perceived the system as eternal yet were simultaneously prepared for its collapse. It analyses late socialism not through the familiar binary oppositions (official/unofficial culture, totalitarian/free language, suppression/resistance, public lie/hidden truth) but through the concept of the performative shift of authoritative discourse and «вненаходимость» (vnenakhodimost, “being simultaneously inside and outside” the discursive field of the system)
Contents. An anthropological study of the “last Soviet generation” — those who came of age in the late Soviet period, in the mid-1950s to mid-1980s — and of the internal dynamics of the system of late socialism that made the collapse of the USSR at once a surprise and something widely expected. The introduction and the concluding chapter set out the central paradox: that the reproduction of the fixed forms of the authoritative discourse of the system was accompanied by a constant internal shift of meaning, so that the very process of reproducing the system changed it from within. The chapters examine the performative shift in Soviet ideology and language, the ethics and poetics of living “ideology turned inside out”, the everyday practice of vnenakhodimost (life simultaneously within and without the discursive field of the system), the “imagined West” as a space of vnenakhodimost, the phenomenon of «Разноцветный коммунизм» (multi-coloured communism) and the reception of Western rock music, and the irony of vnenakhodimost — necro-aesthetics, stiob and the Soviet anecdote. The Заключение (Conclusion) carries the analysis through the years of perestroika to the collapse: the loss of legitimacy of the CPSU in 1990–1991, the disintegration of the fabric of the authoritative discourse, and the end of the Soviet system.
Предисловие (Preface)
Взгляд антрополога на книгу Алексея Юрчака — Александр Беляев introduces the book, situating Yurchak’s anthropological approach to late socialism within the broader discipline of anthropology and the study of the Soviet and post-Soviet world.
Глава 1 — Поздний социализм. Советский субъект и неожиданность обвала системы
Late socialism. The Soviet subject and the unexpectedness of the collapse of the system: the paradox that the system was perceived as eternal yet its fall was not felt as surprising; the inadequacy of binary models (mimicry, dissimulation, divided consciousness) for describing the Soviet subject; and the framing of the book’s analytic approach.
Глава 2 — Гегемония формы. Неожиданная смена парадигм
Hegemony of form. An unexpected change of paradigms: the performative shift in the Soviet authoritative discourse — the shift from the constative (describing facts) to the performative (reproducing fixed forms) function of language — and what this meant for the constitution of the Soviet subject.
Глава 3 — Идеология наизнанку. Этика и поэтика
Ideology turned inside out. Ethics and poetics: how the meaning of ideological forms was transformed while their external forms were faithfully reproduced; the everyday ethics and aesthetics of living within the system.
Глава 4 — Вненаходимость как образ жизни
Vnenakhodimost as a way of life: the principle of “being simultaneously inside and outside” the rhetorical field of the authoritative discourse, neither supporting nor opposing the system, and its role in the reproduction and internal transformation of late socialism.
Глава 5 — Воображаемый Запад. Пространства вненаходимости позднего социализма
The Imagined West. Spaces of vnenakhodimost of late socialism: the constitution of the “imagined West” through foreign goods, music, language and images (the plastic bag with a New York laundromat address, Western rock records), and its function as a space of symbolic otherness within Soviet everyday life.
Глава 6 — Разноцветный коммунизм. King Crimson, Deep Purple, Pink Floyd
Multi-coloured communism. King Crimson, Deep Purple, Pink Floyd: the reception of Western rock music in the late Soviet period, its cultural meaning and its place in the everyday life of the last Soviet generation.
Глава 7 — Ирония вненаходимости. Некроэстетика, стёб, анекдот
The irony of vnenakhodimost. Necro-aesthetics, stiob, anecdote: the ironical and aesthetic practices — including the rock group Laibach and the “necro-aesthetic” fascination with old books and images — through which vnenakhodimost found cultural expression.
Заключение (Conclusion)
Carries the analysis of late socialism through perestroika to the collapse of the Soviet system: the loss of the legitimacy of the CPSU by 1990–1991 as the party’s authoritative discourse was destroyed from within, the “return to Lenin” as a symptom of that breakdown, the disintegration of the fabric of the authoritative discourse, and the argument that the internal dynamics of late socialism — examined throughout the book — made the collapse at once unexpected and inevitable.
